## The real characteristic complement has an exponentially small marked remainder, 23 November

The [full Fourier bound](research_same_index_edge_fourier_characteristic_bound.md)
and its [exponential strengthening](research_same_index_edge_exponential_characteristic_bound.md)
give a general estimate for the actual edge source before gluing.
It also bounds the complementary piece after the original marked
closing, with a polynomial cost. The channel coefficients may be
coupled arbitrarily; no positivity or independence of the edges is
required.

Fix a source template with \(E\ge1\) edges, \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\),
and the actual Newton polynomials \(e_k\). Keep two separate incidence
activities per edge and write
\[
 B_k(z)=e_k(-z-z^{-1}),\qquad
 F_N=\sum_{\mathbf k\in\{0,\ldots,d\}^E}
       \mu_{\mathbf k,N}\prod_{e=1}^E B_{k_e}(z_e)B_{k_e}(y_e).
 \tag{EC1}
\]
Every original activity-independent edge weight, insertion and scalar
remains in its prescribed coefficient or closing functional.
The coefficients in (EC1) can encode fixed short choices and can
depend on \(N\). The remaining fixed signed crossing powers at the
vertices have no largeness hypothesis in this estimate.

Use the full Laurent coefficient norm
\[
 \|F_N\|_{\mathrm{inc}}^2
       =\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^{2E}}|\widehat F_N(m)|^2 .
 \tag{EC2}
\]
Each separate Fourier exponent is in \([-d,d]\).
Let \(\mathcal F_N\) be the exact Gaussian analysis frame of
equation (8) in the Fourier-bound proof, at fixed width \(\sigma>0\).
Its frequency centers range over the full real space, and
\(\int|\mathcal F_Nh|^2d\nu=\|h\|_{\mathrm{inc}}^2\).
This is an incidence norm, not the ordinary-color Plancherel energy.

On the real phase space
\(z_e=e^{i\theta_e}\), \(y_e=e^{i\varphi_e}\),
\(Y_{z_e}=e^{2\pi i\xi_e}\), \(Y_{y_e}=e^{2\pi i\eta_e}\),
let \(p_e\) be the scalar in equation (4) of the exponential proof.
Its prefactor \((1+z_e)(1+y_e)/(z_ey_e)\) is retained, including
its zeros. Put
\(\Omega_\delta=\{\max_e|p_e|\ge\delta\}\).
Uniformly in all coefficient arrays,
\[
 \int_{\Omega_\delta}|\mathcal F_NF_N|^2d\nu
 \le C_\sigma E N^2 e^{-c_\sigma N\delta^2}
                                      \|F_N\|_{\mathrm{inc}}^2,
 \qquad 0<\delta\le1 .
 \tag{EC3}
\]
At a fixed gap this is exponential decay. The same estimate holds
for the complete vector of normalized angular jets
\(N^{-|\alpha|}\mathscr D^\alpha F_N\) of any fixed maximal order,
with sums of squared norms and constants depending on that order.
Their exact triangular commutator forcing is retained.

The input is a literal homogeneous equation for every same-index
edge summand. Thus it survives arbitrary coupled weights and all
endpoint channels. Iterating its adjoint on the known Gaussian
tests gives (EC3); only these explicit tests are continued to
fractional displacements. There is no interpolation of an unknown
source, finite output compression, or discarded Fourier alias.

The original marked gluing can now be applied to a controlled
complementary source. Let \(\mathcal V_N\) be the separately even
Laurent band \([-d,d]\) in every incidence variable, and let
\(\Pi_N\) be its orthogonal projection: retain the band and average
under each \(z_j\leftrightarrow z_j^{-1}\). Define
\[
 Q_\Omega=\Pi_N\mathcal F_N^\dagger
                       \mathbf1_\Omega\mathcal F_N\Pi_N,\qquad
 F_{\mathrm{off}}=Q_{\Omega_\delta}F_N,\qquad
 F_{\mathrm{on}}=Q_{\Omega_\delta^c}F_N
 \tag{EC4}
\]
Each \(Q_\Omega\) is a positive contraction. Since \(F_N\in\mathcal V_N\),
we have \(F_N=F_{\mathrm{on}}+F_{\mathrm{off}}\) exactly and
\(\|F_{\mathrm{off}}\|_{\mathrm{inc}}^2
\le\int_{\Omega_\delta}|\mathcal F_NF_N|^2d\nu\).
Projection back to the full canonical space is part of this definition;
it removes no original Hermite coordinate.

For the literal vertex rules of the original finite-source compiler,
fixed template and fixed powers, its full marked functional obeys
\[
 |\Lambda_{N,s}(h)|\le C_{\mathrm{template},R}N^B
                      \|h\|_{\mathrm{inc}},\qquad
 h\in\mathcal V_N,\quad |s|\le R<1 .
 \tag{EC5}
\]
This is a proved norm comparison in the exponential note.
Fourier coefficient sum costs at most \((2d+1)^E\).
Passing to Chebyshev polynomials and identifying vertex activities
does not increase that sum. The literal fixed crossing polynomials
have polynomial cost; reduction uses each vertex's own relation,
and its original marked top coefficient costs \(N^2/2\).
The full repeated-root normals, pivots and prescribed external
scalars remain. Fixed parameter derivatives have polynomial cost
on smaller disks as well.

Consequently the original scalar splits without commuting a cutoff
through a vertex:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Lambda_{N,s}(F_N)=
       \Lambda_{N,s}(F_{\mathrm{on}})
                     +\Lambda_{N,s}(F_{\mathrm{off}}),\\
 |\Lambda_{N,s}(F_{\mathrm{off}})|
 \le C_{\mathrm{template},R,\sigma}\sqrt E\,N^{B+1}
       e^{-c_\sigma N\delta^2/2}\|F_N\|_{\mathrm{inc}} .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{EC6}
\]
Both pieces use the same original closing. An angular-jet closing
must retain its own literal functional and parity; (EC4) does not
prescribe evenization of an arbitrary differentiated closing.

This controls a general real complementary region, including its
actual marked remainder relative to the full incidence norm.
The remaining step is a coherent lower estimate for the retained
piece at the geometric rate, together with a suitable geometric
estimate for that incidence norm. The real characteristic set has
not been identified with a selected complex hyperbolic branch.
No arbitrary short-component volume lower bound or finite-exception
theorem follows yet. A different compiler or metric still requires
its actual source adapter.

## Fixed meridian jets of the initialized row have polynomial conditioning, 23 November

A fixed number of scaled meridian jets of the actual initialized row
has an explicit asymptotically orthogonal frame. Its Gram has a
polynomial inverse bound, despite its leading rank-one limit.
This concerns the selected full physical row, including its normal
tail. It is not a quotient deleting normal directions from the
whole Gauss operator, nor a lower bound for every closing functional.

Keep the actual data of (QD1)--(QD3), fix an integer \(p\ge0\)
independently of \(N\), and keep \(\alpha_N=\ell/N\) in
\(I\Subset(0,1/2)\). All derivatives in this section are in
\(u=N\mu\) at fixed quantum root. Define
\[
 \widetilde r_N(u)=\frac{r_N(u)}{d_N(u)},\qquad
 v_a=(r_0)_a,\qquad
 b_j=\partial_u^j\widetilde r_N(0),\qquad
 w_j=N^{j/2}(\partial_u-\lambda_{\alpha_N})^j
                         \widetilde r_N(0),\quad 0\le j\le p .
 \tag{JG1}
\]
The quotient is holomorphic through each fixed ordinary zero by
(QD9). Near zero this also follows directly from \(d_N(0)=1\).
Every row above has all \(T+1\) physical coordinates. For the root,
\(v_a=c_*q^{a^2}{\ell\brack a}_Q\) on \(0\le a\le\ell\)
and \(v_a=0\) otherwise; the higher rows need not have that support.

For \(a\le\ell\), write
\(\widetilde r_N(u)_a=v_a g_{N,a}(u)\), where \(g_{N,a}\)
is the exponential and two product ratios in (MC12) after \(d_N\)
is removed. Its logarithm is zero at \(u=0\). Set \(s=a/N\).
On the central interval \(\ell/4\le a\le3\ell/4\), all product
indices stay a fixed fraction of \(N\) away from their roots.
Differentiating the finite products and taking ordinary Riemann
sums therefore gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \partial_u\log g_{N,a}(0)&=L_\alpha(s)+O_I(N^{-1}),\\
 N\partial_u^2\log g_{N,a}(0)&=R_\alpha(s)+O_I(N^{-1}),\\
 \partial_u^m\log g_{N,a}(0)&=O_{I,m}(N^{1-m}),\qquad m\ge2,
 \end{split}
 \quad \alpha=\alpha_N,
 \tag{JG2}
\]
where
\[
 \begin{split}
 L_\alpha(s)&=-1+3\alpha+2s+
   \frac{i}{\pi}\log
       \frac{\sin^2(\pi(\alpha-s))\sin(\pi(\alpha+s))}
            {\sin^3(\pi\alpha)},\\
 R_\alpha(s)&=\frac{
       4\cot(\pi(\alpha-s))-5\cot(\pi\alpha)
                         +\cot(\pi(\alpha+s))}{\pi}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{JG3}
\]
All sine arguments here are in a fixed compact subinterval of
\((0,\pi)\), so the logarithm is of a positive number.
For an explicit sign check, a numerator factor with exponent
\(\nu=4\) has second logarithmic derivative
\(4N^{-2}\csc^2(\pi j/N)\); an inverse denominator factor
with \(\nu=2\) contributes \(-N^{-2}\csc^2(\pi j/N)\).
Their integrals are precisely \(R_\alpha\).
The first derivatives use the two integrals in (MC17), now over
\([\alpha-s,\alpha]\) and \([\alpha,\alpha+s]\), respectively.
Each higher derivative contributes \(O(N^{-m})\) per factor,
which proves the last estimate in (JG2).

Put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \theta_\alpha=\pi\alpha/2,\qquad
 \sigma_\alpha^2=\frac{\tan\theta_\alpha}{4\pi},\\
 \kappa_\alpha=2+i\{\cot(3\theta_\alpha)
                                  -2\cot\theta_\alpha\},\qquad
 \rho_\alpha=
   \frac{4\cot\theta_\alpha-5\cot(2\theta_\alpha)
                                  +\cot(3\theta_\alpha)}{\pi}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{JG4}
\]
Thus \(L_\alpha(\alpha/2)=\lambda_\alpha\),
\(L_\alpha'(\alpha/2)=\kappa_\alpha\), and
\(R_\alpha(\alpha/2)=\rho_\alpha\).
In particular \(\operatorname{Re}\kappa_\alpha=2\), so it never
vanishes. For \(x=(a-\ell/2)/\sqrt N\) in a bounded interval,
(JG2) gives
\[
 \sqrt N\{\partial_u\log g_{N,a}(0)-\lambda_\alpha\}
       =\kappa_\alpha x+O_I((1+x^2)/\sqrt N),\qquad
 N\partial_u^2\log g_{N,a}(0)\longrightarrow\rho_\alpha .
 \tag{JG5}
\]
Every scaled cumulant \(N^{m/2}\partial_u^m\log g_{N,a}(0)\),
\(m\ge3\), tends to zero, by (JG2).
The finite exponential differentiation formula consequently yields
\[
 \frac{(w_j)_a}{v_a}\longrightarrow
 H_{j,\alpha}(x)
   :=j![z^j]\exp\{\kappa_\alpha xz+\rho_\alpha z^2/2\}.
 \tag{JG6}
\]
Here \(z\) is a formal generating variable, not a boundary activity.
This is an identity about fixed derivatives at zero; it does not
assume a whole-row estimate at \(u\) of order \(\sqrt N\).
The polynomial \(H_{j,\alpha}\) has degree \(j\) and leading
coefficient \(\kappa_\alpha^j\).

The limiting physical measure is also explicit. Define
\[
 \nu_N(a)=\frac{|v_a|^2}{\|r_0\|_2^2},\qquad
 x_a=\frac{a-\ell/2}{\sqrt N}.
 \]
The consecutive ratio of its unnormalized weights is
\[
 \frac{|v_{a+1}|^2}{|v_a|^2}
    =\left\{\frac{\sin((\ell-a)\pi/N)}
                   {\sin((a+1)\pi/N)}\right\}^2 .
 \tag{JG7}
\]
Summing its central Taylor expansion gives the Gaussian
\(\exp[-2\pi\cot\theta_\alpha\,x^2]\).
The Gaussian upper tails and central lower bound proved in
(MC14)--(MC15) normalize these Riemann sums and control all
fixed polynomial moments. Uniformly on \(I\), the measures
of \(x_a\) therefore converge, with those moments, to
the centered real Gaussian \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\alpha^2)\).

No omitted coordinate can alter the ensuing Gram limit.
On the whole central interval, the scaled first cumulant in
(JG5) is bounded by \(C_I(1+|x_a|)\), using the bounded
derivative of \(L_\alpha\). All higher scaled cumulants through
order \(p\) are bounded by (JG2).
The exponential differentiation formula then bounds
\(|(w_j)_a/v_a|\) by \(C_{I,p}(1+|x_a|^j)\).
This supplies uniform integrability against the Gaussian tails.
For \(a\le\ell\) outside that interval, use a fixed circle
\(|u|=R\), \(R\notin\pi\mathbb Z\), in (QD6).
The component \(\widetilde r_N(u)_a\) is bounded there by a
polynomial in \(N\) times \(|v_a|\). Cauchy bounds its fixed
derivatives by the same type of polynomial; the extra
\(N^{j/2}\) is still absorbed by the exponentially small root mass.
For \(a>\ell\), (MC11) and the extracted zero factor used in
(QD8) give a polynomial absolute bound on that circle.
Division by \(d_N\) is harmless there. Cauchy and the positive
exponential root norm (FH15) make all those normalized derivative
tails tend to zero. The nonzero normal tail has been retained.

Let \(\mathsf G_N\) be the Hermitian row Gram
\((\mathsf G_N)_{jk}=w_jw_k^\dagger/\|r_0\|_2^2\).
Equations (JG6)--(JG7) and the preceding bounds prove
\[
 (\mathsf G_N)_{jk}
    -\int_{\mathbb R}H_{j,\alpha_N}(x)
              \overline{H_{k,\alpha_N}(x)}
                    \,d\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\alpha_N}^2)(x)
        \longrightarrow0,\qquad 0\le j,k\le p ,
 \tag{JG8}
\]
uniformly for admissible \(\alpha_N\in I\).
The limiting matrix is positive definite: a nonzero linear
combination of these polynomials is not the zero polynomial,
because their leading coefficients are nonzero, and the Gaussian
has positive density on the whole real line.
Continuity and compactness in \(\alpha\) give constants
\(0<c_{I,p}\le C_{I,p}<\infty\) with
\(c_{I,p}I\le\mathsf G_N\le C_{I,p}I\) for large \(N\).

There is an explicit asymptotically orthonormal choice.
Set \(\omega_\alpha=\rho_\alpha+\kappa_\alpha^2\sigma_\alpha^2\),
and take the positive square root \(\sigma_\alpha\).
Define the actual rows
\[
 \widehat w_j=
 \frac{1}{(\kappa_\alpha\sigma_\alpha)^j\sqrt{j!}}
 \sum_{m=0}^{\lfloor j/2\rfloor}
 \frac{j!}{m!(j-2m)!}
        \left(-\frac{\omega_\alpha}{2}\right)^m w_{j-2m},
 \qquad \alpha=\alpha_N .
 \tag{JG9}
\]
Multiplication of the generating series in (JG6) by
\(\exp(-\omega_\alpha z^2/2)\) gives
\(\exp(\kappa_\alpha xz-\kappa_\alpha^2\sigma_\alpha^2z^2/2)\).
Thus the limiting profiles of (JG9) are
\(\mathrm{He}_j(x/\sigma_\alpha)/\sqrt{j!}\), where
\(\exp(yt-t^2/2)=\sum_j\mathrm{He}_j(y)t^j/j!\).
The Gaussian generating integral is \(\exp(st)\); comparison
of coefficients proves their orthonormality.
Consequently the Gram of \(\widehat w_j/\|r_0\|_2\)
converges to the identity, without an inverse physical Gram.
The triangular transformation from \(w_j\) to \(\widehat w_j\)
has fixed size \(p+1\) and is bounded and invertible on \(I\).

For the unscaled derivative rows \(b_j\) of (JG1), let
\(\mathsf B_N=(b_jb_k^\dagger/\|r_0\|_2^2)_{0\le j,k\le p}\).
The centered derivative change has entries
\(\binom jm(-\lambda_\alpha)^{j-m}\), \(m\le j\);
it and its inverse are uniformly bounded. Standardization then
multiplies row \(j\) by \(N^{j/2}\).
It follows from (JG8), by these invertible congruences, that the
eigenvalues in decreasing order satisfy
\[
 c_{I,p}N^{-j}\le\lambda_j(\mathsf B_N)
       \le C_{I,p}N^{-j},\quad 0\le j\le p,\qquad
                    \operatorname{cond}(\mathsf B_N)\le C_{I,p}N^p .
 \tag{JG10}
\]
Replacing \(b_j\) by \(b_j/j!\) changes only fixed constants.
The jets of the undivided row \(r_N=d_N\widetilde r_N\) obey
the same bounds, because multiplication by \(d_N\) and its inverse
has a bounded triangular jet matrix of fixed order at zero.
Original \(\mu\)-jets have the additional row factors \(N^j\);
one must not assign them the same normalization.
For those raw jets the immediate bound is
\(\operatorname{cond}\le C_{I,p}N^{3p}\), still polynomial.

The Gram lower is a norm statement for this fixed finite source-jet
space. A specified cap can still annihilate a combination.
For a fixed polynomial \(P\) and fixed \(Z>0\), (QD11) and Cauchy
give, on the actual collar \(z=q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N}\),
\(|\zeta|\le Z\),
\[
 P(\partial_u)\!\left[\frac{\mathscr S_N(u,z)}{d_N(u)}\right]_{u=0}
 =\mathscr S_N(0,z)
       \{P(\lambda_{\alpha_N})+O_{I,P,Z}(N^{-1/2})\}.
 \tag{JG11}
\]
A relative nonzero conclusion requires a uniform lower bound on
\(|P(\lambda_{\alpha_N})|\). At its zeros (JG11) supplies no
such conclusion. The initialized first normal \(P(z)=z\) is safe
by (MC23); an additional marked scalar or exterior derivative
must retain its own polynomial and possible zeros.
No claim about the full marked closing follows from a jet norm.

The lower bound here concerns one actual initialized row and a fixed
order \(p\), not all physical Hermite channels or arbitrary short
components. Physical coordinates still grow with \(N\).
The complete proof inputs are the adopted (QD1)--(QD12),
(MC1)--(MC23), and (FH1)--(FH21), with their complete matching
sources. The whole vacuum-normal and meridian-frame comparison
texts listed after (MC23) provide different scalar and upper
estimates; neither proves the Gaussian finite-jet Gram lower above.
All original row tails, capped inputs, and external source factors
retain the scopes stated there.

## The divided capped initializer crosses every fixed ordinary meridian zero, 23 November

The initialized capped period has a quantum-dimension factor on every
bounded scaled meridian domain. After this factor is removed, the
actual period is holomorphic, nonzero, and uniformly controlled
through the ordinary meridian zeros. This extends the small disk of
(MC22); it does not extend the original marked knot closing.

Keep the actual two-head data of (MC1), with
\(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(\ell=d-T\ge1\), \(t=N-2\ell>0\),
\(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), and \(\alpha_N=\ell/N\in
I\Subset(0,1/2)\). The root is fixed. Write
\[
 r_N(u)=e_T^{\mathsf T}A(e^{u/N}),\qquad r_0=e_T^{\mathsf T}A_0,
 \qquad a_*=\lfloor\ell/2\rfloor,\qquad
 f_N(u)=\frac{A(e^{u/N})_{T,a_*}}{(A_0)_{T,a_*}} .
 \tag{QD1}
\]
The denominator is nonzero by (FH12). The Laurent products (MC7)
make every component of \(r_N\), and hence \(f_N\), entire in
\(u\). Here entire refers to these entries; the divided expressions
below are asserted on each fixed bounded domain for sufficiently
large \(N\), rather than globally at every fixed level.

Fix \(U>0\), independently of \(N\), and put
\[
 d_N(u)=\frac{D_N(e^{u/N})}{N}
       =\frac{\sinh u}{N\sinh(u/N)},\qquad
 f_N(u)=d_N(u)g_N(u),
 \tag{QD2}
\]
with removable values at zero. Explicitly \(g_N\) is the exponential
and the two central products in (MC12), with \(a=a_*\), after
the factor \(D_N/N\) is removed. On every fixed closed \(u\)-disk
these product indices stay a fixed fraction of \(N\) away from
zero modulo \(N\). Thus, for all sufficiently large admissible \(N\),
\(g_N\) is a holomorphic unit on a neighborhood of that disk.
The same central logarithmic expansion as in (MC16)--(MC17), now
for arbitrary bounded \(u\), proves
\[
 g_N(u)=e^{u\lambda_{\alpha_N}}(1+O_{I,U}(N^{-1})),
 \qquad |u|\le U,
 \quad
 \lambda_\alpha=4\alpha-1+\frac{i}{\pi}
 \log\frac{\sin^2(\pi\alpha/2)\sin(3\pi\alpha/2)}
               {\sin^3(\pi\alpha)} .
 \tag{QD3}
\]
No smallness of \(U\) is needed: each central factor is expanded
in \(u/N\), and the total quadratic remainder is \(O_{I,U}(N^{-1})\).
The factor \(g_N\) and its inverse are consequently bounded on
each such disk. The only zeros of \(f_N\) there are the simple
zeros \(u=i\pi j\), \(j\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\).
For large \(N\) no nonzero multiple of \(i\pi N\) lies in the disk,
so the denominator in (QD2) does not cancel one of these zeros.

The whole row shares those zeros exactly. This requires the
Laurent products, not a continuation of the root support.
In the row formula (MC7), set \(k=T-a\). Apart from its nonzero
constant and monomial, its factors are
\[
 (M^{-2}Q;Q)_k
 (M^{-2}Q^{T+1};Q)_\ell
 (M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a,\qquad M=e^{u/N}.
 \tag{QD4}
\]
At \(M=q^{-j}\), \(1\le j\le\ell\), the middle product contains
the common zero factor with index \(N-j\).
At \(M=q^j\), assume \(t\ge3j+1\). If \(k\ge j\), the first
product vanishes. If \(k<j\), then
\[
 T+a=2T-k\ge2T-j+1=N+t-j-1\ge N+2j .
 \tag{QD5}
\]
The last product therefore contains index \(N+2j\), whose factor is
\(1-M^{-4}Q^{2j}=(1-M^{-2}Q^j)(1+M^{-2}Q^j)\).
In both cases the row entry is divisible by \(1-M^{-2}Q^j\).
The negative case is likewise a literal common Laurent factor.
Since both \(\ell\) and \(t\) grow proportionally to \(N\) on \(I\),
these statements cover every \(u=i\pi j\) in any fixed disk once
\(N\) is sufficiently large.

We next extend the projective estimate, keeping possible numerator
zeros on the boundary. Choose a radius \(R>U\) with
\(R\notin\pi\mathbb Z\). On \(|u|=R\) the nonzero denominators
in (MC6) stay separated from their roots. More precisely, products
of the ratios
\[
 \frac{1-e^{-\nu u/N}Q^j}{1-Q^j}\quad(\nu=2,4),
 \qquad
 \frac{1-Q^j}{1-e^{-2u/N}Q^j},\qquad 1\le j<N,
 \tag{QD6}
\]
over any of the intervals used there have modulus at most
\(C_R(N+1)^{p_R}\), for a fixed \(p_R\).
Only an upper bound is claimed for a numerator ratio.
Indeed its modulus is at most
\(1+C_R/[N|1-Q^j|]\). For inverse denominator ratios, the
finitely many indices within a fixed distance of an endpoint
are controlled by the positive distance of the circle from
\(i\pi\mathbb Z\); for the remaining indices the perturbation is
small relative to \(1-Q^j\). Summing
\([N|1-Q^j|]^{-1}\le C/\min(j,N-j)\) proves (QD6).
Numerator zeros, including half-integer ones, cause no difficulty.

For \(\ell/4\le a\le3\ell/4\), cancel the common \(d_N\)
before comparing \(R_a\) of (MC12) with \(f_N\).
All remaining central factors are units on the fixed disk, and
consecutive logarithmic quotients are \(O_{I,R}(N^{-1})\).
Summation gives
\[
 \left|\frac{R_a(u)}{f_N(u)}-1\right|
 \le C_{I,R}\frac{|a-a_*|+1}{N},\qquad |u|=R .
 \tag{QD7}
\]
The root sine-binomial weights have second moment \(O_I(N)\)
about \(a_*\), as proved in (MC14)--(MC15). They therefore
give an \(O_{I,R}(N^{-1/2})\) relative row error on this interval.
Outside it, but with \(a\le\ell\), their exponentially small
mass absorbs every polynomial loss in (QD6).
For \(a>\ell\), remove the unique factor \(1-M^{-4}\)
from the last product in (QD4). All remaining nonzero-root
ratios satisfy (QD6). The polynomial first-normal tail bound
(MC11), multiplied by \(|1-e^{-4u/N}|=O_R(N^{-1})\), bounds
this whole tail by a polynomial in \(N\). Its ratio to the root
row norm is exponentially small by (FH15).
Thus
\[
 \|r_N(u)-f_N(u)r_0\|_2
       \le C_{I,R}N^{-1/2}\|r_0\|_2,\qquad |u|=R .
 \tag{QD8}
\]

Set \(E_N=r_N-f_Nr_0\). Every component is entire.
By (QD4)--(QD5), \(E_N\) vanishes at every zero of \(f_N\)
inside the circle, and those zeros are simple by (QD2)--(QD3).
Consequently \(E_N/f_N\) has removable singularities there.
On the boundary \(f_N\) is bounded away from zero, since
\(d_N\to\sinh u/u\) and \(g_N\to e^{u\lambda_{\alpha_N}}\).
Apply the maximum principle to every unit linear functional
of the vector \(E_N/f_N\). Since its value at zero is zero,
one may also divide by \(u\). This proves
\[
 \left\|\frac{r_N(u)}{f_N(u)}-r_0\right\|_2
       \le C_{I,U}\frac{|u|}{\sqrt N}\|r_0\|_2,
                    \qquad |u|\le U ,
 \tag{QD9}
\]
with the quotient interpreted removably at the ordinary zeros.
No path avoids or discards those zeros in this argument.

Now keep the frozen \(D,F_c\), literal capped input \(c_T\), and
period \(\mathscr S_N\) of (MC18). Let \(Z>0\) be fixed and put
\(z_N(\zeta)=q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N}\), \(|\zeta|\le Z\).
The genuine capped overlap lower bound (MC21) transfers (QD9)
to the scalar with its original binomial coefficients and carrier.
It gives a holomorphic error \(\varepsilon_N\), including across
the ordinary zeros, such that
\[
 \frac{\mathscr S_N(u,z_N(\zeta))}
      {f_N(u)\mathscr S_N(0,z_N(\zeta))}
      =1+\varepsilon_N(u,\zeta),\qquad
 |\varepsilon_N(u,\zeta)|
       \le C_{I,U,Z}\frac{|u|}{\sqrt N}.
 \tag{QD10}
\]
The root denominator is nonzero by (MC20)--(MC21).
Equivalently the exact local quantum-dimension factorization is
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mathscr S_N(u,z_N(\zeta))
   =d_N(u)\mathscr S_N(0,z_N(\zeta))\,\mathcal U_N(u,\zeta),
 \qquad
 \mathcal U_N=e^{u\lambda_{\alpha_N}}(1+O_{I,U,Z}(N^{-1/2})).
 \quad}
 \tag{QD11}
\]
On every fixed pair of disks, for all sufficiently large admissible
levels, \(\mathcal U_N=g_N(1+\varepsilon_N)\) is holomorphic and
nonzero. This assertion is local on arbitrary bounded scaled domains;
it is not a claim of a globally nonzero quotient at each fixed \(N\).

Thus the only zeros of this capped period in the fixed \(u\)-disk
are exactly the simple zeros \(u_j=i\pi j\ne0\) of \(d_N\).
Their divided normals are nonzero. Explicitly, for each fixed
nonzero integer \(j\),
\[
 \frac{\partial_u\mathscr S_N(u_j,z_N(\zeta))}
      {\mathscr S_N(0,z_N(\zeta))}
   =\frac{(-1)^j}{iN\sin(\pi j/N)}
         e^{u_j\lambda_{\alpha_N}}(1+O_{I,U,Z}(N^{-1/2})).
 \tag{QD12}
\]
This follows by differentiating the exact factorization at its zero,
using \(d_N'(u_j)=(-1)^j/[iN\sin(\pi j/N)]\).
All fixed scaled-\(u\) and \(\zeta\) derivatives in (QD11) obey the
same convergence on smaller disks by Cauchy. An order-\(m\) original
meridian derivative retains the conversion \(N^m\partial_u^m\).

The additional conclusion beyond (MC22) is control through every
fixed ordinary scaled meridian zero, rather than a disk where the
quantum dimension is a unit. The scale remains \(\mu=u/N\);
neither a fixed meridian disk nor colors growing with \(N\) are
covered. All other opposite-kernel factors, their meridian derivatives,
the exterior word, and the original marked closing remain separate.
No arbitrary short-component or closed-knot lower bound follows.
The complete proof inputs are the following adopted (MC1)--(MC23),
(NR1)--(NR12), and (FH1)--(FH21), together with their complete
matching sources and comparison coverage listed in those sections.
The Laurent products, root weights, and capped overlap used here
are precisely those actual source quantities; no general-method
novelty or replacement cycle is asserted.

## The capped Gauss initializer has a controlled whole meridian collar, 23 November

The terminal Gauss column has an exact finite-product formula in the
original meridian family. Its row has a different, explicit transpose
adapter. Together they give a scalar-relative estimate for the actual
capped initializer on a \(1/N\) meridian disk and a complex Gaussian
activity collar. The first normal includes its nonzero endpoint tail.
No inverse physical Gram or unknown closed invariant enters the proof.

Keep the two-head physical degrees of (GA1), with
\(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), \(x_0=-q^{-1}\),
\(\ell=d-T\ge1\), and \(t=N-2\ell>0\).
The quantum root is fixed. Write
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 M=e^\mu,\quad x=-M/q,\quad C=Q^{-T-1}=Q^\ell,\quad
 K_T=M^2C,\quad F_j=(Q;Q)_j,\quad
 g_j(M)=(M^{-2}Q;Q)_j,\\
 H_j(M)=M^jQ^{-j(j+1)/2}g_j(M),\qquad
 A(M)=q_F(M)E_\Sigma(M)^d i_d\big|_{\mathcal H_T}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{MC1}
\]
These are the actual balanced heads and capped Gauss factor of G489.
In particular \(E(M)w_a=(MQ^{-a}-M^{-1})w_{a-1}\), with bottom
zero, \(Fw_a=(1-Q^{a+1})w_{a+1}\), with top zero, and
\(Kw_a=xQ^{-a}w_a\).
Here \(E_\Sigma\) in (MC1) is the original full prefix total.
The remaining-head totals in its Gauss polynomial are
\(E=E_1K_2+E_2\), \(F=F_1+K_1^{-1}F_2\), with
\(\Omega=FE+qK+q^{-1}K^{-1}\).

For \(0\le a\le T\), put \(k=T-a\). The whole-meridian column is
\[
 A(M)_{aT}
   =H_dK_T^d x^{-k}M^{-2k}Q^{Tk}
                  \frac{(M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a}{g_a(M)} .
 \tag{MC2}
\]
Here and below all displayed \(g_j\) denominators have index
\(j<N\), so they are units near \(M=1\). We derive (MC2) before
specialization. Only \((E_1K_2)^n\) acts on \(|T,0\rangle\);
its coefficient is
\(x^nM^nQ^{-nT+n(n-1)/2}g_T/g_{T-n}\).
The raising path to \(|a,T-a\rangle\), for \(n\ge k\), has coefficient
\({n\brack k}_Qx^{-k}Q^{k(T-n)}F_aF_k/F_{T-n}\).
Inserting the literal coefficient
\(Q^{-n}x^{-n}H_d/(F_nH_n)\) and \(K_T^{d-n}\) gives
\[
 A(M)_{aT}=H_dK_T^dx^{-k}Q^{Tk}g_TF_a
   \sum_{r=0}^{a}
    \frac{M^{-2(r+k)}Q^{r(r+k)}}
         {g_{r+k}g_{a-r}F_rF_{a-r}} .
 \tag{MC3}
\]
After extracting \(M^{-2k}/(g_kg_aF_a)\), the sum becomes
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{a}
  \frac{(Q^{-a};Q)_r(M^2Q^{-a};Q)_r}
       {F_r(M^{-2}Q^{k+1};Q)_r}
                  (M^{-4}Q^{T+a+1})^r
 =\frac{(M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a}
             {(M^{-2}Q^{k+1};Q)_a}.
 \tag{MC4}
\]
This is exactly G489's proved finite identity (19),
\(\sum_{r=0}^a(Q^{-a};Q)_r(B;Q)_r(cQ^a/B)^r/
[F_r(c;Q)_r]=(c/B;Q)_a/(c;Q)_a\).
Its own proof clears \((c;Q)_a\) and uses Gaussian Pascal
induction, so no infinite summation or root factorial \(F_N\)
is divided. Since \(g_k(M^{-2}Q^{k+1};Q)_a=g_T\),
(MC3)--(MC4) prove (MC2) on the entire holomorphic germ.

The generic row must not be obtained by differentiating root symmetry.
Set \(h_j=M^{-j}F_j/g_j\) and
\(D_h=\operatorname{diag}(h_0,\ldots,h_d)\); on the pair set
\(\mathcal D_T(M)=\operatorname{diag}(h_a h_{T-a})\).
Direct one-head coefficients give
\[
 E(M)^{\mathsf T}=D_h^{-1}x^{-1}KF D_h,\qquad
 F^{\mathsf T}=D_h^{-1}xEK^{-1}D_h.
 \tag{MC5}
\]
For example \(h_a/h_{a+1}
=M(1-M^{-2}Q^{a+1})/(1-Q^{a+1})\), which gives the first
raising coefficient exactly; the other ratio gives the second
identity. The missing arrows are zero on both sides.
The ordered coproduct preserves these identities, and hence
\(\Omega^{\mathsf T}=\mathcal D_T^{-1}\Omega\mathcal D_T\).
Since the actual \(A(M)\) is a polynomial in \(K,\Omega\),
\[
 \begin{split}
 A(M)^{\mathsf T}&=\mathcal D_T^{-1}A(M)\mathcal D_T,\\
 A(M)_{Ta}
   &=\frac{h_T}{h_ah_k}A(M)_{aT}\\
   &=H_dK_T^dx^{-k}M^{-2k}Q^{Tk}
       \frac{F_T}{g_T}\frac{g_k}{F_k}
                     \frac{(M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a}{F_a}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{MC6}
\]
There are no genuine meridian poles hidden in these formulas.
Indeed \(H_d=(-1)^dM^dg_d=(-1)^dD_N(M)\), where
\(D_N(M)=(M^N-M^{-N})/(M-M^{-1})\) has its Laurent-polynomial
continuation. With
\(\Gamma_a=(-1)^dC^dx_0^{-k}Q^{Tk}\), the two entries are
\[
 \begin{split}
 A(M)_{aT}
   &=\Gamma_a M^{3(\ell+a)}
       (M^{-2}Q^{a+1};Q)_{d-a}(M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a,\\
 A(M)_{Ta}
   &=\Gamma_a\frac{F_T}{F_aF_k}M^{3(\ell+a)}
       (M^{-2}Q;Q)_k(M^{-2}Q^{T+1};Q)_\ell
                                      (M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a.
 \end{split}
 \tag{MC7}
\]
Each line has exactly \(d\) finite product factors. Thus the
entry identities also continue as Laurent polynomials for \(M\ne0\).
The factored germ forms are convenient for estimates.

All first-normal entries are explicit. Write
\(A_j=[\mu^j]A(e^\mu)\), \(v_a=(A_0)_{aT}=(A_0)_{Ta}\),
and \(\Sigma_j=\sum_{h=1}^jQ^h/(1-Q^h)\).
For \(a\le\ell\), logarithmic differentiation of (MC2) gives
\[
 \frac{(A_1)_{aT}}{v_a}
 =2d-3k+4\sum_{j=0}^{a-1}
       \frac{Q^{T+1+j}}{1-Q^{T+1+j}}-2\Sigma_a .
 \tag{MC8}
\]
Here \(H_d'(1)=0\). The row score includes the derivative of
the adapter in (MC6); explicitly
\[
 \begin{split}
 (A_1)_{Ta}&=\tau_av_a,\qquad
 \tau_a=2d-3T+3a
       -4\sum_{j=\ell-a+1}^{\ell}\frac1{1-Q^j}
       +2\sum_{j=\ell+1}^{\ell+a}\frac1{1-Q^j},\\
 |\tau_a|&\le C N\log(N+1).
 \end{split}
 \tag{MC9}
\]
Empty sums are zero. The bound follows from
\(|1-Q^j|\ge4\min(j,N-j)/N\).
For \(a=\ell+r>\ell\), \(1\le r\le t-1\), the numerator in
(MC2) has exactly one zero factor, \(1-M^{-4}\). Thus both
row and column have the same nonzero first-normal tail:
\[
 \begin{split}
 (A_1)_{\ell+r,T}=(A_1)_{T,\ell+r}
   &=4i c_*q^{\ell^2}(-q^\ell)^r
                   \frac{S_\ell S_{r-1}}{S_{\ell+r}},\\
 c_*&=(-1)^{\ell+1}Nq^{2\ell^2+\ell+1},\qquad
 S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j2\sin(\pi h/N).
 \end{split}
 \tag{MC10}
\]
This also follows directly by replacing that zero factor by its
derivative \(4\) in (MC2). No prefactor derivative survives against
the root zero, and the transpose adapter equals one at the root.

The entire tail has polynomial norm. The positive sine-binomial
\(S_{u+v}/(S_uS_v)\) is at least one when \(u+v<N\).
At fixed sum \(n<N\), its ratio at consecutive indices is
\(\sin((n-a)\gamma)/\sin((a+1)\gamma)\), at least one before
the midpoint by sine addition. Its values are symmetric and
have endpoint value one.
Consequently
\[
 |(A_1)_{T,a}|
   =\frac{2N}{\sin(\pi a/N)}
           \left(\frac{S_{a-1}}{S_\ell S_{a-\ell-1}}\right)^{-1}
       \le\frac{2N}{\sin(\pi a/N)},\qquad
 \|((A_1)_{T,a})_{a>\ell}\|_2\le C N^2 .
 \tag{MC11}
\]
The last bound uses \(\sin(\pi a/N)\ge
2\min(a,N-a)/N\) and \(\sum_{j\ge1}j^{-2}<\infty\).
This is a bound for the original occupation tail, not a replacement
of the complementary normal in (GK9).

We now prove the stronger projective estimate on the natural scale.
Fix \(I\Subset(0,1/2)\), \(\alpha_N=\ell/N\in I\), and
\(0<\eta<\pi/4\). Set \(M=e^{u/N}\), \(|u|\le\eta\),
and \(a_*=\lfloor\ell/2\rfloor\).
For \(a\le\ell\), the exact row/root quotient is
\[
 R_a(u)=\frac{A(e^{u/N})_{Ta}}{v_a}
 =\frac{D_N(e^{u/N})}{N}\,
   e^{u[2d-3(T-a)]/N}
   \prod_{j=T+1}^{T+a}\frac{1-e^{-4u/N}Q^j}{1-Q^j}
   \prod_{j=T-a+1}^{T}\frac{1-Q^j}{1-e^{-2u/N}Q^j},
 \qquad f_N(u)=R_{a_*}(u).
 \tag{MC12}
\]
The scalar \(f_N\) is an explicit known product, not an unknown
closed invariant. It is a holomorphic unit on this disk.
Its central indices stay a fixed fraction of \(N\) away from
zero modulo \(N\), so \(f_N\) and its inverse are uniformly
bounded for the indicated \(I,\eta\).
The remaining common factor is exactly
\(D_N(e^{u/N})/N=\sinh u/[N\sinh(u/N)]\), also a bounded unit.

Here are the estimates, including noncentral entries.
For \(\nu=2,4\), \(1\le j<N\), the factor
\(1-e^{-\nu u/N}Q^j\) has no zero on \(|u|\le\eta\).
Its sine representation and \(\eta<\pi/4\) give
\[
 |1-e^{-\nu u/N}Q^j|\ge c_\eta|1-Q^j|,\qquad
 \left|\partial_u\log
       \frac{1-e^{-\nu u/N}Q^j}{1-Q^j}\right|
          \le\frac{C_\eta}{N|1-Q^j|}.
 \tag{MC13}
\]
For example its sine argument is
\((\pi j+i\nu u/2)/N\); its real part stays inside
\((0,\pi)\), a comparable distance from either endpoint.
Analytic logarithms are zero at \(u=0\).
Summing (MC13) gives an \(O_\eta(\log(N+1))\) logarithmic
derivative for every product interval here. Such products and
their inverses are at most a fixed power of \(N+1\).
Their differences from the value at zero vanish linearly in
\(u\), with the same polynomial bound and one harmless logarithm.

On \(\ell/4\le a\le3\ell/4\), consecutive quotients in
(MC12) have logarithm \(O_I(|u|/N)\). Hence
\[
 \left|\frac{R_a(u)}{f_N(u)}-1\right|
     \le C_{I,\eta}\frac{|u|(|a-a_*|+1)}N .
 \tag{MC14}
\]
This follows by summing those logarithms; the exponential remainder
is bounded on the whole central interval.
The root row has \(v_a=c_*q^{a^2}{\ell\brack a}_Q\),
\(0\le a\le\ell\), and zero elsewhere.
The normalized weights \(|v_a|^2\) have variance \(O_I(N)\)
about \(\ell/2\), with mass \(O_I(e^{-c_IN})\) outside
the central interval. Indeed their consecutive ratio is
\([\sin((\ell-a)\gamma)/\sin((a+1)\gamma)]^2\);
the derivative of its logarithm is
\(-2\gamma[\cot((\ell-a)\gamma)+\cot((a+1)\gamma)]
\le-c_I/N\). In a central window it is also bounded below
by \(-C_I/N\). Summing these inequalities gives Gaussian
upper tails and a matching central lower bound, proving the
variance and exponential-tail statements.

Thus (MC14) gives an \(O_{I,\eta}(|u|/\sqrt N)\) relative
row error on the central interval. Outside it but with
\(a\le\ell\), (MC13) bounds the quotient difference by
\(|u|\) times a polynomial, against an exponentially small
root weight. For \(a>\ell\), extract \(1-e^{-4u/N}\)
from (MC6). All remaining factors are bounded by their nonzero
root values times a polynomial, by (MC13).
Equation (MC11) then bounds this whole tail by
\(C|u|N^p\) for a fixed \(p=p_\eta\).
Its ratio to the root norm is exponentially small by (FH15),
whose rate \(S(\alpha)\) is positive uniformly on \(I\).
Combining all parts proves
\[
 \|e_T^{\mathsf T}A(e^{u/N})
                -f_N(u)e_T^{\mathsf T}A_0\|_2
      \le C_{I,\eta}\frac{|u|}{\sqrt N}
                          \|e_T^{\mathsf T}A_0\|_2 .
 \tag{MC15}
\]
This argument has retained, and then bounded, the nonzero meridian
tail rather than differentiating a root support assertion.

There is a simple explicit limit for the known scalar product.
Uniformly on smaller closed \(u\)-disks,
\[
 f_N(u)=\frac{\sinh u}{u}
             e^{u\lambda_{\alpha_N}}(1+O_{I,\eta}(N^{-1})),
 \quad
 \lambda_\alpha=4\alpha-1+\frac{i}{\pi}
       \log\frac{\sin^2(\pi\alpha/2)\sin(3\pi\alpha/2)}
                     {\sin^3(\pi\alpha)} .
 \tag{MC16}
\]
The logarithm is real, of a positive number. To verify this
without a source asymptotic assumption, expand the central
product logarithms in \(u/N\). Their total second-order
remainder is \(O_{I,\eta}(N^{-1})\).
The monomial in (MC12) contributes
\(u(-1+9\alpha_N/2)+O_I(N^{-1})\).
The two first-order sums differ by \(O_I(N^{-1})\) from the
following expressions, with \(\alpha=\alpha_N\):
\[
 u\left\{4\int_{\alpha/2}^{\alpha}
       \frac{e^{-2\pi iv}}{1-e^{-2\pi iv}}\,dv
    -2\int_{\alpha}^{3\alpha/2}
       \frac{e^{-2\pi iv}}{1-e^{-2\pi iv}}\,dv\right\}.
 \tag{MC17}
\]
Use \(e^{-2\pi iv}/(1-e^{-2\pi iv})
=-1/2-(i/2)\cot(\pi v)\).
The real contribution is \(-\alpha u/2\), and the imaginary
contribution is the logarithm in (MC16).
Finally \(D_N(e^{u/N})/N=\sinh u/[N\sinh(u/N)]\)
has the stated limit. The removable value at zero is one.
Uniform holomorphy gives every fixed scaled-\(u\) derivative.

We pass from row norm to the actual capped scalar.
Keep \(D,F_c\) fixed at their root values in (FH1)--(FH3), and set
\[
 h(u)=e_T^{\mathsf T}\overline D A(e^{u/N})\overline D F_c,\qquad
 \mathscr S_N(u,z)=h(u)c_T(z),\qquad k_0=t-1 .
 \tag{MC18}
\]
Here \(c_T\) is exactly (NR1), not a square-root binomial input.
The whole block \(F_c\) is a contraction; on the root input
flag of \(h(0)\) it is unitary. Thus (MC15) gives the same
relative row bound for \(h(u)-f_Nh(0)\).
The original cap has a uniformly nonzero overlap with that
root row on a complex Gaussian collar.

For completeness put \(c=T/2\) and
\(\beta_b=\binom db\binom d{T-b}\).
Both \(P(b)\) of (FH13) and \(\beta_b\) are positive and
symmetric about \(c\). Each has Gaussian upper tails of width
\(\sqrt N\), and is bounded below by a constant times its
maximum on \(|b-c|\le\sqrt N\), uniformly on \(I\).
For \(P\) these are the midpoint and global concavity bounds
in (FH14)--(FH15). For \(\beta\), use its exact ratio
\[
 \frac{\beta_{b+1}}{\beta_b}
       =\frac{(d-b)(T-b)}{(b+1)(\ell+b+1)} .
 \tag{MC19}
\]
The derivative of its logarithm is the negative sum of the
four reciprocal factors, at most \(-4/N\) everywhere it
is used; in the central window its modulus is \(O_I(N^{-1})\).
Summing gives the same tail and central bounds.
In particular
\(\sum_bP(b)\beta_b\ge c_I\|P\|_2\|\beta\|_2\).

Let \(w=e^{\zeta/\sqrt N}\), \(|\zeta|\le R\), with \(R\)
fixed and \(N\) sufficiently large.
The negative-root bound (NR6), followed by palindromy and
the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality, gives
\[
 |\Psi_{N,T}(w)|
   \ge\cos(\arg w/2)^T\Psi_{N,T}(|w|)
   \ge c_R|w|^{T/2}\Psi_{N,T}(1).
 \tag{MC20}
\]
The Gaussian upper tail of \(\beta_b^2\) also gives
\(\|c_T(q^{k_0}w)\|_2
\le C_{I,R}|w|^{T/2}\|\beta\|_2\), by summing its bounded
exponential tilt. Since \(h(0)_b=\eta\sqrt N
q^{-k_0b}P(b)\), these inequalities prove the actual scalar
overlap bound
\[
 |\mathscr S_N(0,q^{k_0}w)|
       \ge c_{I,R}\|h(0)\|_2\|c_T(q^{k_0}w)\|_2 .
 \tag{MC21}
\]
All phases and ordinary-binomial coefficients are used in this
inequality; it is not an arbitrary norm substituted for a closing.

Applying (MC15) through (MC18),(MC21) yields the main result:
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mathscr S_N(u,q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})
   =f_N(u)\mathscr S_N(0,q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})
                       (1+\varepsilon_N(u,\zeta)),\qquad
 |\varepsilon_N(u,\zeta)|
       \le C_{I,\eta,R}\frac{|u|}{\sqrt N}.
 \quad}
 \tag{MC22}
\]
It holds uniformly for \(|u|\le\eta<\pi/4\), \(|\zeta|\le R\),
and all sufficiently large admissible levels with \(\ell/N\in I\).
Both factors on the right are nonzero, and so is the actual
left side. The error is jointly holomorphic. Apply the estimate
first on slightly larger disks with meridian radius below \(\pi/4\);
Cauchy then gives every fixed scaled-\(u\) and \(\zeta\) derivative
as \(O(N^{-1/2})\) on the smaller disks.
An original \(\mu\)-derivative is \(N\partial_u\); its order-\(j\)
conversion retains \(N^j\), rather than asserting an unscaled bound.

The first actual capped normal is itself nonzero eventually.
Equations (MC16),(MC22), differentiated at \(u=0\), give
\[
 \frac{\partial_\mu
       \mathscr S_N(N\mu,q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})|_{\mu=0}}
      {\mathscr S_N(0,q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})}
          =N\lambda_{\alpha_N}+O_{I,R}(\sqrt N).
 \tag{MC23}
\]
The multiplier \(\lambda_\alpha\) never vanishes on \((0,1/2)\).
Its real part can vanish only at \(\alpha=1/4\), where the
positive logarithm argument in (MC16) is \(\sin(\pi/8)<1\).
Thus its modulus is bounded below on \(I\).
The first normal has the same logarithmic modulus rate as
this nonzero root boundary scalar on the stated collar.

This is a fixed-root meridian theorem for the specified initialized
Gauss boundary scalar. The actual \(A(M)\), its lower and upper
occupation entries, generic transpose connection, all binomial caps,
and full unit phase in (FH13) are retained. The frames \(D,F_c\)
are frozen only for this declared boundary presentation.
The opposite kernel still has all external \(\kappa(M)\) scalars,
its original braid routing, turnover,
Cartan divisor, pivots, framing factors and any marked row; their
meridian derivatives must be included in a full source finite part.
No arbitrary short-component stability, quantum-parameter normal,
fixed-radius activity theorem, geometric occurrence, or lower bound
for the original marked knot scalar follows.

Complete proof inputs are the adopted (NR1)--(NR12),
(FH1)--(FH21), and their unchanged complete source texts, together
with G489's actual Gauss operator and finite summation proof at
42e6d6c3a5039859c241a2832de56301eff49d749db86d67868f3534c89aaaaa.
The full two-head balanced meridian conventions also appear in the
whole-meridian fusion proof, at
9ebdf4611802b9091a1c3dc3194e6529ed867933008c3c3d0851212325673b19.
Whole comparison coverage includes
[the earlier vacuum normal](research_actual_gauss_vacuum_meridian_normal.md),
449 lines, at
bfe1861c0219f2de8faca263b643508f8c5e4e71e10f1eb51e99c2ba0f20ba5a,
and [the meridian frames](research_actual_meridian_source_frames.md),
506 lines, at
6f58fba195ba5e8208e1d5180a1d684b933f9f5d50eb28efc56609580fe29976.
Those texts give a different initialized vacuum normal and general
polynomial frame bounds; they do not supply the actual projective
row estimate or capped scalar-relative collar proved here.

## The capped Gauss row has a zero-free slit and a global logarithmic rate, 23 November

The positive row in (FH13) can be contracted with its actual
ordinary-binomial input before a contour estimate. After its specified
linear phase is removed, the resulting polynomial has only simple
negative zeros. Its normalized logarithm consequently has an actual
global limit on the slit plane, initialized by a positive real sum.
The original marked knot closing is not replaced by this boundary row.

Keep the admissible physical data and fixed frames of the following
section: \(d=N-1\), \(\gamma=\pi/N\), \(q=e^{i\gamma}\),
\(\ell=d-T\ge1\), \(t=N-2\ell>0\), and
\(H_+=\mathcal K F_c\). Put
\[
 \beta_b=\binom db\binom d{T-b},\qquad
 c_T(z)=\sum_{b=0}^T\beta_bz^b|b,T-b\rangle,\qquad
 \Psi_{N,T}(z)=\sum_{b=0}^TP(b)\beta_bz^b,\quad
 P(b)=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}2\sin((b+j)\gamma).
 \tag{NR1}
\]
Here \(c_T\) is the original two-head ordinary-binomial input on
the chart \(z_2=1\). Its homogeneous form retains \(z_2^T\) and
the activity \(z=z_1/z_2\).
The entire row formula (FH13), including its unit phase \(\eta\),
gives the exact scalar identity
\[
       e_T^{\mathsf T}\mathcal K F_cc_T(z)
          =\eta\sqrt N\,\Psi_{N,T}(q^{-(t-1)}z).
 \tag{NR2}
\]
All Fourier and diagonal transformations have their corresponding
inverse exterior transformations; none is a new cap normalization.

First let \(f_0(z)=\sum_{b=0}^T\beta_bz^b\).
Leibniz's rule gives the polynomial identity
\[
 \frac1{T!}\frac{d^T}{dx^T}\{x^d(1+x)^d\}
       =x^d(1+x)^{d-T}f_0((1+x)/x).
 \tag{NR3}
\]
Repeated Rolle gives \(T\) distinct zeros in \((-1,0)\),
besides the endpoint multiplicities \(d-T\) at both \(-1\)
and \(0\). Counting degree \(2d-T\) shows that the interior
zeros are simple and exhaust the other zeros.
The map \(z=(1+x)/x\) sends that interval onto
\((-\infty,0)\), with nonzero derivative. Thus \(f_0\)
has exactly \(T\) simple negative zeros.

Apply the already proved sine multiplier of the complete-channel
negative-root theorem, section 3:
\[
 \mathcal L_j f(z)
  =\frac{e^{ij\gamma}f(e^{i\gamma}z)
                 -e^{-ij\gamma}f(e^{-i\gamma}z)}{i},
 \qquad
 [z^b]\mathcal L_j f=2\sin((b+j)\gamma)[z^b]f .
 \tag{NR4}
\]
Its elementary root count can be recalled briefly. If
\(f(z)=a\prod_{h=1}^T(z+r_h)\), with \(a,r_h>0\),
the continuous argument of \(e^{ij\gamma}f(e^{i\gamma}x)\),
as \(x\) increases from \(-\infty\) to \(0\), has derivative
\(\sum_h r_h\sin\gamma/|r_h+xe^{i\gamma}|^2>0\).
Its limiting arguments are
\(-T\pi+(T+j)\gamma\) and \(j\gamma\).
For \(0<j\), \(T+j<N\), these are respectively in
\((-T\pi,-(T-1)\pi)\) and \((0,\pi)\).
Exactly \(T\) multiples of \(\pi\) are crossed transversely.
They give all \(T\) simple negative zeros of \(\mathcal L_jf\);
its leading and constant coefficients are positive.

Every \(1\le j\le\ell\) satisfies \(T+j\le d<N\).
Successive application proves the exact all-level assertion
\[
 \Psi_{N,T}=\mathcal L_\ell\cdots\mathcal L_1f_0
       =a_{N,T}\prod_{h=1}^T(z+r_h),\qquad
            a_{N,T}>0,\quad r_h>0\text{ distinct}.
 \tag{NR5}
\]
On \(\mathfrak D=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]\), fix \(r>0\).
The normalized logarithm and a quantitative comparison are
\[
 \begin{split}
 \operatorname{Log}\frac{\Psi_{N,T}(z)}{\Psi_{N,T}(r)}
   &=\sum_{h=1}^T\operatorname{Log}\frac{z+r_h}{r+r_h},\\
 \left[\cos(\theta/2)\min(1,|z|/r)\right]^T
   &\le\frac{|\Psi_{N,T}(z)|}{\Psi_{N,T}(r)}
       \le\left[\max(1,|z|/r)\right]^T,\qquad
                  \theta=\arg z\in(-\pi,\pi).
 \end{split}
 \tag{NR6}
\]
The logarithms are fixed by their real values at \(r\).
The bounds follow factorwise from
\(|z+\rho|\ge\cos(\theta/2)(|z|+\rho)\), \(\rho>0\),
and the triangle inequality. On \(|z|=r\) they give
\(\cos(\theta/2)^T\le|\Psi_{N,T}(z)|/\Psi_{N,T}(r)\le1\).
This finite angular loss can be exponential in \(N\).

There is also a global logarithmic rate for this actual scalar.
Write \(\alpha_N=\ell/N\in I\Subset(0,1/2)\), and define
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal H(u)&=-u\log u-(1-u)\log(1-u),\\
 J(u)&=\int_0^u\log(2\sin\pi v)\,dv,\\
 F_\alpha(u)&=\mathcal H(u)+\mathcal H(\alpha+u)
                         +J(\alpha+u)-J(u),
                  \qquad 0\le u\le1-\alpha,\\
 \mathcal M_\alpha(r)&=
       \max_{0\le u\le1-\alpha}\{F_\alpha(u)+u\log r\},
                       \qquad r>0 .
 \end{split}
 \tag{NR7}
\]
The entropy is continuous at both endpoints. Uniformly for every
allowed integer \(0\le b\le T\),
\[
 \log\{P(b)\beta_b\}
       =NF_{\alpha_N}(b/N)+O_I(\log N).
 \tag{NR8}
\]
Indeed \(\binom d{T-b}=\binom d{\ell+b}\) exactly.
Uniform Stirling gives
\(\log\binom{N-1}k=N\mathcal H(k/N)+O(\log N)\)
for \(0\le k<N\), including endpoints, by
\(\binom{N-1}k=(1-k/N)\binom Nk\).
Also, for \(S_k=\prod_{j=1}^k2\sin(\pi j/N)\),
\(\log S_k=NJ(k/N)+O(\log N)\) uniformly for \(0\le k<N\).
To check the latter bound at the endpoints, subtract
\(\log v+\log(1-v)\) from \(\log(2\sin\pi v)\).
The remainder is smooth on \([0,1]\), with bounded Riemann-sum
error; the two subtracted sums are factorial sums controlled by
the same uniform Stirling bound. Since \(P(b)=S_{b+\ell}/S_b\),
this proves (NR8) without deleting a finite endpoint.

The maximizer in (NR7) is unique and strictly interior. In fact
\[
 \begin{split}
 F_\alpha'(u)
  &=\log\frac{(1-u)(1-\alpha-u)\sin\pi(\alpha+u)}
                 {u(\alpha+u)\sin\pi u},\\
 F_\alpha''(u)
  &=-\frac1{u(1-u)}
    -\frac1{(\alpha+u)(1-\alpha-u)}
    -\frac{\pi\sin\pi\alpha}
                 {\sin\pi u\,\sin\pi(\alpha+u)}<0 .
 \end{split}
 \tag{NR9}
\]
The first derivative tends to \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\)
at the left and right endpoints. On compact positive \(r\)
and compact \(I\), the maximizer stays uniformly interior.
The upper bound of a positive sum by \(N\) times its largest
term, and a nearest-lattice term for the lower bound, give
\[
       \log\Psi_{N,T}(r)
          =N\mathcal M_{\alpha_N}(r)+O_{I,R}(\log N),
                         \qquad r\in R\Subset(0,\infty).
 \tag{NR10}
\]
All caps and the exact parameter \(\alpha_N\) remain.

Suppose now that \(\alpha_N\to\alpha\in(0,1/2)\), and set
\(L_N(z)=N^{-1}\operatorname{Log}
[\Psi_{N,T}(z)/\Psi_{N,T}(1)]\) on \(\mathfrak D\).
These holomorphic functions are locally bounded there.
For a compact subset of \(\mathfrak D\), the functions
\(\operatorname{Log}[(z+\rho)/(1+\rho)]\) are bounded uniformly
in \(0\le\rho\le\infty\): their arguments form the compact
family of line segments between \(z\) and \(1\), contained in
the same slit plane. Formula (NR5) averages at most \(N\)
such terms. Every normal-family subsequential limit agrees on
the positive axis with
\(\mathcal M_\alpha(r)-\mathcal M_\alpha(1)\), by (NR10).
The identity theorem makes the limit unique. Consequently
\[
 \begin{split}
 L_N&\longrightarrow L_\alpha
      \quad\hbox{locally uniformly on }\mathfrak D
          \hbox{ with every fixed derivative},\\
 L_\alpha(r)&=\mathcal M_\alpha(r)-\mathcal M_\alpha(1),\\
 \frac1N\log|\Psi_{N,T}(z)|
       &\longrightarrow
            \mathcal M_\alpha(1)+\operatorname{Re}L_\alpha(z).
 \end{split}
 \tag{NR11}
\]
This is a proved logarithmic limit, not a relative-amplitude
estimate. It holds along every admissible sequence converging to
\(\alpha\), at both parities and composite levels.

Its selected derivative is also explicit. Put
\(m_\alpha(z)=zL_\alpha'(z)\). On \(r>0\) it is the unique
maximizer in (NR7), by differentiating the maximized value.
The finite functions
\(zL_N'(z)=N^{-1}\sum_h z/(z+r_h)\) have positive imaginary
part in the upper half-plane. Their nonconstant limit does too;
nonconstancy follows as the real maximizer ranges from \(0\)
to \(1-\alpha\). The positive saddle equation and exact
palindromy \(P(T-b)\beta_{T-b}=P(b)\beta_b\) imply
\[
 \begin{split}
 z(1-m_\alpha)(1-\alpha-m_\alpha)\sin\pi(\alpha+m_\alpha)
      &=m_\alpha(\alpha+m_\alpha)\sin\pi m_\alpha,\\
 m_\alpha(1/z)&=1-\alpha-m_\alpha(z),\qquad
 m_\alpha(1)=(1-\alpha)/2 .
 \end{split}
 \tag{NR12}
\]
The first equality holds on the whole slit by the identity
theorem; the marked branch is fixed by (NR11) and the real saddle.
No unrelated solution of this equation is selected.

By (NR2), physical zeros lie on \(q^{t-1}(-\infty,0)\),
not on an unrotated ray. The actual boundary scalar has a
holomorphic logarithm normalized at \(q^{t-1}\) on
\(q^{t-1}\mathfrak D\);
its logarithmic modulus rate at \(z_{\rm phys}=q^{t-1}z\)
is the one in (NR11), since \(|\eta\sqrt N|=\sqrt N\).
The full phase \(\eta\), homogeneous input, and inverse exterior
frame transformations remain. This coefficient observation is
not identified with the original marked knot closing.
No preservation under Conway multiplication or signed turns,
meridian-normal deletion, complex-degree projection, geometric-cycle
coefficient or closed-source lower bound is asserted.

## An actual Gauss boundary row has a positive profile but no scalar Fourier Hermitian phase, 23 November

The actual terminal Gauss source has an explicit positive Fourier-row
envelope and a uniform Gaussian profile at macroscopic degrees. Its
terminal observation can nevertheless be exponentially smaller than
its full row norm. The same exact row fixes the phase in a test of a
possible positive sewing shortcut: no overall phase makes the Fourier
rotation of the whole gauged matrix Hermitian on an infinite family
of initialized macroscopic degrees. The calculations retain the actual
factorial eigenvalues and their algebraic multiplicities.

Use the admissible two-head data of (GA1):
\(N\ge2\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), \(d=N-1\),
\(\ell=d-T\ge1\), \(t=N-2\ell>0\), and \(M=T+1\).
The symbols \(M,T\) in this paragraph are fixed matrix size and degree.
Let \(D_{aa}=x_0^a q^{-Ta}\), \(x_0=-q^{-1}\), and let
\(O=[u_0,\ldots,u_{t-1}]\) be the real orthonormal top-eigenvector
matrix in (JF8). Put
\[
 \mathcal W'=D^\dagger\mathcal W,\quad U=DO,\quad
 \mathcal K=D^\dagger A_0\overline D=OBO^{\mathsf T},\quad
 B=U^\dagger A_0\overline U,\quad C=U^{\mathsf T}U.
 \tag{FH1}
\]
Here \(A_0\) is the actual root Gauss matrix on \(\mathcal H_T\).
Both \(B\) and \(C\) are invertible. For \(B\) this follows from
(JF9). The lower-primary unit in the marked calculus gives invertibility
of \(A_W=U^\dagger A_0U\), and
\[
                         A_W=BC.
 \tag{FH2}
\]
The incoming conjugate flag and all complementary meridian blocks in
(JF9)--(JF10) remain unchanged.

The centered finite Fourier block is
\[
 (F_c)_{ab}=N^{-1/2}Q^{(a-T/2)(b-T/2)},\qquad 0\le a,b\le T.
 \tag{FH3}
\]
Every fractional power in this formula is the displayed exponential.
Summing over \(a=0,\ldots,T\), centered at \(T/2\), proves
\(F_c^\dagger F_c=F_cF_c^\dagger=D^\dagger SD\), the real sine
kernel (JF2). Thus \(F_c\) preserves \(\mathcal W'\) and is unitary
there. This is not a unitary assertion on the whole time block.

Its square on that flag also has an exact interpretation. Extend (FH3)
to the full \(N\)-by-\(N\) matrix \(\mathscr F\), with indices
\(0,\ldots,d\). Diagonal phases reduce it to the normalized Fourier
matrix, so it is unitary. For \(u\in\mathcal W'\), equality
\(\|F_cu\|=\|u\|\) forces every outside output coordinate of
\(\mathscr Fu\) to vanish. The same holds for \(F_cu\).
For physical indices \(a,c\le T\), the full square is
\[
 (\mathscr F^2)_{ac}
  =Q^{-T(a+c-T)/2}\frac1N\sum_{b=0}^{d}Q^{(a+c-T)b}
  =\delta_{a+c,T}.
 \tag{FH4}
\]
The only multiple of \(N\) in \([-T,T]\) is zero; in particular no
half-phase is discarded at a wrapped endpoint. Therefore
\[
 F_c^2|_{\mathcal W'}=R|_{\mathcal W'},\qquad
 (Ru)_a=u_{T-a},\qquad
 \det(R|_{\mathcal W'})=(-1)^{t(t-1)/2}.
 \tag{FH5}
\]
The last equality also follows directly from (JF7): its positive envelope
is invariant under \(a\mapsto T-a\), and reflection reverses its
\(t\) exponential columns, with product of the extra phases equal to one.

We now compute a determinant ratio for the actual \(B\), keeping the
root Casimir multiplicities. Write \(F_n=(Q;Q)_n\), \(s=t-1\).
The finite highest-vector construction in the whole-meridian fusion
proof, (10)--(16), gives the characteristic factors indexed by
\(j=0,\ldots,T\), with root Casimir values
\(qQ^j+q^{-1}Q^{-j}\). Repeated values retain their algebraic
multiplicities. Its two root factorial labels are
\(l=T-j\), \(k=[j-\ell]\). For \(j\ge\ell\), their ordinary sum
is \(s<N\); for \(j<\ell\) it is \(N+s\). The lower labels are
therefore all ordered pairs \((l,s-l)\), \(0\le l\le s\).
The marked lower-unit formula (16) of the factorial calculus gives
the following \(t\) eigenvalues of \(A_W\), with multiplicity:
\[
 \lambda_l=(-1)^dNQ^{-\ell}
                \frac{F_s}{F_lF_{s-l}},\qquad 0\le l\le s.
 \tag{FH6}
\]
This determinant calculation neither diagonalizes away a Jordan entry
nor estimates a primary projector.

Since \(F_n=(-i)^n q^{n(n+1)/2}
\prod_{a=1}^n2\sin(\pi a/N)\), all sine products here are positive,
and \(F_s/(F_lF_{s-l})\) has phase \(q^{l(s-l)}\).
The identity \(\sum_{l=0}^{s}l(s-l)=t(t-1)(t-2)/6\) yields
\[
 \frac{\overline{\det A_W}}{\det A_W}
       =q^{4\ell t-t(t-1)(t-2)/3}.
 \tag{FH7}
\]
For the other determinant, \(D^2=\operatorname{diag}(Q^{\ell a})\)
gives \(C=O^{\mathsf T}D^2O\). Reflection preserves \(\mathcal W'\);
write \(RO=OP\), where \(P\) is a real orthogonal involution.
Reflecting the diagonal entries proves
\[
 \overline C=Q^{-\ell T}PCP,\qquad
 \frac{\overline{\det C}}{\det C}=Q^{-\ell Tt},\qquad
 \frac{\overline{\det B}}{\det B}
       =q^{-2\ell(\ell-1)t-t(t-1)(t-2)/3}.
 \tag{FH8}
\]
The last equality uses (FH2), (FH7), and \(T=N-\ell-1\); its
exponents are compared modulo \(2N\).

Suppose that a scalar \(\rho\) satisfied the proposed Fourier reality
identity on this full actual block:
\[
                    \overline{\mathcal K}=\rho F_c\mathcal K F_c.
 \tag{FH9}
\]
Its restriction to the real space \(\mathcal W'\), followed by
determinants and (FH5), necessarily gives
\[
 \rho^t=(-1)^{t(t-1)/2}
              q^{-2\ell(\ell-1)t-t(t-1)(t-2)/3}.
 \tag{FH10}
\]
The actual terminal column determines \(\rho\) without choosing a
root of (FH10). Set \(k=T-a\), and
\(\eta_T=(-1)^dN(Q^{-T-1})^d\). Expanding the literal Gauss
formula (GK5) on \(|T,0\rangle\), including its missing endpoint
arrows, gives
\[
 (A_0)_{aT}=\eta_T(-1)^kq^kQ^{Tk}
    \sum_{r=0}^{a}Q^{r(r+k)}
          {T\brack a-r}_Q{a\brack r}_Q
  =\eta_T(-1)^kq^kQ^{Tk}{T+a\brack a}_Q.
 \tag{FH11}
\]
For the first equality, the transfer order is \(n=r+k\): lowering
acts only on the first input head, and the ordered raising path puts
\(k\) units on the second head. Before insertion of the Gauss
coefficient, its exact coefficient in \(F^nE^n|T,0\rangle\) is
\({n\brack k}_Q x_0^{n-k}
Q^{-nT+n(n-1)/2+k(T-n)}F_TF_kF_a/F_{T-n}^2\).
Multiplying by (GK5) reduces it to the summand in (FH11).
The second equality is a finite coefficient
identity. Extract \([z^a]\) from
\((-z;Q)_{T+a}=(-z;Q)_T(-zQ^T;Q)_a\), and cancel the common
\(Q^{a(a-1)/2}\). Thus it is valid at the root as a polynomial
Gaussian identity, including when \(T+a\ge N\).

For \(a>\ell\), this last Gaussian is zero, since its product
numerator contains \(1-Q^N\) and its denominators have indices
below \(N\). For \(a\le\ell\), reflecting the \(a\) factors
\(1-Q^{T+j}=1-Q^{j-\ell-1}\) in its numerator proves the entire
terminal column and its generating polynomial:
\[
 (A_0)_{aT}=c_*q^{a^2}{\ell\brack a}_Q\ (0\le a\le\ell),
 \quad c_*=(-1)^{\ell+1}Nq^{2\ell^2+\ell+1},\qquad
 \sum_{a=0}^{T}(A_0)_{aT}z^a=c_*(-qz;Q)_\ell.
 \tag{FH12}
\]
Here \(\ell\le T\) by the admissible degree conditions.
No unknown boundary coefficient is used for this normalization.

More generally the entire terminal row of \(H_+=\mathcal K F_c\)
is explicit:
\[
 \begin{split}
 (H_+)_{Tb}
  &=\frac{c_*}{\sqrt N}\overline{D_{TT}}
                  q^{-Tb+T^2/2}(Q^{b+1};Q)_\ell\\
  &=\eta\sqrt N\,q^{-(t-1)b}P(b),\qquad
 P(b)=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}2\sin\frac{\pi(b+j)}N>0,\quad 0\le b\le T,\\
 \eta&=\frac{c_*}{N}\overline{D_{TT}}q^{T^2/2}
                  (-i)^\ell q^{\ell(\ell+1)/2},\qquad |\eta|=1.
 \end{split}
 \tag{FH13}
\]
Indeed \(A_0\) is symmetric, and its column (FH12), multiplied
by \(\overline{D_{aa}}(F_c)_{ab}\), is evaluated by the same
generating polynomial at \(\overline{x_0}Q^b\).
Every sine is positive, since \(1\le b+j\le d\).
Thus this row is a known linear phase times a positive envelope,
not a sum whose normalization is selected from a presumed saddle.

Here is its uniform asymptotic with its full finite cap. Fix
\(\alpha=\ell/N\) in any compact interval
\(I\Subset(0,1/2)\), and let \(b_*=T/2\),
\(\vartheta=\pi\alpha/2\), and
\(J(u)=\int_0^u\log(2\sin\pi v)\,dv\). Put
\(S(\alpha)=-2J((1-\alpha)/2)>0\).
For actual integer occupations with \(x=(b-b_*)/\sqrt N\)
in a fixed bounded real interval,
\[
 (H_+)_{Tb}
  =\eta q^{-(t-1)b}\sqrt N\,e^{NS(\alpha)}
                e^{-\pi\tan\vartheta\,x^2}
                       (1+O_{I,R}(N^{-1})),\qquad |x|\le R.
 \tag{FH14}
\]
To prove this, the arguments \((b_*+j)/N\) are the exact midpoints
of the \(\ell\) equal subintervals of
\([(1-\alpha)/2,(1+\alpha)/2]\). For
\(f(u)=\log(2\sin\pi u)\), the midpoint error is \(O_I(N^{-1})\)
in the sum, uniformly after shifts of size \(O_R(N^{-1/2})\).
The integral \(\int_{(1-\alpha)/2}^{(1+\alpha)/2}f(u+y)\,du\)
is even in \(y\), with value \(S(\alpha)\) and second derivative
\(-2\pi\tan\vartheta\) at zero. Its fourth derivative is uniformly
bounded on these compact bulk intervals. Taylor expansion therefore
proves (FH14). The identities \(J(1/2)=0\) and
\(J(1-u)=-J(u)\) follow by reflecting the sine integral and using
\(\sin(2v)=2\sin v\cos v\). They also give
\(S(\alpha)=J(\alpha)-2J(\alpha/2)\); both sides vanish at zero
and have derivative \(\log(2\cos(\pi\alpha/2))\).
Positivity follows also from
\(S(\alpha)=2\int_{(1-\alpha)/2}^{1/2}f(u)\,du>0\), since
this interval is contained in \((1/4,1/2)\).

No discarded endpoint can change the norm calculation. On the full
real interval \(0\le b\le T\),
\((\log P)''(b)=-(\pi/N)^2\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}
\csc^2(\pi(b+j)/N)\le-\pi^2\ell/N^2\).
Reflection gives \((\log P)'(b_*)=0\). The midpoint estimate at
\(b_*\) consequently bounds \(P(b)\) by
\(C_Ie^{NS(\alpha)}e^{-c_I(b-b_*)^2/N}\) everywhere.
Dominated Riemann sums applied to (FH14) now prove
\[
 \|(H_+)_{T,*}\|=\|A_0e_T\|
   =N^{3/4}(2\tan\vartheta)^{-1/4}
                         e^{NS(\alpha)}(1+o_I(1)).
 \tag{FH15}
\]
The norm identity uses (FH1), symmetry of \(A_0\), and the
unitarity of \(F_c\) on the input flag of this row. The Riemann
integral is \(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2\pi\tan\vartheta x^2}dx
=(2\tan\vartheta)^{-1/2}\). These estimates are uniform for the
stated real degrees, including integer and half-integer \(b_*\).
The new source identification is (FH12)--(FH13); no new general
method or novelty for the finite Gaussian-binomial norm is claimed.

Its terminal diagonal entry is, by
(FH3),(FH12) and the literal \(D\)-phases,
\[
 h_+=(H_+)_{TT}
   =\frac{c_*}{\sqrt N}\overline{x_0}^{\,T}q^{T^2/2}
                     (Q^{T+1};Q)_\ell,\qquad
 |h_+|=\sqrt N\,|F_\ell|>0.
 \tag{FH16}
\]
Indeed \(-q\overline{x_0}Q^T=Q^{T+1}\) is the argument in
the generating product. Its root reflection is
\((Q^{-\ell};Q)_\ell=(-1)^\ell Q^{-\ell(\ell+1)/2}F_\ell\).
Keeping also the positive-sine phase of \(F_\ell\) gives
\[
 \frac{\overline{h_+}}{h_+}=q^{R_+},\qquad
 R_+=3N\ell-N^2-4\ell^2-\ell-1.
 \tag{FH17}
\]
If \(e^{i\varphi}H_+\) were Hermitian, its nonzero diagonal
entry would force \(e^{2i\varphi}=q^{R_+}\). Because
\(\mathcal K\) is symmetric and supported on the real flag,
Hermiticity multiplied on the left by \(F_c\) also gives (FH9)
with this same \(\rho=e^{2i\varphi}\).
Conversely (FH9) gives \(H_+^\dagger=\rho H_+\) on the flag,
so its nonzero terminal entry already forces \(\rho=q^{R_+}\).
Write the exponent on the right of (FH10) as
\(L=Nt(t-1)/2-2\ell(\ell-1)t-t(t-1)(t-2)/3\).
The exact integer calculation
\[
 tR_+-L=-\binom t3-Nt(t+1)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
                         2N\ \bigm|\ \binom t3
 \tag{FH18}
\]
is therefore necessary. In particular it fails for every admissible
\(t=3\) block. It also fails on the infinite macroscopic family
\[
 N=3^h,\quad h\ge2,\qquad \ell=t=N/3,\qquad T=2N/3-1,
 \qquad (T+1)/N=2/3:
 \quad v_3\!\left(\binom t3\right)=h-2<h.
 \tag{FH19}
\]
The valuation follows from \(t=3^{h-1}\) and the two factors
\(t-1,t-2\), neither divisible by three.

The global Gaussian bound and (FH15) also give the actual observation
loss \(|h_+|/\|(H_+)_{T,*}\|\le C_I N^{-1/4}e^{-c_I N}\)
on each such compact macroscopic interval. This concerns the specified
terminal entry, not an identification of that entry with an arbitrary
original marked knot closing.

The opposite Fourier orientation has its own endpoint phase, which
must not be replaced by (FH17). Directly,
\[
 h_-=(\mathcal K F_c^\dagger)_{TT}
  =\frac{c_*}{\sqrt N}\overline{x_0}^{\,T}q^{3T^2/2}F_\ell,
 \qquad |h_-|=\sqrt N\,|F_\ell|,
 \qquad R_--R_+\equiv-2(\ell+1)(2\ell+1)\pmod{2N},
 \tag{FH20}
\]
where \(q^{R_-}=\overline{h_-}/h_-\).
On the flag \((F_c^\dagger)^2=R\), so Hermiticity of any overall
phase times \(\mathcal K F_c^\dagger\) has the same determinant
condition (FH10), with its new endpoint phase. It requires
\[
                 2N\ \bigm|\
           \binom t3+2t(\ell+1)(2\ell+1).
 \tag{FH21}
\]
On (FH19), the two terms have valuations \(h-2\) and \(h-1\)
respectively; their sum still has valuation \(h-2\). Thus this
orientation also admits no overall Hermitian phase on that entire
initialized macroscopic family.

This excludes that particular scalar-phase Fourier Hermitian, hence
positive, construction. It does not exclude other phase operators or
positive congruences, give a knot counterexample, or bound the original
marked scalar. The exact orthogonal frames, all four meridian-normal
blocks, both source flags, and every sewing/cap factor remain.

Complete proof inputs are the adopted (JF1)--(JF10), (GA1)--(GG3),
and (GK1)--(GK9), with their seven complete matching source texts,
and the entire
[marked factorial calculus](research_marked_gauss_functional_calculus.md)
`7f8c7c0be05331e7c0679c5a26374bbcb4b38b817c36a1f4ac4e16d4c1739095`

The former fixes the original lower-unit normalization, and the latter
proves the actual characteristic multiplicities used in (FH6).
No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build, git
operation, frozen-note edit or public-document edit is used.

## A tridiagonal orthogonal frame for the actual Gauss flag, 23 November

The two-head physical lowering flag has an exact orthonormal construction
which does not invert its Fourier Gram or use its oblique primary
projection. This changes coordinates in the full root source; it does
not remove its complementary first meridian normal or its original cap.

Use the notation and admissible physical degrees of (GA1) below:
\(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), \(x_0=-q^{-1}\),
\(\ell=d-T\ge1\), and \(t=N-2\ell>0\). Put
\(M=T+1=N-\ell\), \(\gamma=\pi/N\), and identify
\(\mathcal H_T\) with occupations \(a=0,\ldots,T\).
Here \(M\) is a matrix size, not a varying meridian. Extend this space
by zero in \(\mathbb C^N\). The twisted Fourier vectors and retained
band are
\[
 f_h(a)=N^{-1/2}x_0^aQ^{ha},\qquad
 Q_B=\sum_{h=-T}^{0}f_hf_h^\dagger,\qquad
 S=P_TQ_BP_T\big|_{\mathcal H_T}.
 \tag{JF1}
\]
The interval \(-T,\ldots,0\) represents the same residues as the
complement of \(1,\ldots,\ell\). By (GA3)--(GA5),
\(\mathcal W=\ker(E^t|_{\mathcal H_T})\) is precisely the
\(1\)-eigenspace of \(S\), and has dimension \(t\). Indeed
\(\langle u,Su\rangle=\|Q_Bu\|^2\); equality with \(\|u\|^2\)
holds exactly when \(Q_Bu=u\).

Define the diagonal unitary and the real sine kernel by
\[
 D_{aa}=x_0^a q^{-Ta},\qquad
 (D^\dagger SD)_{ab}=k_{a-b},\qquad
 k_n=\frac{\sin(M\gamma n)}{N\sin(\gamma n)}\ (n\ne0),
 \qquad k_0=M/N.
 \tag{JF2}
\]
This follows by summing \(Q^{h(a-b)}\) over the literal interval
in (JF1); all half phases are retained. Let \(J_T\) be the real
symmetric tridiagonal matrix
\[
 (J_T)_{aa}=\alpha_a=-\cos(M\gamma)\cos((2a-T)\gamma),\qquad
 (J_T)_{a,a+1}=(J_T)_{a+1,a}=b_a
       =\sin((a+1)\gamma)\sin((T-a)\gamma).
 \tag{JF3}
\]
Use \(b_{-1}=b_T=0\) at the endpoints. Every other \(b_a\) is
strictly positive. The commutation with the real kernel is direct.
For \(n=a-b\) and \(s=(a+b-T)\gamma\), the coefficient differences
are
\[
 \alpha_a-\alpha_b=2\cos(M\gamma)\sin s\sin(n\gamma),\quad
 b_{a-1}-b_b=-\sin s\sin((n-1)\gamma),\quad
 b_a-b_{b-1}=-\sin s\sin((n+1)\gamma).
 \tag{JF4}
\]
Thus each entry of \([J_T,D^\dagger SD]\) is \(\sin s\) times
\[
 2\cos(M\gamma)\sin(n\gamma)k_n
  -\sin((n-1)\gamma)k_{n-1}
  -\sin((n+1)\gamma)k_{n+1}=0.
 \tag{JF5}
\]
The equality is the sine addition formula after division by \(N\).
It includes zero indices by the value of \(k_0\); any unused outside
kernel entry is multiplied by a zero endpoint coefficient.

For clarity, the needed real Jacobi ordering also has an elementary
finite proof. If \(p_j(\lambda)\) is the characteristic polynomial
of the leading \(j\)-by-\(j\) block, then
\[
 p_0=1,\quad p_1=\lambda-\alpha_0,\quad
 p_{j+1}=(\lambda-\alpha_j)p_j-b_{j-1}^2p_{j-1}.
 \tag{JF6}
\]
Induction in this recurrence gives real simple roots and strict
interlacing: at consecutive roots of \(p_j\), the values
\(-b_{j-1}^2p_{j-1}\) have alternating signs, and the monic end
signs give one root in each of the two outside intervals. No adjacent
polynomials have a common root. The eigenvector at a root of \(p_M\) has entries
\(p_a(\lambda)/(b_0\cdots b_{a-1})\), times its nonzero first
entry. The sign variation of \((p_0,\ldots,p_M)\), starting at zero
above all roots, does not change when an interior polynomial vanishes:
its neighbors have opposite signs by (JF6). As \(\lambda\) decreases
past a root of \(p_M\), interlacing makes its sign relative to
\(p_{M-1}\) change from equal to opposite, adding one variation.
At the \(j\)-th largest root, omitting the final zero therefore gives
exactly \(j\) sign changes, \(0\le j<M\). An interior zero is also
omitted; its two neighbors have opposite signs, giving the same count
as either nearby value of \(\lambda\). This proves the stated
ordering for every eigenvector, as well as simplicity.

The part of that ordered basis giving \(\mathcal W\) is explicit.
Writing \(A(a)=\prod_{h=1}^{\ell}\sin((a+h)\gamma)>0\), the exact
reflection formula (GA4) gives
\[
 D^\dagger\mathcal W
   =\left\{\left(A(a)\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}
         z_j e^{i(t-1-2j)\gamma a}\right)_{a=0}^T:
                       z_j\in\mathbb C\right\}.
 \tag{JF7}
\]
For example, the common nonzero factor discarded in this span is
\(\gamma_{\!\rm GA}(-2i)^\ell
e^{i\gamma\ell(\ell+1)/2}\), where \(\gamma_{\!\rm GA}\) is the
constant in (GA4). Every sine in \(A(a)\) has argument strictly
between \(0\) and \(\pi\), including both physical endpoints.

The span in (JF7) is invariant under conjugation. A real vector in it
therefore comes from a real trigonometric polynomial: uniqueness of
its \(t\) coefficients on the \(M\ge t\) distinct samples forces
the conjugate-reversal relation on the coefficients. That polynomial
has at most \(t-1\) zeros on \(0\le\theta\le T\gamma<\pi\),
unless it is zero. To see this, multiply it by
\(e^{i(t-1)\theta}\); the result is a polynomial of degree at most
\(t-1\) in \(e^{2i\theta}\), whose points on this arc are distinct.
Consequently every nonzero real vector in (JF7) has at most \(t-1\)
sign changes.

Equations (JF1), (JF5) and the simple spectrum make this span a sum of
real eigenspaces of \(J_T\). Its dimension is \(t\), so the ordering
proved from (JF6) forces
\[
 D^\dagger\mathcal W
       =\operatorname{span}\{u_0,\ldots,u_{t-1}\},\qquad
 P_{\mathcal W}=D\left(\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}u_ju_j^{\mathsf T}\right)D^\dagger,
 \tag{JF8}
\]
where \(u_j\) is a real orthonormal eigenvector of \(J_T\), ordered
by decreasing eigenvalue. This is an exact tridiagonal construction;
no lower bound for its eigenvalue gap is asserted.

It also gives complete sewing coordinates. Set
\(U=D[u_0,\ldots,u_{t-1}]\),
\(U_c=D[u_t,\ldots,u_{M-1}]\), and \(V=[U,U_c]\).
For the actual root Gauss matrix \(A_0\), the landing and ordinary
transpose identities (GK4)--(GK6) imply
\[
 A_0=U B U^{\mathsf T}
     =V\begin{pmatrix}B&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}V^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 B=U^\dagger A_0\overline U=B^{\mathsf T},\quad \det B\ne0.
 \tag{JF9}
\]
The incoming flag is \(\overline{\mathcal W}\). It is not silently
identified with the outgoing \(\mathcal W\). Keep this full root
frame fixed for the meridian germ:
\[
 A_N(e^\mu)=V\mathcal B(\mu)V^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 \mathcal B(\mu)=V^\dagger A_N(e^\mu)\overline V.
 \tag{JF10}
\]
All four blocks of \(\mathcal B_1\) remain. In particular its
complementary block \(U_c^\dagger A_1\overline{U_c}\) is invertible
by (GK9), restricted to this degree. No symmetry of \(\mathcal B_1\)
or whole-germ projected identity is needed.

For a literal coefficient pairing \(I\), the full overlap between
two such frames is \(V_i^{\mathsf T}V_j\), a unitary matrix because
\(V_i^{\mathsf T}\overline{V_i}=I\). The retained rectangular
overlap \(U_i^{\mathsf T}U_j\) is a contraction. More generally an
actual seam \(C\) becomes \(V_i^{\mathsf T}CV_j\), with exactly
the same operator norm as \(C\); its retained block has norm at most
\(\|C\|\). Nonidentity turns, inverse pairings and pivotal factors
are kept in \(C\). Open vectors and the original marked row are
transported by the same exact substitutions. No overlap or compressed
block is inverted, and no nonidentity seam is declared unitary.
For a Hermitian pairing the corresponding formula is instead
\(V_i^\dagger CV_j\), again norm preserving for the full frames.
Extending the block frames by the identity on the other physical
degrees and self sectors gives a unitary coordinate change on the
whole two-head space; no omitted sector or source row is set to zero.

This eliminates dense inverse Grams and oblique primary inverses from
the orthogonal root-coordinate construction and its exact sewing
form. It supplies no nonzero marked overlap, geometric asymptotic,
source-compatible window or scalar lower estimate after arbitrary
short components. The physical size \(M\), flag dimension \(t\),
and occupation degree \(T\) grow with \(N\); they are distinct from
the fixed auxiliary polynomial degree in the earlier variational
and coefficient-filter constructions. The statement is for the
two-remaining-head blocks specified above, not a general-width flag
basis theorem.

The complete proof inputs are the two following adopted ledger
sections, (GA1)--(GG3) and (GK1)--(GK9), and their seven complete
matching sources: C549
`b4fb801a1482316aebb4799f1d0b80d5b43ced39138d903c04cfde811ca166b0`,
F428 `7589bb0f796a874608b9e558aac1f78699884f0003da4a73ba52778c1edba66e`,
