proves that small-ball volumes do not collapse anywhere in the
retained core. The next two arguments use this estimate to construct
the limiting metric without using the flattened tetrahedra as charts.

The [regular injectivity estimate](research_regular_corner_injectivity_away_axes.md)
now supplies uniformly sized hyperbolic coordinate neighborhoods
on every fixed buffer around the retained core that stays a fixed
positive distance from genuine cone axes. The proof uses the
preceding ball-volume lower bound. A short covering displacement
would produce many distinct lifts of every point of a fixed-radius
ball, all inside one bounded hyperbolic ball in a local universal
cover. Counting their volume rules out such a displacement.
The proof also excludes short finite-order repeats and does not
assume that the entire universal cover is complete.

The [marked-limit theorem](research_regular_corner_marked_metric_limit.md)
assembles these coordinate neighborhoods into a complete limiting
cone metric on the original filled topology. Finite metric nets
give a compact limit. The injectivity bound makes its small
neighborhoods full hyperbolic balls. Averaging the local chart maps
then gives actual diffeomorphisms between the compact cores, with
smooth convergence of their metrics. The original generators can
be represented by uniformly bounded paths, so their transported
homotopy classes stabilize after taking a subsequence. This fixes
the original marking, including the filling slopes and peripheral
logarithms. The explicit ends complete the resulting metric.

The [relative deformation theorem](research_relative_cone_holonomy_deformation.md)
starts with this supplied marked cone metric and constructs nearby
metrics for nearby representations satisfying the same full
peripheral equations. On the compact core it averages equivariant
developing maps; at the ends it uses the prescribed tube and cusp
models. The construction therefore continues the geometry even
when some original tetrahedra have lost their positive orientation.
It needs the actual base metric and its marked atlas, which the
preceding limit theorem supplies.

The same relative theorem proves a local comparison and an analytic
volume formula. Two developments close in the supplied marked atlas,
with the same representation and compatible full end models, give
marked isometric metrics. The constructed volume is real analytic.
Consequently, along a real-analytic one-parameter branch, a volume
calibration on an accumulating sequence of positive metrics extends
across the corner, provided those metrics have the required marked
convergence. Equality of holonomy alone is not used to identify
their volumes.

The [geometric continuation theorem](research_regular_corner_geometric_continuation.md)
now assembles these results and strengthens the calibration to a full
real charge neighborhood. Fix a nonempty proper selected set in the
connected original circle tree, with its integer slopes and carriers.
Suppose actual positive cone metrics approach a regular one-square
configuration with positive limiting core lengths and cone charges.
There is then a unique local analytic solution of the original
primitive equations. Every sufficiently late member of the supplied
sequence is on this branch, by the implicit-function theorem's
local uniqueness. For all nearby real charges with
\(0<\chi_v\le1\), it gives actual marked complete cone metrics and
\[
 \operatorname{Vol}(g_{\boldsymbol\chi})
 =2\pi\Re\left[
   \sum_{e\in E}\psi_e(t_v,t_w)
   +\frac{i}{4\pi}\sum_{v\in S}n_vt_v^2
   -i\sum_{v\in S}\chi_vt_v
 \right].
\]
Here the angles solve the continued primitive equations,
\(n_v=\eta_v-2p_v\), and every original edge is included with
its original additive constant. The full periods retain
\(U_v+p_vV_v=-2\pi i\chi_v\).

The proof of this neighborhood statement uses more than the
convergence of a sequence. At a late strictly positive point,
small deformations of the actual tetrahedral face and edge
neighborhoods give a smoothly varying marked family of positive
metrics. The local comparison therefore identifies the two
families on a nonempty open set of real charges. The positive
volume identity holds there for arbitrary real charges, and the
real-analytic identity theorem extends it throughout the connected
corner neighborhood. This justifies the volume equality also
where some of the old tetrahedra have become negatively oriented.

These are local results at a supplied regular one-square limit.
They do not prove that every short partial filling can be reached
along such a path. The metric argument does not yet cover a
two-square corner or a singular face chart. A geometric stationary point also still
needs a nonzero contribution in the original finite quantum sum,
together with a bound on its complementary contribution.

## The primitive equations at two-square limits

The [two-square theorem](research_radial_two_square_primitive_lift.md)
now treats the remaining finite corner alternatives for a supplied
positive radial sequence. Its hypotheses are a proper nonempty
selected set in a connected original circle tree, integer powers,
complete outside angles, and a supplied positive solution at charge
one. The charge varies by one common real value. The radial
compactness theorem supplies bounded periods, positive limiting
core heights and the sharp corner equations.

At a boundary charge strictly between zero and one, no selected
real angle can reach either endpoint \(\pm\pi\). Such an endpoint
would propagate a component of equally signed endpoints. At a
boundary vertex of that component its exact row would read
\(2\chi=|n_v|+d_0\), where the integer power is nonzero and
\(d_0\ge1\) counts adjacent zero-real-angle vertices. This
contradicts \(\chi<1\). Compactness consequently gives a uniform
margin from both angular endpoints on closed positive-charge
intervals.

If both square factors of an edge degenerate, its two endpoint
real angles are zero and both imaginary returns are \(-\pi/2\).
Every other incidence at either endpoint has strictly negative
imaginary return. The charge rows therefore force these edges to
form a matching, with \(\chi>1/2\). The common charge excludes a
leaf at either end; every other edge incident to these vertices
is strictly positive.

This structure regularizes the full system of primitive equations,
including a vanishing square root. Write a fold edge as
\(a_v=-iA,\ a_w=-iB,\ A,B>0,\ A^2+B^2=1\). Retain \(q_e\)
as an independent coordinate with
\[
 q_e^2-1-\tan^2(t_v/2)-\tan^2(t_w/2)=0.
\]
The linearized constraint is
\(B\,dt_v+A\,dt_w=0\). On that constrained tangent the edge's
angular return variation vanishes, while its \(q_e\) column is
\(i(B,A)^T/(AB)\). The remaining positive and regular-corner
edges give a positive definite Hermitian form. Pairing the
linearized primitive equations with their angular variation
forces that variation to vanish. The disjoint fold supports then
force every \(dq_e=0\). Hence the augmented square Jacobian is
invertible and the original logarithmic equations continue
holomorphically for independent nearby complex charges.

The result supplies a local analytic branch at every finite
corner alternative admitted by this radial limit theorem.
It does not prove that the positive radial set is connected or
that the two-square limit is an actual completed cone metric.
It also does not infer a scalar Gaussian phase after the wire
coordinate has been eliminated.

The [full phase calculation](research_unsummed_two_square_morse_lift.md)
keeps the internal summation coordinate \(x_e\) as well as the
angles. It proves that the joint holomorphic Hessian is nonsingular
at these same limits, including \(q_e=0\). This is stronger than
regularity of the primitive equations alone.

The reason is an exact identity. In local coordinates
\(q_e=\cot(\pi x_e)\), put
\[
 f_e=q_e^2-1-\tan^2(t_v/2)-\tan^2(t_w/2).
\]
The full phase gradient is an invertible triangular holomorphic
matrix times the vector consisting of the \(f_e\) and the
primitive equations. Its Hessian at their common zero is therefore
invertible. The coordinate change remains regular because
\(dq_e/dx_e=-\pi(1+q_e^2)\ne0\). At a fold the wire-only second
derivative vanishes, but the mixed wire--angle derivatives do not.
Eliminating the wire too early loses precisely those terms.

This gives a local descending disk for the phase. The exact
factorial source is holomorphic nearby, with the original trace
and both level parities retained. Neither statement proves a
nonzero asymptotic amplitude there or a nonzero coefficient of
that disk in the original integration cycle. The theorem applies
to the specified same-index phase; a free boundary polynomial
or a reversed-index factor needs its own phase analysis.

The [factorial amplitude theorem](research_two_square_factorial_amplitude.md)
now also proves that the factors on each two-square edge have a
nonzero local asymptotic coefficient. With the original internal
coordinate \(x\) and endpoint angle \(t\), the actual factor satisfies
\[
 B_N(x,t)=\frac{e^{Nb_0(x,t)}}{2N\sin(\pi x)}
                    \bigl(1+O_{\mathrm{hol}}(N^{-1})\bigr).
\]
The result includes an expansion to every order. Its phase is the
original continued phase, including its constant. The proof starts
from the exact finite logarithmic derivative of the canonical
factorial and uses midpoint summation on a slit domain. A contraction
of the positive approach identifies that domain's logarithms with
the original marking.

At a two-square limit \(q=iQ\), both factors are holomorphic and
nonzero on one neighborhood for every \(N\ge2\). Their paired
leading coefficient, after extracting the phase and \(N^{-2}\),
is \((1-Q^2)/4>0\). At the fold it is \(1/4\).
Thus these degenerating edges cause neither a vanishing joint
Hessian nor a zero of their own leading factorial coefficient.
The theorem does not assign a single asymptotic branch to unrelated
factors or show that the complete integration cycle retains this
local contribution.

## A nonzero marked Fourier term in the local density

The [local Fourier-sector theorem](research_tree_factorial_marked_fourier_sector.md)
assembles all same-index factorial factors of the stated tree,
including factors whose exact values can vanish. A negative-real-part
factorial argument has the form
\[
 z_j=\tfrac12-x_e+\frac{\varepsilon_jt_v}{2\pi},
 \qquad \varepsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
The exact factorial shift expresses it as a nonzero normalized
factor times two exponentials. Bounds on the continued sine
logarithms identify which exponential carries the original
geometric phase, including its constant. They do not select it
merely because it is the larger exponential.

After extracting that marked phase and a specified exact common
factor, the remaining finite multiplier is
\[
 \prod_j\bigl(1+e^{-2\pi iN\sigma_jz_j}\bigr),
 \qquad \sigma_j\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
There is at most one such argument per incidence. On a tree their
linear frequencies are independent: the wire equations pair
incidences on an edge, and a leaf then forces its remaining
coefficient to vanish. Thus the factorial multiplier has constant
coefficient one.

The theorem also retains the angular denominators. Their terms
are indexed by \(k_v\ge0\), with coefficient
\((k_v+1)(-1)^{(N-1)k_v}\). Any contribution to the marked frequency
must pair opposite wall signs on each used edge. The affine
constants then cancel, and angular balance forces \(\sum_vk_v\)
to be even. Every resonant contribution is consequently positive
at both parities. At unit charge their sum is an explicit integer
\(\mathcal M\ge1\); the empty choice contributes one.
At the classified common radial charges \(1/2<\chi<1\), the other
cosine term cannot resonate with these integer frequencies. The
coefficient is then \(2^{-|S|}\mathcal M>0\).

This proves a nonzero marked term in this exact local decomposition.
Its normalized coefficient and the full Hessian give a nonzero
formal local Gaussian coefficient at the classified critical
points. The conclusion is tied to the specified factorial
representative and common factor. Exponentially small terms in
that factor can matter alongside larger competing modes; they
are not removed from the exact expression.

For use in the original source, every replaced endpoint must
satisfy the traced-end convention or have a separate proved
adapter. Setting a free outside angle to zero does not authorize
replacing its cardinal polynomial by a factorial. The result also
does not compute the coefficient of the descending local disk in
the original relative cycle or bound the rest of that cycle.
Those are still required for a volume limit.

Multiply its exact ratios before identifying shared boundary

Absorbing \(Q_N\) into the specified common factor preserves its

The ratio is a unit for sufficiently large levels; no all-level

## Compactness on bounded real-period sets

The [real-period compactness theorem](research_real_period_image_compactness.md)
strengthens the earlier inverse-period description. Fix positive
charges \(c\), complete outside angles and a strict feasible
assignment of the original angle constraints. For the positive
solutions of
\[
 P_n(t)=u-\pi i c,\qquad \|u\|_1\le R,
\]
all imaginary angles, real returns and square covectors are bounded
uniformly, without a sign assumption on the imaginary angles and
without assuming that the real-period image is connected.
The proof perturbs one incidence at each selected vertex in the
ambient convex angle body. The supporting inequality bounds the
sum of the absolute imaginary angles; the original positive
pairing then bounds each return.

Every finite image-boundary approach therefore has subsequential
finite limiting data. Noninterior square factors are sharp corners,
with the limiting covectors satisfying the exact corner equality.
For a proper selected subset, vanishing of a half-angle cosine would
propagate along the original tree to a complete outside vertex,
where that cosine is one. This excludes that degeneration and,
together with the positive charge rows, bounds the half-angle
sines and full sines away from zero.

These bounds do not imply bounded stationary wire coordinates.
The general tilted corner problem still permits \(q_e=\pm i\);
the inverse cotangent may diverge there. The radial matching
classification used above has additional hypotheses and is not
imported into this more general image problem.

The calibrated action retains a strict gap on every compact
real-period annulus away from the supplied center. This supplies
classical control at finite image boundaries. It does not match
those boundaries to the original angular endpoints or wire seams.
Moreover, the entire positive inverse slice need not stay below
the real angular axes. The note exhibits real points of that slice
which meet genuine original trace poles at infinitely many odd
levels. It does not place those points in the center's component
or rule out valid contour detours. The unresolved task is to
construct and estimate the connecting relative chain, including
its pole detours and wire faces.

The real-period compactness theorem is adopted at

## The descent contour over a convex domain of real angles

The [reduced-angle theorem](research_reduced_angle_inverse_period_graph.md)
gives an explicit domain for the geometric contour. For fixed real
angles \(s\), minimize the original convex energy over the incidence
angles \(g\), keeping the prescribed imaginary period rows:
\[
 e_c(s)=\min_g\mathcal E(s,g),\qquad
 \sum_{e\ni v}g_{v,e}-n_vs_v/2=-\pi c_v.
\]
The strict feasible real-angle domain is the bounded convex polytope
\[
 |s_v|<\pi,\qquad
 |n_vs_v-2\pi c_v|+\sum_{e=(v,w)}|s_w|<\pi d_v .
\]
Here \(d_v\) is the original degree, and complete outside angles are
zero. Strict feasibility alone does not guarantee an interior fiber
minimum.

Where the fiber minimum is interior it reconstructs exactly one
positive point \(t=s+i h(s)\), with
\[
 P(t)=\nabla e_c(s)-\pi i c .
\]
Every positive point of this real-period slice arises this way. If
\(J=P_t=A+iB\), then
\[
 h_s=-A^{-1}B,\qquad \nabla^2e_c=A+B A^{-1}B>0 .
\]
For every energy level below the full boundary-energy gap, the
previous inverse-period collar is exactly the graph over the convex
sublevel \(D_\delta=\{s:e_c(s)<E_0+\delta\}\). On this graph its
action is \(mM_\infty-e_c(s)/\pi\), with a strict quadratic drop from
the center and the prescribed boundary loss \(\delta/\pi\).

This is a more useful parametrization of the existing contour, not
yet a representation of the original quantum integration class.
The same calculation determines the cost of a vertical connector:
within a positive chart its action increases away from the graph.
A short connection to the constant geometric-height contour has a
strict boundary gap. A connection all the way to real height is
different. At a nonreal center, every sufficiently small projected
collar has its entire real rim above the target action, because
\[
 \Re\Phi_c(s)-\Re\Phi_c(s+i h(s))
       =\{e_c(s)-\mathcal E(s,0)\}/\pi>0
\]
at the center. Consequently this simple vertical completion cannot
supply the missing global bound. A larger deformation must retain
and control the combined angular and wire boundary contributions.

The reduced-angle theorem is adopted at

## The exact contribution at an escaping stationary wire

The [stationary-wire boundary calculation](research_stationary_wire_escape_current.md)
now determines what the original source retains when an internal
stationary coordinate tends to infinity. Write \(D=N-1\),
\(w=e^{-2\pi ix}\), and retain the actual cardinal representatives
at the two ends of an edge. Their product has the finite expansion
\[
 F_N(w)=\sum_{m=-D}^{D}A_m w^{-m},\qquad
 A_0=K_T/N,\qquad A_D=\kappa^{-2}(R\otimes R)/N^2 .
\]
Here \(K_T=\sum_j e_j\otimes e_j\) is the original turn kernel,
\(R\) is the physical crossing, and
\(\kappa=\exp(\pi i(N-1)^2/(2N))\) is its prescribed scalar.
The extreme coefficient inserts one crossing at each endpoint and
deletes the edge. The whole wire-boundary integral does something
different: it retains the original coupling. Precisely,
\[
 F_N\,dx=-\frac{K_T}{2\pi iN}\frac{dw}{w}
       +d_w\left(\sum_{m\ne0}\frac{A_m w^{-m}}{2\pi i m}\right).
\]
This equality also holds in the joint source after the remaining
differentials and all original exterior factors are attached.
The clockwise wire period and its factor \(N\) recover \(K_T\).

The complete lower lattice correction has zero residue, since
\(w^NF_N\) vanishes to order at least \(N-D=1\). For the literal
factorial representative before physical contraction, the exact
covering factor can also be retained: on a sufficiently small fixed
wire circle, its completed lower correction has arbitrarily small
prescribed exponential rate, uniformly on compact endpoint-angle
sets. This estimate concerns a complete circle. It neither bounds
an incomplete arc nor makes the main \(K_T\) residue small.

At the classical escape \(q_e=\sigma i\), the limiting return is
\[
 r_{ve}=-\sigma i t_v/2+\pi i k_{ve},\qquad \sigma\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
The two integers satisfy an odd parity constraint. Exactly one
endpoint has real angle \(s_v=\epsilon\pi\); the other has real
angle zero. The nonzero integer is \(k_{ve}=\sigma\epsilon\).
Deleting this edge changes its endpoint row to power
\(n_v+\sigma\) and charge \(c_v+k_{ve}\), with the original lift
retained. A unit charge can therefore become zero or two; a
nonzero-charge deletion comparison is not automatically available.

There is an elementary restriction on where this can happen. At
the saturated selected endpoint the original imaginary period row
gives
\[
 \epsilon n_v-2c_v=\frac2\pi\sum_{e\ni v}g_{v,e},\qquad
 |\epsilon n_v-2c_v|\le d_v .
\]
Every escaping edge consequently meets a vertex with
\(|n_v|\le d_v+2c_v\), in particular \(|n_v|\le d_v+2\) at unit
charge. This localizes this boundary phenomenon to short powers.
It does not make the associated filling assignments finite, since
the other coordinates remain unrestricted.

The original factorial/cardinal primitive and its moving-seam
currents are still required on a partial angular patch. They have
not been identified with scalar vertex deletions. The remaining
construction must pair or estimate those angular sides and seam
terms while keeping the geometric contribution. The new boundary
identity specifies these obligations without assuming that an
extreme Fourier coefficient equals a complete period.

## Reflection and periodic translation retain different boundary terms

The [joint angular-face calculation](research_joint_angular_face_source_identities.md)
settles the proposed reflection completion. Reflection \(t_v\mapsto-t_v\)
preserves the exact joint differential, its factorial/cardinal primitive
\(\Theta\), and its moving-wire currents. It also fixes the spectral
coordinate \(z_v=-2\cos t_v\). A patch and its pushforward reflection
therefore have the same oriented spectral image, including their
boundaries. They add. The factor \(1/2\) in the original full-lens
trace compensates this double covering; it is not a boundary
cancellation.

Periodic translation is a different operation. With polynomial
spectators retained, \(t\mapsto t-2\pi\epsilon\) multiplies the
Gaussian angular form by
\[
 M_{n,\epsilon}(t)=(-1)^{nN}e^{-inN\epsilon t}.
\]
At \(t=\epsilon\pi+ih\), this is \(e^{nN\epsilon h}\).
The oriented partial-face pair retains the defect \(M-1\).
Only after the entire original residue window has been evaluated
does translation by \(r\) full turns give the scalar
\((-1)^{nr}\). In particular the symmetric full-turn current is
zero for even powers and four times the original source for odd
powers. Neither assertion permits dropping partial angular faces.

All these angular operations act separately on each wire Fourier
coefficient. They preserve the distinction between the original
\(K_T\) residue and the edge-deleting extreme coefficient. The
classical crossing and charge shifts at a wire escape consequently
do not, by themselves, cancel its quantum residue.

The charge shifts themselves now have an exact full-normal formula.
Let \(C_c\) be the original cosine coupon and put
\[
 D_c=[\eta^{-1}\sin(Nt)\sin(N(1-c)t)],\qquad \eta=(-1)^{N-1}.
\]
The brackets denote its full Hermite class in
\(\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2)\). Then
\[
 C_{c+k}=\eta^k(C_c+kD_c)\quad(k\in\mathbb Z),\qquad
 D_cD_d=0,\qquad C_{1+k}=\eta^k .
\]
The element \(D_c\) has zero physical values but generally nonzero
first normals. Thus reflecting a selected classical charge channel
does not justify changing the exact coupon from \(C_c\) to
\(C_{-c}=C_c+2D_c\).

The remaining boundary calculation must retain the partial
Gaussian defect and the \(\Theta,V_N\) side integrals, or replace
them by a proved identity for the entire original contraction.
The reflection and periodicity shortcuts supply no such identity.

## The exact energy on a saturated angular face

The [saturated-face calculation](research_saturated_angle_face_energy.md)
now treats the entire fixed-angle minimization, with arbitrary positive
charges. Let \(C\) be the vertices whose real angles are fixed at
\(s_v=\varepsilon_v\pi\), and delete those vertices and their incident
edges. Keep every surviving selected vertex, its original power and
charge, including any isolated vertex. Write \(r_C\) for the number
of deleted edges and \(G'\) for the remaining forest.

For a specified surviving real-angle vector \(s'\), extension to the
original closed angle body is possible exactly when the retained fiber
is feasible and
\[
 |\varepsilon_v n_v-2c_v|
 \le \sum_{\substack{e=vw\\w\notin C}}
                  (1-|s_w|/\pi)\qquad(v\in C).
\]
The removed incidence variables form independent interval sections.
Every removed edge has constant boundary energy \(\pi M_\infty\),
where \(M_\infty=4G_{\rm Cat}/\pi\). Consequently
\[
 e_{G,c}(\varepsilon\pi,s')
       =r_C\pi M_\infty+e_{G',c'}(s').
\]
Here \(e\) denotes the minimum energy over the incidence variables,
with the displayed real angles and the original charge rows fixed.

If the original problem has a positive central solution, its energy
minimum \(E_0\) is separated from the angle boundary by
\(\Delta_c>0\). The compatible retained action therefore satisfies
\[
 (m-r_C)M_\infty-e_{G',c'}(s')/\pi
 \le mM_\infty-E_0/\pi-\Delta_c/\pi.
\]
This comparison requires no large-power assumption. It applies to
the compatible fibers just described, not to every state of an
unconstrained deleted quantum source.

At a bounded real-period limit, every cut neighbor of \(C\) has
real angle zero. Writing \(\tau_v=\operatorname{sgn}\Im t_v\), the
original rows sharpen the compatibility inequality to
\(\varepsilon_vn_v-2c_v=\tau_v d_0(v)\), where \(d_0(v)\) counts
the cut edges. Such a neighbor need not be a complete cusp: its
imaginary angle can remain nonzero. Deletion also changes its real
period by the removed real returns. Neither change is suppressed.

## Joint angular translations and escaping wires

The [joint deck calculation](research_joint_angular_wire_deck_multiplier.md)
gives the exact multiplier of the canonical factorial halfwire:
\[
 B_N(x,t-2\pi)
  =\frac{w^N-\eta e^{-iNt}}{1-\eta e^{-iNt}w^N}B_N(x,t),
 \qquad w=e^{-2\pi ix},\quad\eta=(-1)^{N-1}.
\]
It composes at arbitrary degree, retaining every incidence and its
orientation. At prescribed wire ends, the multiplier splits into a
Gaussian factor with the effective exponent \(n+\sum\sigma_e\)
and rational corrections of order \(v_e^N\). A correction belongs
to the regular-alias ideal only when the remaining boundary
multiplier is identically one, not merely one at a stationary point.

The matched signs above restrict a possible resonance at unit charge:
there is exactly one cut edge, that edge escapes, the vertex has
negative height, and it must also have a saturated neighbor. Strict
feasibility excludes an isolated saturated star, even if only some
of its wires were proposed to escape.

The full relative source retains more than this multiplier. On an
admitted continuation chart, with polynomial coupons,
\[
 D^*\Omega_{\rm mix}-\Omega_{\rm mix}
  =(M_n-1)\Omega_{\rm car}
    +d(D^*\Theta_{\rm mix}-\Theta_{\rm mix}).
\]
The cardinal term still has the original \(K_T\) wire residue.
The primitive and wire-seam terms need not vanish on a partial
angular face. Thus effective-exponent cancellation does not remove
the original source current or identify it with the compatible
deleted fiber in the preceding section.

## A positive path from the inverse-period graph to real angles

The [radial height-contraction theorem](research_positive_radial_height_contraction.md)
verifies an additional geometric hypothesis needed by the earlier
vertical action identity. For an original positive configuration
\(t_v=s_v+ih_v\) with \(|s_v|\le\pi/2\), all original edge
tetrahedra remain positive under
\[
 t_v(\lambda)=s_v+i\lambda h_v,\qquad 0\le\lambda\le1.
\]
The heights and real angles may have arbitrary signs. Complete
outside vertices stay complete, and all logarithmic markings remain
on their canonical branches.

The proof rewrites the exact edge positivity condition as a
hyperbolic-cosine polynomial. When its cross term is negative,
division by \(\cosh((|h_v|+|h_w|)\lambda)\) leaves a
nonincreasing function, so positivity at \(\lambda=1\) implies
positivity throughout the contraction. The cases of zero real
angles reduce directly to monotonicity of \(\tanh^2\).

At an inverse-period point \(P(s+ih)=u-\pi i c\), let
\(J=\partial P/\partial t\) and
\(g(\lambda)=\Re\Phi_c(s+i\lambda h)\). Then
\[
 g(\lambda)-g(1)=
 \frac1\pi\int_\lambda^1(r-\lambda)
 h^{\mathsf T}\Re J(s+irh)h\,dr.
\]
This is strictly positive for \(h\ne0\) and \(\lambda<1\).
Compact positive families give uniform upper and lower quadratic
bounds for this increase.

This is an ascending path to the real projection. It neither
decreases the already identified real-rim excess nor supplies a
completed dual cycle. Original residue poles, endpoint faces and
wire seams still have to be treated in the quantum integral.
No assertion is made that every short filling lies in the stated
real-angle sector.

The result is adopted at

## Exact one-sided charge families with the same unit-charge value

The [finite charge-polarization note](research_polarized_charge_heat_source.md)
constructs two entire charge coupons in the original spectral algebra.
At each double node \(c_a=-2\cos\tau_a\), with its positive physical
angle \(\tau_a\), define the class \(L_N\) by
\[
 L_N(c_a)=\tau_a,\qquad L_N'(c_a)=\frac1{2\sin\tau_a}.
\]
Its value at the odd simple node is zero. Its square is exactly the
original squared-angle class, including the first normals. Therefore
\[
 Q_{N,\pm}(\chi)=\exp_{\mathcal A_N}
                         (\pm iN(1-\chi)L_N)
\]
satisfies
\[
 \tfrac12(Q_{N,+}+Q_{N,-})=\mathcal C_{N,\chi},
 \qquad Q_{N,\pm}(1)=1.
\]
Inserting either coupon retains the original trace and recovers
the original source exactly at unit charge. The charge reflection
\(\chi\mapsto2-\chi\) exchanges the two families rather than
forcing either one to have zero derivative at that endpoint.

Each polarized source has the same carrier-normalized heat equation
in the filling powers and the same exact Gaussian evolution. Its
finite charge space contains one sign of the Fourier frequencies,
with the linear factors required by repeated roots. Extracting that
space from the cosine family is a projection of the whole charge
function; it cannot be applied to a local asymptotic expansion as
though it were a fixed-order derivative.

The original positive-angle nodal cycle gives an exact contour
formula for this polarization, including the odd simple-node term.
A literal exponential on the full symmetric angular contour instead
averages back to the cosine coupon. These are different sources away
from unit charge. The polarized small-charge initializer and its
central and outer connector estimates remain to be proved for this
finite-coupon construction.

## An initialized contour polarization

The [pattern-adapted contour construction](research_pattern_adapted_polarized_heat_initializer.md)
supplies a different polarized family with a proved initializer.
First expand the actual source by the subset \(S\) of physical
rows outside the central angular interval. For each such summand,
freeze the contour heights at its own reduced small-charge saddle.
Replace only the retained horizontal cosine by one of its two
exponentials. Keep the vertical integrals and removed physical
rows, including every first normal, unchanged.

The sign average of these families is the original entire cosine
source. Every sign choice has exactly the original value when all
charges equal one. The fixed contours also give the exact
carrier-removed heat equation and Gaussian evolution; no moving
endpoint term is omitted.

For the fixed same-index graphs of the small-charge theorem, with
complete outside data and arbitrary fixed real powers, the all-plus
family has the actual holomorphic expansion
\[
 \mathfrak Z_{N,+}
   =2^m N^{3(m-e)/2}A_\Gamma(\chi)e^{NS(\chi)}
                              (1+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-1}))
\]
on a complex neighborhood of any specified small positive base
charge. Here \(m\) is the number of selected vertices, \(e\) the
number of kernel edges, and \(A_\Gamma\) is the original nonzero
small-charge amplitude. Every other sign choice has a strict
exponential gap there. Freezing heights separately for each
removed subset is essential: a single common height would not
justify importing the archived reduced-source estimates.

These are prescribed contour families, not the finite polarized
coupons of the preceding section. Their global charge growth also
contains \(H_*|1-\Re\chi|\), where \(H_*\) is the largest frozen
height. The local heat theorem applies with this cost included in
both its tail slope and its excess constant.

This removes the charge-reflection obstruction to a one-branch
continuation argument for an actually initialized family. It does
not show that the certified initial classical angles reach every
unit-charge target, or that the necessary global tail bounds
survive that continuation. Those remain the substantive missing
steps toward arbitrary short partial fillings.

## Exact changes of height and local source recentering

The [height-current theorem](research_polarized_height_current_transport.md)
now calculates the difference between two frozen contour choices,
rather than treating their unit-charge equality as a continuation
argument. In one coordinate, changing the height of the horizontal
exponential together with its retained cosine vertical integral gives
an explicit endpoint current. Its charge factor is
\(\sin(N(1-\chi)(a\pm ih))\), with the original midpoint kernel
\(-\eta/(4\cosh^2(Nh/2))\). Both endpoint evaluations of the
original spectral spectator remain.

For real \(0\le\chi\le1\), the coupon/kernel part is bounded by
\[
 \min\{1,N|1-\chi|\sqrt{a^2+h^2}\}\,e^{-N\chi h}.
\]
This is the same exponential envelope as the previous vertical
current. The exact formula assembles across the removed-row
patterns and retains their first normals.

Consequently sufficiently close height tables near a certified
small-charge table differ by
\[
 O\!\left(N^p\|\mathbf h-\widehat{\mathbf h}\|_1
                      e^{N(\Re S-\gamma)}\right),\qquad\gamma>0,
\]
uniformly on a common complex charge neighborhood, with complete
outside data. All asymptotic coefficients, including the nonzero
leading one, are unchanged. This proves local recentering of the
initialized source.

At the full midpoint \(a=\pi\), zero power and integral
\(N(1-\chi)\) give an additional exact cancellation, coefficientwise
for ordinary spectral spectators. Its charge derivative is generally
nonzero. This periodic lattice identity does not replace the missing
complex continuation estimate, and the full midpoint is not silently
substituted for the initialized truncated cutoff.

The current vanishes at unit charge. Approaching that endpoint at
distance \(O(N^{-1})\) gives no automatic exponential improvement.
A global recentering argument still needs a boundary-current gap
beyond the known small-charge region.

## The full positive charge cube for zero-power components

The [zero-power charge-cube theorem](research_zero_power_charge_cube_positivity.md)
sharpens the earlier sufficient degree condition for the original
positive subdivision. Let the selected vertices form a connected
proper subtree, set their crossing powers to zero, keep outside
angles complete, and suppose every original selected degree is at
least three. Then the original positive primitive solution exists
uniquely for every \(0<c_v\le1\), except when the selected component
is exactly two adjacent trivalent vertices and both charges are one.

The proof minimizes the actual convex height potential
\[
 \mathcal L_{\mathbf c}(H)
       =\sum_{e=vw}V(H_v,H_w)-\sum_v c_vH_v.
\]
Its coercivity and local strict convexity give a unique finite
positive minimizer throughout the cube. If an edge were saturated,
it would contribute \(\pi/2\) to each endpoint's angular row.
Writing \(r_v=\sinh(H_v/2)\), the remaining incidences give
\[
 \arctan r_v\le\frac{\pi(c_v-1/2)}{d_v-1}\le\frac\pi4,
 \qquad
 \arctan r_w\le\frac{\pi(c_w-1/2)}{d_w-1}\le\frac\pi4.
\]
Saturation also requires \(r_vr_w\ge1\). Equality is therefore
forced throughout: both degrees are three, both charges are one,
both \(r\)'s equal one, and neither vertex has another selected
neighbor. This proves the classification without enumerating
tangle words.

Every regular endpoint is connected analytically to completeness
by its radial charge path. Compact subsets of the positive charge
cube avoiding the exceptional corner stay in the positive domain.
No uniform assertion is made for arbitrary partially zero-charge
faces, which can change the effective selected components.

At unit charge the stated degree condition is also necessary,
since every original return has imaginary part strictly between
\(-\pi/2\) and \(\pi/2\). The exceptional pair has internal
\(q=0\); this is a failure of the original positive subdivision,
not a claim of nonhyperbolicity. The broader zero-power knot
family was already handled by the separate Newton/Conway
construction. The new result supplies its positive charge
geometry, not a charged quantum continuation theorem.

## Quantitative reconstruction from the full charge lattice

The [finite reconstruction theorem](research_finite_charge_quantitative_reconstruction.md)
recovers the canonical polarized source from the original cosine
source at \(N\) lattice charges in each selected coordinate. The
first derivatives at repeated spectral roots are retained. They
appear as the linear factors in
\[
 F_\sigma(y)=
 \sum_{a<\lfloor N/2\rfloor}(u_a+yv_a)
       e^{\sigma i\pi(N-1-2a)y}
       +\mathbf1_{N\ {\rm odd}}u_*,
 \qquad y=1-\chi.
\]
The exact charge reflection determines a second sample block from
the first. A finite Fourier transform then recovers both coefficients
of every linear factor.

If the errors in the original \(N\) cosine samples are at most
\(\delta_N\), the reconstructed polarized function satisfies
\[
 |\Delta F_\sigma(y)|
 \le N(1+2|y|)\delta_N
          e^{\pi(N-1)(-\sigma\Im y)_+}.
\]
The corresponding tensor estimate holds for any fixed number of
selected vertices, with the product of the polynomial factors and
the sum of the directional exponential costs. Thus real
reconstruction has polynomial cost, while complex reconstruction
has an explicit cost that cannot in general be removed.

This is useful only when the whole sample block has a uniform
error estimate at the required exponential scale. The known
small-charge interval does not supply that block; extrapolation
from such a short interval can have exponential cost even in the
exact finite source space. Nor does this theorem identify the
contour-polarized family with the canonical one away from lattice
charges. Their difference can vanish at every lattice sample
without belonging to the finite charge space.

## A full lattice-source estimate on a substantial charge range

The [charged high-sector theorem](research_zero_power_half_charge_high_gap.md)
settles the preceding divided-difference estimate on the lower half
of the charge cube. Let the selected vertices form any fixed
connected proper subtree, with all crossing powers zero and original
degrees at least three. For every lattice tuple
\(1\le J_v\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), put \(\chi_v=J_v/N\).
Then the original full source and its all-low part differ by
\[
 \sup_{\mathbf u\ {\rm real}}
 |Z_N(\boldsymbol\chi;\mathbf u)-Z_N^{\rm low}(\boldsymbol\chi;\mathbf u)|
 \le C N^p
       \exp\{N[M(\boldsymbol\chi)-\gamma]\},
 \qquad
 \gamma=\frac{4G}{\pi}-\log3>\frac{31}{990}.
\]
The constants are uniform over this entire nonzero lattice block,
at both level parities. High boundary indices are included.

Here \(M(\boldsymbol\chi)\) is the minimum of the original height
functional \(\sum_e V(H_v,H_w)-\sum_v\chi_vH_v\), and \(G\) is
Catalan's constant. The proof first contracts each high factor by
its exact divided-difference formula. Its coefficients have absolute
value at most two; its charge coupon contributes only a physical
value of modulus at most one. The remaining low factors have a
joint positive Laurent majorant.

For a high-edge matching \(A\), this majorant deletes exactly the
edges in \(A\) and makes their selected endpoints complete and
untraced. Every other edge remains, including edges joining two
different matched pairs. If \(M_A^{\rm cut}\) is the corresponding
minimum, evaluating the original variational problem with those
endpoint charges set to zero gives
\[
 M(\boldsymbol\chi)-M_A^{\rm cut}(\boldsymbol\chi)
 \ge |A|\frac{4G}{\pi}
       -\sum_{v\in T_A}\chi_vH_v(\boldsymbol\chi).
\]
The height bound \(H_v\le\log3\) for \(\chi_v\le1/2\) proves
the gap. Thus this argument controls the actual charged trace
without assuming its Newton coefficients are nonnegative.

If every original selected degree is at least twelve, the same
argument covers the whole nonzero lattice block \(1\le J_v\le N\).
Its uniform gap is
\[
 \gamma=\frac{4G}{\pi}
             -4\operatorname{arsinh}(2-\sqrt3)>\frac4{99}.
\]
The estimate remains uniform when some charges approach zero at
the lattice scale. At every surviving cut vertex the minimizing
height is bounded below by \(c\chi_v\ge c/N\), so the exact
Fourier denominators stay controlled.

On compact subsets of the interior charge cube where this gap
holds, the written all-low contour proof now gives a nonzero
asymptotic for the original full source. Its phase is the marked
geometric action and its leading coefficient is positive at
complete outside angles. The factor \(2^{-|S|}\) from the selected
cosine branches is retained.

This last asymptotic is asserted at lattice charges. A uniform
low-source formula at the charge endpoints, and the required
complex-charge reconstruction and signed-filling estimates, remain
separate tasks. In particular this theorem does not yet add a
knot family to the frozen volume theorem or settle finite exceptions.

## Stability of the high-index gap near unit charge

The [near-unit charge theorem](research_near_unit_charged_high_sector_gap.md)
provides a second charge region for every fixed zero-power subtree
whose unit-charge minimizing geometry is regular. There are
\(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) such that, uniformly over all lattice
tuples \(1-\varepsilon\le J_v/N\le1\),
\[
 \sup_{\mathbf u\ {\rm real}}
 |Z_{N,\mathbf c}(\mathbf u)-Z^{\rm low}_{N,\mathbf c}(\mathbf u)|
       \le CN^A e^{N(M(\mathbf1)-\delta)}.
\]
Since \(M(\mathbf c)\ge M(\mathbf1)\) for \(\mathbf c\le\mathbf1\),
this is also a strict gap below the charged geometric action.
Both level parities, all high boundary indices, and a fixed complex
boundary strip with every fixed derivative are covered.

The exact coupon \(T_{N-J}(-z/2)\) has Newton degree \(k=N-J\).
For \(k<\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), its Newton coefficients have absolute
value at most \(2N\). Full Frobenius duality therefore expresses
the charged trace as a polynomially bounded combination of the
original product coefficients with outputs \(D,D-1,\ldots,D-k\),
where \(D=N-1\). This retains the derivative data at repeated roots.

The proof keeps each vertex's final binary product before relaxing
its output. The resulting positive comparison has the same shared
edge labels and a continuous action on nested compact polytopes.
At output \(D\) the old internal and boundary high-index estimates
give a strict gap. Compactness preserves that gap when all outputs
are sufficiently close to \(D\). No positivity of the charged trace,
or concavity of the enlarged high-boundary envelope, is assumed.

The adopted charge-cube classification makes the regularity
hypothesis explicit: among connected proper zero-power subtrees
with original degrees at least three, only the selected adjacent
trivalent pair fails it at unit charge. This does not extend the
new estimate through that pair's degenerate corner.

The lower-half and near-unit estimates are separate regions.
For small original degrees they may leave a middle charge range
uncovered. The degree-at-least-twelve result above controls the
high terms throughout the nonzero charge grid. It still needs a
uniform analysis of the low terms near charge zero and charge one.
Near one the Fourier companion can have the same exponential
scale; near zero the selected Gaussian coefficient tends to zero.
Neither contribution may be discarded in assembling the full
sample block. Subsequent complex reconstruction must also meet
its explicit error requirement; interior relative errors alone
do not imply that requirement.

## Uniform source asymptotics at the nonzero zero-charge endpoint

The [zero-charge transition theorem](research_zero_charge_uniform_low_source.md)
now controls the all-low source uniformly for every lattice tuple
\(1\le J_v\le c_*N\), for each fixed \(c_*<1\). It permits some
charges to tend to zero while others remain in the interior. With
\(\chi_v=J_v/N\) and \(p=3(|\partial S|-1)/2\), the formula is
\[
 Z_N^{\rm low}(\boldsymbol\chi;\mathbf u)
 =N^{-p}\Bigl(\prod_v\chi_v\Bigr)e^{NW(\boldsymbol\chi,\mathbf u)}
       \bigl(\beta(\boldsymbol\chi,\mathbf u)+O(N^{-1})\bigr).
\]
The coefficient \(\beta\) extends across the zero-charge faces and
is a nonzero holomorphic function of the ordinary boundary variables
near completeness. The relative error is uniform down to \(J_v=1\).

The vanishing factor is forced by the exact antisymmetric Fourier
differences in the original trace. Fixed contours adapted to each
zero face produce holomorphic interpolants odd in its zero
coordinates. Dividing their normalized remainder by those
coordinates preserves the \(O(N^{-1})\) bound. These interpolants
agree with the actual principal contribution on its charge lattice;
they are not identified with the off-lattice cosine source.

Higher Fourier aliases have a fixed action gap even when the
minimizing heights tend to zero. The proof increases one height by
a fixed small amount in a coordinate where the alias has an
additional charge. Its linear penalty beats the quadratic change
in the original stationary action.

At the completely zero corner the theorem gives the explicit
\(J_v=O(\sqrt N)\) transition. Combining it with the adopted high
gap proves the same nonzero asymptotic for the full original
source on the entire nonzero lower-half lattice block. Exact
charge zero is excluded: there the principal difference vanishes,
and the other aliases supply the trace. Uniform exponential
sampling errors and off-lattice continuation are not asserted.

## Retaining the Fourier companions through unit charge

The [unit-charge companion theorem](research_unit_charge_companion_uniformity.md)
controls every regular unit-charge face, including sequences
\(J_v=N-O(1)\). For each coordinate near one, both effective
charges \(c_v\) and \(2-c_v\) remain in the leading sum. They have
the same geometric continuation near the regular unit minimum,
and each has a positive leading Gaussian coefficient at complete
outside angles.

Keeping these finitely many companions gives a uniform nonzero
leading factor on a fixed complex boundary neighborhood. The
stationary derivative
\(\partial_{\lambda_v}W=-it_v^*\) has strictly negative real part
there. Thus reflected contributions are bounded relative to the
unreflected exponential. Their positive sum at completeness and
Cauchy estimates give a lower bound on a common smaller complex
neighborhood, independent of the level and the endpoint distances.

The formula includes the original trace normal weights and both
parities. Every fixed inverse-level order has a uniform remainder.
The adopted near-unit high gap transfers it to the full source
near a regular unit tuple; the degree-twelve high bound also
applies to its mixed interior/unit-coordinate sets.

This theorem keeps its nonendpoint coordinates a fixed distance
from zero. The preceding zero-charge theorem keeps all coordinates
a fixed distance from one. Their separate statements therefore
do not yet give a uniform theorem at simultaneous zero/unit
corners. That assembly must retain both the vanishing zero-charge
factors and the unit-charge companion sums. Fixed-order
remainders also remain distinct from exponentially accurate
reconstruction errors.

## Exponentially accurate errors on the full charge grid

The [growing-order remainder proof](research_full_charge_grid_exponential_remainder.md)
strengthens the preceding zero-power source theorem. It has the same
scope: a fixed connected proper selected subtree, original selected
degrees at least twelve, and every nonzero charge \(J_v/N\) with
\(1\le J_v\le N\). It retains both level parities, all mixed endpoint
faces, the finite companion sum, and ordinary outside spectral data.
For expansion order \(L\le aN\), its normalized remainder satisfies
\[
 |\mathcal R_{N,L}|
 \le C^{L+1}L!N^{-L}+Ce^{-\delta N}.
\]
Choosing \(L\) to be a sufficiently small fixed multiple of \(N\)
gives a relative error \(O(e^{-\kappa N})\), with \(\kappa>0\).

The proof obtains factorial coefficient bounds from the exact
midpoint factorial formula, controls the growing-degree tails of
the joint wire and angular Gaussian integral, and divides by the
vanishing charge factors on fixed complex neighborhoods of the
zero faces. The original higher Fourier aliases and high Newton
terms retain their separate exponential gaps. Thus the estimate
concerns the actual finite source, rather than a formal expansion.

The positive error rate depends on the analytic neighborhood
radii and the contour gaps. It has not been shown to exceed the
loss between the complete action and a proposed filled action.
On the entire sample array the absolute error can still be as
large as a polynomial times
\(\exp\{N(|E_S|M_\infty-\kappa)\}\).
The exact complex reconstruction also has its previously stated
directional exponential cost. Neither the asymptotic of the
reconstructed approximation nor arbitrary short-filling coverage
follows from this remainder estimate.

 \le C_{a,b}N^{2+2a+2b}.

This has zero exponential rate. In contrast, taking absolute values
before summing the low Newton indices can give a positive rate.

The proof identifies every physical kernel row with the already
proved Racah polynomial whose roots lie strictly above two. Its
normalized value is at most one on the short interval from the
largest physical root to two, and the same root product controls

high radical is restored with its own polynomial bound. Cauchy
and polynomial derivative estimates retain all first normals and
every fixed mixed derivative, at both parities.

\[
 \big|\phi_N((\partial_w^aK_N)(2,z)A(z))\big|
 \le C_a N^{5+2a}\|A\|_{\rm H},

where the seminorm retains the spectator's physical values,
first normals at double roots, and odd simple value. The spectator
has not been estimated or replaced. A separate fixed small-height
continuation gives an upper exponential rate tending to zero as
the endpoint and other angular heights tend to zero.

## The endpoint current as an exact sum of smaller sources

The [full-period current formula](research_full_period_current_charge_convolution.md)
keeps the original trace at every vertex not put on a vertical side
of the contour. If \(L_v=H_v+V_v\) denotes the full trace, its lower
horizontal integral, and its paired vertical integral, respectively,
the exact identity is
\[
 \prod_{v\in S}L_v
 =\prod_{v\in S}H_v+
 \sum_{\varnothing\ne C\subseteq S}(-1)^{|C|+1}
       \left(\prod_{v\in C}V_v\right)
       \left(\prod_{w\in S\setminus C}L_w\right).
\]
Each vertical integration evaluates the removed color at
\(2\cosh h_v\). The incident kernels are multiplied at each common
surviving vertex before any further trace is taken. Edges between
removed vertices, all crossing scalars, and every first normal remain
in the formula.

Expanding each such polynomial product in Chebyshev polynomials gives
an exact finite convolution in the surviving charge variables.
Consequently the current is bounded by actual smaller charged sources,
with their remaining powers and traces intact. It is no longer
bounded merely by an absolute norm of an unfilled spectator.

There is a uniform version with endpoint heights
\(H_v=\alpha_v/N\), \(0<\alpha_v\le\alpha_0<\pi\). The endpoint
operator then costs only a fixed power of \(N\):
\[
 |I_{C,N}|
 \le C N^{2(e_C+b_C)+q_C}\mathcal M_{C,N}.
\]
Here \(e_C\) counts edges inside \(C\), \(b_C\) counts edges leaving
\(C\), \(q_C\) counts surviving selected vertices incident to \(C\),
and \(\mathcal M_{C,N}\) is the explicitly specified maximum of the
actual smaller sources at the shifted charges. Fixed outside
derivatives cost further powers of \(N\). This estimate uses the
shrinking root disk directly; it does not substitute a varying
height into a fixed-height asymptotic.

The shifted sources still have to be controlled coherently. Even one
endpoint kernel has nonzero coefficients of order \(N^{-2}\) at
charges \(1/N\) and \(2-1/N\) when the original charge is one.
Thus no locality in charge, same-charge face bound, or contributing
geometric coefficient follows from this reduction alone.

## Folding the remaining charges without losing the normal terms

The [shared endpoint-coupon reduction](research_endpoint_coupon_half_band_folding.md)
improves the preceding convolution. At each surviving vertex it
interpolates the values of the entire product of incident endpoint
kernels, including the original charge factor. The interpolating
polynomial has degree at most
\(J=\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor\). Its Chebyshev expansion therefore
uses only the original charges \(1-k/N\), \(0\le k\le J\).
Their coefficient norm is \(O(N)\), independently of the number of
cut incidences. Repeating the reduction keeps these traced charges
in the same interval \([1-J/N,1]\).

The interpolant agrees with the physical values but need not agree
with their first derivatives. The difference belongs to the
square-zero ideal of the original physical algebra. Its prescribed
trace is an explicit sum of physical evaluations, with total
coefficient norm \(O(N^3)\). This is an equality of the full trace,
not a replacement of the derivative data by values.

The graph formula retains a single shared color at every evaluated
vertex. In particular, edges between two evaluated vertices remain
present, as do all powers at the remaining traced vertices. The
result is an exact polynomial-cost reduction to smaller sources
with upper-half charges and specified physical boundary colors.
It removes the previous growth of the charge range with cut valence.

The original high Newton contribution has additional phase structure:
its physical coefficient is
\(\eta(-1)^a g_a\), with \(g_a>0\) for an individual real endpoint
kernel. Since
\[
 (-1)^a=i^{-(N-1)}e^{iN\tau_a/2},
\]
it carries a definite alternating Fourier character. Products of
low interpolants introduce a separate normal correction, which the
formula also retains. No positivity or action bound for their sum
has been inferred from the polynomial coefficient estimates.
Controlling this coherent sum remains necessary for arbitrary
short fillings.

## An explicit amplitude for the endpoint's alternating normal sum

The [endpoint character calculation](research_endpoint_radical_half_character_amplitude.md)
now resolves the coefficients of the original high Newton endpoint
coupon near the complete physical color. Write
\(w=2\cosh(\alpha/N)\), \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\), and
\(c_a=-2\cos\tau_a\) for the original double roots. Its prescribed
trace is exactly
\[
 \phi_N(B^{\rm high}_{N,\alpha}f)
   =\eta\sum_a(-1)^a\gamma_{a,N}(\alpha)f(c_a).
\]
The spectator \(f\), including any crossing, remains in this formula.
The weights are positive for real \(\alpha\), while their alternating
signs are retained separately.

For \(0<\tau_a\le1/10\), these weights agree exactly with a finite
analytic interpolant \(\Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau_a)\). On
\(|\alpha|\le1,\ |\tau|\le1/5\), its leading profiles are
\[
 \Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle \frac{2\cosh(\alpha/2)}N\tan(\tau/2)
       +\frac{\sin\tau}{N}O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2}),&N\text{ even},\\[4pt]
 \displaystyle \frac{2\cosh(\alpha/2)}N
          \frac{\sin^2(\tau/2)}{\cos(\tau/2)}
       +\frac{\sin\tau\sin(\tau/2)}N O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2}),
                                      &N\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\]
All fixed derivatives are controlled on smaller domains. The
remaining analytic factors are nonzero. The proof starts from an
exact central sine-product normalization and sums the backward
Newton ratios only as far as a fixed linear cutoff. At the relevant
physical rows the later terms vanish exactly. In the complex domain
the retained ratios have a uniform geometric majorant.

The alternating character has an exact simple-pole sampling contour.
Its lower horizontal kernel is
\[
 \frac{e^{-iNt/2}}{1-\eta e^{-iNt}}
   =\sum_{j\ge0}\eta^j e^{-iN(j+1/2)t}.
\]
Thus the actual central normal contribution begins at effective
charge \(1/2\), with all higher modes retained. The formula also
retains the explicit vertical integral and its original midpoint
phase. The opposite parities have the correct reflection at zero;
the odd simple node contributes zero to this radical term.

This gives a concrete Fourier estimate to pursue for the actual
coefficients. It does not bound the vertical integral, the remaining
physical rows, or their combination with the low Newton term at the
filled action. The finite-exception theorem therefore remains open.
Earlier distinct-node observation notes already used half-charge
sampling; the new calculation concerns this endpoint coupon's
analytic weights and microscopic-height normalization.

## The amplitude on an explicit complex domain

The [general-domain extension](research_endpoint_radical_general_domain.md)
replaces the preceding small bidisk by a family of explicit domains.
For a fixed cutoff \(0<\delta<1/2\), put
\[
 \mathcal D_\delta
 =\{t:|\cos t-\cos(2\pi\delta)|<1+\cos(2\pi\delta)\}.
\]
On every compact subset, uniformly for bounded complex microscopic
endpoint parameter \(\alpha\), the normalized finite amplitude is
\[
 H_N^\delta(\alpha,t)=\sec^2(t/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2}),
\]
with all fixed derivative bounds and eventual nonvanishing. The exact
physical-row interpolation holds for any fixed window
\(0<\tau_a\le b<2\pi\delta\). A uniform amplitude estimate additionally
requires that window or its chosen complex contour to lie in the
stated domain.

The criterion comes from the exact maximum of the limiting backward
ratios. Writing \(z=\sin^2(t/2)\) and \(a=\sin^2(\pi\delta)\), that
maximum is
\[
 \max\left\{|z|,\frac{|z-a|}{1-a}\right\}.
\]
It is less than one precisely on \(\mathcal D_\delta\). In the
coordinate \(\zeta=e^{it}\), the same condition is a polynomial
inequality in \(\zeta\) and its complex conjugate. It therefore gives
an explicit condition to check on a proposed geometric contour.

For example, at \(\delta=1/8\) the entire closed rectangle
\[
 |\Re t|\le\pi/4,\qquad |\Im t|\le\log3
\]
lies strictly inside the domain. Thus the analytic estimate is
available well beyond the original small neighborhood. The
half-charge contour identity still includes its vertical integral,
all higher modes, and the unestimated remainder of the original
source. This extension is an amplitude-domain theorem; it supplies
no new assertion about contributing cycles or knot coverage.

## The controlled amplitude is an exact band of the original source

The [central-band source identity](research_endpoint_central_band_half_charge_source.md)
identifies the preceding analytic amplitude with an ordinary polynomial
factor of the original kernel. Set \(k_0=\lceil N/2\rceil\) and
\[
 B^{[L]}_{N,\alpha}(z)
   =\sum_{l=0}^{L}e_{k_0+l}(2\cosh(\alpha/N))e_{k_0+l}(z),
                 \qquad 0\le L\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor-1.
\]
At even levels this polynomial equals the original half-charge coupon
times \(\mathcal H_{N,L,\alpha}(z)\), with its exact scalar of order
\(N^{-2}\). At odd levels the charge factor is the difference of
the neighboring coupons at \(1/2+1/(2N)\) and \(1/2-1/(2N)\).
The identities hold before taking the physical quotient, so they
retain every required derivative.

Consequently the replacement can be made inside any coupled graph.
It keeps all remaining powers, traces, shared colors, incident
edges, and joint spectators. The odd difference uses the same
amplitude in its two terms and must be summed coherently.

The omitted high band contracts exactly to physical rows with
angles at least \((2L+3)\pi/N\) at even levels and
\((2L+4)\pi/N\) at odd levels. Its coefficient norm is
\(O(N^{5/2})\), multiplying the actual remaining traced sources.
Thus \(L=\lfloor\delta N\rfloor\) leaves an explicit macroscopic
physical-row tail. The construction is an exact source split,
not an uncontrolled replacement of an off-grid amplitude.

The low endpoint polynomial remains present. A comparison of the
central high contribution alone with a geometric action cannot
replace the cancellation between the low and high terms.

## Exponential cancellation between the low and central high endpoint terms

The [endpoint cancellation theorem](research_endpoint_low_high_exponential_cancellation.md)
now estimates the sum of these two parts, rather than either part
separately. Write \(w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N)\), let \(Q_N\) be
the monic polynomial whose roots are the distinct physical colors,
and put
\[
 P_N^\delta(\alpha,Z)
   =\sum_{j=0}^{\lceil N/2\rceil+\lfloor\delta N\rfloor}
          e_j(w_N(\alpha))e_j(Z),\qquad 0<\delta<1/2.
\]
Here \(P_N^\delta\) denotes a partial kernel, not the polynomial
defining the physical quotient. On each fixed compact subset of
\[
 \mathcal D_\delta\cap\{\operatorname{Im}t<0\},\qquad
 Z=-2\cos t,
\]
and uniformly for \(|\alpha|\le A<\pi\), the proved estimate is
\[
 \left|\frac{P_N^\delta(\alpha,Z(t))}{Q_N(Z(t))}\right|
      \le C e^{-\kappa N},\qquad \kappa>0.
\]
It holds at both parities. All fixed derivatives are controlled;
each derivative in the endpoint variable \(w\) costs at most a
factor \(N^2\).

The proof uses an exact finite difference equation. Division by
\(Q_N\) changes its leading multiplier to a function converging
to \(4\cot^2(t/2)\), which is nonzero on the stated domain.
The forcing is an explicitly bounded product of
\(\lfloor\delta N\rfloor\) factors of modulus less than one.
An a priori bound for the actual quotient comes from interpolation
of its physical values. Repeated Cauchy estimates on nested complex
domains then give the exponential bound. No formal series is used
to assert an exponentially small remainder.

For several endpoint factors at a shared vertex, the same argument
gives their product estimate while retaining the entire remaining
integrand. The exact central trace formula still contains its
vertical integral. The omitted high terms remain an explicit sum
over the original outer physical rows with their normal weights.

This is a quantitative improvement for a specified part of the
original source. It is not a bound for the complete invariant:
\(Q_N\) itself grows off the real interval, the effective Fourier
character is retained in the horizontal integral, and neither the
outer rows nor the vertical integral has been bounded at the filled
geometric action. The constant \(\kappa\) has not been compared
with the loss required by that action.

## A decay estimate for the omitted physical rows

The [outer-row estimate](research_endpoint_outer_row_decay.md) adds
an explicit angular penalty to the preceding exact decomposition.
For an endpoint parameter \(|\alpha|\le A<\pi\), the omitted-band
coefficient at the original physical angle
\(\tau_a=(N-1-2a)\pi/N\) satisfies
\[
 |\omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha)|
 \le C_A\min\left\{N^{3/2},
       N^4\sin^{2L+2}(\tau_a/2)\right\}.
\]
This holds at both parities and uniformly in the cutoff \(L\).
The proof uses the exact finite products for the normal weights.
On the physical grid their angular factor is bounded by
\(\sin^2(\tau_a/2)\); the remaining cosine ratios and microscopic
endpoint perturbations have only polynomial cost.

For \(L=\lfloor\delta N\rfloor\), the decay is exponential at
each fixed angle below \(\pi\). More explicitly,
\[
 |\omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha)|
   \le C_A N^4
       \exp\left[-\delta\pi^2(a+\tfrac12)^2/N\right].
\]
The weights therefore have an endpoint scale of order \(\sqrt N\).
This statement concerns the weights alone. Multiplying by the
remaining source can change the relevant scale and exponential rate.

For any fixed number of endpoint factors at a shared vertex, their
exact product rule retains the same estimate with a fixed multiplicative
constant. Applying this identity at several vertices gives a weighted
sum of actual remaining traces, with all shared colors and edges
retained. No estimate for those remaining traces at the filled
geometric action is supplied by the weight bound.

The note also rules out a proposed shortcut for the truncated
kernel. Its exact finite difference equation gives a lower bound
on the maximum of the quotient at three neighboring complex points.
For certain allowed heights \(H\ge\log3\), the forcing decays at
rate \(I_\delta(H)<H/2\). Consequently a uniform bound with rate
\(H/2\), which would cancel the growth of the distinct-node
polynomial, is false for this truncation. The obstruction is not
a lower bound at the center point alone. The remaining bands and
vertical integrals must be included in any stronger estimate.

## Physical endpoint rows are positive charge convolutions

The [physical-row transport theorem](research_physical_row_charge_transport.md)
now keeps the remaining state sum in the endpoint estimate. For an
original physical color \(c_a=2\cos((2a+1)\pi/N)\), write
\[
 F_{a,N}(z)=K_N(c_a,z),\qquad M_{a,N}=F_{a,N}(-2).
\]
All \(a\) roots of this degree-\(a\) polynomial lie above \(2\).
Factoring by those roots gives a symmetric finite probability law
on integers \(K_a\in[-a,a]\), with the exact identity
\[
 F_{a,N}(-2\cos t)=M_{a,N}\,\mathbb E(e^{iK_at}).
\]
It follows, including all physical first derivatives, that
\[
 F_{a,N}\mathcal C_{N,\chi}
       =M_{a,N}\,\mathbb E\mathcal C_{N,\chi-K_a/N}.
\]
This is a positive expansion of one specified kernel row. It does
not say that the remaining quantum source has nonnegative terms.

The coefficient mass has the explicit bound
\[
 M_{a,N}\le(a+1)
       \left[\frac{\pi^2e^4}{4}\left(\frac Na\right)^2\right]^a
       \quad(a\ge1),\qquad M_{0,N}=1.
\]
At a surviving vertex, multiply all incident physical rows before
using their convolution law. Their charge supports add, and every
other edge, crossing, insertion and full trace remains in the same
descendant source. Starting at unit charge, exact cosine reflection
folds these shifts to charges at or below one.

Consequently, rows \(a_v\le\varepsilon N\) cost only
\(O_G(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))\) in the exponential rate
and \(O_G(\varepsilon)\) in the charge labels. The theorem gives a
precise induction input: if the actual decorated descendant sources
have a uniform strict rate margin in the corresponding below-unit
lattice charge window, a sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\)
preserves half that margin after the original endpoint rows are
summed. A bound at unit charge alone does not supply this hypothesis.

The positive row mass also explains why the preceding Gaussian
weight estimate cannot simply be called a subexponential deletion
cost. At \(a/N=x>0\) near zero, even one complete outside incidence
has mass of rate at least \(2x\log(1/x)+O(x)\), whereas the actual
omitted-row penalty has rate
\(\pi\tan(\pi\delta)x^2+O(x^4)\). Their product can therefore grow
exponentially. A supplied geometric margin may absorb this cost;
otherwise the original row phases must be used. The exact integer
phase and all remaining contour terms are retained in the note.

## The geometric margin survives the below-unit charge shifts

The [closed-angle endpoint-window theorem](research_endpoint_window_closed_action_induction.md)
connects the physical-row transport to the original convex action.
Assume an original positive unit-charge solution with complete outside
angles. Let \(H_v=-\operatorname{Im}t_v^0>0\), and let \(\delta_0>0\)
be the boundary minimum of the energy after subtracting its supporting
affine function at that solution. For a nonempty removed set \(U\),
write \(Y=S\setminus U\).

At each surviving charge \(\mathbf c'\), maximize the deleted
angle action over all weak assignments satisfying its original
charge rows. Denote this closed variational rate by
\(M_U^{\mathrm{cl}}(\mathbf c')\). No positive deleted critical
point is needed, but the assignment set must be nonempty. For
\(\mathbf c'\in[1-r,1]^Y\), the proved comparison is
\[
 M_U^{\mathrm{cl}}(\mathbf c')\le M_G-\Delta_U(r),\qquad
 \Delta_U(r)=\frac{\delta_0}{\pi}
   +\sum_{v\in U}H_v\left(\frac{|n_v|}{2}-1\right)
   -r\sum_{w\in Y}H_w .
\]
It follows from the exact supporting-plane identity on the ambient
angle body. The comparison therefore extends the earlier
above-unit-charge result to the charges actually produced by the
new positive row law.

If all removed powers have absolute value at least two, one
strictly positive margin works on a fixed below-unit box and for
all such removed subsets of the fixed graph. If the surviving
powers also have absolute value at least two, every charge in
\((0,1]^Y\) has a weak assignment: set all incidences to zero
and \(s_w=2\pi c'_w/n_w\). This includes isolated survivors and
works for arbitrarily large fixed trees.

The quantum transfer has a precise remaining hypothesis. The actual
decorated descendant sources must have uniform upper bounds
\[
 |Z_{G_U,N}^{A_{N,\mathbf a}}(\mathbf c')|
     \le q_N e^{N M_U^{\mathrm{cl}}(\mathbf c')},
                 \qquad \log q_N=o(N),
\]
at every sampled charge. The spectator includes all retained
partial coupons and other insertions. A bound for an undecorated
source does not imply this one. Under this hypothesis, the
positive row law and its \(O(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))\)
mass cost prove that a sufficiently small fixed endpoint window
is exponentially below \(M_G\). No descendant lower bound or
nonzero leading coefficient is required for this implication.

This transfer explicitly requires nonempty sampled angle problems.
Replacing the rate of an empty global problem by zero is not a valid
general repair: an isolated power \(1\) or \(-1\) can have an empty
near-unit angle problem but a nonzero unit-modulus quantum trace.
Alongside a positive-rate component, that trace leaves the component's
rate intact although the global angle problem is empty. Such
descendants remain part of the finite-exception target. They cannot
be removed by imposing zero growth or vanishing.

## Terminal reductions retain small boundary polynomials

The [charged leaf reduction](research_low_degree_charged_leaf_reduction.md)
extends the original exact reductions at terminal powers \(0,1,-1\)
to the low-degree polynomials produced by nearby lattice charges.
Let \(P\) have ordinary degree \(k<\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), let \(T\)
be the original turn, and let \(R\) be the original crossing.
For \(\sigma=\pm1\), define
\[
 U_\sigma P=\kappa^\sigma T(R^{-\sigma}TP).
\]
Then
\[
 T(R^\sigma P)=R^{-\sigma}U_\sigma P,\qquad
 \deg U_\sigma P\le k,\qquad
 \|U_\sigma P\|_{\mathrm{New},1}
       \le2^k\|P\|_{\mathrm{New},1}.
\]
Thus eliminating a unit-power leaf changes its neighbor's power by
\(-\sigma\) and transfers a polynomial of the same degree. Every
other factor at the neighbor remains in its original trace. For a
free neighbor, the canonical representative is taken before any
ordinary boundary substitution.

A zero-power leaf instead gives an exact sum over the physical
colors \(c_a\), \(0\le a\le k\). Its neighbor's entire remaining
factor is evaluated at that same color; the other incident kernels
become their actual rows \(K_N(c_a,z)\). Two such zero leaves at one
traced neighbor annihilate the source because both transmitted
factors lie in the square-zero radical. Isolated zero and unit
components likewise have explicit trace formulas. These statements
apply to joint spectators coefficientwise, with their variable
dependence retained.

For the near-unit charge polynomial \(P=T_k(-z/2)\), conversion
of \(U_\sigma P\) to cosine coefficients costs at most
\[
 2N^3\exp\!\left\{
 N\left[\varepsilon\log2+
       2\varepsilon\log\frac{e}{2\varepsilon}\right]\right\},
 \qquad k\le\varepsilon N< N/2.
\]
It therefore introduces a rate tending to zero with the charge
window. A fixed positive window does not have a polynomial cost.
The transmitted degree adds to any polynomial already at the
neighbor; the restriction on total degree must be checked at every
subsequent reduction.

This supplies actual operations for some degenerate descendants,
without assuming that intermediate exteriors are hyperbolic or
assigning an arbitrary rate to an empty angle problem. It does not
bound arbitrary high-degree endpoint factors or the remaining
branching contractions.

remove a terminal power \(\pm1\) and adjust its neighbor's power;

\[

       e^{N\Phi_G(\varepsilon)}

This is a bound for arbitrary-size fixed forests with the stated
reduction order. It does not assert that every short component has
such an order. It also requires a closed source with controlled
local polynomials; full endpoint kernels of degree comparable to
\(N\) remain outside the theorem.

## The actual omitted rows now have a controlled complex continuation

The [analytic degree interpolation theorem](research_physical_row_analytic_degree_interpolation.md)
addresses a missing step in deforming the omitted physical-row sum.
The original row \(F_{j,N}(Z)=K_N(c_j,Z)\) had a proved growth rate
at integer \(j\). Substituting a complex degree into the full Newton
kernel can revive terms that vanish at those integers. The new
construction instead interpolates the actual rows with their proved
growth rate.

Fix \(0<a<b<1/2\), and keep the exterior spectral color in a bounded
closed subset of \(\operatorname{Re}Z<2\). There is a fixed complex
strip about \([a,b]\) and a holomorphic function
\(\mathfrak F_N(x,Z)\) such that
\[
 \mathfrak F_N(j/N,Z)=F_{j,N}(Z),\qquad
 N^{-C}e^{N\operatorname{Re}\Psi(x,Z)}
 \le|\mathfrak F_N(x,Z)|
 \le N^C e^{N\operatorname{Re}\Psi(x,Z)}.
\]
Here
\[
 \Psi(x,Z)=\int_0^x\log\lambda(u,Z)\,du,\qquad
 \lambda+\lambda^{-1}=2+(2-Z)\cot^2(\pi u),
\]
with the growing root and logarithm fixed by the original positive
row. Its normalization is the original edge action, with boundary
value zero at angle \(\pi\). Matching is an identity in \(Z\), so
every exterior spectral derivative is retained.

The proof first iterates the contracting Riccati recurrence for a
number of steps proportional to \(N\). An Euler--Maclaurin primitive
with truncation order proportional to \(N\) then interpolates the
row products with exponentially small nodal error. A finite sum of
Gaussian-localized sinc functions corrects that error exactly.
The localization bounds its cost throughout one fixed strip over
the whole interval. There is no need to match separate interpolants
at artificial subdivision boundaries.

The same construction applies to the actual omitted-row weight
\(\omega_{j,N,L}=\eta(-1)^j\gamma_{j,N}\), where
\(L=\lfloor\delta N\rfloor\), provided \(b<1/2-\delta\).
Its finite product sum is truncated before every original terminating
index, and the omitted part is bounded relative to that prefix.
The exact corrected interpolation \(\mathfrak G_N\) has rate
\[
 -J_\delta(x)
 =\int_0^\delta
     \log\left(1-\frac{\sin^2(\pi x)}{\cos^2(\pi u)}\right)\,du.
\]
Consequently a single omitted-row amplitude, including all its
incident physical rows, has an exact contour representation with
noncharacter growth bounded by
\[
 C N^C\exp\left\{N\operatorname{Re}
       \left[-J_\delta(x)+\sum_e\Psi(x,Z_e)\right]\right\}.
\]
The original alternating sign, crossing Gaussian, residue kernel,
and shared spectators remain in that integral.

This supplies the complex continuation needed to use the row
phases. It does not estimate the two outer connecting segments,
the endpoint \(x=0\), the terminating boundary \(x=1/2-\delta\),
or exterior colors approaching \(2\). Nor does its growth bound
by itself compare the resulting integral with the filled geometric
action or prove a nonzero contribution.

## Full endpoint data force a large periodic-strip norm

The [endpoint representative theorem](research_endpoint_periodic_hermite_strip_obstruction.md)
rules out one proposed way of estimating the retained full endpoint
factors. Put \(w_N=2\cosh(\alpha/N)\), with \(\alpha\) in a fixed
bounded real interval. Suppose an even periodic holomorphic function
\(h_N(t)\) agrees with \(K_N(w_N,-2\cos t)\) in every physical value
and every required first spectral derivative. On every fixed strip
of height \(H>0\), its norm must satisfy
\[
 \|h_N\|_H\ge c_{A,H}N^{-2}e^{NH}.
\]
This holds for any such periodic representative, including one
obtained by adding a holomorphic multiple of the spectral relation.

The proof applies the existing full-Hermite Fourier folding formula
to the actual top coefficient
\[
 b_{N-1}=\frac{e_{N-1}(w_N)}{N^2},
 \qquad |b_{N-1}|\ge c_A N^{-2}.
\]
The physical derivatives eliminate its low-frequency alias.
Fourier decay on a strip then forces the displayed lower bound,
at both parities. The odd simple node needs only its original
value; evenness supplies the zero angular derivative.

This is an obstruction to a global periodic norm estimate, not
to the desired scalar volume bound. Indeed the same kernel has
the exact bounded trace
\[
 \phi_N(K_N(w_N,z))=e_{N-1}(w_N)=O_A(1).
\]
It also does not obstruct the new interpolation in an interior
degree interval after a radical has consumed the normal.
Local or nonperiodic representatives retain boundary terms;
they cannot be substituted into a whole-period trace without
those terms.

## The full endpoint product has an exact relative contour

The [two-half-plane endpoint theorem](research_endpoint_two_half_plane_relative_source.md)
gives a constructive replacement for the unavailable moderate
periodic representative. At a traced vertex, multiply every
microscopic endpoint kernel first and take its full Hermite
remainder \(C_N\). Its Fourier coefficient sum is polynomially
bounded for any fixed incidence count and bounded complex microscopic
parameters. This reduction retains the values and first derivatives
before any contour is split.

Writing
\[
 C_N(-2\cos t)=\beta_0+
       \sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\beta_k(e^{-ikt}+e^{ikt}),
 \qquad z=e^{-it},
\]
the lower representative replaces \(z^{-k}\) by
\(2\eta z^{N-k}-z^{2N-k}\); the upper representative is its
reflection. Each separately preserves all physical jets and has
polynomial norm in its assigned half-plane. With
\[
 W_N=\frac{z^N}{(1-\eta z^N)^2},\qquad
 A_-=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\beta_k z^{N-k},\qquad A_+(t)=A_-(-t),
\]
the exact identities are
\[
 C_NW_N=C_-W_N+A_-=C_+W_N+A_+.
\]
The full trace rectangle therefore equals its lower exterior
integral with \(C_-\), its upper exterior integral with \(C_+\),
and the real interface integral with \(A_--A_+\).
All four vertical half-sides, the original crossing Gaussian,
and the shared spectator remain. The interface has no sampling
poles, but its continuous Fourier integrals include zero frequency;
it is not an automatically small remainder.

This construction uses the full endpoint product, so no artificial
Newton cutoff occurs in the final identity. It applies
coefficientwise and in tensor products of traced variables.
It does not reduce an ordinary free variable or estimate the
remaining spectator at the filled rate.
