## Composition from physical bounds and exact boundary windows

The [composition theorem](research_physical_window_short_contraction_class.md)
starts with actual incoming polynomials \(H_{a,N}\). Their values and
required first derivatives at every physical node obey
\[
 |\partial_C^b H_{a,N}(c_j)|
 \le \exp\{o(N)+N[M_a-\gamma_a(1-\cos\tau_j)]\}.
\]
Here \(c_j=-2\cos\tau_j\), \(0\le\tau_j<\pi\), and
\(b\) ranges over the multiplicity of that node. On a specified
central window these same data are supplied exactly by a holomorphic
function with logarithm \(NW_a(t)+o(N)\), where \(C=-2\cos t\).
There is no assumption about the canonical polynomial between the
remaining physical nodes.

For the outgoing function
\[
 H_{\mathrm{out},N}=T\!\left(R^p\prod_a H_{a,N}\right),
\]
the theorem gives explicit sufficient conditions on the known phases.
Their sum with the outgoing edge action must have strictly negative
real second derivative on the selected rectangle. The charged action
must have an interior stationary point on its lower horizontal side.
The two real endpoints and the bound on the untouched physical rows
must lie strictly below that stationary action. These hypotheses pay
both vertical sides, the entire Fourier denominator, and every
unselected physical row, including all derivative terms in the trace.

The conclusion is a physical bound of the same form, with a positive
outgoing Gaussian loss. Near the complete boundary color there is also
a holomorphic representative with exact physical values and first
derivatives and a nonzero Gaussian leading coefficient. Its domain
can shrink. At the next vertex the required contour must fit in that
domain or in a separately proved continuation.

At the final root, omit the outgoing edge and impose the corresponding
conditions on the sum of the incoming phases. The theorem then proves
a nonzero leading coefficient for
\[
 Z_N=\phi_N\!\left(R^p\prod_a H_{a,N}\right)
\]
along both level parities. This is the original scalar closing, not
only a norm estimate. The result proves finite-tree closure under
explicit input checks; it does not assert that hyperbolicity implies
those checks or identify a new scalar rate with manifold volume.

## A positive measure and an exact bound for the Ward correction

The [Ward measure theorem](research_positive_ward_measure_and_coherent_cauchy_tail.md)
uses
\[
 P_N(C)=2T_N(C/2)+2,\qquad
 d\mu_N(x)=
 \frac{N^3}{4\pi\sin(\pi/N)P_N(x)}
 \tanh\!\left(\frac N2\operatorname{arcosh}(x/2)\right)dx,
 \qquad x>2.
\]
This measure is positive and has finite moments through degree \(N-2\).
For the double physical nodes
\(c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N)\), put \(F_j(C)=K_N(c_j,C)\).
Their exact orthogonality is
\[
 \int F_jF_k\,d\mu_N
 =\frac{\delta_{jk}}
 {4\sin(\pi/N)\sin((2j+1)\pi/N)}.
\]
At odd level the remaining simple row has a divergent squared norm
and is not included in this identity. Its value is retained separately
in the original source and closing.

For any actual input \(A\), let \(H_A=\operatorname{can}(TA)\).
Its Ward representative has the form
\(\widehat H_A=Y_A+\widetilde Q_N L_A\), with
\[
 L_A(C)=4(-1)^{N-1}\sin(\pi/N)
       \sum_{j\ {\rm double}}\sin((2j+1)\pi/N)A(c_j)F_j(C).
\]
The theorem proves the exact Cauchy formula
\[
 \frac{\widehat H_A(C)-H_A(C)}{P_N(C)}
 =\frac1{N^2}\int_2^\infty\frac{L_A(x)}{x-C}\,d\mu_N(x).
\]
The quotient extends holomorphically through all physical nodes.
Orthogonality therefore gives, off the cut,
\[
 \left|\frac{\widehat H_A(C)-H_A(C)}{P_N(C)}\right|
 \le \frac1{N^2\operatorname{dist}(C,[2,\infty))}
       \sum_{j\ {\rm double}}\frac{|A(c_j)|}{|F_j(C)|}.
\]
Every zero of \(F_j\) lies on the cut, so these denominators are
nonzero. The bound also controls fixed derivatives with a polynomial
cost. For \(A=R^p\prod_aH_a\), every integer \(p\) is allowed and
\(|A(c_j)|=\prod_a|H_a(c_j)|\).

This is a bound for the complete correction, not separate bounds for
its two large Ward terms. The positive measure also gives an exact
Plancherel identity for \(L_A\). It does not make the original
two-source closing positive: that closing has a cut pairing with
matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&2Q_{\mathrm R}\end{smallmatrix}\right)\)
and determinant \(-1\), as well as the odd simple-node term.
Control of the remaining representative on a parent contour is still
necessary.

## Positive Cauchy remainders for every physical value row

The [row factorization](research_physical_rows_positive_ward_remainder.md)
uses the same positive measure and orthogonal polynomials. Write
\(m=\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\), and
\(h_j=\int F_j^2\,d\mu_N\). For a real input color \(c<2\), define
\[
 L_c(C)=\eta\sum_{j<m}\frac{F_j(c)F_j(C)}{h_j},
 \qquad K_c=\sum_{j<m}\frac{F_j(c)^2}{h_j},
\]
\[
 V_c(C)=\int_2^\infty
       \frac{L_c(x)^2(x-c)}{x-C}\,d\mu_N(x).
\]
The evaluation identity
\(\int L_cf\,d\mu_N=\eta f(c)\) for \(\deg f<m\) implies
that \(L_c\) is orthogonal to every polynomial of degree below
\(m-1\) for the positive measure \((x-c)d\mu_N\). Consequently
its \(m-1\) roots are simple and lie in \((2,\infty)\).
The Cauchy integral \(V_c\) is positive on the real interval
\((-\infty,2)\), has positive imaginary part in the upper half-plane,
and has no zero in \(\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus[2,\infty)\).
Its defining measure has infinite total mass at even levels, but
the Cauchy integral converges.

For the original free-color row \(A_c=K_N(c,\cdot)\), the exact
canonical turn and its Ward representative are
\[
 H_{A_c}(C)=\frac{\eta}{N^2}
                  \frac{P_N(C)-P_N(c)}{C-c},\qquad
 \widehat H_{A_c}(C)=
       \frac{P_N(C)V_c(C)/L_c(C)-\eta P_N(c)}{N^2(C-c)}.
\]
At every physical color \(c\), including the odd simple color \(-2\),
this gives
\[
 \widehat H_{A_c}
    =\frac{P_N V_c}{N^2(C-c)L_c},
 \qquad
 \frac{\widehat H_{A_c}}{TA_c}=\frac{\eta V_c}{L_c}.
\]
The last ratio extends to a holomorphic nonvanishing function on
\(\Omega\), is positive below \(2\), and equals one at \(C=c\).
Thus the zeros of the representative are exactly those of
\(P_N(C)/(C-c)\), with their original multiplicities.

For each fixed compact \(K\Subset\Omega\), the theorem proves
\[
 a_KN^{-2}\le \frac{|V_c(C)|}{K_c}\le b_K
       \qquad(C\in K)
\]
uniformly in the level and in every physical color. Positivity
prevents cancellation in the integral after a common rotation of
its integrand. The distance \(2-c\ge 4/N^2\) supplies the lower
bound. This controls the normalized remainder at subexponential
scale; it does not bound the exponential contributions of \(K_c\)
or \(1/L_c(C)\).

For complex input color, the quotient in the exact formula means
\[
 J_c(C)=\frac{V_c(C)}{L_c(C)}
       =\int_2^\infty L_c(x)\frac{x-c}{x-C}\,d\mu_N(x).
\]
This expression is polynomial in \(c\), and \(J_C(C)=\eta\)
removes the apparent pole on \(C=c\). At a double physical node,
differentiation gives the original normal row:
\[
 \widehat H_{G_j}(C)=\frac{P_N(C)}{N^2}
       \left.\partial_c\frac{J_c(C)}{C-c}\right|_{c=c_j}.
\]
No positivity of that derivative is asserted. The term involving
\(P_N(c)\) disappears together with its first derivative at a
double node. It cannot be omitted during a general continuation in
the input color; the two terms also cancel each other's diagonal
pole.

The unstripped ratio \(\widehat H_1/L_{c_0}\) is neither Herglotz
nor anti-Herglotz when \(N\ge3\). Its Pick kernel has at least
\(m-1\) negative squares, forced by its distinct double zeros.
This does not contradict positivity of \(V_c\), which is obtained
only after the explicit spectral divisor is separated.

## The action and derivative bounds of the physical Ward kernel

The [Christoffel–Darboux theorem](research_physical_ward_cd_action_and_normals.md)
determines the factors left explicit by the preceding result.
Put \(d=\lfloor N/2\rfloor-1\) and \(R_d=F_{d-1}/F_d\).
For \(d\ge1\), the original Jacobi recurrence gives
\[
 L_c(C)=\frac{\eta F_d(c)F_d(C)}{h_d}B_c(C),
 \qquad
 B_c(C)=1+b_d\frac{R_d(C)-R_d(c)}{C-c}.
\]
Here \(b_d>0\) is the last downward Jacobi coefficient.
The resolvent representation of \(R_d\) makes \(B_c\) one plus
a positive Cauchy transform for real \(c<2\). It has polynomial
upper bounds and a uniform positive lower bound on compact output
subsets of the slit plane, for all \(c\in[-2,c_0]\).
No recurrence beyond the ordinary physical-row range is used.

Write
\[
 \Psi(C)=\int_0^{1/2}
 2\operatorname{arsinh}
   \left(\frac{\sqrt{2-C}}2\cot(\pi s)\right)\,ds,
\]
with the branches fixed by positivity for real \(C<2\).
The existing row asymptotics, the exact symmetry
\(F_d(c_l)=F_l(c_d)\), and
\(\Psi_x(-2)=\Psi(2\cos(2\pi x))\) give, uniformly on the entire
real input interval,
\[
 \log K_c=2N\Psi(c)+O(\log N),\qquad
 \Log U_c(C)=N[\Psi(c)-\Psi(C)]+o_K(N).
\]
On compact subsets of \(\Re C<2\), the second error is
\(O_K(\log N)\). Fixed output derivatives obey the corresponding
estimates. The endpoint \(c_0\to2\) is handled by the symmetry
and a half-step estimate, rather than by applying a fixed-margin
asymptotic at a moving endpoint.

The same factorization and a Cauchy–Schwarz estimate in the positive
measure give
\[
 |\partial_c U_c(C)/U_c(C)|\le C_KN^5.
\]
For a double physical node this bounds the original normal row by
\[
 |\widehat H_{G_j}(C)|
 \le C_KN^5
       \left|\frac{P_N(C)}{N^2(C-c_j)^2}\right||U_{c_j}(C)|.
\]
The quotient involving \(P_N\) is a polynomial, including at
\(C=c_j\). A separate reverse-parameter identity shows that, for
fixed real \(C<2\), \(J_c(C)\) is a degree-\(\lfloor N/2\rfloor\)
orthogonal polynomial for \(d\mu(c)/(c-C)\). Its roots lie above
\(2\). This gives polynomial bounds on every fixed input derivative
and positivity of the stripped first-normal ratio when \(C\le c_j\).
It does not supply a general lower bound for the normal row.

The operator distinction remains essential. If
\(\widehat B(c,C)=\widehat H_{K_N(c,\cdot)}(C)\), then
\[
 \widehat T A(C)=\phi_c[\widehat B(c,C)(TA)(c)].
\]
Thus \(\widehat B\) represents Ward regularization of the identity
under the Frobenius pairing, rather than the original turn alone.
The actual \(TA\) coefficients, their normals, and the free-color
\(P_N(c)\) term still enter a general contraction. No hypothesis
of the arbitrary short-component composition theorem has been
removed by treating the action difference as a change of gauge.

## Polynomial propagation of both Ward channels

The [full crossing theorem](research_ward_cut_jet_crossing_propagation.md)
uses the same positive cut measure and the same polynomials \(F_j\)
as the Ward correction theorem. Write
\[
 h_j=\int |F_j|^2\,d\mu_N
 =\frac1{4\sin(\pi/N)\sin((2j+1)\pi/N)},\qquad
 a_j=4-c_j^2.
\]
The two degree-less-than-\(\lfloor N/2\rfloor\) polynomials associated
with an actual input \(A\) are \(L_A\) and \(Y_A^0\); the latter
omits the separately retained odd simple term from \(Y_A\).
They satisfy
\[
 Y_A^0=\mathscr D_NL_A+J_A,\qquad
 J_A=(-1)^{N-1}\sum_{j\ {\rm double}}
       (a_jA'(c_j)-c_jA(c_j))F_j.
\]
Here \(\mathscr D_NF_j=R_j/c'(0)\), where \(R_j\) is the derivative
of the original common-shift Jacobi determinant. This identity
retains every input derivative.

The main estimate is
\[
 \|\mathscr D_N\|_{L^2(\mu_N)\to L^2(\mu_N)}
 \le CN^3(1+\log N).
\]
The proof uses the exact original \(G_jG_k\) Gram matrix. A contour
around the Ward cut identifies the Hermitian part of
\(\mathscr D_N\) with a compressed multiplication form for the real
part of the Ward function. Degree preservation makes the connection
triangular, so that identity determines its entries. The required
logarithmic moments are \(O(\log N)\). The proof treats the even final
row directly; its first moment diverges and is never used.

Let \(\mathscr U_pF_j=R(c_j)^pF_j\), an exact unitary operator for
the cut measure, and
\[
 \mathscr VF_j=\frac{i(N-1-2j)}{4\sin(\pi/N)}F_j.
\]
For every integer \(p\), the original multiplication crossing obeys
\[
 \binom{Y_{R^pA}^0}{L_{R^pA}}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \mathscr U_p&
 [\mathscr D_N,\mathscr U_p]+p\mathscr U_p\mathscr V\\
 0&\mathscr U_p
 \end{pmatrix}
 \binom{Y_A^0}{L_A}.
\]
At odd levels \(A(-2)\) is multiplied by the original unit
\(R(-2)^p\). This gives a positive definite norm
\[
 \|A\|_{\rm cut}^2
 =\|Y_A^0\|_{\mu_N}^2+\|L_A\|_{\mu_N}^2
       +\mathbf1_{\rm odd}|A(-2)|^2
\]
on the full original algebra, with
\[
 \|R^{\pm p}A\|_{\rm cut}
 \le C\{1+N^3(1+\log N)+|p|N^2\}\|A\|_{\rm cut}.
\]
All physical values and derivatives can be recovered from these
coordinates. In particular, the original closing is
\[
 \phi_N(A)=Y_A^0(c_0)+\mathbf1_{\rm odd}A(-2),\qquad
 |\phi_N(A)|\le\sqrt5\,\|A\|_{\rm cut}.
\]
Its exact dual norm is \(2\) at even levels and
\(\sqrt{4\sin^2(\lfloor N/2\rfloor\pi/N)+1}\) at odd levels.

This removes the loss of normal information in the earlier positive
quotient. It does not remove cancellation in this specified linear
observation. In particular the theorem estimates multiplication by
\(R^p\), not the turn \(T\), and does not pay the exponential cost
of forming products. The next estimate must use the received
coefficients in the oscillatory kernel and its explicit normal
connection, rather than replacing them by an arbitrary norm bound.

## Positive tetrahedra do not protect every pointed projection

The [pointed-module counterexample](research_positive_tetrahedron_pointed_projection_zero.md)
tests the proposed inference from positive shapes and primitive
projector rank to a nonzero distinguished vector. It uses the literal
tetrahedron relation \((X+Y-1)p=0\), with
\[
 N=3,\quad R=e^{-2\pi i/3},\quad s^3=-R,\quad t=s^{-1},\qquad
 X=s\,\operatorname{diag}(1,R,R^2),\quad
 Ye_j=t\,e_{j+1\bmod3}.
\]
The central shape is \(z=-R=e^{i\pi/3}\), and all three central
triad shapes are the same positive regular shape. The specified
pointing is
\[
 p=\bigl(1,\,[s(1-sR)]^{-1},\,s(1-s)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Every coordinate is nonzero. Nevertheless, for \(U=XY\),
\[
 \Pi=\tfrac13(I+RU+R^2U^2),\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\Pi=1,\qquad \Pi p=0.
\]
Indeed \((1,R,R)\) is the left eigenrow of \(U\) at \(R^2\),
and its pairing with \(p\) vanishes after the exact substitution
\(s^3=-R\). The monomial exponent \((1,-1)\) in the
\((X,Y^{-1})\) lattice is primitive; its character has the
required central power. The proof also transports the pointing
and projector through all independent cube-root choices.

The limitation of this test matters. Its minimal local incidence
counts are \((2,0,1)\), with angle sum \(\pi\), not \(2\pi\).
No actual face pairing completes an interior edge in this example.
It therefore disproves the unrestricted projection inference, not
nonvanishing for a geometrically glued knot triangulation, and not
an asymptotic volume statement. It tells us which additional
geometric constraints a projected-generator argument must use.
The existing finite-branch, cut-norm and contour calculations have
not supplied that global argument.

## A genuine positive edge preserves the pointed tensor

The [single-edge theorem](research_single_edge_pointed_nonvanishing.md)
retains the actual incidence counts
\((a_j,b_j,c_j)\in\{0,1,2\}^3\) in every tetrahedron, its positive
angles \(\alpha_j+\beta_j+\gamma_j=\pi\), and the edge equation
\[
 \sum_j(a_j\alpha_j+b_j\beta_j+c_j\gamma_j)=2\pi.
\]
Faces are paired in distinct occurrences, and the nonzero edge row is
primitive in the integral tetrahedron lattice. Let \(p_j\) be the
original pointed tetrahedron generators, \(U_e^N=1\) the normalized
original Weyl edge operator, and \(\chi\) any prescribed compatible
character. Then, at every \(N\ge2\),
\[
 \Pi_{e,\chi}\bigotimes_jp_j\ne0,\qquad
 \Pi_{e,\chi}=\frac1N\sum_{h=0}^{N-1}\chi^{-h}U_e^h.
\]

The proof has three parts. The incidence counts classify each local
factor, after exact pointed shape-order changes, as central, a first
or second power of a shape axis, or a mixed monomial \(XY\).
The first shape power has all \(N\) spectral characters on its
pointed vector; the second has \(N/\gcd(N,2)\).
In the mixed eigenbasis, the original tetrahedron equation gives
an invertible three-term recurrence. Two zero coordinates cannot
have cyclic distance one or two. Its support therefore has at least
\(\lceil2N/3\rceil\) characters, strictly more than \(N/2\).

Supports of distinct local factors add in \(\mathbb Z/N\).
Different local eigenvalue tuples belong to a finer direct sum,
so tuples with the same global character cannot cancel each other.
Two supports whose sizes sum to more than \(N\) cover every character.
Primitivity leaves only one potential exception: a single mixed
tetrahedron with every other incidence factor central.

The positive angle equation forces that exception to consist of a
mixed \((2,0,1)\) tetrahedron and exactly one \((1,1,1)\)
tetrahedron. Their face incidences cannot be paired. The mixed
tetrahedron has face counts \(\{1,1,2,2\}\). The other three marked
edges form either a star, giving \(\{0,2,2,2\}\), or a triangle,
giving \(\{3,1,1,1\}\). Thus there would be five count-two faces
in the first case or five count-one faces in the second. Face
pairing requires each count to occur an even number of times.
Tetrahedra with no occurrence of the edge add only zero-count faces
and cannot fix this contradiction.

This proves nonvanishing for the prescribed character using the full
\(2\pi\) geometry and incidence, rather than selecting a favorable
root lift. If the independent edge lattice has rank one, this is
already the full edge projection. In larger rank, complete marginal
supports do not determine joint support. Local restrictions of
different commuting global edge operators need not commute within
one tetrahedron, and the first reduction destroys the product form
used in the proof. The remaining task is simultaneous pointed
nonvanishing, followed by the original-source and scalar comparison.
No level-uniform quantitative lower bound or volume limit is inferred.

## Simultaneous edge projection under an incidence condition

The [joint character theorem](research_joint_edge_character_bootstrap.md)
uses the same original tensor \(p=\bigotimes_t p_t\) and the full
commuting edge projectors. Let \(E\) be the primitive edge lattice,
\(G=\operatorname{Hom}(E,\mathbb Z/N)\) its character group, and
\(v_\chi=\Pi_\chi p\). For each tetrahedron \(t\), define
\(\alpha_t,\beta_t\in G\) by the commutators of its operators \(X_t,Y_t\)
with the normalized edge operators. The original tetrahedron relation
gives the exact coupled equations
\[
 v_\chi=X_tv_{\chi-\alpha_t}+Y_tv_{\chi-\beta_t},
 \qquad
 v_\chi=Y_t^{-1}v_{\chi+\beta_t}
        -Y_t^{-1}X_tv_{\chi-\alpha_t+\beta_t}.
\]
These equations retain the components after all edge projections;
they do not assume that those components are product vectors.

Starting with \(H=0\), enlarge \(H\) by both \(\alpha_t,\beta_t\)
whenever one of \(\alpha_t,\beta_t,\alpha_t-\beta_t\) already belongs
to \(H\). The set of zero components is invariant under each enlarged
subgroup. For example, if \(\alpha_t\in H\) and \(v_\chi=0\), the first
equation and invertibility of \(Y_t\) force
\(v_{\chi-\beta_t}=0\). The second equation proves the rule for
\(\alpha_t-\beta_t\in H\). Finite character orders supply the reverse
translations.

Write \(H_\infty\) for the resulting subgroup. If \(e\) is one genuine
edge satisfying the positive single-edge theorem and
\[
 \ker\!\left(G\longrightarrow\mathbb Z/N,\ \chi\longmapsto\chi(e)\right)
 \subset H_\infty,
\]
then every \(v_\chi\) is nonzero. Otherwise a zero component would force
all components with the same value on \(e\) to vanish; their sum is a
single-edge projection already proved nonzero. The same construction
in \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,\mathbb Z)\), with no saturation, gives an
all-level sufficient condition. At composite levels the required
statement is a subgroup inclusion, not a comparison of dimensions.

The criterion also describes precisely where this argument stops.
In \(G/H_\infty\), every tetrahedron has either three equal classes
\(0,\overline\alpha_t,\overline\beta_t\), or three pairwise distinct
classes. For a genuine edge with local opposite-pair counts
\((a,b,c)\), the shifts evaluate to \(c-b\) and \(c-a\).
Thus a first integral step requires two opposite pairs with the same
multiset of global edge labels. If every tetrahedron has six distinct
global edge labels, no step starts at any level. This is a limitation
of the criterion, not a vanishing result.

No new knot family is claimed from this test. The complete geometric
incidence theorem below now proves that its hypothesis fails at every
\(N\ge3\) when the edge rank is at least two. Passing to another complete
positive geometric triangulation does not remove this obstruction.
Even where the abstract test succeeds, it gives neither a uniform lower
bound nor the comparison with Kashaev's prescribed scalar. The
finite-exception theorem and the frozen long-twist theorem are unchanged.

## Complete geometry rules out the initial propagation step

The [geometric incidence theorem](research_complete_positive_no_axis_incidence.md)
applies to an oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic manifold with
torus cusps and a positive geometric ideal triangulation. It does not
assume a global lift of the holonomy to \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C)\).
The proof works directly with its canonical action on
\((\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\})/\{\pm1\}\).

A complete peripheral subgroup is conjugate to translations and fixes
a nonzero vector class in this space. Choose one at each cusp and extend
equivariantly to all lifted ideal vertices. If \(v_i,v_j\) are endpoints
of a lifted edge, then
\[
 d_e=\det(v_i,v_j)^2
\]
is independent of endpoint signs, edge reversal and deck translation.
It is therefore a number attached to the global unoriented edge, and
is nonzero by nondegeneracy of the incident tetrahedra.

In a positively ordered tetrahedron let \(A,B,C\) be the multisets of
global edge labels in the pairs \(01/23,02/13,03/12\), and let
\(D_A,D_B,D_C\) be their products of \(d_e\). Direct determinant
calculation gives
\[
 z^2=D_B/D_C,\qquad
 (z')^2=D_C/D_A,\qquad
 (z'')^2=D_A/D_B.
\]
If any two multisets coincide, one of the three shapes has square one.
That is impossible for a positive tetrahedron. Completeness is the
reason the vector classes and the \(d_e\) descend; no such conclusion
is asserted for arbitrary incomplete peripheral holonomy.

This applies exactly to the attempted character propagation. Its first
step requires one of \(c-b,c-a,a-b\) to vanish modulo \(N\) on every
genuine edge row. The coordinates lie in \([-2,2]\), so at \(N\ge3\)
this means equality of two integral opposite-pair multisets. Hence
\(H_\infty=0\). For edge rank at least two it cannot contain the kernel
of evaluation on a primitive genuine edge. At level two, accidental
parity equalities remain possible. Rank-one edge reduction is already
covered by the single-edge theorem and needs no propagation.

There is also a useful description of local rank one. The three
distinct multiplicity vectors have coordinate sum two and are
collinear, so they must be
\[
 2\mathbf e,\quad \mathbf e+\mathbf f,\quad 2\mathbf f.
\]
In the corresponding cyclic shape ordering the determinant equations
give \([z(1-z)]^2=1\). The negative choice has only real roots; positivity
forces \(z=e^{i\pi/3}\). Thus every such tetrahedron is regular and
contributes angle \(\pi\) to each of its two global edge labels.

If two of these tetrahedra share a global edge, they exhaust its
\(2\pi\) angle. Every face of either contains that label, so all their
face partners belong to the same two tetrahedra. In a connected
triangulation they are the whole triangulation. Consequently, for
\(T>2\), the pairs of labels belonging to rank-one tetrahedra are
disjoint. Euler characteristic gives \(T\) global edges for a
torus-cusped ideal triangulation. There are therefore at most
\(\lfloor T/2\rfloor\) rank-one tetrahedra and at least
\(\lceil T/2\rceil\) with rank-two local edge constraints.

This rules out the proposed initial shape-axis elimination even after
changing to another complete positive geometric triangulation. It
does not imply that the joint projected vector vanishes. It directs
further work toward simultaneous non-axis relations and the original
source comparison, rather than seeking a geometric justification of
the propagation condition.

## Finite covers can remove every initial cancellation loop

The [finite-cover theorem](research_complete_positive_cover_neighbor_matching.md)
examines the exact relations obtained immediately from one zero
component \(v_\chi=\Pi_\chi p=0\). With
\(v(\delta)=v_{\chi+\delta}\), the tetrahedron equation gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 v(-\alpha_t)&=-X_t^{-1}Y_t\,v(-\beta_t),\\
 v(\alpha_t)&=Y_t\,v(\alpha_t-\beta_t),\\
 v(\beta_t)&=X_t\,v(\beta_t-\alpha_t).
 \end{split}
\]
These are invertible transports between six neighboring labels. A loop
would impose a fixed-vector equation. Two loops with noncommuting
holonomies could force another component to vanish. The question is
whether complete geometry supplies such loops.

The theorem gives a general obstruction to that inference. Let \(D\)
be the maximum edge valence of a finite complete positive geometric
triangulation. A finite normal cover can be chosen so that every dual
ball of radius \(2D\) in the universal triangulation injects on its
tetrahedra. The proof includes finite separation of the deck group:
its faithful adjoint holonomy has entries in a finitely generated
complex ring, and reduction to a suitable finite field separates any
prescribed finite collection of nonidentity elements.

The bounded-ball condition first makes the six edges of every cover
tetrahedron globally distinct. If two signed opposite-pair differences
were equal, their four supporting edges would have the same labels.
One common edge puts lifts of both tetrahedra in a single bounded
edge star. Injectivity forces the other three edge identifications to
use the same lifts. The four actual edges determine the same four
ideal vertices and hence the same convex geometric tetrahedron.
Thus all indexed signed differences are distinct. Their coefficients
are \(0,\pm1\), so they remain distinct modulo every \(N\ge3\).

Consequently the displayed initial relations form exactly three
disjoint edges per tetrahedron. There are no initial holonomy loops
in this cover, including no pair with a nontrivial commutator.
This does not rule out propagation from further zero components or
relations involving several tetrahedra. It does not assert that the
cover is an \(S^3\) knot exterior, that its edge lattice is primitive,
or that a selected quantum state descends to the original manifold.
It establishes only the stated geometric limitation of the immediate
loop mechanism.

## The threading identity holds before closing the tangle

The [open threading theorem](research_open_star_even_threading_scalar.md)
uses the original same-colored tangle tensor in a ball, with arbitrary
balanced Casimir coupons and its literal marked cap. Every boundary
index is fixed before the internal sums are taken. For a closed
auxiliary loop \(\gamma\) inside the ball, define its relative linking
number \(\ell\) by intersecting a Seifert surface with the oriented core
strands. The surface avoids the coupon boxes. Balanced orientation
makes this integer independent of the surface and of the continuations
inside the boxes; it agrees with any oriented closure outside the ball.
That closure is used only to interpret the integer.

At \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(U=M^{2N}\), the exact entrywise formula is
\[
 \mathcal K^{S,C_{2N}(\gamma)}_{\mathbf b;\mathbf a}(M)
   =(U^\ell+U^{-\ell})
       \mathcal K^S_{\mathbf b;\mathbf a}(M).
\]
The proof first applies the integral Weyl-module sequences to the
closed auxiliary trace, retaining all core indices. They replace the
Chebyshev threading by the sum of two one-dimensional colors of
weights \(2N\) and \(-2N\). Each crossing with either color is a
scalar times the flip on the entire core space. The scalar on the
actual dual is reciprocal to that on the primal color. These scalars
commute with every original coupon, including the marked cap; no
intertwining property of that cap is assumed. Removing the auxiliary
loop gives \(U^\ell\) and \(U^{-\ell}\), respectively.

For \(\ell=0\), the difference
\(\mathcal K^{S,C_{2N}(\gamma)}-2\mathcal K^S\) and all its
fixed-\(q\) meridian derivatives vanish entrywise. An exterior
contraction cannot turn them into a nonzero source coefficient.
This closes a proposed way of obtaining the source extension merely
by retaining the boundary indices. It does not exclude a relative
construction with varying central character or a geometric saddle
in the original sum. The required scalar lower bound remains open.

## A specified first normal before specializing the root

The [Weyl-normal calculation](research_even_threading_weyl_normal_source.md)
fixes a regular family in which the core is the genuine integral color
\(D_{N-1}(q)\), with \(M=-q^N\). It retains the original source
pivots and prescribes the marked matrix by
\(\mathsf D(q)=g(q)^{-1}e\), so that
\(\operatorname{Tr}(g(q)\mathsf D(q)T)=\operatorname{Tr}(eT)\)
before specialization. Root-only simplifications of the marked cap
are not differentiated as though they were generic identities.

For the entrywise vanishing defect
\(\Delta_\gamma(q)=\mathcal K_\gamma(q)-2\mathcal K(q)\), this gives
the exact normal
\[
 J_{\gamma,N}
  =\left.\frac{\Delta_\gamma(q)}{1-q^{2N}}\right|_{q=e^{\pi i/N}}
  =-\frac1{2N}
       \left.q\frac{d\Delta_\gamma}{dq}\right|_{q=e^{\pi i/N}}.
\]
It is a finite sum with one differentiated crossing, turn, coupon,
pivot, mark or framing factor in each term. The proof gives every
crossing coefficient, including the divided-power terms which vanish
at the root but can contribute to its derivative. At a crossing with
the \(N\)-dimensional core those high terms are absent; they cannot be
invoked as a nonzero contribution there.

An exterior contraction differentiates by the product rule. Its
derivative multiplies the zero root defect, so the resulting normal
is exactly the root exterior applied to \(J_{\gamma,N}\). This
localizes the calculation without discarding the source adapters.
It does not make the result independent of the prescribed off-root
family, nor does it establish a nonzero global coefficient.

## The first annular normal is nonzero, but a turn can kill its closing

The [pair normal theorem](research_even_threading_first_normal_casimir_radical.md)
computes the preceding derivative for a zero-framed annulus around two
complete strands. Its off-root family is fixed: genuine integral Weyl
colors, the literal annular braid, one auxiliary closing cut, and the
original source pivot \(K^{1-N}\). The genuine dual identifies an
opposite-oriented pair without extending the root-only dual parameter
formula off root.

Let \(q_0=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(D=N-1\), and let \(\Omega(q)\) be the pair
Casimir. Its generic minimal polynomial is
\[
 P(q,C)=\prod_{j=0}^{D}
   \bigl(C-q^{2N-1-2j}-q^{-2N+1+2j}\bigr).
\]
The exact normal of the even threading minus twice the identity is
\[
 J_N=r_N(\Omega(q_0)),\qquad
 r_N(C)=-\frac2N
       \left.q\frac{\partial P(q,C)}{\partial q}\right|_{q_0}.
\]
The proof keeps the auxiliary-pivot correction. Its derivative is a
trace with one \(H\) insertion. At the root the two one-dimensional
auxiliary colors have weights \(2N\) and \(-2N\), giving cancelling
contributions on the complete pair. Thus the stated source normal
agrees with the computed ordinary-pivot normal for this fixed annulus.

At each double node \(c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N)\), \(j<D-j\), the value
of \(r_N\) is zero and its derivative is
\[
 r_N'(c_j)=
  \frac{4N(D-2j)}{q_0^{2j+1}-q_0^{-2j-1}}\ne0.
\]
The odd-level simple value is zero as well. Therefore \(J_N^2=0\),
but \(J_N\ne0\), and multiplication by \(r_N\) generates every
double-node radical channel from its corresponding value channel.
Scalar eigenvalue derivatives miss this: the colliding eigenvalues
have second-order zeros, while their divided difference has only a
first-order zero.

This is also an already specified original crossing operator. With
\(R=\kappa u_N(\Omega(q_0))\), \(\kappa=q_0^{D^2/2}\), the full
crossing values and derivatives give
\[
 r_N=4(1-u_N^{2N}),\qquad
 J_N=4(I-(-1)^{N-1}R^{2N}).
\]
The power \(2N\) depends on the level; this is an operator identity,
not a theorem for a new fixed filling. Existing full-normal crossing
estimates already apply to its multiplication.

The original closing detects it exactly:
\[
 \phi(r_N)=-\frac{4i(-1)^{N-1}N^2}{\sin(\pi/N)}.
\]
More generally \(\phi(r_N f)\), after a common phase is removed,
is a sum of \(f(c_j)\) with strictly positive weights. That does not
replace the original closing by a positive norm: the resulting
quadratic form vanishes on \(r_N\) itself, although \(\phi(r_N)\ne0\).
There is an equally explicit obstruction to transporting this local
nonzero value. For the original unscaled quarter-turn \(\mathcal R\),
the literal cup and cap contraction gives
\[
 \phi(\mathcal R f)=f(c_0),\qquad
 \phi(\mathcal R(r_Nf))=0
       \quad\text{for every }f\in\mathcal A_N.
\]
Thus a permissible exterior can annihilate the entire locally detected
family. The needed theorem must control the specific exterior and
geometric contribution belonging to the knot. This calculation does
not supply that global lower bound or enlarge the proved knot class.

## A positive center does not regularize every feasible fiber

The [fiber example](research_strict_feasible_nonregular_angle_fiber.md)
uses two adjacent selected vertices of degree three, each with two
complete outside neighbors. Both selected charges are one. At fixed
real angles \(s_v=s_w=0\), the incidence constraints and energy are
independent of the signed filling powers. There is a strict feasible
assignment, with every selected incidence equal to \(-\pi/3\).
Nevertheless the unique minimizing fiber has
\[
 g_{v,vw}=g_{w,vw}=-\pi/2,\qquad
 g_{a,e}=-\pi/4
 \quad\hbox{on the four selected outside incidences}.
\]
The internal edge is degenerate. This same fiber persists for every
power pair.

For equal sufficiently large positive signed powers \(\nu\), the
unchanged filling equations also have an interior positive solution
\[
 t_v=t_w=\frac{2\pi}{\nu}
              -\frac{6\pi i}{\nu^2}+O(\nu^{-3}).
\]
This follows by applying the holomorphic implicit-function theorem
to the original equations at completeness. Hence the domain of regular
fiber minima is a nonempty proper subset of the strict feasible
real-angle domain even when a positive filling center exists.
The compact low-energy collars around that center remain valid;
extending them requires control of the degenerate fibers.

## Compactness and the precise convex extension at a corner

The [strict-base compactness note](research_strict_base_fiber_compactness_and_corner_subgradients.md)
proves uniqueness and continuity of the closed fiber minimum throughout
the strict feasible real-angle domain \(D\), including where it is
degenerate. For \(K\Subset D\), an explicit continuous strict section
has a common square-coordinate margin \(\alpha>0\). Write
\(E_{\max}=4mG_{\rm Cat}\), where \(m\) counts the original included
edges, and \(n_{\max}=\max_v|n_v|\). Every supporting period/height pair
for the marginal energy satisfies
\[
 \|h\|_1\le \frac{E_{\max}}{\alpha},\qquad
 \|u\|_1\le \frac{(1+n_{\max})E_{\max}}{\alpha}.
\]
The two tests perturb the strict section, first at fixed real angles
and then at fixed charge rows. This cancels the unwanted multiplier
term in each supporting inequality. The bounds therefore apply to
all convex supporting pairs, including at nonregular fibers.

At regular points these are the actual geometric heights and real
periods. Their returns and square covectors are also bounded.
Every genuine nonregular limit over \(K\) is consequently finite and
has corner factors. If the positive filling center exists, the
original energy gap puts these limits strictly below its classical
action. The regular compact-base consequence could already be
obtained from convex difference quotients and the earlier bounded-period
theorem; the explicit bounds for all supporting pairs are the refinement.

At a signed square corner, let \(U,W\) be the two covector components
after multiplying by the signs of their corresponding corner coordinates.
The exact convex subdifferential is
\[
 U>0,\qquad W>0,\qquad \sinh(2U)\sinh(2W)\ge1.
\]
Limits of genuine interior geometric gradients require equality.
The strict-inequality region therefore cannot be interpreted as a
continuation of the original geometric branch merely because its
vectors support the convex energy.

## Isolating the interior wire and retaining its boundary currents

The [fixed-wire collar theorem](research_fixed_wire_collar_source_reduction.md)
splits the original half-wire source into an interior segment and
two local endpoint pieces. Write
\[
 a=-\frac1{2N},\qquad b=\frac{N-1}{2N},
 \qquad \mathcal R x=2b-x.
\]
Here \(F_N\) is the original product of two factorial kernels and
\(I_N\) is its established inverse representative. For fixed small
\(\delta,H>0\), set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 M_{H,\delta}&=N\int_{[a+\delta,b-\delta]+iH}F_N(y)\,dy,\\
 R_{H,\delta}&=N\int_{[a,a+\delta]+iH}F_N(y)\,dy
                 +N\int_{[a,b+\delta]-iH}I_N(x)\,dx.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The extension of the inverse segment has positive orientation:
reflection of the removed right collar reverses both its
parameter direction and its differential.

The original source and \(M_{H,\delta}+R_{H,\delta}\) have
the same complete physical values and spectral normals. On common
even slit domains their difference belongs to the ideal generated
by the endpoint polynomials \(P_N\). Complete original traces
annihilate that difference, including all shared product derivatives.
The enlarged upper slit starts at real coordinate \(-2\pi\delta\);
the lower slit ends at \(2\pi\delta\). Their detours and winding
remain part of the contour.

For joint chains the precise statement is Stokes' identity
\[
 \int_\Gamma(\Omega_{\rm old}-\Omega_{\rm new})
       =\int_{\partial_{\rm extra}\Gamma}\Theta.
\]
Every term of the angular primitive \(\Theta\) contains every wire
differential. Its pullback is therefore zero on any coordinate-fixed
wire face, even when the angular variables vary along that face.
It also vanishes on the designated angular endpoint faces.
Additional angular, slit or exterior faces generally remain.
Bare equality of the two bulk integrals requires their total
primitive current to vanish. This corrects the stronger bare-equality
wording in the preceding draft.

On a buffered angular compact, the two endpoint pieces satisfy
\[
 |R_{\rm left}|+|R_{\rm inverse}|
 \le C N^B
 \exp\!\left\{N\left[
 8\pi\epsilon+
 C_{\mathcal K}(\epsilon+\delta)
                 (1+|\log(\epsilon+\delta)|)\right]\right\},
 \qquad \epsilon\le H\le2\epsilon.
\]
The polynomial exponent is chosen before the small fixed
\(\epsilon,\delta\). Polynomial-distance pole detours, grouped
collision residues, endpoint connectors and fixed derivatives obey
the same rate with polynomial losses. This rate tends to zero with
the two small parameters. It is a bound for these factors, not
for their product with the remaining graph.

The original action at the interior segment's fixed endpoints still
matters for any proposed contour through its saddle. Smallness of
the replaced endpoint pieces does not bound the unchanged interior
connecting paths or the extra-face current. Both remain part of
the global noncancellation problem.

## Why separate absolute wire bounds cannot finish the proof

The [interior wire-barrier theorem](research_positive_wire_absolute_barrier.md)
disproves a proposed uniform absolute-contour estimate on the general
positive domain. It concerns the actual same-index factorial kernel,
with the endpoint angles fixed during the wire deformation.

For its original real envelope \(\mathcal B(y,t)\), put
\(z=\sin^2(\pi y)\) and \(A=\cos^2(t/2)\). At real
\(-\pi<t<\pi\), \(y=\xi+iH\), \(0<\xi<1/2\), \(H>0\),
\[
 \Im z>0,\qquad
 \partial_H\mathcal B(\xi+iH,t)
   =-\Arg\!\left(\frac{A-z}{z}\right)>0.
\]
The original branch puts that quotient in the lower half-plane.
Conjugation gives the same increase in \(|H|\). Thus the envelope
has its vertical minimum on the real wire.

Fix a small interval \(I\) about \(\xi=1/4\) and let
\(\beta=\min_I\mathcal B(\xi,0)>0\). As a fixed real angle
\(t_0\) approaches \(\pi\), the selected action
\(\psi(t_0,0)\) tends to zero and its selected saddle approaches
the left endpoint. Nevertheless
\[
 \mathcal B(\xi+iH,t_0)+\mathcal B(\xi+iH,0)\ge\beta
 \quad(\xi\in I,\ H\in\mathbb R).
\]
This strict excess persists on an open family of complex positive
pairs, including pairs with both imaginary angles negative.

At finite level, choose a vertical slab of width \(1/(20N)\) in
\(I\), separated from the five relevant real projections of the
factorial-zero, inverse-pole and integer lattices. The exact midpoint
estimates and reflection formula give, for every fixed height bound,
\[
 |F_N(y;t,u)|,\quad |I_N(\mathcal R_Ny;t,u)|
 \ \ge c_MN^{-2}e^{N(\Re\psi(t,u)+\gamma)}
\]
throughout that slab, with \(\gamma>0\). The slab can depend on the
level and parameters; its width and lower-bound constants are uniform
on the fixed positive family.

Every rectifiable path crossing the slab has total variation within
it at least its width, even if the path changes height or backtracks.
Its absolute integral, with the original multiplier \(N\), therefore
has the same excessive exponential rate. If a fixed cut divides the
original main path from a reflected inverse tail, concatenate the
main path with the reversed reflected tail. The concatenated path
still crosses the slab. The sum of their two absolute integrals
retains the lower bound, regardless of the cut.

This excludes simultaneous absolute bounds at the selected edge
rate for those pieces throughout the general positive domain.
It gives no lower bound for their signed sum, no estimate after
the original angular trace, and no contradiction to a volume identity.
The parameter family is not asserted to solve the integer filling
equations. It shows why the global method must use coherent
cancellation, coupled angular deformations, or an exact change of
source representative. The finite-factor theorem covers contours
with any fixed height bound, not heights diverging with \(N\).

## Complete inverse-half periods on common slit domains

The [slit-domain source comparison](research_inverse_half_slit_domain_source_comparison.md)
constructs the common angular domains required for exact full-trace
height comparison. For a lower wire at height \(-H\), its angular
poles lie on the two relative slits
\[
 [0,\pi)+2\pi iH,\qquad (-\pi,0]-2\pi iH.
\]
Remove them from \(|\Re t|<\pi\). The remaining domain is even,
connected and simply connected and contains the whole physical
real interval. Finite intersections for different heights retain
these properties. Fixed original reciprocal halfwires are
holomorphic there as well.

Finite Hermite interpolation in each endpoint now gives a global
decomposition of the difference between two representatives:
\[
 K_H(t,u)-K_{H'}(t,u)
       =P_N(-2\cos t)A(t,u)+P_N(-2\cos u)B(t,u),
\]
with jointly holomorphic even coefficients on the common product
domain. The construction retains the original odd simple node
and all repeated-root derivatives. No bound for these coefficients
is asserted.

For any fixed network, telescope this decomposition over the
traced variables. In each term one spectral polynomial cancels
its original trace kernel. The remaining integrand is odd and
holomorphic in that variable, with a path-independent primitive
vanishing at both symmetric endpoints. Its integral over the full
lower angular lens is therefore exactly zero. This proves equality
of the complete original periods for all specified height choices,
with crossings, charge coupons, shared variables and unreduced
free polynomial coefficients retained.

The proof applies on explicit slit domains even when a rectangular
domain would cross inverse poles. The lower lenses keep their
detours around the slit tips and their original physical winding.
On a patched geometric contour the primitive differences on
individual interface faces are still present. Only the complete
full-trace height difference has been canceled. The main-half
integrals and angular detours still need their source estimates.

## Uniform bounds for inverse-contour detours and connectors

The [inverse-contour theorem](research_inverse_half_strip_contour_bounds.md)
extends the additive regularization estimate from finitely many
horizontal segments to an entire thin wire band. Fix a compact angular
set, then an exponent \(C>2\), and finally a sufficiently small fixed
\(\epsilon>0\). At distance at least \(N^{-C}\) from the actual pole
lattices, every point of the band
\[
 a_N-O(N^{-C})\le\Re x\le b_N+O(N^{-C}),\qquad
 \epsilon-O(N^{-C})\le-\Im x\le2\epsilon+O(N^{-C})
\]
satisfies
\[
 |N I_N(x;t,u)|
 \le C_{\epsilon}N^B
 \exp\!\left\{N\left[8\pi\epsilon+
                 C_{\mathcal K}\epsilon(1+|\log\epsilon|)\right]\right\}.
\]
The exponent \(B\) is fixed independently of \(\epsilon\).
The proof uses the canonical factorial's two-sided midpoint estimate
and exact reflection. The latter costs only a power of \(N\) at the
allowed polynomial distance from a pole. The nonnegative real-wire
potential controls the remaining exponential rate.

There are four pole lattices, each with spacing \(1/N\). At scale
\(N^{-C}\), a connected cluster therefore contains at most four
centers. Detouring around their grouped disks produces bounded-length
paths with \(O(N)\) pieces. Integrating the same pointwise bound
controls these paths, the sum of the absolute grouped residues,
and both endpoint connectors. Grouping precedes taking residues at
a collision. Freezing each contour on a parameter neighborhood of
polynomial radius also gives all fixed parameter derivatives at a
polynomial cost.

For two admitted heights \(H_1<H_2\), the exact lower-half transition
is the difference of the left and right upward connectors plus the
retained grouped residues. Every one of these inverse terms has the
displayed small rate. For a fixed graph, products of finitely many
such terms have the sum of the rates and a polynomial prefactor.
The original crossing phases, angular traces and unchanged edge
factors remain spectators; this does not bound those factors.

The theorem retains the full relative descent
\(\Omega_i-\Omega_{\rm car}=d\Theta_i\). On admitted common domains,
\(J_{ij}=\Theta_j-\Theta_i\) has zero alternating triple-overlap sum.
Thus there is no additional unknown corner form. The main-half
contributions to \(\Theta_i\), however, have not been bounded.
Nor does this result supply the common even holomorphic domains
needed to make their integrated face terms vanish.

## An exact finite transformation retaining the independent derivatives

The [finite Sears source theorem](research_finite_sears_full_normal_source.md)
now gives a second local representation of the original edge kernel,
including the derivatives required at repeated spectral roots. It is a
finite identity with its cutoff term retained.

Put \(D=N-1\), \(\theta=\pi/N\), and
\(c(\alpha)=2\cos((2\alpha+1)\theta)\). Let \(G_N\) be the canonical
factorial, normalized by \(G_N(0)=1\) and
\(G_N(z+1)=2\sin(\pi(z+1)/N)G_N(z)\). Define
\[
 T_k(\alpha,\beta)=
 \frac{G_N(\alpha+\beta-k)^2}
 {G_N(\alpha-k)^2G_N(\beta-k)^2G_N(k)^2},
 \qquad S_M=\sum_{k=0}^M T_k.
\]
For a physical degree \(0\le j\le\lfloor D/2\rfloor\),
\[
 K_N(c(j),c(\beta))=S_j(j,\beta).
\]
The finite Sears transformation proves this equality with its full
scalar normalization. An explicit rational telescoper gives
\[
 A(\alpha)S_M(\alpha+1,\beta)
 +C(\alpha)S_M(\alpha-1,\beta)
 -[A(\alpha)+C(\alpha)+c(0)-c(\beta)]S_M(\alpha,\beta)
 =\mathcal H_{M+1}(\alpha,\beta),
\]
where \(A,C\) are the original row-recurrence coefficients and
\(\mathcal H_{M+1}\) is the displayed finite boundary flux in the note.
At \(\alpha=j\), a sufficiently extended regular cutoff makes this
flux vanish to second order in \(\alpha-j\). A cutoff ending exactly
at \(j\) does not permit the same inference: a denominator in the flux
can cancel the summand's double zero.

Differentiating the extended finite recurrence and using the exact
initial derivative
\[
 \left.\partial_\alpha T_0(\alpha,\beta)\right|_{\alpha=0}
       =2[g_N'(\beta)-g_N'(0)]
\]
proves the original normal normalization, where \(g_N=\log G_N\).
It is the independent spectral derivative of the source, not merely
the derivative of its terminating sampled values.

At a physical pair \((j,l)\), any cutoff with
\(\max(j,l)\le M\le j+l\) and \(M<N\) gives a jointly holomorphic
local representative. Its value, both first derivatives, and mixed
first derivative agree with those of \(K_N(c(\alpha),c(\beta))\)
whenever those derivatives are prescribed. Different such cutoffs
have identical full physical data. The odd simple node is handled
by local reflection before descending to the spectral variable;
there is no division by the derivative of \(c\) at that fold.
Products and subsequent original traces preserve these identities.

The local restriction is essential. For instance an excessive
summand near \((0,0)\) has the divisor
\(\alpha^2\beta^2/(\alpha+\beta)^2\), up to a holomorphic unit.
Separate vanishing does not make it jointly holomorphic. Nor does
agreement of physical derivatives bound a transition away from
the physical grid. The result supplies an exact representation and
finite transport equation; the global contour and endpoint estimates
remain to be proved.

## The actual bulk Fourier coefficients have a moderate analytic amplitude

The [single-endpoint Fourier theorem](research_endpoint_bulk_fourier_interpolation.md)
provides an exact formula for another part of the boundary problem.
Write the original ordinary kernel as
\[
 K_N(2\cosh(\alpha/N),-2\cos t)
   =b_{0,N}+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}b_{k,N}(e^{-ikt}+e^{ikt}),
 \qquad \alpha\in\mathbb R.
\]
For \(1\le s\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), its coefficient is
\[
 b_{N-s,N}=\eta(-1)^{s-1}\beta_{s,N},
 \qquad \beta_{s,N}>0.
\]
The positive magnitude is an explicit finite sum. On each fixed
interval \(0<a\le s/N\le b<1/2\), consecutive terms of this sum
have ratio at most \(q_b<1\), uniformly for all sufficiently large
levels. This is proved from the exact sine products.

A prefix of length \(\lfloor\sigma N\rfloor\) therefore has
exponentially small relative error. Its dependence on \(x=s/N\)
uses finite products of sines, so it is analytic on a fixed complex
strip. The theorem identifies a positive analytic function
\(\mathcal B_\alpha(x)\) for which
\[
 N\widehat\beta_N(x,\alpha)
       =\mathcal B_\alpha(x)+O_{\mathrm{hol}}(N^{-2}).
\]
A localized sinc correction makes the interpolation exact at every
degree node in the interval while changing it by only an exponentially
small relative amount. The resulting function
\(\mathfrak b_N\) satisfies \(c/N\le|\mathfrak b_N|\le C/N\)
on a smaller fixed strip.

The alternating sign remains the explicit character
\(-\eta e^{i\pi Nx}\). Thus the actual coefficients have a bounded
analytic amplitude after this known character is removed. The
finite sum has an exact residue representation with this amplitude,
its sampling kernel and all connecting contours retained. This
supplies the analytic coefficients needed for a coherent Fourier
estimate; their positivity alone does not bound the interface.

The interval excludes both its endpoints and the midpoint
\(s/N=1/2\). Shared endpoint products require convolution and full
Hermite folding, including their signs. Neither these complementary
regions nor the whole boundary current is covered by the theorem.

## A general interpolation theorem retains the endpoint values and normals

The [two-channel interpolation theorem](research_microscopic_endpoint_two_channel_interpolation.md)
removes the need for a scalar nonvanishing assumption in the
microscopic physical rows. Its first part is a general analytic
statement. If
\[
 y_{j+1}=T_N(j/N)y_j,\qquad T_N(x)=I+O(N^{-1}),
\]
with the matrices uniformly analytic on a fixed buffered interval,
then polynomially bounded nodal vectors have an exact holomorphic
interpolant on a smaller fixed strip, with a polynomial bound there.

The proof uses local Newton interpolation. Analyticity of the
recurrence bounds its repeated differences, so Newton polynomials
through a number of consecutive nodes proportional to \(N\) stay
bounded on fixed disks. Adjacent polynomials have proportionally
many common zeros; their difference is exponentially small on the
overlap. A Cauchy integral corrects the resulting small
\(\bar\partial\) error, and a finite sinc sum restores every nodal
value exactly. This proof applies to vectors and to holomorphic
external parameters. It does not divide by a component of the
solution.

For the original endpoint kernel, put
\[
 F_j=K_N(c(j),2\cosh(\alpha/N)),\qquad
 G_j=\partial_zK_N(c(j),2\cosh(\alpha/N)).
\]
The original difference equation and its differentiated version
give a four-component recurrence for the values, their consecutive
differences, the scaled normals, and their differences. On every
fixed interval \(0<a\le j/N\le b<1/2\), this matrix is
\(I+O(N^{-1})\), uniformly for bounded complex \(\alpha\).
The original endpoint kernel bound supplies polynomial initial
size. The general theorem therefore gives exact analytic
interpolants \(\mathcal F_N,\mathcal G_N\) for both \(F_j,G_j\),
with polynomial norms on one fixed strip.

Their product rule also handles any fixed number of endpoint
kernels sharing a surviving vertex. In the original trace they
are used as separate value and normal functions. The theorem does
not assert that
\[
 \partial_x\mathcal F_N(x,\alpha)
       =N c'(Nx)\mathcal G_N(x,\alpha).
\]
A scalar contour replacement must retain this possible difference.
The physical endpoints, the resulting normal contribution, and
the whole-current comparison with the geometric action remain
outside this interpolation theorem.

## The remaining radical frequencies concentrate at the midpoint

The [Fourier fold theorem](research_endpoint_fourier_fold_transition.md)
now treats the midpoint excluded by the bulk Fourier theorem.
Fix \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), remove the actual Newton terms with
\(1\le m\le\lfloor\varepsilon N\rfloor\), and let
\[
 \mathcal H_N(Z)=
 \sum_{m=\lfloor\varepsilon N\rfloor+1}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}
            e_{N-m}(2\cosh(\alpha/N))e_{N-m}(Z).
\]
The low physical-value interpolant is separate and remains in
the original kernel. For real bounded \(\alpha\), the upper Fourier
coefficient at frequency \(N-s\) has the known alternating sign
and a positive magnitude \(B_{s,N}\). Uniformly at both parities,
\[
 B_{s,N}\le C_{\varepsilon,A}N^{-3/2}
       \exp\!\left[-2\varepsilon(N/2-s)^2/N\right].
\]
Thus these remaining coefficients lie in a window of width
\(\sqrt N\) about \(s=N/2\).

Their profile is also identified. With \(u=(N/2-s)/\sqrt N\),
\[
 N^{3/2}B_{s,N}\longrightarrow
 \frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}{2\pi}
 \int_{\tan(\pi\varepsilon)}^\infty
                 v^{-3/2}e^{-\pi u^2v}\,dv ,
\]
uniformly on bounded \(u\)-intervals. The amplitude is derived
from the original finite product \(P_N(w)/P_N(2)\), including
the odd simple root. Gaussian domination gives the total Fourier
coefficient mass, which is of order \(N^{-1}\). The reflected
lower frequencies and the half weight at the even midpoint are
retained exactly.

The theorem also gives the original normal contribution as a
cosine transform of these coefficients. A pointwise profile is
not substituted into that oscillatory transform without an error
estimate suitable for its cancellation. On a complex angular
contour, \(H=|\operatorname{Im}t|\), the proved envelope is
\[
 |\mathcal H_N(-2\cos t)|
 \le C N^{-1}
       \exp\!\left[N\left(H/2+H^2/(8\varepsilon)\right)\right].
\]
This still has an exponential cost. It is a quantitative bound
for the stated radical terms, not a bound at the filled volume
rate for the complete source.

## The scalar derivative mismatch has an exact trace contribution

The [normal-defect calculation](research_endpoint_normal_defect_bulk_primitive.md)
specifies what would be lost by differentiating only an interpolation
of the physical values. For any exact value interpolant \(f_N\), put
\[
 \Delta_j=Nc'(j)G_j-\partial_x f_N(j/N).
\]
Replacing the actual normal by the derivative of \(f_N\), while
keeping the other rows unchanged, changes the original trace by
exactly
\[
 -\frac{\eta}{\pi}\sum_{j/N\in I}
       \sin((2j+1)\pi/N)\,\Delta_j A_N(c(j)).
\]
Here \(I\) is the chosen interior row interval and \(A_N\) is the
entire remaining source, including its crossing and all shared
variables. The odd simple value is unchanged. For products of
endpoint kernels, the mismatch obeys the ordinary product rule;
no division by a possibly zero value is used.

The exact Fourier decomposition expresses \(\Delta_j\) through
the derivative of the low physical-value polynomial and a sine
transform of the positive high-frequency magnitudes. Their
alternating signs cancel within that transform. On a fixed
interior frequency interval, a finite geometric series in the
forward-difference operator supplies an exact summation primitive.
Analyticity bounds its remainder exponentially. The two terminal
terms remain, and cancel at artificial subdivisions when the same
primitive is used throughout.

There is a further structural reduction. The two-component
derivative mismatch satisfies the original value transfer equation
with exponentially small forcing on a buffered bulk interval.
The forcing is the derivative of the value interpolant's
difference-equation residual. That residual has polynomial
analytic norm and vanishes at all grid points; the dense-zero
estimate makes it and its derivative exponentially small on a
smaller strip. The actual initial mismatch has not thereby been
set to zero. It is fixed by the original normal data and their
endpoint source.

## Two actual coefficients determine the interior derivative mismatch

The [two-mode transport theorem](research_endpoint_normal_defect_two_mode_transport.md)
makes the preceding reduction precise. On any fixed buffered
interval inside \(0<j/N<1/2\), the derivative mismatch is independent
of the choice of a polynomially bounded analytic value interpolant,
up to exponentially small errors. Its two-component recurrence has
uniformly bounded forward and inverse products. Consequently two
actual coefficients at one interior reference index determine the
whole mismatch there, to exponential accuracy.

The limiting transport is explicit. Its scalar equation is
\[
 f''+\pi(3\cot(\pi x)+\tan(\pi x))f'
       +(\pi^2+\alpha^2)\cot^2(\pi x)f=0.
\]
For \(\alpha\ne0\), its solutions include
\(\sin(\pi x)^{-1\pm i\alpha/\pi}\). At \(\alpha=0\), use
\(\csc(\pi x)\) and
\(\csc(\pi x)\log\sin(\pi x)\). A basis entire in \(\alpha\)
has Wronskian \(\pi\cos(\pi x)/\sin^3(\pi x)\).
The exact finite-level transfer differs from this fundamental
matrix transport by \(O(N^{-1})\), uniformly on the buffered
interval. The two source coefficients themselves have not been
assigned a leading value.

There is an exact local criterion: a single scalar analytic
interpolant with polynomial norm can match both physical values
and normals on a fixed interior interval if and only if those
two coefficients are exponentially small. Necessity follows from
the dense common zeros of two value interpolants. For sufficiency,
exact transfer makes every derivative discrepancy exponentially
small, and a finite sinc-squared sum corrects all first derivatives
without changing any value. This is a local criterion; it does not
produce a full-period representative or discard its connecting
integrals.

The source also calibrates the parameter dependence. At
\(\alpha=\pm i(2b+1)\pi\), with \(b\) fixed, the endpoint is the
physical color \(c_b\); the original kernel is then an ordinary
polynomial of degree \(b\). Its two coefficients are exponentially
small. On each bounded parameter disk, subtracting an explicitly
exponentially small finite interpolation correction therefore gives
\[
 \mathbf a_N(\alpha)=\cosh(\alpha/2)\mathbf h_N(\alpha)
                            +\mathbf r_N(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \|\mathbf h_N\|\le CN^p,\quad
 \|\mathbf r_N\|\le CN^p e^{-cN}.
\]
This equality retains the correction and is proved at the actual
physical parameters. At this stage the quotient \(\mathbf h_N\)
was unknown. Since \(\cosh(\alpha/2)\) has no real zeros, the
factorization alone did not settle real-parameter compatibility.
The later bulk scalar theorem below proves exponential smallness
of the actual coefficients by a different argument. Noncancellation
in the knot source remains separate.

## The original endpoint derivative has a controlled two-ended limit

The [endpoint-normal limit](research_endpoint_normal_two_ended_limit.md)
computes an actual initial datum for the differentiated recurrence.
For \(w_N=2\cosh(\alpha/N)\), let
\[
 Q_N(\alpha)=
       \left.\partial_Z K_N(Z,w_N)\right|_{Z=c_0}.
\]
Differentiating the original Newton factors gives exactly
\[
 \frac{Q_N(\alpha)}{N^2}
   =\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}
          \frac{(-1)^i e_i(w_N)}{N^2s_1s_i}.
\]
Terms with \(i\) fixed and terms with \(N-i\) fixed both contribute
to its limit. The intervening indices are controlled uniformly,
including complex parameters, by
\[
 \left|\frac{(-1)^i e_i(w_N)}{N^2s_1s_i}\right|
             \le \frac{C_A}{\min(i,N-i)^2},
 \qquad |\alpha|\le A.
\]

Put
\[
 E_m(\alpha)=
 \frac{(1/2+i\alpha/(2\pi))_m
       (1/2-i\alpha/(2\pi))_m}{(m!)^2},
\]
where \((a)_m=a(a+1)\cdots(a+m-1)\). The resulting even entire
function is
\[
 \mathcal Q(\alpha)=
 \frac{1}{4\pi^2}\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{E_m(\alpha)}m
 +\frac{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)}{4\pi^4}
                  \sum_{m\ge1}\frac{1}{m^3E_m(\alpha)}.
\]
The second series is read term by term with its removable
singularities filled in. Both series converge normally on every
bounded parameter disk. The theorem proves
\[
 N^{-2}Q_N(\alpha)=\mathcal Q(\alpha)+O_A(N^{-1/2})
\]
uniformly on those disks, with the same rate for fixed parameter
derivatives on smaller disks. Its proof retains the exact zeros
through a product of analytic units; it does not divide by a
vanishing limiting polynomial. Every summand is positive for
real \(\alpha\), so \(\mathcal Q(\alpha)>0\) there.

In the original index coordinate this gives
\[
 c'(0)Q_N(\alpha)
       =-4\pi^2\mathcal Q(\alpha)+O_A(N^{-1/2}).
\]
This fixes the endpoint normal itself. It does not compute the
two interior compatibility coefficients, which also involve the
coefficient-shift solution and the propagated endpoint forcing.
The later bulk scalar theorem resolves their compatibility by
analytic uniqueness on two parity subgrids. Positivity of
\(\mathcal Q\) is still not a lower bound for the original
oscillatory knot sum.

## The actual endpoint values and normals are compatible in the bulk

The [bulk scalar compatibility theorem](research_microscopic_endpoint_bulk_scalar_compatibility.md)
settles the local obstruction isolated above. Fix any compact interval
\(I\Subset(0,1/2)\), and any bounded complex set of microscopic
endpoint parameters \(\alpha\). There is one scalar holomorphic
function, with polynomial norm on a fixed neighborhood of \(I\),
whose values and first spectral derivatives agree exactly with
those of \(K_N(2\cosh(\alpha/N),Z)\) at every physical node of
that interval. The neighborhood may be thin. Both parities are
included, and any fixed product of endpoint kernels sharing that
variable has the same property.

The proof uses two different analytic descriptions of the true
derivative mismatch. Let \(f_N\) be a moderate exact value
interpolation, and \(L_N\) the ordinary low-degree polynomial
interpolation of all distinct physical values. Dividing
\(L_N(c_N(x))-f_N(x)\) by the distinct-root polynomial removes
every grid zero. The quotient has polynomial norm: on a rectangle
with vertical sides midway between grid points, the denominator's
growth matches or exceeds the low polynomial's growth.

The full high normal has an exact analytic amplitude on a suitable
local chart at every interior physical angle. Its cutoff is chosen
so the actual lowering chain terminates inside the analytic
contraction domain. Combining these two expressions gives
\[
 \Delta_{j,N}=(-1)^j A_N(j/N)
\]
with \(A_N\) polynomially bounded and analytic. Independently, the
two-channel theorem represents the same \(\Delta_{j,N}\) by a
polynomially bounded analytic function \(d_N\). Thus \(d_N-A_N\)
vanishes on the even subgrid, while \(d_N+A_N\) vanishes on the
odd subgrid. Each has a number of zeros proportional to \(N\)
in every fixed chart. The disk Blaschke estimate makes both
functions exponentially small on a smaller chart.

Consequently the actual derivative mismatch and both intrinsic
two-mode coefficients are exponentially small. No initial normal
was chosen or discarded. Locally an exact scalar representative
is the literal partial Newton sum
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{\lceil N/2\rceil+\lfloor\delta N\rfloor}
       e_k(2\cosh(\alpha/N))e_k(c_N(x)).
\]
Its full values and normals are correct on the chosen chart;
the proof bounds it on a sufficiently thin complex neighborhood.
A finite sinc-squared correction gives one representative over
the full compact interval. Products preserve all shared normals
by the ordinary product rule.

This result supersedes the earlier open local compatibility
question. It does not cover either endpoint of the physical
interval, a full period, arbitrary contour heights, the connecting
integrals, or the remaining graph factors. Those restrictions
prevent using it as an unproved whole-source bound.

## Explicit bulk values and actual spectral normals

The [value connection theorem](research_endpoint_value_connection_and_overlap.md)
computes the leading endpoint values with a power-saving error.
For real bounded \(\alpha\), set \(\nu=\alpha/\pi\) and, away
from zero, define
\[
 k_\pm(\nu)=
   \frac{\Gamma(\pm i\nu)}
        {\Gamma(1/2\pm i\nu/2)^4},\qquad
 g_\alpha(s)=k_+s^{-1+i\nu}+k_-s^{-1-i\nu}.
\]
The combined expression is regular at \(\alpha=0\), where
\[
 g_0(s)=\frac{2}{\pi^2s}
                 \bigl(\log s+\gamma_E+4\log2\bigr).
\]
Here \(\gamma_E\) is Euler's constant. Write
\[
 S_N(x)=\frac N\pi\sin(\pi x),\qquad
 c_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi/N).
\]
On every fixed compact physical bulk interval there is
\(\epsilon>0\) such that
\[
 K_N(c_j,2\cosh(\alpha/N))
       =g_\alpha(S_N(j/N))+O(N^{-1-\epsilon}).
\]
All fixed derivatives of the actual moderate value interpolation
have the corresponding real-interval estimate, after decreasing
\(\epsilon\) if necessary.

The connection constants are derived from an exact generating
function for the limiting endpoint recurrence and Euler's beta
integral. A growing intermediate index \(J=N^\kappa\) is then
compared with the exact finite-level recurrence. Transport in the
explicit Euler basis controls the passage from \(J\) to the
physical bulk. Thus the proof does not interchange a fixed-index
limit with a bulk limit. Derivative estimates use shrinking
complex strips of width proportional to \(1/\log N\); no
fixed-strip small-error estimate is asserted.

Combining this theorem with the now-proved scalar compatibility
gives the actual spectral normal:
\[
 \left.\partial_ZK_N(Z,2\cosh(\alpha/N))\right|_{Z=c_j}
 =\frac{\left.\partial_x g_\alpha(S_N(x))\right|_{x=j/N}}
        {-4\pi\sin(2\pi j/N+\pi/N)}
       +O(N^{-1-\epsilon}).
\]
The denominator is a unit on the fixed bulk interval. This follows
by subtracting the exponentially small true derivative defect;
it uses the original normal, not a common-index coefficient
derivative.

For example, at \(\alpha=0\), put
\[
 L_N(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{N\sin(\pi x)}{\pi}\right)
                              +\gamma_E+4\log2.
\]
The last display becomes
\[
 \left.\partial_ZK_N(Z,2)\right|_{Z=c_j}
       =\frac{L_N(j/N)-1}{4\pi N\sin^3(\pi j/N)}
                                   +O(N^{-1-\epsilon}),
\]
after taking \(\epsilon<1\). At nonzero real \(\alpha\), the
leading value oscillates in \(\log N\); no uniform nonzero
amplitude is claimed. These local estimates still leave the
original endpoint and whole-trace contributions to be controlled.

## Complex asymptotics and a nonzero local multiplier

The [fixed-neighborhood theorem](research_endpoint_fixed_strip_asymptotics.md)
extends the real value asymptotic to a fixed thin complex
neighborhood, with a smaller positive power saving. Its proof
uses a harmonic barrier in a rectangle: a holomorphic function
bounded by \(N^P\) on the rectangle and by \(N^{-1-\epsilon}\)
on its real diameter is bounded by
\(N^{-1-\epsilon/2}\) in a sufficiently thin fixed subrectangle.
The thickness depends on the buffers, \(P\), and \(\epsilon\),
but not on \(N\). This applies to the difference between the
actual scalar representative and its explicit leading function.

There is also a useful uniform nonzero regime. For real
\(\alpha_N=\beta/\log N\), with \(|\beta|\le B<\pi^2\),
\[
 h_N(x,\alpha_N)=
 \frac{2\log N}{\pi N\sin(\pi x)}
       \frac{\sin(\beta/\pi)}{\beta/\pi}
       \left\{1+O_{\mathrm{hol}}\!\left(\frac1{\log N}\right)\right\}.
\]
The sine quotient has its value one at zero. It is positive
and bounded away from zero on this real parameter interval.
Thus the displayed leading factor and the actual representative
are nonzero on the smaller complex bulk neighborhood for large
\(N\). Fixed products retain this property and all shared normals.
This includes the complete endpoint \(\alpha=0\); it does not
extend the nonzero claim to every fixed nonzero real \(\alpha\).

If a local saddle contour and its nonzero bare leading coefficient
have already been established within that neighborhood, these
factors multiply the coefficient by a nonzero factor and change
only powers of \(N\) and \(\log N\). The proof bounds the
multiplier's variation by \(O(1/\log N)+O(|x-x_*|)\) and
integrates against the absolute Gaussian bound.
It does not establish that the original closed trace contains
this contour, that the geometric saddle lies in the thin
neighborhood, or that another contribution cannot cancel it.

## Interpolation approaching both physical endpoints

The [shrinking-buffer theorem](research_microscopic_endpoint_shrinking_buffer_compatibility.md)
removes the requirement that the physical interval stay a fixed
distance from its endpoints. There are uniform constants such
that, for \(M/N\le\rho\le\rho_*\), the interval
\[
                   I_\rho=[\rho,1/2-\rho]
\]
has a scalar representative on a complex neighborhood of width
\(c\rho\). It matches the actual values and first spectral normals
exactly, has norm at most \(CN^P\rho^{-P}\), and differs from
the value interpolation by at most
\[
                    CN^P\rho^{-P}e^{-cN\rho}.
\]
The actual analytic derivative mismatch has the same bound.
Both parities and all bounded complex microscopic parameters
are included.

The proof rescales \(x=\rho y\). The exact value-and-normal
recurrence then has step \(I+O((N\rho)^{-1})\) on a fixed-width
complex neighborhood in \(y\). Its interval has length
\(O(\rho^{-1})\), but local interpolation and gluing cost only
polynomial factors: the actual nodal data are already
polynomially bounded, so no long transfer product is used to
estimate them.

Near the first physical endpoint, the finite lowering ratios
need not individually contract. Their entire product is bounded
instead by a telescoping cosine ratio and a reciprocal-square
estimate. This gives a uniform polynomial bound on the exact
alternating normal amplitude. Dense even and odd subgrids then
give the factor \(e^{-cN\rho}\), followed by exact Hermite repair.
There is no condition that \(N\rho^2\) tend to infinity.

Consequently the representative overlaps the endpoint region at
any growing index \(j=N^\kappa\), \(0<\kappa<1\), with error
\(\operatorname{poly}(N)e^{-cN^\kappa}\). Taking
\(\rho=K\log N/N\) gives any prescribed negative power of \(N\)
by choosing a sufficiently large fixed \(K\). The construction
still omits the endpoint rows. Its complex width shrinks, and
the exact outer vertical integrals remain; none can be discarded
on the strength of this interpolation estimate alone.

## The original trace on a compact angular window

The [bulk contour assembly](research_endpoint_bulk_annulus_full_trace.md)
uses one scalar representative throughout an interior window
\(0<a<b<\pi\). It reproduces both the original values and first
spectral derivatives of every microscopic endpoint factor.
Multiplication preserves all derivatives of factors sharing a
variable; the other graph factors remain in their joint spectator.

For midpoint boundaries \(a_N,b_N\) and a sufficiently small fixed
height \(H>0\), write
\[
 g_N(t)=\sin t\,\widehat Q_N(t)A_N(-2\cos t)
                   e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)},\qquad
 W_N(t)=\frac{e^{-iNt}}{(1-\eta e^{-iNt})^2},
 \quad C_{N,n}=e^{\pi in(N-1)^2/(4N)}.
\]
Here \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\), \(\widehat Q_N\) represents the shared
endpoint product, and \(A_N\) retains the remaining source.
The original trace restricted to the positive physical angles
between \(a_N\) and \(b_N\) equals
\[
\begin{split}
 -\frac{N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi i}
 \left(\int_{-b_N-iH}^{-a_N-iH}
             +\int_{a_N-iH}^{b_N-iH}\right)g_N(t)W_N(t)\,dt
 {}+\frac{\eta N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi}
 \int_{-H}^{H}
 \frac{g_N(b_N+iv)-g_N(a_N+iv)}
                         {4\cosh^2(Nv/2)}\,dv .
\end{split}
\]
The scalar is reflected to the separate negative window; no
extension through zero is assumed. The residue calculation retains
the derivative multiplier in every Fourier term:
\[
 W_N(t)=\sum_{\ell\ge1}\ell\eta^{\ell-1}e^{-i\ell Nt}
                         \qquad(\Im t<0).
\]
Using the same scalar on adjacent rectangles makes their common
vertical integrals cancel exactly. The two displayed outer
integrals remain. For several traced vertices the formula
tensorizes, including every intersection of these outer faces.

This establishes the placement of the new scalar in the original
finite functional. It does not bound the remaining spectator,
remove the endpoint rows, or establish a whole-source volume rate.

## A limit of continuation inside one positive subdivision

The [small-real-power corner calculation](research_trivalent_pair_real_power_corner_persistence.md)
tests a proposed general shortcut. On an original selected trivalent
pair, at explicitly specified charges strictly below one, the
zero-power minimizer is interior. Assigning sufficiently small
opposite real powers makes the unique minimizer a corner, even
though the old positive assignment remains strictly feasible.

The proof constructs the exact convex optimality certificate,
including all four original outside edges and their fixed
logarithmic branches. Its corner covector is a strict supporting
covector; it is not a finite original geometric period at a
regular corner. Thus zero-power positivity and comparison of
minimum energies cannot alone justify continuation inside the
same positive subdivision.

This is a test of a general proposed implication, not an additional
knot case. The powers are small and nonintegral. No conclusion
about hyperbolicity, integer fillings, another subdivision, or
the quantum geometric contribution follows from the example.

## Exact comparison of the two polarizations at the final readout

The [heat-readout quotient theorem](research_polarized_endpoint_heat_readout_quotient.md)
identifies precisely which changes of the charge function leave
every independent heat evolution and final unit-charge evaluation
unchanged. Put \(y_v=1-\chi_v\), let \(R_v\) reflect \(y_v\),
and set \(E=\prod_v(1+R_v)/2\). On the actual entire functions
of exponential type, the common kernel of all independent heat
readouts is exactly \(\ker E\). These are sums of parity
components odd in at least one coordinate. The converse uses
heat parameters in an open real or complex set, not integer
parameters alone.

Both the canonical finite polarization and the initialized
frozen-contour family have the same all-even component: the
original cosine source, with all physical normal data. Their
difference therefore has exactly zero final readout after every
signed heat evolution. This permits using the initialized contour
family directly as a representative of the canonical family's
readout class. Equality of the two functions away from unit
charge is unnecessary.

The distinction matters analytically. For the actual kernel
network with complete outside ends, the canonical polarization
has an explicit contribution of the complete exponential rate
in its contractive charge half-planes. The theorem calculates
it at both parities, including every physical normal and bounded
real crossing powers. Thus one cannot infer its geometric
leading term merely from the cosine source's lattice asymptotics.

The exact difference of representatives can be removed before
the complete heat integral is estimated. Subtracting only the
leading endpoint expression, or a finite angular Taylor jet,
would leave errors at the same exponential rate. Likewise a
truncated saddle contour need not annihilate an odd component:
the identity applies to the complete readout.

This resolves the exact comparison between the two constructions.
It does not extend the contour representative's current
initialization domain or prove the global tail estimates and
geometric contribution for arbitrary short fillings. Those remain
the critical analytic requirements.
