proves \(|dq/ds|<41/60\) throughout the original convex own-four
image. These are bounds for critical coordinates. They do not assert
that the endpoint map preserves that domain, or bound the cost of
moving the indices back to the real physical rows.

One portion of the physical complement is now fully below the
geometric rate. The [exact endpoint-tail bound](research_mixed_fourier_right_cap_wall_endpoint_tail.md)
first sums the outgoing index coherently, as above. The remaining
rows sufficiently near their upper endpoint then increase by a
factor greater than two. Their complete sum in modulus is bounded
by twice the literal final row, including when its incoming
polynomial vanishes. That final row has the exact allocated rate
\[
 E_{\rm end}(a;y)=2\pi(-\Im a)_++\pi\Im y
                                      -\eta\Re g(a)/2.
\]
The [cardinal-action comparison](research_mixed_fourier_right_cap_endpoint_payment.md)
proves \(\Re\ell_{q_*}(y)-\Re\ell_0(y)>1/200\).
Its proof decreases the height to zero, uses real concavity, and
bounds the two endpoint dilogarithm series by explicit terms and
geometric tails. Combining this with the already completed inner
last-row comparison gives
\(E_{\rm end}<B_\eta-387/70000\). Consequently a fixed
positive-width high-index strip of the actual finite two-index
source has a uniform exponential gap \(1/200\), with both
parities and every original scalar retained. This is a bound for
that complete strip. The following comparisons extend it across
the rest of the high-index interval; the real outgoing faces and
remaining retained-index currents are separate.

There is also a direct comparison on the first part of the high-index
range. Let \(E_\eta(s;a)\) be the exponential upper rate of one
retained physical row after the complete outgoing contraction, including
the original incoming allocation. Put \(X=e^{-2\pi ia}\) and
\(S=e^{-2\pi is}\). In terms of \(J(s)=\Re g(s)\) and the
Wall action \(I\) above, it is
\[
 \begin{split}
 E_\eta(s;a)={}&\int_0^s\log|1-Xe^{-2\pi iu}|\,du
       -2J(s)-2\pi(\Im a)s\\
       &+\Re I(1-s,Y)+\pi\Im y-\frac\eta2\Re g(a).
 \end{split}
\]
The exact product rate and the completed Wall action give
\[
 E_\eta'(s;a)=\log
   \frac{|X^{-1}-S|}{|1-S|^2|R_{\rm out}(1-s,Y)|}.
\]
This derivative is strictly negative for \(1/2\le s\le3/4\).
Indeed \(|X^{-1}|<2\) on the original incoming heights, and the
certificate gives \(|R_{\rm out}|>1\). For \(s\le2/3\),
the numerator is less than three and \(|1-S|^2\ge3\).
For \(2/3\le s\le3/4\), write \(t=1-s\). The angle between
\(X^{-1}\) and \(S\) has absolute value at most \(2\pi/5\),
so the squared numerator is at most \(6-\sqrt5<4\), while
\(|1-S|^2\ge2\). The primitive rate is continuous through any
incoming numerator zero; its logarithmic derivative tends to minus
infinity there, so such a zero does not interrupt the decrease.
This reduces the interval to the rate at \(s=1/2\). The
[retained-rate theorem](research_mixed_fourier_right_cap_coherent_retained_rate.md)
also provides a finite algebraic candidate list for the remaining
interval, as a fallback.

The [Wall rate-convexity theorem](research_mixed_fourier_right_cap_wall_rate_convexity.md)
now removes the need to estimate those interior candidates. Its
elementary complex bounds give \(|1-q_t|<1\) and \(|QR|<2\)
on \(0\le t\le1/4\), where \(Q=e^{-2\pi iq}\) is the
original outgoing root and \(R\) the initialized degree root.
These imply
\(\partial_t\log|R|>-2\pi\cot(\pi t)\). Consequently
\(E_\eta(1-t;a)\) is strictly convex before the incoming
numerator crossing and strictly increasing after it, when that
crossing occurs in this interval. Together with the preceding
decrease this proves
\[
 E_\eta(s;a)\le
       \max\{E_\eta(1/2;a),E_{\rm end}(a;y)\},
                       \qquad 1/2\le s\le1.
\]
The true endpoint is already below the geometric rate, leaving
the coherently summed half-index face \(E_\eta(1/2;a)\).

That last comparison is now proved in the
[complete coherent high-tail theorem](research_mixed_fourier_right_cap_coherent_high_tail_payment.md).
The outgoing saddle at \(s=1/2\) satisfies
\(11/50<\Re q_c<3/8\), so it lies in the original allowed
real target interval. For
\(K(q)=g(1/2+q)-g(q)+\ell_q(y)\), the original logarithmic
equation gives \(K'(q_c)=0\), while \(\Re K''<0\) along
its entire negative-height vertical line. Its real action is
therefore a vertical minimum. Comparing it with the value at the
original reference height uses the already proved individual
inner half-row estimate, with unchanged action and allocations.
It gives \(E_\eta(1/2;a)<B_\eta(a)-1/35000\).

Consequently the **entire original high-index part**, with
\(j\ge\lceil N/2\rceil\), has finite exponential gap
\(1/70000\) below the geometric supporting plane, uniformly on
the stated actual incoming families and at both level parities.
The proof first sums every outgoing row within each retained
index. It retains its initial condition, exact scalars and incoming
polynomial zeros. It does not bound the old low-outgoing wedge
separately: that wedge is included inside the full coherent
contraction. The next whole-cap argument must split the retained
index first and preserve this grouping. Low retained indices,
their contour joins and the complete right-cap remainder are
still unproved by this theorem.

The next closure estimate now has an
[exact prepared-cap source](research_mixed_prepared_three_four_cap_source.md):
\(G_{34,N}(y,w)=v_N(w)^TA_{3,N}A_{4,N}h_N(y)\), with the
original ordinary closing vector. There are exact four-index and
coherent three-index formulas, including their scalar and physical
support. The original endpoint action replaces one Fourier incidence
in the earlier paired kernel. The cap curvature and the two triangle
forms prove strict accretivity of this new phase on a complete
four-variable rectangle. The
[enlarged height domain](research_mixed_prepared_cap_typed_height_rectangle.md)
contains the actual two-letter critical point and retains the exact
finite-row expansion. Consequently its local stationary current has
power \(N^{-1}\) and a nonzero coefficient. The earlier paired
kernel's action and numerical gaps are not reused for this different
boundary vector.

The [physical-tail reduction](research_mixed_prepared_cap_physical_tail_reduction.md)
now bounds the remote index regions explicitly and reduces the remaining
real tails to eight faces of a four-variable rectangle. Each face has
a strictly concave rate function. This reduction uses the asymptotic
of the actual incoming coefficient before taking absolute values; it
does not discard its internal cancellation. The resulting face maxima
have now been compared with the new critical action. Seven pass, but
the upper private-index face does not. The failed comparison is a
genuine obstruction to this absolute-tail decomposition, as explained
below.

The [rational critical curve](research_mixed_prepared_three_four_cap_critical_curve.md)
expresses the prepared cap's critical equations by rational functions
of one endpoint shape. Its domain conditions select the original
logarithms. The new existence theorem supplies its admitted preimage
on the enlarged domain, where the same argument proves nonramification.

The original [complete source criterion](research_mixed_prepared_cap_full_source_criterion.md)
isolates sufficient comparisons for the four-index decomposition.
The explicit remote-region
bound and eight real boundary maxima must lie strictly below the new
critical action. Eight additional maxima bound all discrete Fourier
corrections. The proof retains every contour term and shows that
simultaneous joining contours require no extra family of comparisons.
The prescribed calculation proves fifteen of the sixteen inequalities.
The remaining real-face inequality is false, so this sufficient
criterion cannot be applied with the stated private-index cut. The
completed coherent argument below retains cancellation across that cut.
A whole-period bound compatible with further attachments, and control
of the remainder under composition, are still needed for mixed-word
propagation. The explicit outgoing-period bound above supplies an
initial source estimate but does not establish that compatibility.
The finite-exception theorem and the completed knot-family scope are
unchanged.

The [action-enclosure lemma](research_mixed_prepared_cap_action_enclosure.md)
provides a way to measure those gaps using the already established
critical point. The full five-variable Hessian has norm less than
\(120\) on its original convex domain. A certified gradient residual
that places the root within radius \(r\) of a rational center therefore
bounds the complex action error by \(60r^2\). The formula retains every
original additive constant and the full uncertainty in the algebraic
Fourier parameter. The
[face and alias protocol](research_mixed_prepared_cap_face_alias_protocol.md)
uses one supporting-plane bound for each complete domain, with all
signed gradient terms retained. Both prescribed calculations are now
complete. The [action record](../repro/results/research-mixed-prepared-cap-action.json)
certifies
\[
 2.120165258<\Re\Phi_{\mathrm{cap}}<2.120165259.
\]
The [comparison record](../repro/results/research-mixed-prepared-cap-face-alias-budget.json)
encloses all sixteen cases. The seven successful real-face bounds have
gap greater than \(1/400\), and all eight Fourier-correction bounds
have gap greater than \(1/20\). At an explicit rational point of the
remaining face, \(s=49/100\), the real summand rate exceeds the true
critical rate by more than \(1/60\). The
[saved-data assessment](research_mixed_prepared_cap_face_alias_attempt.md)
gives the exact witness. Higher precision or a sharper upper bound
cannot remove that excess. It concerns the modulus of separate rows,
not their signed sum; it does not contradict the volume conjecture.

The [three-index argument](research_mixed_prepared_cap_three_index_sheet.md)
performs the whole first internal sum before taking absolute values,
using the exact polynomial \(U_{0,N}\). It proves a nonzero asymptotic
on the critical-height integration sheet and an exponential bound
for the physical indices outside its three-dimensional box. The latter
uses only the six already successful outer-face comparisons: an
outside outer coordinate remains on its corresponding face throughout
the original clipping argument. No new numerical evaluation is involved.
This regrouping avoids the failed private cut. The
[contour completion](research_mixed_prepared_cap_coherent_contour_completion.md)
now controls its remaining discrete Fourier corrections and connecting
contours. For terms with a Fourier penalty, the cap's real-index
envelope and the original height bounds reduce the estimate to a
successful outer face or alias. For the unpenalized connecting
contours, choose the private contour height to vary with the outer
height. Convexity of the five explicit source profiles compares the
two ends of this deformation: the saved real-face or alias bounds at
one end, and the proved cap supporting bound at the other.
The separate endpoint ceiling is also below the action. This proves
the whole prepared-function asymptotic stated at the start of this
section. The proof includes a contour lemma that can be applied to
longer sources once its stated hypotheses have been verified.

There is also an [exact terminating formula](research_mixed_prepared_cap_terminated_chart.md)
for that same prepared source. The rearrangement is made at the finite
level before interpolation, so it does not replace the original cap
polynomial by an off-grid continuation of a terminating identity.
Its phase has the same original critical value and a strictly negative
real Hessian on the complete required rectangle. The
[logarithmic derivative bounds](research_mixed_prepared_cap_terminated_gradient_strips.md)
prove analytically that every paid Fourier height can be reset toward
zero. Its [physical-tail reduction](research_mixed_prepared_cap_terminated_tails.md)
leaves two new private-face comparisons: the upper-half Newton rows
already have a gap greater than \(3/10\), and the outer physical
complement is controlled by keeping the first cap summed. These are
alternative source and contour tools, not additional knot results.
In particular the six old coherent outer-face estimates cannot be
transferred to the absolute Newton rows of this new formula.

The [uniform repeated-word estimate](research_mixed_uniform_repetition_bound.md)
now removes the polynomial and small exponential losses from the
upper spectral bound. There are constants \(C_*,N_*\), independent
of the positive three/four word \(w\), its length \(\ell\), and
the repetition count \(r\), such that
\[
 |\operatorname{tr}(W_N^r)|\le\mathfrak Z_N(w^r)
       \le C_*^{r\ell}e^{NrM_w}\qquad(N\ge N_*,\ r\ge1).
\]
Here \(\mathfrak Z_N\) is the total absolute integral of the
complete conditional representation on its original hybrid graphs;
the conditional sums are performed before taking their moduli.
Sharp central block powers cancel the Gaussian integration powers.
Only blocks near a noncentral or selected coordinate need the
coarser finite-source estimates, whose losses are paid by that
coordinate's occupation penalty. This gives one constant per letter,
with no level-dependent loss per repetition. The same proof bounds
the complete contribution outside the unselected central region by
\(C_1^{r\ell}e^{N(rM_w-1/2000000)}\), with universal constants.
This comparison is with the literal central integral; its Gaussian
asymptotic is not asserted uniformly in growing word length. The normalized matrix
determinants also converge on a fixed disk for each fixed word.
That disk is zero-free and does not establish spectral projections
or actual closing coefficients. The new upper estimate applies even
when the word varies with the level; the corresponding nonzero
asymptotic has not been proved in that varying-word regime.

The [full retained-period boundary potential](research_mixed_full_alphabet_boundary_potential.md)
extends the finite-memory open-chain inequality to the zero seam,
right half and every selected symbol. Its exact conditional-to-Fourier
operator norm also records the cost of changing representations.
This provides interior transport with boundary terms retained. It
does not supply the calibrated bound for the actual cap when a
neighbor changes its height, nor remove the closing coefficient.

The [spectral-radius theorem](research_mixed_word_spectral_radius.md)
now covers every fixed nonempty word \(w=(n_1,\ldots,n_\ell)\)
with \(n_j\in\{3,4\}\). For the original matrix product
\(W_N=A_{n_1,N}\cdots A_{n_\ell,N}\), it proves
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\rho(W_N)=M_w,
\]
where \(\rho\) is the spectral radius and \(M_w\) is the real
part of the original cyclic geometric action. The upper estimate
comes from finite-source bounds uniform in the number of repetitions
of the word; the lower estimate comes from its nonzero trace
asymptotic. The repetition limit is taken at fixed level before the
level tends to infinity. A positive inner product adapted to this
one product also follows. Its conditioning and the overlap with
the actual closing vectors are not controlled, so this does not
yet extend the knot-volume theorem to every such word.

The [diagonal obstruction](research_mixed_paired_schur_raw_diagonal_obstruction.md)
also identifies a limitation of the proposed absolute-value bound.
On an explicit interval near the geometric parameter, that raw
bound exceeds the required rate on the diagonal, where any scalar
boundary weight cancels. Consequently a sufficiently small local
chart combined with that unchanged exterior bound cannot prove
the desired weighted estimate. This concerns the proposed bound,
not the actual oscillatory kernel. A larger region with controlled
cancellation, a different contour, or a sharper exterior estimate
is required.

An [exact crossing-filter calculation](research_mixed_ordinary_crossing_filter.md)
clarifies a different possible way to close the source. At odd
squarefree levels the ordinary mark is a polynomial in the crossing
with coefficient absolute sum one. Its trace formula involves
crossing powers up to \(4N+1\), so the three/four word theorem
does not estimate it. At levels \(N=p^2\), for every odd prime
\(p\ge5\), a noncomplete physical node has exactly the complete
node's crossing eigenvalue. No function of that single crossing can
separate their required mark values. This is an obstruction to that
all-level filter construction, not to the volume identity or to
noncommuting operator constructions.

The [complete three-four kernel theorem](research_mixed_contracted_pair_full_kernel.md)
now controls the entire original paired quantum sum near its
alternating complex boundary parameters. Its asymptotic is
\[
 \mathcal K_{34,N}(x,y)=\kappa_N^3N^{-1/2}B_{34}(x,y)
             e^{N\Phi_{34}(x,y)}(1+O(N^{-1})),
 \qquad B_{34}\ne0.
\]
The original action and scalar are retained, both level parities
are covered, and normalized derivatives of every fixed order have
the same local control. In particular this gives an actual lower
bound for the complex sum, not only a nonzero formal saddle
coefficient. The proof treats all physical rows, joining contours
and discrete Fourier corrections. This completes the paired-kernel
estimate at its specified boundary parameters. Iteration still needs
a bound on the whole incoming boundary function and on its remainder
outside that neighborhood; the finite-exception theorem is unchanged.

The [complete three-crossing boundary theorem](research_three_full_boundary_source_propagation.md)
now restores the original matrix at every step of the homogeneous
Fourier induction. For every fixed chain length at least three, the
actual function \(v(-2)^T(JM^3)^m h(y)\) has the same nonzero
local asymptotic and the same bound on the entire real Fourier
period as the previously treated function with truncated matrices.
The total restoration error is at least \(19/100\) below the
central exponential rate, independently of the fixed length; on
the local output domain the relative gap is at least \(17/100\).
These estimates follow from the existing action drift and corner
bounds, without a new numerical calculation. They retain complete
ordinary-color jets. They do not give a global envelope at arbitrary
complex outside colors, or an induction for arbitrary incoming
functions. The concrete use is that the original homogeneous
boundary functions are now available for exact changes of basis
and subsequent tangle attachments, without an unestimated
truncation error.

The [exact Fourier change of coordinates](research_mixed_conditional_fourier_message_bridge.md)
identifies each full conditional transfer with attachment by the
original matrix \(JM^3\) or \(JM^4\), including its scalar
normalization. The preceding restored homogeneous family therefore
provides actual conditional messages with controlled Fourier images.
This is an identity of the entire finite functions, not only an
agreement of critical equations. A mixed interface moves outside
the domain of the existing homogeneous analytic estimates, so its
global bound still has to be proved.

For the alternating three/four interface there is now an
[invariant holomorphic phase and leading amplitude](research_mixed_alternating_interface_invariant_germ.md).
The proof first selects the unique complex Gaussian width with
positive real part. It then uses a contraction on bounded
holomorphic functions to construct the entire local phase germ,
and a convergent product to construct its nonzero amplitude.
The original nonzero boundary momentum and action constant are
retained. Thus the local construction is more than a finite Taylor
expansion. It concerns the local integral near the geometric
critical point. The connection to the actual cap's geometric phase
is now proved below; a bound for the rest of the input period is
still required for a mixed-source induction.

The [local stability theorem](research_mixed_alternating_interface_local_entrance_basin.md)
now extends that construction to an open family of nearby holomorphic
phase gradients. Their critical points, first derivatives and Gaussian
widths may vary. Repeated local paired attachment contracts the phase
gradients toward the invariant one and preserves a class of nonzero
leading amplitudes. The proof carries each exact stationary action
increment; its difference from the invariant increment is quadratic
in the gradient perturbation, so the accumulated correction converges.
This supplies a stable local family for a possible composition theorem.
The finite quantum boundary function still needs a full asymptotic
estimate in that family, including control of its error under
repeated attachment.

The [actual cap-phase entrance theorem](research_mixed_alternating_cap_phase_entrance.md)
now connects this local family to long alternating prefixes with the
original complete ordinary cap. It does not replace that cap by an
assumed invariant input. In the original leg coordinates, the complex
Hessian is uniformly accretive and has nonzero blocks only between
neighboring vertices. A convergent geometric series for its inverse
shows that the effect of changing the left endpoint decreases
exponentially with distance. Comparing the actual half-chain with
the tail determined by the invariant phase then proves convergence
of the outgoing phase gradient on a fixed complex disk. The exact
change to the Fourier boundary coordinate preserves this conclusion
and the original action constant. The local coefficient supplied by
the actual cap and conditional factors is nonzero. This establishes
entrance for the geometric phase and its local contribution; the
other terms of the original finite boundary function remain to be
bounded relative to that contribution.

The same theorem now permits any preceding word in positive powers
three and four. The trial keeps that entire actual prefix and
replaces only its alternating tail. Only the two vertex groups at
the join acquire a residual, so the phase approaches the invariant
one exponentially in tail length, with constants independent of
the prefix's length and letter order. Thus the required preparation
length for the phase is uniform over this source class. The prefix's
action constant and local coefficient are retained. Amplitude and
finite-source error constants may still depend on that prefix; this
does not allow its length to grow with the quantum level.

For attachment of a different fixed short piece, Section 7 of that
note isolates a precise additional condition. Eliminating the
uniformly accretive infinite tail leaves a finite Schur complement
at the short piece. Its invertibility is equivalent to absence of
a compatible square-summable linearized deformation. When it is
invertible, the finite attachments have uniformly bounded inverses
and the response to boundary forcing decays exponentially along the
tail. The condition holds at an already constructed compact positive
geometric attachment; existence of such an attachment remains a
separate requirement. An explicit tridiagonal example shows why
positivity of every finite approximation alone is insufficient:
the limiting Schur complement can vanish and the far-end response
can grow exponentially. This is a limitation of the proposed
argument, not a counterexample arising from a knot.

The earlier [paired Fourier-period analysis](research_mixed_paired_fourier_period_criterion.md)
separates one possible global estimate into explicit inequalities for
the original contours. Each vertex has 25 contour contributions and
one complementary part of the original index triangle. Pairing them
at their shared Fourier variable gives 676 sufficient comparisons;
these are a criterion, not 676 established estimates. One part now
has an analytic proof: with both index contours at their original
critical heights, the joint real action is strictly concave throughout
the shared-variable interval \(0\le\Re z\le1/5\). Consequently
this contribution decreases quadratically away from the geometric
point. The [negative-arc argument](research_mixed_paired_main_negative_wire_arc.md)
extends its strict comparison over the entire remaining part to
the left, down to \(\Re x_0-1/2\). It first bounds the maximizing
shared indices by their exact phase derivatives, then proves that
the action increases toward the already controlled endpoint zero.
The other comparisons in that particular sufficient criterion were
not completed. The exact contraction below now proves the full
paired kernel near its boundary reference without requiring those
separate bounds. A whole-function composition estimate still has
to control the actual incoming remainder.

There is also a way to estimate that same full paired kernel without
bounding two separate vertices at every Fourier angle. The
[contracted four-index theorem](research_mixed_contracted_pair_rectangle.md)
uses the exact shared-wire contraction before taking any modulus.
All three triangular constraints on the four remaining indices are
retained. Its combined phase has a uniformly positive negative real
Hessian on the entire original complex index rectangle, and its
critical value is the original geometric action. The resulting
local contribution has an explicit nonzero coefficient and power
\(N^{-1/2}\). Its global completion uses the enlarged rectangle
and the physical and lattice comparisons proved below. This formulation keeps
the shared-wire cancellation inside the exact source, so those
comparisons can replace the earlier separate far-wire tests.

The physical part of this comparison now has a finite reduction.
[Monotonicity of the original rate](research_mixed_contracted_pair_outer_index_elimination.md)
first bounds a distant region by a value at least \(1/200\)
below the geometric action. The
[nine-face theorem](research_mixed_contracted_pair_nine_face_tail.md)
then moves every remaining tail point, without decreasing its rate,
onto one of the eight faces of the original central rectangle or
onto the extra face \(s=0\). Each restriction is strictly concave.
Consequently nine outward tangent bounds at chosen rational points
would bound the entire physical remainder. Their
[fixed calculation protocol](research_mixed_contracted_pair_nine_faces_protocol.md)
retains all nine comparisons and does not assume that the proposed
supporting points are exact optimizers. The single execution of that
protocol produced seven strict bounds and two failures. At saved
rational points on \(s=9/20\) and \(t=1/4\), the rate itself
exceeds the actual geometric action, by more than \(1/100\) and
\(1/500\), respectively. These are not failures of the optimizer
or interval precision. The
[saved-data diagnosis](research_mixed_contracted_pair_nine_faces_diagnosis.md)
proves them from the recorded enclosures without new evaluations.
Thus the full physical remainder for those cuts cannot be discarded
by its absolute row rate. The failed certificate is retained. A
larger central domain now resolves that particular obstruction.
[Whole complex-rectangle accretivity](research_mixed_contracted_pair_enlarged_rectangle.md)
and the [new tail-preserving clips](research_mixed_contracted_pair_enlarged_tail_reduction.md)
hold on
\(C'=[1/4,1/2]\times[1/5,9/20]\times[1/5,21/50]^2\),
with the original contour heights and phase. The
[exact saved-gradient transport](../repro/results/research-mixed-contracted-pair-saved-face-transport.json)
then certifies all nine new face bounds using only the previous
rate and full-gradient enclosures. In particular it keeps the
negative contribution of moving \(s=9/20\) to \(s=1/2\),
and the positive derivative multiplied by the negative displacement
from \(t=1/4\) to \(t=1/5\). No new support point or function
evaluation is used. The entire physical complement of this new box
has upper rate at most \(2261/1500\), giving a gap larger than
\(19/3750>1/200\) below the actual geometric action.

The [simultaneous contour translation](research_mixed_contracted_pair_simultaneous_contour.md)
moves all four zero-frequency coordinates with one common height
parameter. Its boundary integrals have a strict gap whenever the
eight physical central faces do: convexity in this common height
interpolates between those face bounds and the already controlled
faces at critical height. The complete discrete Fourier correction
is retained separately in the exact source identity. The established
physical-tail certificate therefore controls these zero-frequency
boundary integrals as well.
Sections 4--5 further prove an original logarithmic-gradient bound:
every imaginary index derivative has magnitude less than \(2\pi\)
on the old complex rectangle. After the exact Fourier coefficient
penalty is included, the rate therefore decreases as any absolute
height increases from zero. This pays every vertical lattice term
by the corresponding physical face and reduces all horizontal
products to eight single-coordinate height comparisons. The enlarged-rectangle theorem proves
the same gradient strips and contour reductions on \(C'\), where
the physical-face bounds now hold. Consequently the physical
remainder, simultaneous joining terms and all vertical lattice
corrections are controlled there. The
[eight-alias certificate](../repro/results/research-mixed-contracted-pair-eight-aliases.json)
now proves all eight remaining comparisons. Their upper rates are
less than \(73/50\), hence at least \(1/20\) below the actual
geometric action. The full source consequently has the nonzero
leading term and two-sided bound stated at the beginning of this
section. No remaining contour contribution is omitted from this
paired-kernel conclusion.

The [whole-message criterion](research_mixed_paired_whole_message_schur_criterion.md)
states precisely what is still required for iteration. A weighted
integral bound must control the full-period transform, and its
part outside the central saddle arc must be exponentially smaller
for local output. Given those estimates and an actual incoming
packet with a whole-period envelope, exact linearity and stationary
phase propagate the packet, its original action and nonzero
coefficient, and its error for any fixed number of attachments.
The kernel's own now-proved coefficient is used throughout. The
weighted exterior estimate and the initial whole-message envelope
are hypotheses still to establish; local phase entrance alone
does not supply them.

An earlier [exact contour regrouping](research_exact_vertical_current_regrouping.md)
supplies the identity used in these bounds. The vertical join
from moving the zero-frequency integral cancels part of the
original cotangent coefficient. Below the negative critical height,
and above real height zero, the combined coefficient is exponentially
small. Between the critical height and zero it has no such penalty.
The argument retains the signs, both horizontal corrections, and
all products of contour sides. It supplies an improved bound for
use in the global comparison; the whole-kernel proof above now
combines it with the completed physical and horizontal comparisons.

There is a second exact simplification at the right boundary.
The [suffix reversal formula](research_mixed_coherent_suffix_reversal.md)
sums any fixed suffix completely and expresses it as the generalized
cap for the reversed word followed by one explicit transform. It
retains all Fourier alternatives at the eliminated coordinates.
The local geometric action, its surviving boundary derivative, and
the polynomial power of \(N\) are unchanged. In particular this
allows the problematic ending \((4,3,3+\epsilon)\) to be treated
as one signed boundary function. An estimate for that entire
function would avoid proving the four earlier selected-term
inequalities individually. The exact identity does not yet give
that estimate or exclude cancellation of its local geometric term.

The [completed endpoint extension](research_mixed_cap_upper_target_completion.md)
enlarges the first cap's outgoing real-coordinate interval from
\([.22,.45]\) to \([.22,.5]\), at its original contour height.
It bounds the entire original finite cap with its allocated Fourier
weight, all physical tails and contour terms included. The estimate
retains strict decay away from the complete real ordinary color,
both level parities, and fixed ordinary derivatives. Its proof
combines the extended concavity bound, all cut and alias comparisons,

The [shared-index cancellation theorem](research_mixed_terminal_shared_index_gain_cancellation.md)
further reduces their added cost. For its exact scalar gain \(G\),
with reference \(s_R\), the two forces satisfy \(u<0<v\).
The original curvature decreases toward the right endpoint of the
target interval, and the interval contains the reflection of every
allowed left displacement. Hence \(G(-q)\le G(q)\) for \(q\ge0\).
The positive part of the extra shared-index cost obeys
\[
 [G(u+v)-G(v)]_+
 \le\min\left\{
       \left(1-\frac{v}{-u}\right)_+G(u),
       (1/2-s_R)(-u-2v)_+
       \right\}.
\]
In particular no extra shared-index cost is needed when \(-u\le2v\).
That force-ratio condition has not been proved uniformly and is not
assumed: the displayed bound remains valid when it fails. Substituting
it gives two smaller sufficient inequalities. The fixed calculation
below proves their signs using the linear positive-part bound, with
the common force variables retained throughout.

The [signed boundary-compensation lemma](research_stationary_reference_signed_boundary_compensation.md)
gives another general form of the extension argument. For the original
phase defect \(D\), subtracting
\[
 C=\frac12\Re\sum_{j\in B}\lambda_jp_j\overline{r_j}
\]
removes the signed boundary response exactly, leaving a subharmonic
function \(D-C\). Harmonic measure expresses the correction as a signed
covariance of the boundary derivatives and coordinates. On a disk,
at its center, this covariance is their Fourier inner product; Cauchy
coefficient bounds give an explicit tail estimate if a larger regular
disk is available. The correction also adds under gluing, and matching
internal boundary derivatives cancel before any absolute value is taken.
No favorable covariance sign or new numerical inequality is asserted. In particular,
the Fourier coefficients here belong to the holomorphic boundary functions,
not to Kashaev's invariant. The current first-type-three calculation
continues to use the already reviewed absolute-response bound.

There is also a stronger form specific to concave reference phases.
Center the same compensation at any canonical reference. If every
boundary height follows its reference with coefficient one and the
negative real Hessian of the reference phase is nonnegative along
connecting segments, this centered compensation is nonpositive.
Consequently a uniform negative boundary bound for \(d-C\), where
\(d\) bounds the original phase defect, extends to the whole domain.
The original pair-Hessian theorem verifies these extra premises for
both first endpoint types in the current central and half-row problems.
This criterion uses boundary values and a certified anchor, without
inverse-Jacobian or boundary-derivative bounds. Its boundary inequality
has not been evaluated; it supplies a possible stronger comparison if
the current absolute-response calculation is insufficient.

The [stationary boundary-energy law](research_stationary_reduced_boundary_energy.md)
also gives a compositional version of this method. The energy between
two stationary boundary states equals the sum of the local energies
after exact matching, including at branching vertices. The original
imaginary quadratic filling terms contribute zero to this energy,
although their changes in a selected-height target phase must still
be retained. This supplies a general way to assemble an upper
comparison on regular original domains. It does not establish that
every short filling stays in such a domain or that its whole finite
source has a nonzero geometric contribution.

The [local germ estimate](research_source_germ_truncation_and_turn_remainders.md)
clarifies the separate observation problem. On a fixed regular chart,
logarithmic Taylor order suffices to preserve the proved local
Gaussian packet. However, the original turn can promote a remainder
that is exponentially small on that input chart. What still needs
control is the complementary original source after the actual short
operation, at the new calibrated action. Local jets alone do not
supply that estimate.

The critical path therefore remains explicit. First finish the missing
boundary configurations beyond the first two retained positions,
including combinations with those now treated, and control the
contributions outside the retained plateau. Establish the required
whole-source outside-color gap as well. The geometric action germ for
these positive three/four components is now proved separately above.
Then prove that the whole original source retains its nonzero geometric
term under arbitrary fixed short partial fillings. The finite-branching
deduction would turn that stability theorem into finitely many exceptions
for each fixed template. It would still not give finitely many exceptions
over all templates.

The [rational propagation theorem](research_mixed_rational_critical_transport.md)
provides a simpler description of the reference data for that inequality.
All endpoint exponentials are rational functions of one parameter, and
each adjoining block acts by an invertible rational map preserving the
same differential two-form. A mixed chain of any fixed length is a
composition of these maps with a final endpoint matching condition.
The original logarithmic branches and nonvanishing denominators remain
part of the assertion. This describes the classical critical equations;
it does not prove that a critical point contributes to the quantum sum.

A [bounded exploratory calculation](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-correlated-selected-boundary-curvature/README.md)
used these correlated reference data. Of 25 prescribed inputs, three
passed the necessary local filters; each was evaluated at eight heights.
The largest sampled effective curvature divided by pi was approximately
4.9193, below the proposed bound of six. This is floating evidence only.
The retained inputs are not certified as references of complete words,
the height intervals and reference domain were not covered, and the
forced branch was not optimized. No additional source certificate was
run. The inequality remains unproved.

Two deductions clarify how this work bears on the finite-exception
target. The [residual-edge reduction](research_mixed_short_component_edge_reduction.md)
shows, conditionally on a complete two-boundary theorem, how mixed
three/four chains would remove one family of adjacent short assignments
from the partial-filling induction. It does not remove pendant or
branching components, other short powers, or infinite parameter fibers.
The [power-transfer obstruction](research_mixed_power_transfer_obstruction.md)
also proves that replacing the exponent in the three/four formula by
the crossing power minus one does not give the general crossing source.
An exact level-two calculation already rules out that extrapolation.
The general composition problem therefore still needs the full crossing
operator or a separately derived transfer formula.

There is a separate exact result for the proposed Fourier and positive
metric approach. The [twist-observation theorem](research_original_twist_observation_tomography.md)
keeps the full values and first derivatives at the original spectral
nodes. These define a positive norm at every level, polynomially
equivalent to the physical value-and-derivative norm. Multiplication by
any fixed twist transports this norm with distortion at most one plus
the absolute twist power, independently of the level. At odd prime
level \(N\), observations at \(2N\) closing powers of one permitted
parity reconstruct a polynomially equivalent norm. This supplies a
precise positive Fourier average and an exact transport law. The
observation window grows with the level;
it gives no lower bound for a prescribed fixed filling. Any fixed finite
window has an exact nonzero kernel for large levels, and at infinitely
many composite levels a nonzero derivative direction is invisible even
to every integer closing twist. Finally, in any positive metric on the
full original space, the product of the operator norms of the physical
turn and the triple twist grows exponentially. Thus a universal norm
argument with subexponential cost for both operations cannot work.
Almost invariance or controlled transport of a specified geometric
source direction remains possible and requires its own proof.

The [actual-vertex observability theorem](research_actual_vertex_twist_observability.md)
does remove the collision obstruction for a particular genuine source
class: a fixed crossing power times a fixed product of bare edge
kernels at real outside colors. The normal coefficients within each
coincident-eigenvalue group have the same phase. Their scalar twist
observations therefore control the complete physical-jet norm with
polynomial loss at every level. Fixed twists and multiplication preserve
this class; physical turns have not been shown to do so. The all-level
single-parity version requires even total exponent. For the isolated
filled sources whose scalar asymptotic is already known, the exponential
loss from the unfilled norm to the prescribed observation is exactly
the calibrated filling-action decrease. Thus observability does not
remove the need to pay that action change and prove the nonzero
coefficient when composing a new short piece.

A separate [global critical-value audit](research_global_filled_critical_scope.md)
distinguishes the fully expanded original crossing expression from
collapsed filling expressions. The original regular full critical
points already give marked knot-group representations and the volume
upper bound. In a collapsed expression, a repeated peripheral
eigenvalue can instead satisfy the scalar filling equation without
satisfying the matrix relation. An explicit original local coupon
demonstrates this loss of an additive transport condition; it is not
asserted to be a stationary point of a closed knot expression.

The [matrix extension theorem](research_saturated_matrix_filling.md)
repairs this on the scheme-theoretic closure of the distinct-eigenvalue
filling locus. Components supported entirely on the repeated-eigenvalue
divisor require a separate source argument. The
[original crossing identities](research_original_power_ward_component_exclusion.md)
provide one such local test: any regular formal expansion of the whole
signed-power kernel must obey the full Hurwitz transport, not just its
eigenvalue equation. A formal phase sector with the wrong additive
transport has zero aggregate amplitude to every order. The theorem
requires the identities to act on that whole expansion; it cannot be
applied independently to an arbitrary interpolation's saddles. It
also gives no exponential remainder bound and no nonzero coefficient
for the allowed geometric sector. Those are the next analytic
requirements for using this route in the short-filling theorem.

The [quantitative shift estimate](research_quantitative_power_ward_exclusion.md)
now makes the first of those requirements explicit. The exact original
shift equation gives any fixed inverse power of the level under smooth
symbol bounds. If the normalized whole contribution is holomorphic and
polynomially bounded on a fixed larger complex neighborhood, repeated
Cauchy estimates instead give a fixed exponential loss, with every
localization residual retained. For the explicit parabolic coupon,
one specified generator discrepancy has modulus at least \(7/8\)
for every integer crossing power; the local nonzero-symbol hypothesis
is therefore explicit, although the chart constants depend on the
fixed power. The original factorial factors have
the required local analytic bounds on regular compact sets. Establishing
the corresponding bound and shift-compatible residual control for an
assembled wrong-transport contribution remains open. A homogeneous
shift example proves that vanishing to all formal orders alone would
not justify an exponential gap.

There is now a general consequence for the actual scalar period,
proved in [the growth-characteristic theorem](research_regularized_period_growth_characteristics.md).
For every fixed knot, the whole regularized meridian period \(R_N(Y)\)
obeys a fixed finite-order equation with a polynomially bounded affine
source. Its original finite crossing formula gives locally uniform
exponential bounds; an annulus argument carries those bounds across
the ordinary-color quotient roots. No separate saddle expansion is
assumed. In a logarithmic meridian chart \(Y=e^x\), let
\(\mathcal U\) be the upper growth rate allowing both the level
and a nearby meridian to vary. At every finite positive first-order
upper contact with complex slope \(p\),
\[
                  B_{\rm cl}(e^x,e^{2\pi i p})=0,
\]
where \(B_{\rm cl}\ne0\) is the principal symbol of the original
primitive normal-state operator. Such characteristic contacts approach
every finite positive envelope point. On a positive \(C^1\) region
with simple nonzero symbol roots, the envelope is necessarily the real
part of one local action primitive, plus a constant and an integer
multiple of \(\Re x\). This identifies the differential of actual
smooth growth with a characteristic action without choosing a formal
WKB solution first.

The [common-modulus regularity theorem](research_regularized_growth_single_modulus.md)
removes that differentiability premise when the simple nonzero roots
have one common modulus on a positive disk. After subtracting one
harmonic action, the upper-contact slopes are real and lie in a finite
union of integer translates. A directional comparison makes the
remainder independent of the imaginary meridian coordinate;
subharmonicity then makes it convex in the real coordinate. Interior
convex slope bounds leave only finitely many translates. Thus the
growth is locally a finite maximum of harmonic actions. This does
not choose a geometric root or determine the additive constants.
Different root moduli require a separate argument.

For arbitrary simple nonzero roots on a regular meridian disk,
[vertical regularity](research_regularized_growth_vertical_regularity.md)
now proves that the positive part of the growth envelope is continuous.
It is locally Lipschitz in the imaginary coordinate, locally Holder
of exponent \(2/3\) in the real coordinate, and has finitely many
analytic action pieces on each compact vertical interval. The proof
uses the finite possible vertical slopes of an upper test and then
subharmonicity; it does not assume differentiability or a positive
neighborhood. In particular every positive point has a positive
neighborhood inside the regular-root region. A two-dimensional
finite action decomposition for general root moduli, and control at
a degenerate complete fiber, are not conclusions of this result.

For [two strictly separated modulus classes](research_regularized_growth_two_moduli.md),
the two-dimensional conclusion is now proved as well. A slice has at
most one upward switch. Continuity and fixed vertical buffers give
open strips belonging to the two classes. Their horizontal residuals
are convex with discrete slopes, and the whole intervening envelope
is their maximum. Thus finitely many harmonic actions suffice locally.
This does not cover a modulus-crossing point or establish which action
belongs to the hyperbolic geometry.

The [null-support theorem](research_regularized_growth_null_riesz_support.md)
now gives a general two-dimensional conclusion for arbitrary simple
nonzero characteristic roots. The support of the Laplacian of the
positive growth envelope has area zero on every regular-root disk.
Off that closed set, each component is either a zero-growth region
or follows one actual characteristic action, with a fixed logarithmic
integer and additive constant. The proof retains the zero-growth
locus and all crossings of root moduli. It first proves that pure
vertical intervals persist as open pieces, and then controls their
convex horizontal residuals. This supplies a previously missing
regularity premise, without assuming a stationary-phase expansion.
Finitely many branches near every accumulation point, geometric
branch selection, and the complete-value lower bound remain open.
The support conclusion extends to the entire logarithmic meridian
plane: the squarefree nonzero root set of the nonzero classical
polynomial is regular outside finitely many meridians, and the
remaining discrete fibers have area zero. This describes the same
classical zero set off those fibers; it does not replace the exact
operator or cancel its peripheral factors at the complete point.

The same note compares the original and regularized whole functions.
Their positive joint rates differ only by
\(\max(0,\Re x)\), and agree on the unit circle. The latter
statement uses rectangles whose boundaries avoid the root orbit,
followed by the maximum principle; it does not divide at a quotient
zero. The full ADO monomial and its shift sign are retained separately.
These conclusions concern nearby-meridian upper growth. They do not
give a lower bound at the single complete value \(R_N(1)\).

The distinction from the geometric A-polynomial is still necessary.
The existing partial geometric-support theorem identifies its factor
before the last two framing contractions. The actual full scalar
certificate leaves explicit framing endpoint and logarithmic-carry
currents. Their geometric contribution has not been removed. Thus
the new characteristic theorem neither selects the geometric root
nor fixes the additive growth constant. Even at the complete meridian
the principal symbol may have a vanishing common meridian factor.
Those source and normalization issues, together with pointwise
noncancellation, remain obligations for the volume identity.

The exact original root-orbit norm makes the missing observation
estimate especially concrete. If
\(H_N=N^{-1}\sum_{Y^N=1}|F_N(Y)|^2\), the ordinary-color bound
gives \(H_N=|K_N|^2/N+O(D_N^2)\), with \(D_N\) polynomially
bounded. A positive exponential lower bound for this particular norm
would therefore give the desired positive rate at the complete value.
The other positive Fourier norms already estimated in the research
notes are not interchangeable with \(H_N\): they concern different
observations and can have a strictly larger exponential rate. The
compulsory pivotal closing is not a positive functional, as its
identity and nilpotent test in
[the source positivity obstruction](actual_quantum_source_positivity_obstruction.md)
show. A special positive presentation or an estimate of the signed
observation would have to be proved for the actual source.

There is also a separate level quantifier. The growth envelope uses
\(\limsup_N\), so even a sharp comparison with the complete-value
norm would initially give only a subsequential lower rate. The volume
limit needs a lower bound along all sufficiently large levels. Neither
noncancellation at one level nor a positive upper envelope supplies
that additional conclusion.

The [orbit-jet growth theorem](research_regularized_orbit_jet_growth.md)
now supplies an intermediate quantitative observation under the
explicit condition \(b_0(1,1)b_d(1,1)\ne0\) on the actual recurrence.
For every prescribed rate error, finitely many scaled meridian
derivatives at \(d\) neighboring root-orbit points capture the positive
joint rate within that error. The derivative order is fixed before
the level varies, but may depend on the error. The proof keeps all
central aliases: Hermite Fourier reconstruction uses the fixed linear
Laurent-degree bound from the original crossings, recurrence transport
controls a short arc, and a polynomial factor suppresses its complement.
This does not prove growth of the single complete value, nor address
an operator whose end coefficients vanish there.

The [singular-arc extension](research_regularized_singular_orbit_jet_growth.md)
now handles vanishing end factors whose nearby divisors split
analytically in the quantum parameter. It keeps their whole leading
germs and costs only \(O(\alpha(1+|\log\alpha|))\) in rate. This
applies to the specified actual figure-eight operator. Its existing
microscopic profile then identifies the whole joint complex growth
at completeness with \(\operatorname{Vol}(4_1)/(2\pi)\); this is
an upgrade from microscopic to joint growth, not a new complete-value
volume proof. The actual generic color pointing also forces a double
\(L=1\) root whenever \(B_{\rm cl}(1,L)\) is not identically zero.

[The unnormalized Weyl identity](scaled_meridian_regular_profile.md),
Section 4.1, gives a direct comparison with one derivative at the
complete point: its first scaled meridian derivative equals
\(-(N-1)R_N(1)/(2N)\) plus a polynomially bounded error.
Consequently the complete value and this first derivative have
the same positive limsup and liminf rates. This uses no division
by \(K_N\) or prior growth assumption. Higher even balanced
derivatives remain independent observations.

The [fixed microscopic-disk theorem](research_regularized_microscopic_disk_growth.md)
now removes the divisor-splitting assumption at the function level.
Provided the two end coefficients are not identically zero as
classical Laurent polynomials, one disk of radius
\(3+2\pi(d-1)\) in the scaled coordinate \(Y=e^{\zeta/N}\)
has exactly the positive joint growth rate. The common microscopic
contour avoids all nearby divisor zeros; their fixed lattice spacing
controls the whole leading product without an arithmetic separation
assumption. This covers ramified and arbitrarily close roots and
retains every peripheral factor. Comparing this particular disk norm
to \(e^{o(N)}(1+|K_N|)\) is now a precise sufficient source estimate
for the complete-value limsup. Classical end-degree loss and an
all-level lower bound remain separate issues.

The [microscopic variation and radius theorem](research_subexponential_variation_meridian_observation.md)
now makes the radius in that observation immaterial: any two fixed
positive microscopic disks have norms differing by at most
\(\exp(O(N/\log N))\), after taking their maximum with one.
The proof applies Hadamard's three-circle inequality between those
disks and a disk of radius proportional to \(N\) in the scaled
coordinate, where the original Laurent-degree and growth bounds apply.
This comparison is levelwise, so both limsup and liminf rates agree.
It still does not compare a disk norm with its central value.

Consequently the existing strict long-twist Conway theorem, with its
original component, framing, parity and strictness qualifications,
gives the regularized disk-norm volume limit on every fixed microscopic
disk. The old profile before the first resonance suffices; the new
comparison extends its norm rate across any fixed number of ordinary
resonances. This does not extend the knot class or assert a nonzero
pointwise profile at every resonance. A further identification with
the unscaled joint envelope still requires the recurrence's classical
end condition.

For an exact paired-factor representation, the same note proves that
subexponential total variation relative to \(1+|K_N|\) suffices for
the desired microscopic bound. Unlike profile convergence, this upper
bound needs no concentration of private indices away from their
endpoints. The full ordinary-color subtraction and maximum principle
carry the estimate through the resonant zeros. Actual multiplication
and cap formulas prevent deriving the variation hypothesis by taking
absolute values entry by entry: some moving tensor terms revive with
an exponential excess, and some private-row sums already lose an
exponential factor before the next contraction. A successful argument
must retain the relevant signed contractions or justify an equivalent
integration cycle. The existing grouped long-filling proof does so
in its stated class; arbitrary short components remain untreated.

The [differentiated-crossing identity](research_actual_microscopic_derivative_coupons.md)
now specifies the whole meridian derivative as a finite list of actual
signed crossing insertions, with the pivot derivative and ordinary-color
subtraction retained. A sublinear relative bound for their summed
contraction on one fixed microscopic disk would imply the desired
observation estimate by integration along radial segments. This argument
does not divide by \(K_N\), so it also applies at levels where the
complete value vanishes. The required signed bound is unproved; the
coefficientwise logarithmic bound controls total variation instead and
cannot replace it. Weyl symmetry controls the odd balanced derivatives;
the second even derivative is the first remaining boundary datum.

The [paired short-crossing formula](research_actual_paired_crossing_boundary_transport.md)
makes the local transport of that datum explicit. Pairing the two
coalescing Casimir channels and dividing their difference by the scaled
meridian displacement gives a two-dimensional observation which retains
the complete derivative channel. Every fixed signed crossing power and
its inverse act by an explicit uniformly bounded matrix, and the
original closing row has polynomial norm. Earlier source bounds already
allowed all such fixed twists and their parameter derivatives; this is
an explicit refinement of their transport, not a new hyperbolic knot
class. Changes of pairing still retain the original complete turn, and
the boundary observation is not bounded by one closing scalar. The same
calculation shows why the second even central derivative depends on
the first thickening of the complete Casimir algebra, rather than on
values in that algebra alone.

The [coherent contour construction](research_actual_coherent_polarization_transport.md)
preserves the exact finite source while moving its resolutions through
bounded regular complex critical data. One actual crossing already
leaves the original positive real coherent sphere, so positivity of
that original sphere does not give automatic propagation. Adapted
spheres repair the contour representation, but their metric changes
can have exponential condition numbers. The
[local Hessian gluing test](research_actual_coherent_gluing_hessian.md)
now gives explicit conditions on the original coupon derivatives under
which their real quadratic forms compose to a negative form after
transverse closure. Those local inequalities have not been proved for
arbitrary signed crossings and turns. The geometric channel Hessian
does not control the separate magnetic directions, and the original
framing radical must be retained until its external pairing is made.
No general nonzero geometric coefficient follows from these reductions.

The [level-dependent metric theorem](research_geometric_transport_level_dependent_metric_obstruction.md)
strengthens the earlier obstruction from a single parabolic loop.
It allows arbitrary positive definite metrics on the full
\(N\)-dimensional symmetric-power fibers, with no conditioning bound
and no requirement that they be induced from two-dimensional metrics.
For complete finite-volume cusp holonomy, two conjugate parabolics
have distinct fixed flags. After normalization they are
\[
 P=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\b&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad ab\ne0.
\]
A fixed integer \(n\) with \(n|ab|>4\) makes
\(L=P^nQ\) loxodromic. Write \(\rho(L)=e^\gamma>1\).
For a fixed closed geometric transport path
\(g_\ell\cdots g_1=\pm L\), every choice of successive positive
metrics, returning to the same initial metric, satisfies
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^{\ell}
   \|\operatorname{Sym}^{N-1}g_j\|_{H_{j-1,N}\to H_{j,N}}
        \ge e^{(N-1)\gamma}.
\]
This follows from submultiplicativity and the metric-independent
spectral radius of the loop. Therefore not all these edge norms can
be \(\exp(o(N))\), even when the metrics depend on \(N\).
Every finite-index subgroup contains \(L^k\) for some positive \(k\).
Along the literal repeated lift, its rate per edge remains
\(\gamma/\ell\). Normality of the cover is unnecessary.

The finite-volume assertion and the metric and cover statements have
direct proofs in the note. The result applies to the flat geometric
local system along the specified loop. It does not assert that a
particular quantum wire graph contains that loop, or that an original
quantum crossing is its symmetric-power transport. Exact frame
cancellation in the original scalar and nonflat choices of contour
are unaffected. This removes an asymptotically inexpensive flat-metric
proposal; it supplies neither a geometric coefficient nor a new
volume-equality family.

The complete final proof and both complete direct-source implications
were checked by author, separate peer and root at SHA256
bd2698727e9577f4b8bbdba28154e6499827cf89725ebdababfea39ce7662f64.
The coherent-contour and gluing-Hessian source versions are respectively
10423fbb5c38b162a68173c1aa3fd2ec7af0f0433878b77390cb7b659e8db2af
and 86fdd6c3bcb1eabefd733b24e63fcc8c62b1fb5411e73239f9b4ab9caefcb217.
No mathematical program or numerical check was used.

The [operator end-loss calculation](research_actual_operator_end_loss_and_coefficient_space.md)
also rules out repairing a minimal recurrence's lost classical ends
by taking another finite homogeneous annihilator of the same original
normal state. The two end losses add under exact Ore multiplication,
and the original Weyl symmetry makes them equal. This obstruction
does not rule out a separately justified affine equation with a
controlled source. A formal reduction to the smaller classical order
retains a remainder containing the unknown whole period; a fixed
power of \(N^{-1}\) does not supply an exponential gap.

Independently of end preservation, the exact coefficient recurrence
has at most \((2A+1)D\) free coefficients on support \([-AN,AN]\),
where \(D\) is the shift span of the extreme meridian coefficient
of the fixed operator. Thus its affine polynomial solution set has
bounded dimension as the level grows. This is an algebraic reduction,
not a conditioning estimate or a complete-value lower bound. The
same calculation shows that positive complete-value growth rules out
a monomial classical symbol, and therefore implies end preservation
for an actual minimal normal operator of order at most two. No
general order bound or positive-growth theorem is inferred from it.

The [actual Green obstruction](research_actual_weyl_green_obstruction.md)
also prevents replacing the complete observation by a left zero-mode
overlap. The cyclic determinant of the whole normal equation vanishes
identically, and all left zero modes annihilate its first normal
forcing. The correct dual equation has the point source on its
right side. A primitive-minimal actual unknot calculation verifies
this distinction with the original ordinary data and root rank.
No non-diagonal duality or further estimate of the inhomogeneous
pairing is ruled out.

For the full scalar geometric-factor question,
[a finite first-symbol test](research_full_certificate_first_symbol_test.md)
now expresses a sufficient condition directly in the coefficients of
the original finite-array certificate. It retains the transverse
moment weights and both framing differences. An explicit mixed first
moment explains why the existing existence construction and the
normalized cut do not supply the needed extra quantum order.
The valuation test, or its weaker principal-current cancellation
version, has not been verified for a broad class of certificates.
This is a concrete test for the missing bridge, not its proof.

A complementary [adjoint shift estimate](research_whole_kernel_adjoint_ward_localization.md)
localizes a contour observation by applying the exact shifts to an
analytic test function. It retains every translated endpoint or face
current. It gives exponential suppression if the weighted contour norm,
the original residual and the translated boundaries have the required
rates; those rates have not been established for an arbitrary short
component. In particular its boundary factor of \(N^{-1}\) is only
a polynomial saving and cannot replace an exponential gap.

There is now also a
[whole type-three terminal bound at selected incoming heights](research_mixed_terminal_three_selected_height_completion.md).
For a type-four incoming coordinate, it allows every selected height
in \([0,.014]\) while retaining the actual Fourier halfweight and
all original transform and Newton indices. The low physical strip
is transported to a real-index anchor before the incoming-height
comparison is applied; the complex joins are controlled by separate
height convexity. The result is a horizontal upper plane, not a new
Gaussian contribution. Relative to the original complex affine plane,
the term \(\Im p\,(h-c)\) remains, where \(p\) is the terminal
phase's incoming derivative. It must still be combined with the
neighboring factor in the global proof.

The corresponding
[type-four selected-height theorem](research_mixed_terminal_four_selected_height_completion.md)
is now proved as well. Its different private-index sectors retain the
whole inner endpoint polynomial, and its full physical partition
includes the even-level half row exactly once. The
[saved-bound extraction](research_mixed_terminal_four_alias_reserve.md)
and [completed exact checker](../repro/results/research-mixed-terminal-four-alias-reserve.json)
supply gap \(1/10\) for all twelve aliases on the necessary actual-reference
set, without evaluating new roots or source functions. Corollary 2 of
the same theorem also proves unselected height attenuation from the
actual negative height to zero, for both terminal types. All these
bounds retain the original imaginary affine term when they are used
against a neighboring factor.

The [terminal tangent sign](research_mixed_terminal_height_tangent_sign.md)
now proves that this remaining term is strictly positive for either
terminal type when the incoming coordinate has type four:
\(\Im p>7\pi/100\). Moving its height from \(c\) to \(k>c\)
therefore leaves a fee greater than \(7\pi(k-c)/100\) relative
to the original complex affine plane. The neighboring ordinary
complex tangent does not cancel a term already omitted from the
terminal horizontal bound. A separate strict loss or a joint
comparison is necessary. This is a limitation of those two upper
bounds, not a positive defect of the actual quantum expression.

The [first boundary-region theorem](research_mixed_first_collar_full_terminal_completion.md)
now treats every fixed mixed word of length at least three, with either
terminal type. The first integration coordinate is near zero, the
second stays in its specified type-dependent interval, and the later
coordinates range independently over the plateau with their unselected
Fourier terms. Both allowed selections at the first coordinate and at
a type-four second coordinate are included. The terminal height bounds
cancel the adjacent real linear terms exactly. The whole contribution
of this region is at most a polynomial times
\(e^{N(M_{\rm open}-1/50)}\), after choosing one total error tolerance;
\(M_{\rm open}\) is the real action at the geometric critical point.
This removes a competing region for every such chain length. Later
selected coordinates and coordinates outside the stated intervals are
not covered by this theorem.

The [two-block boundary estimate](research_mixed_two_vertex_first_collar.md)
treats the missing length-two case. Here the same coordinate enters
both end factors, so the longer-chain plateau argument cannot be
used. A direct bound for the exact terminal sum, combined with the
first-cap bound and the actual geometric action, gives loss \(1/20\)
on a sufficiently small fixed interval near zero. The contour is
exactly real there for both Fourier selections. Both block types at
either end, both level parities, and small ordinary-color neighborhoods
are included. This remains a bound on that boundary region alone.

Exact [transposition of the full finite source](research_mixed_reversed_complete_collar.md)
transfers these estimates to the other end in the opposite retained
coordinate chart, with both ordinary boundary colors and all Fourier
weights preserved. It does not identify two localized integrals in
the same chart. An exact level-two calculation shows that the chart
integrands can differ by nonzero Fourier terms whose full constant
term vanishes but whose integral over a short arc does not. Thus
the two collar estimates cannot simply be added as parts of one
partition of the original integral.

The [endpoint real-color theorem](research_mixed_endpoint_real_color_decay.md)
also proves decay away from the complete outside color for the exact
endpoint coefficient and both complete first caps. With the ordinary
color written as \(w=-2\cos\theta\), their upper exponent loses
\(c(1-\cos\theta)\), where \(c>0\), uniformly over the full real
angle interval. The proof includes the original finite rows, including
rows that vanish at the complete color and reappear at other colors.
It uses an exact factorial inequality on the existing integration
contours and separate bounds for the omitted rows. Near the actual
outgoing critical values it also gives a quadratic bound for small
imaginary changes of the outside angle. The analogous estimate for
the entire chain still requires control of its remaining regions.

The [complete terminal real-color theorem](research_mixed_terminal_real_color_decay.md)
supplies the corresponding calibrated angular loss for both terminal
types on the whole unselected plateau. Its proof checks the upper
Newton rows at general real colors and keeps every revived product
on the complex contours. In the type-four partition, removing the
complete initial transform rows permits deletion of globally zero
private columns; it does not justify a triangular truncation after
contour deformation. This gives the compact physical-index bound
needed for the remaining whole endpoint coefficients.

Consequently the [central-region boundary theorem](research_mixed_central_region_boundary_colors.md)
now proves the real outside-color gap and the quadratic complex
boundary bound for the plateau contribution with all the controlled
interior selections included. This restricted integral is still an
entire polynomial of ordinary degree less than the level at each end,
because its integration domains and heights are fixed independently
of the colors. Its original nonzero local asymptotic and the real gap
therefore satisfy the precise hypotheses of the stability lemma.
The complement of that region must still be bounded before these
conclusions can be used for the whole open source in a filling theorem.

The lower estimate for the central region comes from a nonzero
stationary-phase coefficient and an exponentially smaller remainder
within that region. It does not use positivity of all summands, and
neither Parseval's identity nor Cauchy--Schwarz alone gives a lower
bound for the complete signed invariant. No universal estimate from
almost-invariant vectors has been established.

The remaining critical path is to control the other Fourier alternatives
and the regions outside the plateau, then establish stability under
arbitrary short partial fillings. The finite-branching deduction will
give the requested per-template finite-exception theorem only after
that stability theorem is proved.

The [stability reduction](research_mixed_open_source_stability_reduction.md)
separates two analytic requirements that must not be conflated. A
complete local asymptotic for the open source needs control of all its
retained contour regions near the complete outside colors. Subsequent
fillings also require a strict bound for the entire polynomial at
outside colors away from those complete values. The new reduction
proves that a local packet and this calibrated real-color gap imply
the needed quadratic complex-strip bound; the local angular Hessian
already follows from the endpoint marginals. A marked geometric
boundary germ remains a separate input. Moreover, arbitrary short
components and reductions still have to be covered: the strict-padding
example produces infinite assignment families for one unresolved core,
so a finite list of unresolved cores would not establish the stated
finite-assignment goal.

## Earlier results and attempts

The account below records the intermediate hypotheses and stopped
attempts that led to the completed comparisons above. Statements that
a cap or terminal certificate was pending refer to those earlier
stages, not to the current status.

The main new result is the
[complete type-three terminal theorem](research_mixed_terminal_three_full_completion.md).
For this entire finite boundary polynomial, we have proved the original
geometric asymptotic with a nonzero leading coefficient, along all
integer levels and with every fixed ordinary-color derivative. The
proof controls every summation row and every Fourier term, rather than
only its central integral. It also gives the upper bound needed to
attach this terminal block to a specified first-collar source sector.
The analogous type-four estimate, the remaining regions of the full
open source, and stability under arbitrary short partial fillings are
still open. Thus this is a completed analytic input to the research
goal, not the finite-exceptions theorem itself.

The completed terminal estimate now gives a
[nonzero contribution from a larger integration region](research_mixed_terminal_three_plateau_slab.md)
for every fixed word length at least two, provided the terminal block
has type three. The first retained coordinate stays in the neighborhood
where the first-cap asymptotic is proved; every later retained real
coordinate ranges independently over the full interval \([.22,.45]\).
All retained coordinates use their unselected Fourier alternative and
their original critical heights. Multiplying the complete factor bounds
cancels every linear term in the exponent and leaves a strictly negative
quadratic term away from the geometric critical point. Integration over
this entire region therefore has the original nonzero leading term,
with power \(N^{-3/2}\) after normalization. The regions excluded by
these hypotheses still have to be estimated before this conclusion can
be asserted for the whole open source.

The [height-transport theorem](research_mixed_terminal_three_height_transport.md)
also extends the complete terminal upper bound toward the real contour
when its incoming coordinate has type three. It transports each term
or integral in the existing finite decomposition, preserving the
cancellations already used within each term. Combined with the first-pair
estimate, this settles the first boundary region for the length-three
words \((3,3,3)\) and \((4,3,3)\). These are additional controlled
integration regions, not new knot-volume theorems.

The same transport argument now has a
[common formulation for both terminal types](research_mixed_terminal_height_transport.md).
Their physical rows have exactly the same incoming factor, and their
complex transform-index phases have the same incoming derivative.
Transporting each part of the original decomposition therefore gives
the same bound for a type-three incoming leg. The type-three application
is complete. The type-four application, including the corresponding
length-three first-boundary regions, remains conditional on its complete
terminal source comparisons.

For a type-four incoming coordinate, a separate
[selected-height calculation](research_mixed_terminal_selected_height_rows.md)
now treats every physical transform row with index at least
\(3N/20\). After including both alternatives in the actual Fourier
halfweight, moving the incoming height from its negative reference
value to any selected height in \([0,.014]\) costs no additional
exponential rate. The proof uses the exact Poisson derivative of the
finite-product rate, reflection across the real axis, and an explicit
integral bound on the relevant Poisson arcs. It preserves each whole
incoming-independent coefficient; it does not transport cancellation
between different outer rows. For complex transform indices with real
part at least \(.21\), the analogous rate transport also has no added
cost. On the remaining strip \([.15,.21)\) the note retains an explicit
possible cost. In every case the original imaginary affine term must
still be matched by the neighboring factor. The small physical indices
and that complex strip prevent this result from being a complete
selected-terminal theorem.

The type-three alias bounds have also been strengthened without a new
source computation. An
[exact saved-bound extraction](research_mixed_terminal_three_alias_reserve.md)
and its [completed record](../repro/results/research-mixed-terminal-three-alias-reserve.json)

For the other terminal type, the

The [oriented ordinary-map extraction](research_mixed_first_cap_oriented_plateau_certificate.md)

The latest boundary calculation keeps the last block and its endpoint

The [terminal end-tail theorem](research_mixed_terminal_transform_tails.md)

For type three, a second

The [two-variable difference system](research_mixed_terminal_three_marked_difference_system.md)
now characterizes this finite source exactly. An auxiliary variable

Their classical equations agree with the

The [joint phase estimate](research_mixed_terminal_three_joint_zero_mode.md)

The exact double-summand interpolation transfers its supporting-plane

The [mixed-face acceptance rule](research_mixed_terminal_three_mixed_face_certificate.md)

The resulting [zero-mode theorem](research_mixed_terminal_three_zero_mode_completion.md)

\[
 Z_N^0=\frac{2\pi}{N}
       \frac{\mathcal A_*}{\sqrt{\det H_*}}
       e^{N\mathcal P_0}(1+O(N^{-1})),
 \qquad \mathcal A_*\ne0.
\]
Here \(\mathcal P_0\) is the selected terminal action,
\(H_*\) is the negative Hessian in the two internal variables,
and \(\mathcal A_*\) is the amplitude of the original interpolated
summand. The Gaussian branch specifies the square root. This proves

The [exact alias reduction](research_mixed_terminal_three_alias_reduction.md)

The [right-triangle theorem](research_mixed_terminal_three_right_triangle.md)
