## Earlier development and certificate attempts

The remainder records the deductions and incomplete attempts that led
to the results above. Their original unresolved comparisons are retained
to explain the development; the completed records above govern the
current status of the ordinary row and type-three terminal work.

The earlier completed endpoint estimates cover every first-pair type
\(33,34,43,44\), and the terminal right half near the actual
geometric reference of every three/four word of length at least two.
The latter comparison has a common finite loss \(1/5000\); its
neighborhood may depend on the fixed word. The proof uses the actual
neighboring gluing equation in the one family where an independent-disk
estimate is false. The [type-three](research_mixed_three_first_vertical_phase.md)
and [type-four](research_mixed_four_first_vertical_phase.md) phase
comparisons also cover the full first-collar height changes, with the
next reference fixed. The complete finite sums along those paths are
now controlled by keeping the original reference contours. The
[second-three transport](research_mixed_three_first_source_transport.md)
gives first-cap and first-two-edge losses \(1/40\) and \(1/50\)
for prefixes \(33\) and \(43\). The
[second-four transport](research_mixed_four_fixed_contour_transport.md)
gives loss \(1/25\) for both \(34\) and \(44\), including
the selected second coordinate. The third target is unchanged and
unselected in these statements. Their proof retains all original rows,
the two Fourier alternatives, and every contour current; it does not
require a nonzero asymptotic at the transported parameter. Attaching
these bounds to the existing coherent endpoint buffers is now proved
in the [full-collar buffered theorem](research_mixed_full_collar_buffered_sectors.md):
the whole integrand retains left loss \(1/100\) with an arbitrary
mixed interior, provided the two prescribed plateau corridors and
the small neighboring buffer neighborhoods remain present. This removes
the old first-subcollar and second-selection restrictions, but does
not cover configurations outside those buffers and corridors.
Neither these results nor the cyclic theorem below imply the full
ordinary knot contraction.

The horizontal extension now has a complete cancellation of its
remaining real boundary force on the already admitted source domain.
The [uniform-floor tangent theorem](research_mixed_first_collar_horizontal_tangent.md)
keeps the actual first cap fixed and varies the neighboring real
coordinate in its full typed interval. The old phase lower bound is
uniform on that interval, and concavity places it below the original
tangent line. The next part of the chain has the opposite slope.
Combining the two bounds therefore pays every admitted horizontal
displacement, retaining a common finite loss \(1/50\) and a quadratic
loss in the free real coordinates. All four first-pair types and both
allowed second-coordinate Fourier choices are covered. This earlier version needs
the original complete-source domain, but no extra bound on the
boundary slope and no first-wire sign condition.

The new fixed-reference proofs remove that source-domain hypothesis
from the ordinary part of the left prefix, while retaining explicit
unproved row comparisons. The
[ending-three proof](research_mixed_first_collar_fixed_reference_completion.md)
and [ending-four proof](research_mixed_four_enlarged_contour_transport.md)
allow every later unselected real coordinate to vary independently
in \([.22,.45]\), at its actual height. The second real coordinate
stays in its full typed interval; its entire physical height path,
including the selected type-four branch, is allowed. Every critical
point used in the estimate remains at the original reference.

More precisely, let \(D_j\) be the positive part of the larger of
the midpoint and final-row rates minus the original quadratic
supporting plane of ordinary factor \(j\). For a prefix ending
at an ordinary cut \(3\le h\le m-1\), the new bound is
\[
 \frac1N\log\mathcal L_{h,N}
 \le M_h+\Re P_{h,b}d_h-\delta
       +\sum_{j=3}^hD_j
       -\frac{d_2^2+2\sum_{j=3}^{h-1}d_j^2+d_h^2}{2500000}
       +\tau+O_h(\log N/N).
\]
Here \(\mathcal L_{h,N}\) is the literal prefix modulus with
its full internal Fourier weights and one cut halfweight,
\(M_h\) is its original reference action, \(d_j\) is the
real displacement, and \(P_{h,b}\) is the derivative at the
cut. The reserve \(\delta\) is \(3/100\) for prefix 33,
\(3/125\) for 43, and \(4/125\) for 34 or 44.
All internal linear terms cancel by the original gluing equations;
the surviving cut tangent cancels its opposite boundary term when
the prefix is attached. There is one prescribed total tolerance
\(\tau\), rather than a fixed loss charged on every edge.
If the displayed excesses vanish, all four cases retain a common
loss \(1/50\). The existing safe corridors still pay their
pinning costs with their stronger curvature. Terminal factors,
later selected coordinates and the rest of the ordinary closure
remain outside this extension. The two row comparisons have not
been assumed true in its unconditional inequality.

The [asymmetric-contour theorem](research_mixed_horizontal_asymmetric_contour.md)
supplies a complete finite upper bound on the full horizontal
plateau without following a new critical point. Its lower contour stays
at height \(-1/5\); its upper contour is moved to height \(1\).
Both horizontal additional-frequency contributions lie strictly below
the original supporting plane. The vertical contributions are bounded
by the real cuts, and the zero-mode joins by their endpoints. The
[half-index extension](research_mixed_half_index_contour.md) moves the
right real cut from \(.49\) to \(1/2\), retaining these estimates.

The [right-tail theorem](research_mixed_right_tail_endpoint_bound.md)
then proves that every row between \(1/2\) and \(1\) is bounded
by one of those two endpoints. It holds for both block types, all
real arguments in \([.22,.45]^2\), and all fixed heights of
absolute value at most \(.108\), which includes the actual reference
heights. Reflection of the product integrals reduces the proof to a
one-variable derivative comparison. The remaining numerical-looking
constants are proved by finite rational inequalities and bounds for
convergent series. The row-independent factorial factors are retained.
No interior quartic or sextic root needs to be estimated.

Consequently the complete finite upper rate for this conditional factor
is \(\max(B,T_*)\), up to an arbitrary prescribed tolerance, where
\(B\) is the original supporting plane with its quadratic horizontal
loss and
\[
 T_*=\max\{R(3/20),R(1/2),R(1)\}.
\]
Here \(R(u)\) is the full allocated absolute-row rate at row fraction
\(u\). The left-tail maximum is already known to occur at \(3/20\).
All original rows and both level parities are included. The three
remaining values are explicit functions of the outer arguments; they
are not three fixed numerical tests. Proving \(T_*\le B\), or paying
its positive excess in the actual chain, remains necessary. In
particular, a fixed loss per edge cannot be accumulated over unbounded
word lengths. This upper-bound reduction supplies no lower bound by
itself.

There is also a [boundary principle](research_mixed_horizontal_tail_reference_boundary.md)
for that comparison. Strict concavity shows that a deficit larger than
the known negative reference gap must attain its maximum on the
ordinary boundary of the reference parameter domain. This leaves
circle-times-disk faces; the older checks on two circles do not cover
them. The [last-row optimization](research_mixed_horizontal_revived_endpoint.md)
gives an exact scalar maximum and a strict bound in specified favorable
directions. A bound on all the boundary faces is still missing. The
right-tail theorem uses the smaller actual height range and must not
be applied automatically to the entire auxiliary boundary domain.

The proposed stronger comparison on the full auxiliary reference domain
is now known to fail at the old left cut. A
[single coupled reference](research_mixed_left_cut_independent_reference_obstruction.md)
of own type four, with external types three and four, gives
\(R(3/20)-M-p_ad_a-p_bd_b>1/1000\). Its original logarithmic
equations and strict excess have been checked with one outward root
witness and a saved higher-precision replay. All its individual heights
are smaller than \(.108\) in absolute value. It has not been realized
as the reference of a whole word, and a bound for an absolute row is
not a lower bound for the complete sum. This example rules out the
stronger auxiliary-domain argument, not the desired knot theorem.

For own type four, a [smaller left cutoff](research_mixed_four_left_cut_extension.md)
offers a way past this particular obstruction. The extra index
factorial makes the full three-variable Hessian positive on the added
strip down to \(1/8\), even though the separate pair estimates need
not hold there. Moving the upper contour to height \(5/4\) also
keeps every additional-frequency contribution below the same supporting
plane. Thus the complete bound now uses
\(\max\{B,R(1/8),R(1/2),R(1)\}\) for this own type, and
\(R(1/8)<R(3/20)-1/80\) uniformly. The original cutoff remains
available for own type three.

The [uniform comparison at the new cutoff](research_mixed_four_left_cut_support.md)
now proves \(R(1/8)<B-1/2000\) for every ordinary own-four
reference in the reduced input products, both conditional orientations,
and every horizontal target in \([.22,.45]^2\). The proof reduces
the reference domain to its ordinary boundary faces and uses strict
target concavity to control all targets without a target grid. All

saved replay, with the same 64,469 root witnesses and no refinements.
For these ordinary references the complete finite upper bound therefore
reduces to \(\max\{B,R(1/2),R(1)\}\), with the prescribed

comparison.

The [own-three comparison](research_mixed_three_left_cut_support.md)
is now complete as well, at its original cutoff \(3/20\).
It proves \(R(3/20)<B-1/2000\) on every ordinary reduced
reference product, in both conditional orientations and for every

supplied the sixth from an already completed equal-type face.
Every transported witness was directly validated before assembly.
The original checker then replayed all six faces at 320 bits, with
299,951 saved root witnesses, no proposals and no refinements.
Thus both own types now have the complete finite upper maximum
\(\max\{B,R(1/2),R(1)\}\), with one prescribed tolerance.
This removes the left-row comparison for ordinary factors; the
half row, last row and different terminal endpoint graphs remain.

The [half-row comparison](research_mixed_half_row_vertical_comparison.md)
settles one of them on an explicit region. With index height \(y_0\),
outer heights \(h_a,h_b\), and real targets \(x,z\), define
\[
 q=\sin(2\pi x)+e^{2\pi h_b}\sin(2\pi(x-z))
                  -e^{2\pi(h_a+h_b)}\sin(2\pi z).
\]
If \(y_0q\le0\), direct vertical integration gives
\(R(1/2)\le B-\mu(1/2-\Re s_0)^2/2\), where
\(\mu=1/1250000\) is the existing joint curvature constant.
In particular this applies when all three heights are nonpositive
and \(x\ge z\). The original logarithmic lift, marginals and
halfweights are retained. The complement of this region remains open.

A [stronger curvature estimate](research_mixed_half_row_horizontal_payment.md)
gives a quantitative comparison beyond that sign region. On the
relevant fixed-height index strip \(.23\le\Re s\le.5\), the
joint negative real Hessian is greater than \(I/10\). Let
\(d_s=.5-\Re s_0\), let \(d_a,d_b\) be the two real target
displacements, and put \(\Theta_0=\Im F_s(.5;a,b)\) on the
original logarithmic lift. Then
\[
 R(1/2)\le M+p_ad_a+p_bd_b
  -\frac{d_s^2+d_a^2+d_b^2}{20}
  +y_0\Theta_0-\frac\pi{12}y_0^2.
\]
This pays additional regions with \(y_0\Theta_0>0\), as specified
in that note. Its sufficient inequality has not been proved over all
actual references and targets.
The [uniform half-row certificate design](research_mixed_half_row_support.md)
instead optimizes both target coordinates by strict concavity and
tests the ordinary reference boundary. Its bounded author attempt
completed one of the twelve faces before reaching the time limit;
the partial opposite face and its exact pending boxes are saved in
[the incomplete record](../repro/results/research-mixed-half-row-support-partial.json).
No point obstruction was certified, but the missing coverage prevents
a uniform half-row conclusion. A later continuation can use the exact
input/root exchange on equal-type faces; it must preserve the original
coupled roots, Fourier allocations and full target square.
The [optimized-envelope method](research_mixed_half_row_optimized_envelope.md)
provides a sharper alternative acceptance rule. It proves target
curvature greater than \(720\pi/781\), encloses the unique clipped
maximizer, and differentiates the maximized value with respect to the
reference. The midpoint requires a target-optimization remainder;
the rest of the cell is controlled directly by the derivative of
that maximized value. This rule has a written proof and an
[implementation](research_mixed_optimized_half_row_support.md).
Its [bounded pilot](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-optimized-half-row-support-pilot/README.md)
resolved exactly the same parameter volume and retained the same
frontier as the previous pilot: \(535/262144\), with fourteen
pending boxes. Six accepted boxes changed on each side, but there
was no net coverage gain. A
[diagnosis using three saved witnesses](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-optimized-half-row-performance/README.md)
shows that widening the optimizer interval increases the derivative
bound enough to offset the smaller midpoint error. It also shows
substantially different costs in the three parameter directions.

on a sufficiently small ordinary-color neighborhood. An exact
derivative identity handles the full compact private-index interval;
separate finite-product estimates cover both endpoint tails. Thus the
argument requires only two fixed action evaluations, rather than a
grid of private indices. The focused checker and its saved 320-bit
replay verify the scalar inequalities and bind the inherited results.
The adjacent conditional factor and its reference tangent are still
absent from these ceilings, so the full boundary comparison remains
open.

For a [prefix of two type-three blocks](research_mixed_three_cap_collar_comparison.md),
one calibrated comparison is now proved. The literal cap and its
adjacent conditional factor have a loss of \(1/40\) on the first
real collar \([0,1/1000]\), when the second real coordinate is at

of that second coordinate. This retains the surviving complex

real root disks and scalar budgets passed their saved higher-precision
replay. Other prefixes and the remaining boundary completion are
not covered by this estimate.

The [four-three prefix](research_mixed_four_three_cap_collar.md)
now has its own proved comparison. An asymmetric cotangent-domain
argument controls the conditional root along the first negative-height
segment. Its phase increases along that segment, and the complete first
Fourier weight remains in the action and in the finite source. The

collar, throughout the actual attenuation of the second height. Both
first selections, both level parities and ordinary-colour derivatives
are included. The focused scalar and exact-identity check has a saved

beginning \((4,3)\); the rest of the global boundary comparison
remains separate.

The [prefixes with second type four](research_mixed_second_four_cap_collar.md)
are now covered as well. A one-sided cubic-root domain supplies

and twelve previously checked real phase values give the required

weight, the second halfweight, and both second selections. It gives

sufficiently small fixed first collar. Its exact identities and scalar
inequalities have a saved 320-bit replay. Thus all four first-pair
type combinations in a three/four word have a calibrated collar
estimate; this statement concerns the allocated pair, not the entire

The [following-edge phase theorem](research_mixed_four_first_vertical_phase.md)
removes a phase obstruction to enlarging the first-collar estimate when

or selected interval, with the next reference unchanged. The proof

Bernstein coefficient tables; its symbolic and scalar checks have a

pays the following phase change without a small height reset.
This is a phase theorem. Its sharper moving-phase upper bound,
equation (18), remains unproved. The fixed-reference source estimate
described below now supplies the weaker bound actually needed for the

alternatives.

The [type-three following-edge comparison](research_mixed_three_first_vertical_phase.md)
now supplies the complementary phase deduction for prefixes \(33\)
and \(43\). Its first marginal has argument strictly between zero
and \(\pi\) on the entire required height path. Moving a negative
height to zero decreases the next phase; moving a positive height to
zero costs at most \(\pi(c-k)\). The already proved convex
first-pair budget pays exactly that cost. Keeping the two supporting
tangents until they cancel gives raw reserves greater than \(.03\)
and \(.024\), respectively, on the full collar. This is an exact
written deduction with the next reference unchanged. Its equation
(14) asks for a sharper moving-phase finite bound; the following
fixed-reference argument avoids that unnecessary requirement.

The [complete second-three source transport](research_mixed_three_first_source_transport.md)
uses the same angular inequality for every point of the original
index contour, not just for its critical point. Exact differentiation
of each finite real row expresses its height derivative through a
positive Poisson kernel. The real tails therefore obey precisely the
same allowance as the central contour. The original half-grid cuts,
zero mode, endpoint joins and aliases remain present. This proves
finite first-cap and first-two-edge losses \(1/40\) and \(1/50\)
throughout the collar for prefixes \(33\) and \(43\), at the
unchanged third reference.

For a second type-four coordinate, the
[real-tail transport](research_mixed_four_first_vertical_source_transport.md)
gives rate at most the fixed reference action plus \(1/250\),
including wrapped rows and both selected Fourier branches. The
[fixed-contour proof](research_mixed_four_fixed_contour_transport.md)
bounds the central contribution by that same reference action plus
\(13/2000\). It uses the correct terminal attached-leg height
\(-.108\), including length three. Vertical curvature bounds all
endpoint and alias currents. Combining the two regions takes the
maximum of their allowances, not their sum. The full next factor
therefore has upper rate at most the reference action plus
\(13/2000+\eta\). The retained first-pair reserve pays this
increase and leaves finite loss \(1/25\) for both \(34\) and
\(44\), with either second selection. No moving-root enclosure,
new source grid, or sharp moving-phase asymptotic is needed.

The more general [contour-allowance lemma](research_mixed_conditional_contour_allowance.md)
records why a small positive excess would have sufficed. It bounds the

above a chosen critical rate, retaining all contour pieces. It also

There is also a [terminal right-sector reduction](research_mixed_terminal_right_endpoint_reduction.md).
At complete ordinary color the terminal rate
\(h(e)=J(e)+\Re S(e)\) decreases on \((1/2,1)\); its value at

envelope, with loss at least \(\pi^2(e-1/2)^3/6\), for arbitrary
fixed complex neighboring height.

The [polynomial endpoint argument](research_mixed_endpoint_polynomial_collar.md)
now closes the previously separate endpoint layer. The complete
terminal rate \(h\) is symmetric about \(1/2\) and tends to zero
at both ends. Multiplying the original degree-\((N-1)\) polynomial
by a power of \((1+Y)/2\), and applying an elementary Chebyshev
estimate across one missing arc, gives arbitrarily small exponential
growth on a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of \(Y=1\).
The proof retains a whole ordinary-color neighborhood, all fixed
derivatives and both parities. Thus the joint right-half comparison
holds uniformly through its endpoint for any compact set of complex
neighboring heights. Its loss is
\(K(e)=-\int_{1/2}^{e}\log\sin(\pi t)\,dt\), with
\(K(1)=(\log2)/2\). This reduces the terminal right region to
the full row envelope at \(e=1/2\); comparing that envelope with
the geometric action remains necessary.

At the half point itself, the

\([.27,.33]+i[-.057,-.001]\), for both terminal block types.
The difference of the original optimized endpoint action and its

Its boundary checks reuse the old endpoint root cells; the saved

The [full-row comparison on those same rectangles](research_mixed_terminal_raw_half_gap.md)

The [terminal supporting-plane theorem](research_terminal_supporting_plane.md)

The negative real Hessian remains at least \(6\pi/49\) when

There is now a [full-source estimate with an arbitrary mixed interior](research_mixed_buffered_endpoint_sectors.md)
when the two physical endpoint buffers remain in specified local

The assembled left losses are \(1/50\) for \((3,3)\),
\(3/200\) for \((4,3)\), and \(9/200\) when the second type
is four. In the last case the second selection must be absent, so its
height approaches the actual reference at the seam. Each estimate
leaves room for the shared source tolerance.
The later terminal theorems remove the old \(R_3/R_4\) restriction
on that reference, with common right loss \(1/5000\).
Exact cancellation of the internal affine terms and the existing
pinning argument pay the corridor errors. The interior may retain
its original selected, seam and right-half coordinates. Thus these
endpoint losses suppress a region of the complete finite integrand,
rather than only its endpoint factors. Configurations outside the

The [full-collar extension](research_mixed_full_collar_buffered_sectors.md)
now strengthens that assembled result. The complete three-factor
transport has a common reserve \(1/50\) at the unchanged third
target. Its fixed-contour and zero-safe full-row majorants are uniformly
continuous on compact parameter sets. Small real changes of the second
and third coordinates, the retained third tangent, and one aggregate

All later buffer heights stay at their reference values, including

second selections are admitted. Small coherent neighboring buffers
and the two plateau corridors are still required.

There is a new [all-row bound for the larger-height question](research_mixed_terminal_half_row_envelope.md).
For any complex neighbor \(a\), put \(H=\max(-\Im a,0)\).
Every upper-half row at the terminal half-period is bounded by
\(\max\{2\pi H,b_2/2+\pi H\}\). Reflection turns its
remaining potential into a convex function, so only two endpoint
values are needed. On \(0<\Re a<1/2\), the lower-half
maximum is uniquely determined by a strictly concave scalar function
at every height; its critical equation is a quartic or sextic in
\(\tan(\pi u)\). Thus the complete row envelope is bounded
by that scalar maximum and the two explicit height terms. Their
maximum is subharmonic. No geometric gap on the larger domain is
claimed from these row bounds alone.

The [test on the full neighboring disks](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-terminal-raw-full-disk-boundary/README.md)
now identifies a limitation of that proposed extension. For a type-three
terminal block and a type-three neighboring input, the exact point
\(a=967/3200+7i/128\) lies inside the smaller admitted disk. At the
single real row \(v=67/250\), a validated original critical-point
enclosure gives
\[
 h(1/2)+E_0(a,v)-\Re P_0(a)>7/10000.
\]
Here \(P_0\) is the optimized terminal action and \(E_0\) is the
absolute row rate defined in the terminal half-row note. Thus the
desired absolute-value comparison is false on the whole independent
disk; tightening the numerical bounds cannot prove it there. A
[separate compatibility calculation](research_mixed_terminal_inverse_constraint.md)
now proves that this particular input cannot occur at the critical
point of an actual open word. At length at least three it would force
the opposite leg of the penultimate block outside even the coarse
geometric rectangle; at length two it violates the first endpoint's
attached-height bound. The calculation uses the original logarithmic
root enclosure and exact exponentiated equations, with a saved
320-bit replay. It excludes one point, not the entire problematic
region. A large absolute row also does not imply a large oscillatory
sum. The proved rectangle estimates are unaffected. The remaining
question is whether the coupled equations give a strict gap throughout
the actual reference set, or whether the comparison must keep
cancellation between those blocks. The other three type combinations
passed the bounded circle test, but that diagnostic has not been
promoted to a new source theorem.

The [neighbouring-equation reduction](research_terminal_coupling_barriers.md)
now retains the missing algebraic constraint. For a word of length at
least three, the terminal input determines the exponentials of both
legs needed to reconstruct the preceding ordinary block, by explicit
rational formulas. The proved geometric domains impose lower modulus
bounds on two resulting holomorphic functions. Subtracting nonnegative
multiples of their logarithmic moduli from the terminal gap preserves
superharmonicity. A positive boundary bound for this corrected gap
would therefore prove the desired comparison at every admissible
critical input, even if the unrestricted disk bound fails. The note
proves this implication and specifies finite linear inequalities for
the multipliers. It does not assert that those inequalities are
feasible, or impose critical-point equations on every integration
target.

For an [actual word ending in two type-three blocks](research_mixed_terminal_coupled_disk_gap.md),
the corrected comparison has now been proved. The single multiplier
\(1/200\), applied to
\(\log|\mathcal U(a)|+13\pi/100\), gives a boundary gap greater
than \(1/4000\) on the whole smaller type-three input disk.
Second-order bounds on the same 165 old parameter cells retain the
ordinary-row optimizer response and the exact circle geometry; the
saved 320-bit replay verifies all 660 branch inequalities. The
superharmonic minimum principle and the preceding ordinary block's
height bound therefore give the gap at every actual reference for
words of length at least three ending \((3,3)\). A small ambient
neighbourhood and the finite-source tolerance leave a terminal loss
\(1/5000+K(e)\) throughout \(1/2\le e\le1\). This removes the
earlier neighbouring-rectangle restriction for this type combination
at actual references. It does not impose critical equations on the
ambient integration targets, cover arbitrary changes of their height,
or treat length two as an ordinary penultimate block.

The [two-block word \((3,3)\)](research_mixed_two_three_terminal_compatibility.md)
now satisfies the same terminal comparison by a different argument.
Reflection preserves its full open action, so uniqueness forces its
terminal input to be a fixed point of the endpoint map. Exact
intersection with the saved output bounds leaves six of the original
1,645 parameter cells. On those cells a fixed-point expression for
the coupling function satisfies the required modulus inequality.
Its equality with the original function is used only at the actual
fixed point. The saved 320-bit replay verifies this extraction.
Consequently the finite terminal loss \(1/5000+K(e)\) also holds
near the length-two reference, without an ordinary-vertex substitution.

The [remaining three terminal type families](research_mixed_terminal_remaining_disk_gaps.md)
have now passed the full smaller-disk comparison without a multiplier.
The proof gives a raw gap of \(1/500\) and a finite terminal loss
of \(1/1000+K(e)\); its saved 320-bit replay covers all 457 old
circle cells and 1,828 branch inequalities. Together with the coupled
three-three theorem and the separate two-block compatibility proof,
this gives the common finite loss \(1/5000+K(e)\) near every
actual terminal reference of every three/four word of length at least
two. Both terminal selections, when present, and both level parities
are retained. This completes the type and length coverage for that
terminal sector. Other boundary regions, arbitrary neighbouring
height attenuation and the whole open-sum lower bound remain open.

The alternative Fourier route now has a precise
[marked-trace formulation](research_mixed_marked_trace_observation.md).
Homogeneous-three buffers detect only spectral diagonal information;
the original ordinary endpoint vectors also see off-diagonal terms.
An exact commutator identity expresses those additional observations
as terms at the original type-four insertions. A
[Casimir-mark identity](research_mixed_ordinary_boundary_casimir_mark.md)
further expresses the complete ordinary coefficient at odd levels as
a trace with the primitive idempotent of the complete color inserted.
Its scalar polynomial is the existing Fejér kernel divided by \(N\).
At even levels the complete color is not a root of the physical
polynomial; the corresponding exact formula is a forced resolvent
observation. The even correction is retained explicitly. These
identities specify the actual observation that a Fourier or spectral
estimate must control. Neither the positivity of the scalar Fejér
kernel nor the unmarked cyclic theorem proves the missing marked
asymptotic.

The [marked-vertex contraction](research_mixed_marked_vertex_contraction.md)
carries that insertion through the original finite algebra before
taking absolute values. It changes only one vertex, and its physical
expansion retains endpoint values and first normals. The Newton
color estimate gives an explicit exponential saving for physical
colors a fixed distance from \(-2\), both in the twisted trace and
in the even-level resolvent decomposition. These savings are relative
to a known matrix-norm envelope; that envelope has not been placed
below the geometric rate. The odd Fejér contraction also cancels
the far physical-color terms exactly. Its remaining complete-color
observation is still the original unresolved open source.

There is also a [composition criterion for the actual observation](research_source_adapted_observation_composition.md)
that applies to arbitrary signed crossing powers and branching trees.
At each exact linear map it separates a proposed source direction
from its orthogonal complement. A lower bound requires control of
both directions of coupling, complementary evolution, and the final
physical boundary row. The error radius for several incoming branches
is exactly bounded by \(\sqrt{\prod_i(1+\rho_i^2)-1}\).
Under the stated inequalities, the original scalar is a product of
its proposed amplitudes times controlled nonzero complex factors;
no positivity assumption is made. This supplies an explicit general
target for the almost-invariance proposal. The current local Hessians
and upper source bounds do not establish its hypotheses for arbitrary
short fillings, and the physical boundary overlap cannot be omitted.

The new open critical point is now identified with the marked positive
geometric branch. The [identification theorem](research_mixed_geometric_source_identification.md)
proves this for every fixed nonempty three/four word, including lengths
one and two. Consequently the nonzero local quantum contribution has
the original cell-volume rate. The rest of the finite source and the
boundary estimates for attachment remain open. The geometric proof
develops the following earlier reductions. The
[positive-geometry comparison](research_mixed_positive_geometry_action_route.md)
gives a larger convex injectivity chamber and isolates the missing
unit-period range and logarithmic-lift conditions; positivity alone
does not imply them. The
[unit-period elimination lemma](research_mixed_unit_period_leg_elimination.md)
now gives the precise algebraic part: with inverse legs \(U,V\),
the original unit filling equation implies
\(2\cos\tau=UV-U-V-1\) for type three and
\(2\cos\tau=-U-V\) for type four. All cancelled factors are
nonzero on the positive geometry. This algebra alone does not settle
the required coordinate ranges or the zero logarithmic lifts.
The individual inverse-leg range is now proved for every power at
least three. The [sine-lens theorem](research_mixed_all_leg_half_plane.md)
gives \(|\sin(\tau/2)|<1\) throughout the positive path charge
family. At type three, a putative failure confines each of the two
real returns below \(21/20\), while their sum exceeds \(13/8\).
Concavity then forces their total negative argument above \(23/56\),
contradicting the original imaginary period, which puts it below that
number. Together with the cosine bound, the lens inequality excludes
every real crossing of an inverse leg during charge continuation.
Thus all inverse legs stay in the lower half-plane and have continuous
principal logarithms with real coordinates in \((0,1/2)\).
The complete-vertex case is included directly. This argument uses
analytic inequalities and exact rational comparisons, with no new
root search.

The [wire-before-leg theorem](research_mixed_wire_before_inverse_leg.md)
now also proves \(0<\Re x<\Re s<1/2\) at every incidence of
this geometric family. Its proof bounds the imaginary part of the
wire cotangent using two exact Bernstein polynomial certificates,
then proves that \(e^{2\pi ix}e^{-2\pi is}\) lies strictly
below the real axis. The saved exact replay checks all polynomial
identities; no geometric roots are proposed. These inequalities keep
the original source logarithms and dilogarithms on their regular branches.

The [source logarithmic-lift theorem](research_mixed_geometric_source_log_lifts.md)
uses this regularity to prove the original stationary equations with
zero integer lifts. For a type-four vertex the calibration keeps its
own charge equal to one while varying the other charges from zero;
the own unit equation therefore remains valid throughout the argument.
The shared-wire equation is instead calibrated by scaling all charges
from completeness, since that identity is independent of the charges.

The [geometric action calibration](research_mixed_geometric_action_calibration.md)
now fixes the additive constants as well. The original incidence
derivatives agree with their angular counterparts along the whole
geometric family. Keeping the own charge one then makes each vertex
action difference constant. The type-three constant is the already
calibrated purely imaginary constant; the isolated type-four cubic
places that vertex in its existing calibrated chart, where the constant
is zero. An explicit regular path fixes the shared-wire contraction's
constant to zero. Summing these identities with the endpoint identity
proves
\[
 \nabla\mathcal F_m(z_{\rm geom})=0,\qquad
 2\pi\Re\mathcal F_m(z_{\rm geom})=V_{\rm cells}.
\]
The calibration theorem itself is evaluated at the geometric inverse;
the new identification theorem below supplies its equality with the
localized source point \(z_*\). The written calibration retains the
full complex constants; its exact checker and saved replay verify the
supporting algebra, not the continuation arguments by themselves.

A [separate extraction of the source witnesses](research_mixed_reduced_disk_pair_sums.md)
proves \(109/200<\Re(a+s),\Re(t+b)<77/100\) for every
ordinary block in the reduced disks. Five of the six internal vertex
types also satisfy the desired sum bound greater than \(1/2\).
For a type-four vertex between two type-three neighbors, the certified
lower enclosure is only \(.49653824\); it proves neither the bound
nor its failure. These conclusions reuse the same 4,409 affine witnesses,
with no new root search or subdivision. They do not alone establish
a common injectivity chamber for the geometric and source points.

There is now another sufficient chamber that avoids internal sum
conditions. The [cotangent criterion](research_mixed_cotangent_cone_injectivity.md)
proves strict concavity of each ordinary pair whenever both legs have
\(|\Im\cot(\pi z)|<1\). The convex strip
\(1/5<\Re z<1/2,\ |\Im z|<3/20\), together with the stated
endpoint inequalities, contains every localized source point and has
an injective full gradient. Inclusion of the geometric inverse in this
strip was not established by that criterion. The note also gives an
exact counterexample to simply dropping the old type-four sum condition
with unrestricted heights. The new identification avoids both of
these gaps by controlling the particular segment between the two points.

The [unit cotangent theorem](research_mixed_unit_cotangent_bounds.md)
proves \(0<\Re\cot\pi s<2\), \(|\Im\cot\pi s|<1\)
for every geometric leg. For type four, an exact sum of squares
excludes a crossing of imaginary cotangent \(-1\) while the own
charge remains one. The type-three lower bound follows directly
from the own cosine square. Complete outside incidences satisfy
their own strict barrier, and the shared-edge equation then excludes
imaginary cotangent at least one. The unit equations also bound the
real cotangents. Together with the earlier angle bounds they give
\[
 1/8<\Re s<1/2,\qquad
 |\Im s|<\frac{\log(1+4\sqrt3)}{2\pi}.
\]
The [type-three endpoint lemma](research_mixed_three_endpoint_pair_sum.md)
supplies the remaining endpoint sum inequalities by exact elimination.

These bounds do not make the cotangent domain convex. Instead the
identification proof checks the straight segment from the geometric
point to the source point. Below real part \(1/4\), the boundary
of the cotangent domain is
\(\pm f(x)\), where \(f(x)=-\log\cos(2\pi x)/(2\pi)\).
For a geometric real part below \(.23\), its tangent line lies
above every allowed source height; convexity of \(f\) therefore
keeps the segment inside the domain. At larger real parts the uniform
height bound suffices. Endpoint order and sums persist linearly.
The original Hessian is strictly negative in real part along this
whole segment. Its integral excludes two distinct zero-gradient points,
proving
\[
 z_*=z_{\rm geom},\qquad
 2\pi\Re\mathcal F_m(z_*)=V_{\rm cells}.
\]
Thus the local quantum exponential rate has its intended volume
normalization for every word. This is still a local contribution to
the finite sum, so it does not enlarge the established knot family
without the remaining global and attachment estimates.

The saved branch algebra, action calibration and source-side sum
extraction can be reproduced without changing their canonical records:

```sh
python3 repro/run_research_checks.py mixed-geometric-calibration
```

The finite-exception target also requires stability under arbitrary fixed
short partial fillings, including connected short components and the
peripheral data of the original template. Those requirements remain
open, so this cyclic result alone adds no claim for a new knot family.

Assignments must also remain distinct from knot types. In the original
tree grammar, the [padding theorem](research_original_tree_padding_equivalence.md)
produces infinite assignment fibers for the same knot. Cofiniteness for
every such template would therefore imply the volume identity for every
represented hyperbolic knot. An unresolved finite collection of short
knots cannot simply be discarded on those infinite fibers.

The following paragraphs preserve earlier reductions and diagnostics as a
historical research record. Statements below about a missing cyclic region
or interface sign describe the stage at which that approach was developed;
the complete cyclic theorem above supersedes those gaps. Limitations for
open boundary sources and arbitrary short fillings remain current.

The original endpoint-neighborhood theorem controlled independent zero
collars whose neighbors lay near \(1/10\) or \(1/2\), with a loss
of \(1/100\). Its isolation and neighborhood restrictions have now
been removed in the closed-half theorem above.

Two connector lower bounds gave that earlier region theorem. The
[half-angle comparison](research_mixed_half_angle_connector_lower.md)
combines the exact half-angle source rates with the orientation-dependent
curvature costs. A complete calculation on the original reference-window
boundary, repeated at higher precision, proves its uniform reserve.
The [real connector theorem](research_mixed_low_endpoint_connector_lower.md)
uses joint concavity to reduce all real neighboring angles in
\([1/10,1/2]\) to 64 scalar corner inequalities. This real lower bound
applies at the three endpoint pairs containing \(1/10\); the half-angle
theorem handles the remaining pair \((1/2,1/2)\), whose repaired middle
coordinate remains complex. Continuity gives their common neighborhoods.

The assembly replaces every isolated collar coordinate by its reference
real coordinate and removes its selection, solely for a phase comparison.
The repaired graph belongs to the already controlled half-period. The
two incident source blocks at each collar have a strict reserve against
their repaired coherent rates. The pairs share no physical edge, and only
adjacent noncollar heights change. Their remaining edge errors are bounded
uniformly and absorbed by choosing the neighborhoods small enough.
This works for arbitrary numbers of collars, including shared neighboring
vertices and two-symbol runs; no boundary-potential optimization is used.

Those two earlier certificates can be reproduced together without overwriting
their canonical records:

```sh
python3 repro/run_research_checks.py mixed-seam-connectors
```

An earlier theorem
[reduces the seam attenuation parameters to finitely many values](research_mixed_seam_attenuation_vertices.md).
Fix the other real coordinates, the actual reference and the Fourier
selection. Each neighboring height is a fixed multiple of the minimum
of seam attenuations and fixed cutoffs. On each region where those minima
choose fixed arguments, the original coherent upper rates and the retained
source profiles give a convex bound. Its maximum occurs where every
attenuation equals zero, one, or a neighboring fixed cutoff. A single
seam requires at most four values. The same deduction applies to the
exact boundary-repair comparison, including two-symbol runs with one
joint edge correction and the original short-cycle incidences.
This eliminates the attenuation variables, but by itself leaves a
continuous comparison over the other real coordinates and geometric
references. At that stage the uniform sign outside the endpoint
neighborhoods was missing. The subsequent closed-half proof above
uses the larger height triangles and acute gradient bounds to complete
the required seam estimate.

The [saved attenuation tests](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-seam-attenuation-vertices/README.md)
evaluate 214 candidate values at the earlier physical configurations and
their two saved inner-halo choices. All are negative; 348 interior
probes agree with the cellwise convexity calculation. These are floating
bookkeeping tests, not a sign certificate on the remaining parameter
domain. Their driver now uses only repository-local helpers and inputs.

An [expansion of the corrected boundary expression](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-seam-proxy-corners/README.md)
cancels all target-dependent tangent terms. It identifies the remaining
task as a lower bound for four coherent connector rates, minus the exact
physical boundary corrections. When both neighboring real angles are
at least .22, two reference connector rates cancel and only two varying
connector rates remain. The existing full-matrix curvature estimate gives
a valid lower bound on its unselected plateau domain, but its constant
is too coarse even for a previously tested alternating configuration.
Rotating the orientation-dependent estimates gives smaller one-coordinate
lower costs, \(11/2\) and \(151/20\). At that same fixed reference,
combining them with the exact half-angle source bound changes the scalar
comparison from positive to negative. The archived reference substitution
is a floating diagnostic; it is not a uniform reference certificate.
A bounded test of 784 corner configurations found no failure of the
actual corrected comparison. Those tests did not prove the general-angle
connector lower bound. The later proof uses complete concavity and
rational polynomial reductions, rather than promoting these tests
to a uniform sign assertion.

The reduction uses the recent near-zero seam improvements through
[height-dependent finite-source bounds](research_mixed_height_resolved_seam_sources.md)
and an [admissible-halo and exact boundary-repair theorem](research_mixed_admissible_boundary_halos.md).
The first retains each neighbor's actual height instead of taking a maximum
over its whole band. The second replaces an unnecessarily restrictive
virtual boundary choice by an exact admissible choice, or records the
exact change in the affected physical edge. Together with the exponential
memory estimate below, these are general analytic improvements to the
boundary comparison. These tools alone supplied no universal seam sign;
the closed-half proof now completes that part by a different assembly.
Neither result enlarges the proved knot family or establishes the
all-but-finitely-many theorem.

The height-dependent bounds interpolate nineteen certified source knots
on thirteen height intervals using the squared original Laurent rows.
They retain every row, both level parities, the first-argument chirp and
the actual Fourier forcing. For example, a type-three block with a selected
type-four moving leg has the full-band source ceiling .386681 in place of .447948;
the actual height profile can be sharper still. This extracts information
from completed certificates and their independent replays, with no new
outward cover.

The halo theorem identifies every virtual coordinate that reproduces an
endpoint row. When that endpoint has angle \(1/2\), its height is zero
and a reference halo is exactly admissible. In general, replacing the two
halos by reference symbols changes only the first and last physical
half-period edges. Keeping their exact differences gives an explicit
three-step entry/exit upper bound; a two-symbol run uses one joint
correction, and a singleton has none. The actual tangent and each Fourier
halfweight remain counted once. The
[exact-repair diagnostic archive](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-seam-exact-halo-repairs/README.md)
records negative upper proxies at all 49 saved configurations, also after
a bounded grid over the two additional halos. These are floating tests,
not a continuous parameter cover or a universal sign proof.

Another completed general result is the
[exponential bound on the effect of incoming histories](research_mixed_exponential_incoming_memory.md).
An incoming path whose weight is within \(\varepsilon\) of the
optimal weight has the same property at every earlier boundary state:
otherwise replacing its prefix would improve the whole path. Closing
each prefix by three reference symbols converts this observation into
a backward geometric recurrence for its total occupation penalty.
It follows that the common boundary potential is approximated by a
length-\(h\) incoming optimization with relative error decreasing
exponentially in \(h\). The constants are uniform in word length,
although their coarse compact bounds have not been numerically evaluated.
Every sufficiently nearly optimal incoming history also has all its
selected or transition symbols within a uniformly bounded number of
positions before its prescribed terminal state. Earlier symbols are
unselected plateau symbols; they need not be exactly at their references.

Together with the [exact finite-depth inequality](research_mixed_finite_depth_subaction.md),
this gives a finite function \(V\) for which each controlled block
obeys \(w_i\le V_{i+1}-V_i-\theta\Psi_{i+1}/6\).
Here \(w_i\) is its phase excess over the original geometric tangent
and \(\Psi\) is the occupation of the three-symbol boundary state.
Summing along a chain cancels the interior potential values without
an accumulated approximation error. This supplied a possible approach to the former right-half gap:
raw-source decay would pay the difference between the same boundary
potentials. A universal sign for that particular potential comparison
was not needed in the completed cyclic proof, which instead uses
minimum transport and direct seam repair.

At the near-zero seam, the
[exact virtual-halo construction](research_mixed_seam_boundary_potential_reduction.md)
places the physical neighboring heights in this same framework.
The complete saved two-block certificate also supports finite loss
\(7/25\), stronger than its originally rounded \(1/5\), with
the same reserved quadratic term. Disjoint incident pairs retain the
full loss at isolated seam vertices. The literal source comparison
contains more information than this uniform constant: it retains the
actual geometric tangent plane. A
[bounded diagnostic](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-seam-boundary/README.md)
shows that dropping that dependence can turn a favorable comparison
into an unfavorable one. The recorded numerical incoming maxima do
not certify differences of the true potentials, so they guide the
next estimate and do not supply a new full-period theorem.

The [half-angle source refinement](research_mixed_half_angle_seam_source.md)
now gives exact one-variable maxima for the full original rows when
either neighbor of the seam has angle \(1/2\). It includes the odd
levels' upper rows and the actual Fourier forcing. If both neighbors
have that angle, the raw rate improves by more than .097534 for every
type choice; one-sided versions retain the old bound on the other
neighbor. The improvement persists on a fixed neighborhood, whose
width is not evaluated. The note states the full comparison using the
actual tangent plane and makes clear that the reserved quadratic term
must not be subtracted again.

The earlier [fixed closure obstruction](research_mixed_seam_closure_obstruction.md)
remains valid for its particular forced-halo, independent entry/exit
relaxation: at a homogeneous type-three reference that upper proxy exceeds
the available pair reserve by more than .59. The new halo theorem avoids
that relaxation in the same example. Reference halos are admissible at
its half-angle endpoints, and the resulting incoming and outgoing states
coincide at the same periodic layer, so their common-potential difference
cancels exactly. The certified obstruction never asserted a positive
actual potential difference; neither this repair nor the bounded tests
settle the sign for all other configurations.
The [new actual-plane diagnostics](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-seam-actual-plane/README.md)
preserve all 29 bounded searches and the single deeper follow-up.
At their largest positive three-step estimate, using the same incoming
four- or five-step functions at both ends gives negative trial values.
Differences of these lower estimates for maxima remain uncertified;
they do not prove a universal boundary comparison.

The seven focused boundary-memory checks are available together
without rewriting their canonical source records:

```sh
python3 repro/run_research_checks.py mixed-boundary-memory
```

Their outputs are written to temporary files. The checks cover the
stated exact identities, scalar bounds and saved-source dependencies;
the general analytic arguments remain the written proofs, and the
unproved boundary comparisons remain unproved.

An earlier region theorem included every coordinate between the fixed
near-zero collar and slightly beyond one half. More precisely, for a fixed
hybrid collar width \(\rho>0\), there is a positive
\(\delta_\rho\) such that the original selected integral on
\([\rho,1/2+\delta_\rho]^m\) retains the central nonzero coefficient,
with error \(O(N^A e^{N(M-1/8000)})\). This holds for every fixed
three/four word and both level parities. The width is not numerically
evaluated and is not asserted uniform as \(\rho\) tends to zero.

Two written deductions give this extension. The
[real low-coordinate theorem](research_mixed_deep_low_half_region.md)
proves that either real coordinate of the conditional action has positive
derivative up to \(1/6\). Raising a coordinate in \([\rho,.1]\)
to .1 leaves every contour height unchanged, so the previous phase
inequality extends to \([\rho,.5]^m\). Its finite-source proof includes
the half endpoint and uses the absolute Fourier bound at its forcing tie.
The [coherent half-endpoint collar](research_mixed_coherent_half_endpoint_collar.md)
then uses the already proved open neighborhoods of the complete finite
sources. The extra true Fourier rate beyond .5 is retained, including
for unselected type-four coordinates. A compact derivative bound spends
less than the existing loss at the clamped half endpoint. These are
arbitrary-length arguments, not further numerical word examples. Neither
argument controls the near-zero seam or the entire right half-period.

The [upper-transition/right extraction](research_mixed_upper_transition_right_support.md)
also confirms that the existing right-core profiles already enclose full
independent height bands on the moving interval [.4,.5]. Hence an upper
transition next to a real right argument has a complete absolute-row gap
1/2000, even when another neighbor attenuates its height. The proof uses
the original complete covers and their saved independent replays; no
new numerical cover was run. The weak positive right-edge ceiling is now
needed only for certain partially attenuated type-four plateau legs
below .4.

The latest local estimate now covers a
[left-transition argument next to the real right half-period](research_mixed_transition_right_support.md).
The transition coordinate ranges over [.1,.22], with all its allowed
negative or selected positive heights, including further attenuation by
neighbors. The other coordinate ranges over [.5,1] at height zero.
In both orientations, the complete sum of absolute finite rows is at
least 1/2000 below its original geometric tangent in exponential rate.
The proof retains both Fourier alternatives and the full selected height
at the comparison angle .13. All 720 scalar supports and 512 reference
products passed complete interval coverage and a fresh 320-bit replay.
This supplied a formerly missing local comparison. Its actual boundary
costs are now included in the completed middle-region assembly.

There is also a new general deduction from the cyclic phase inequalities.
The [open-chain boundary theorem](research_mixed_nonlow_open_chain_boundary.md)
bounds any chain with coordinates in [.1,.5] by six explicit boundary
terms, independently of its length. Closing the chain with reference
coordinates proves the inequality. The same argument constructs a
continuous potential whose differences dominate the edge weights.
The [additive loss theorem](research_mixed_nonlow_occupation_loss.md),
with its [sharper extracted curvature constants](research_mixed_extracted_plateau_curvature.md),
strengthens this: each selected coordinate or coordinate outside
[.22,.45] costs at least 1/4000 in phase rate, and unselected plateau
coordinates also pay a quadratic displacement cost. The same
six boundary terms control the sum of these losses on an open chain.
Consequently a chain close to the maximal rate has a bounded number
of such departures, independently of its length. The bound uses a
compact supremum that has not yet been numerically evaluated.
The improvement uses the whole-cell eigenvalue lower bounds already
saved in the completed reset certificate and its 320-bit replay. They
prove local curvature greater than 1/5 and cyclic curvature greater
than 2/5. No new numerical cover was needed; the earlier weaker
occupation statement remains valid.
The [weighted transfer estimate](research_mixed_nonlow_weighted_transfer.md)
then gives an ordinary Cauchy–Schwarz operator bound in a specified
weighted Hilbert norm. After geometric normalization, fixed-length
products have no positive exponential growth in that norm; specified
input regions away from the reference retain the additive loss. The physical
endpoint vectors still have to be estimated in it; no almost-invariant
vector or universal lower bound is asserted.

The [plateau boundary-forgetting theorem](research_mixed_plateau_boundary_forgetting.md)
now supplies a quantitative reduction for long unselected plateau
segments. Keep their actual reference heights and allow arbitrary real
endpoints in [.22,.45]. The unique maximizing interior responds to the
ends with Euclidean contraction factor 99/101. Fixing the middle at its
reference values and optimizing the first and last 295 interior
coordinates changes the optimal action by less than 1/2000; depth 315
gives error less than 1/4000. The same depths work at every chain length
and type word, and shorter chains are retained in full. The proof handles
active constraints and bounds the entire interior tail at once. It is a
variational statement at fixed unselected heights, not an asymptotic for
the finite sum or a bound for altered transition heights.
It removes the length of a good plateau segment from the quantitative
comparison. The number and arrangement of intervening transition or
endpoint regions remain unrestricted, and their combined estimates
still have to be proved.

The previous completed integration-region result was the
[full half-period theorem above the low cutoff](research_mixed_full_nonlow_half_region.md).
Normalize the real integration parameters to period one, and let \(m\)
be the number of blocks in a fixed cyclic word. On \(A_m=[.1,.5]^m\),
the original sum, including every Fourier selection, retains its nonzero
geometric leading coefficient. Its remaining error is exponentially
smaller. This includes arbitrary mixtures of left and right transition
coordinates, at every fixed word length and both level parities.

The proof uses the same [exact periodic contour](research_mixed_split_cutoff_hybrid_contour.md)
as the earlier regional estimates. At a right-transition coordinate,
the [selected-height comparison](research_mixed_right_selected_height_removal.md)
first removes its selection at the same real coordinate. Then the
[unselected clamping theorem](research_mixed_unselected_right_clamping.md)
moves it to .45. Every other row height stays fixed. These comparisons
bound the original rate by a point on the left region's right face,
where the established left estimates give a strict loss. They do not
push an integral forward under a clamping map. Both inputs have complete
outward certificates and fresh 320-bit saved replays: 939 selected-height
domains and 288 unselected-clamping domains. The written assembly handles
cycles of lengths one and two separately where necessary.

The [left/right interface source theorem](research_mixed_left_right_interface_source.md)
supplies the full finite-sum asymptotic on the new local products,
including .5. Its nonzero symbol, all rows and all Fourier corrections
are retained. All 84 boundary products also passed a 320-bit replay.

At zero, the [new two-block estimate](research_mixed_hybrid_zero_pair_support.md)
gives finite loss 1/5 with arbitrary other real angles and physical
height states. It uses the middle critical equation and a three-circles
bound on actual Laurent rows. The
[hybrid low/plateau assembly](research_mixed_hybrid_low_plateau_clusters.md)
then gives loss 1/200 on every box in
\(([0,.1]\cup[.22,.45])^m\) containing a low coordinate. A half-weight
allocation of overlapping pairs and a degree-two incidence count use
each original edge and each height-change charge once.

The far right region \(V_m=[.22,1]^m\) remains proved on this same
contour. The [partial-reset right bound](research_mixed_partially_reset_right_support.md)
also has its complete certificate and 320-bit replay. Its new local
ceiling permits the [hybrid low/plateau/right assembly](research_mixed_hybrid_low_plateau_right_clusters.md):
arbitrary mixtures of \(L=[0,.1]\), \(P=[.22,.45]\), and
\(R=[.5,1]\) now retain the central coefficient on this exact contour.
Every box containing a low coordinate has finite loss 1/2000. This
repairs the previous contour mismatch; no estimate from a different
coupled graph is imported.

The three regions \(A_m\), \(V_m\), and \((L\cup P\cup R)^m\)
have a common central contribution. Their proofs give pointwise strict
bounds off the unselected plateau, so their union retains that
contribution once. At that earlier stage, two kinds of configurations
remained outside the union:

1. A coordinate below .1 together with a coordinate in one of the
   transition intervals \((.1,.22)\) or \((.45,.5)\).
2. No coordinate below .1, but both a coordinate in \((.1,.22)\)
   and one above .5.

The completed middle-region and seam raw-exterior theorems now control
both kinds, and the full-period assembly proves that the common central
coefficient survives. The older open-chain boundary terms remain useful
for the separate problem of attaching pieces with external variables.

The earlier coherent-collar theorem removed every configuration
in that list whose coordinates all lie in
\([\rho,1/2+\delta_\rho]\). At that stage an untreated low/transition
configuration had to enter the near-zero seam or exceed the right
collar. Without a low coordinate, an untreated right coordinate had
to exceed \(1/2+\delta_\rho\). The width remains
unquantified, so this is a genuine enlargement with a precise qualitative
scope, not a numerical threshold for the remaining integral.

The [interface reduction](research_mixed_nonlow_interface_reduction.md)
now writes the leftover nonlow comparison using four explicit closing
weights for each intervening half-period chain, with every physical
edge and Fourier halfweight counted once. It also gives fixed-depth
optimized closing functions and the signs needed to use one common
boundary potential at both ends. The unoptimized four-cost test has a
positive floating diagnostic, so its nonpositivity is not a theorem.
Merely moving a cut one edge deeper cancels algebraically and supplies
no improvement. That approach required a sharper boundary potential or additional
coherent cancellation; the completed cyclic proof uses different
comparisons.

The earlier [finite-depth theorem](research_mixed_finite_depth_boundary_potential.md)
gave a general way to approximate that same potential at both ends. It
leaves a fixed fraction of the occupation loss unused. This bounds the
number of symbols far from their geometric values in any nearly optimal
incoming path. A block of five nearby unselected symbols then permits
the earlier part of the path to be discarded, with error at most
\(40d^2\). The retained depth is independent of the word length and
is \(O(e^{-1})\) for requested error \(e\). The exponential theorem
above improves this to logarithmic dependence on \(1/e\). Its compact size constant
has not yet been numerically evaluated. The resulting interface formula
uses one incoming potential for both signs; independently optimizing an
entrance and an exit need not remove the gap between them.

This reduces approximation of the boundary potential to a specified
finite optimization problem. It does not prove that the resulting
interface functions are negative. A bounded floating trial using the
same incoming potential is promising at the earlier problematic
configuration, but differences of trial maxima are not certified upper
bounds. The [archived diagnostic manifest](../repro/diagnostics/2026-11-05-mixed-interface/manifest.json)
preserves those calculations and the positive four-cost examples,
separately from the proof certificates.

Two stronger proposed estimates have
[explicit counterexamples](research_mixed_right_clamping_obstructions.md):
the selected rate need not decrease along its own taper, and an
absolute-row envelope cannot always be bounded by the clamped phase.
The completed comparisons avoid both assertions.

A further [geometric-center replacement obstruction](research_mixed_geometric_right_replacement_obstruction.md)
is now exact: on an actual alternating four-cycle, the raw two-edge
rate exceeds the proposed coherent replacement by more than 3/50.
Its author calculation and independent 320-bit check retain the actual
critical branch, physical rows and Fourier weights. This rules out that
shortcut only; it does not contradict the signed kernel, the whole-cycle
asymptotic or the volume conjecture.

The remaining periodic integral is now bounded by the full cyclic
theorem. Estimates with the original external boundary variables retained
and stability under arbitrary fixed short fillings are the next tasks.
That broader stability is needed for the finite-branching deduction of
finitely many exceptions per fixed template.

There is an additional scope issue that must remain explicit. In the
original tree grammar, zero fillings can give infinitely many assignments
of the same knot. The [padding theorem](research_original_tree_padding_equivalence.md)
shows that cofiniteness for every template in this class would imply
the volume identity for every represented hyperbolic knot, with no
exceptions. An unresolved finite list of short knots cannot simply be
left on those infinite assignment fibers. The objective is unchanged.

The preceding major step was the
[full left-region theorem](research_mixed_full_left_region.md). For every
fixed cyclic word of three- and four-crossing blocks, the original sum
over \([.1,.45]^m\), including every Fourier selection, retains its
nonzero geometric leading coefficient. All other contributions within
that region are exponentially smaller. The assembly requires complete
local certificates and their separate replays; its checker validates
all 495 domains and every source input. The later full-period theorem completes the cyclic integration problem.
Estimates retaining external boundary variables remain a separate
requirement before applying these words as arbitrary open pieces.

The inner finite sums already have a nonzero leading coefficient for
all real neighboring parameters in the half-period, uniformly on
compact sets away from zero, including the endpoint one half. Explicit
complex neighborhoods also include adjacent left-transition parameters.
At that stage the cyclic problem was cancellation in the parts of the
outer integral outside the completed regions; the new full-period
theorem controls that remainder.
Two proposed absolute estimates for its left region have explicit
counterexamples, described below. These failures concern the estimates,
not the cyclic integral or the volume conjecture.

There is now a positive estimate uniform at zero: when both target
real coordinates are in \([0,.10]\), the
[whole raw-source bound](research_mixed_both_low_raw_support.md)
gives an exponential loss of \(1/100\) below the original geometric
plane. It includes the original complex quadratic taper, every finite
row and every Fourier selection. Its proof maximizes the row entropy
in the angles, then uses convexity in height and a one-variable bound
over the complete row period. It does not use a saddle approximation
at the zero endpoint. The [cyclic consequence](research_mixed_small_region_assembly.md)
removes the entire all-small box \([0,.10]^m\), for every fixed cyclic
three/four word and every selection, with loss \(m/100\).

For real targets, the [global concavity theorem](research_mixed_real_outer_support.md)
gives supporting planes on the entire open half-square. Finite real
tangents then prove a [both-small comparison](research_mixed_real_small_support.md)
and the stronger [one-small comparison](research_mixed_real_one_small_support.md):
if one real coordinate is at most .10 and the other is anywhere in
\((0,.5)\), the phase lies at least \(11/200\) below every permitted
complex geometric plane. The original finite source has loss \(1/20\)
uniformly on compact subsets. This last assertion is not yet uniform
at zero over the entire interval allowed for its other argument.
The [extended real zero collar](research_mixed_real_zero_collar_extension.md)
now allows the other argument anywhere in \([.1,.5]\) and supplies
a uniform raw-source loss of \(3/50\) on \([0,.001]\), including
zero itself. All 64 reference boundary products and 975 cells passed
at 256 bits and in a fresh 320-bit calculation. It uses the exact forced recurrence of the Fourier polynomial
to transport an estimate from a fixed positive angle down to zero.
The [uniform real low-angle corollary](research_mixed_uniform_real_low_support.md)
joins that collar to the compact one-small estimate. It gives finite
loss 1/20 for a low coordinate anywhere in [0,.1] and a real neighbor
in [.1,.45], with all types, orientations and selections. This loss
can reserve one full oriented plateau reset cost and still leave
loss 1/50. Both heights must be zero in the low block; the literal
neighboring-block interpretation keeps its stated plateau and
unchanged-height hypotheses. No derivative at a zero target is used.

The [single-height reset bound](research_mixed_single_height_reset.md)
also pays for the neighboring blocks when their exterior arguments
stay fixed at their references: resetting one height costs at most
\(7h^2\), even after optimizing its real coordinate. Combining it
with the one-small comparison gives the four-block estimate in the
small-region assembly note. Its fixed exterior arguments are an
explicit restriction. The stronger
[full height-reset theorem](research_mixed_full_height_reset.md)
now allows both real coordinates to readjust. It bounds the entire
matrix obtained by completing the real quadratic, giving a cost of
at most \(10\sum h_j^2\) for the reset heights. An incidence count
then pays these costs from neighboring small-coordinate losses for
arbitrary cyclic word length. The explicit coupled graph differs from
the old independent graph on the right half; its earlier right-half
estimates cannot be imported unchanged.

Those estimates now assemble into the
[zero-uniform low/plateau theorem](research_mixed_uniform_low_plateau_clusters.md).
For every fixed cyclic three/four word, on the specified unselected
coupled graph, let \(L=[0,.10]\) and \(P=[.22,.45]\). Every part of
\((L\cup P)^m\) containing a low coordinate has an absolute integral
bounded by a polynomial times \(e^{N(M-1/100)}\), uniformly through
zero. Here \(M\) is the original geometric critical rate. Low--plateau
edges pay for neighboring height changes, while low--low edges retain
their raw gap. The proof uses a degree-two incidence inequality, valid
at every word length, including the repeated incidences in lengths one
and two. Thus the nonzero central coefficient survives throughout
\((L\cup P)^m\) for the term without an additional Fourier frequency.
The [all-selection extension](research_mixed_selected_low_plateau_clusters.md)
now includes every original outer Fourier term on this same real
region, each on its specified exact coupled graph. Its additional
input is the [selected-reset block bound](research_mixed_selected_reset_plateau_support.md):
a selected plateau coordinate next to a real reset coordinate gives
a finite-source loss of \(1/200\), with both true Fourier branches
retained. Blocks incident to low coordinates are real, so their
selected factors have modulus one. All other selected plateau blocks
already have their established strict loss. The same incidence
argument therefore retains the \(1/100\) gap on every box with a
low coordinate, and a \(1/200\) gap for nonempty selections on
\(P^m\). The full original sum over \((L\cup P)^m\) has the same
nonzero geometric coefficient, carrier and level power as the
unaliased central plateau. The intervals \((.10,.22)\) and
\((.45,1]\) on these coupled contours are not yet fully controlled; this
is not yet the complete cyclic asymptotic or a new knot theorem.

The [minimum-neighbor contour](research_mixed_minimum_neighbor_contour.md)
replaces the product of three cutoffs by their minimum. It preserves
the exact finite integral and agrees with the proved contour on every
low/plateau box. It also keeps the critical equations in a common
convex complex domain. For unselected variables whose real coordinates
lie in \([.1,.45]\), the total change in height is at most three
fifths of the real displacement from the geometric point, in Euclidean
norm, independently of word length. This reduces the height changes
caused by adjacent transition coordinates. It gives a precise class
of displacements for a further Hessian comparison, not that comparison
or a new finite-source theorem.

The [orientation-dependent reset estimate](research_mixed_oriented_height_reset.md)
improves the cost of changing only the first or only the second height
to \((11/2)h^2\) or \((151/20)h^2\), respectively, while both
real coordinates remain free. These sharper costs matter in the
right-region comparison; replacing them by the older common cost
can consume the entire available margin.
For two type-four arguments, the
[same-sign extension](research_mixed_same_sign_height_reset.md)
also permits both negative heights to be reset together, with cost
\((11/2)h_0^2+(151/20)h_1^2\). Its proof uses a negative
off-diagonal entry on the certified boundary and extends the fixed
quadratic inequality harmonically. It applies to height changes of
the same sign; it does not claim a diagonal matrix bound for all
directions. This supplies the local estimate for doubly reset plateau
edges in the right-coordinate assembly below.

The [correlated right-region theorem](research_mixed_right_pair_correlated_support.md)
now estimates the complete finite sum when a right-half coordinate
lies between two plateau coordinates. Its proof first reduces all
finite rows to a concave two-variable support. It then compares the
two incident blocks together, using the actual critical equations to
cancel the dependence of their tangent planes on the right coordinate.
A five-vertex window enclosure retains the relations between the
geometric reference values and pays both neighboring reset costs.
The [right-run source bounds](research_mixed_right_run_supports.md)
now treat the ends of longer right-coordinate runs and runs of length
two. The [complete plateau/right assembly](research_mixed_full_plateau_right_clusters.md)
therefore allows every arrangement in \((P\cup R)^m\), where
\(R=[.5,1]\), for every fixed word length, including one and two.
If a box has \(r\ge1\) right coordinates, each original selected
contribution is bounded by a polynomial times \(e^{N(M-r/20000)}\).
The proof assigns disjoint sets of original edges to the ends and
interiors of the runs, then pays each neighboring plateau reset once.
The pure plateau term retains its established nonzero coefficient.

The [three-region assembly](research_mixed_low_plateau_right_clusters.md)
now also allows arbitrary mixtures of low, plateau and right coordinates.
A concave tangent proves that the previously certified right-neighbor
support values already bound every neighboring real coordinate in
\([0,.45]\), including zero. The exact forced Fourier recurrence
supplies the uniform bound at zero. The remaining mixed reset costs
are paid from low/plateau losses, with each original edge and each
charge used once. Consequently the complete selected sum over
\((L\cup P\cup R)^m\) has the original nonzero central coefficient;
every contribution outside the unaliased plateau is at least
\(1/20000\) lower in exponential rate. The two open intervals
\((.1,.22)\) and \((.45,.5)\) remain outside this combined result.

For the left transition, the
[isolated-transition phase theorem](research_mixed_isolated_transition_phase.md)
proves a uniform loss of at least \(1/6400\), after paying for
the adjoining plateau height change. It allows all four ordered type
pairs and both positions of the low argument. Its proof bounds the
Hessian along the actual straight displacement, completes the square
in the free real coordinate, and reduces the remaining imaginary
directions to five vertices of a convex polygon. This is a phase
theorem for one common suppression factor and unselected heights.
The [complete transition source theorem](research_mixed_transition_whole_period_source.md)
now supplies the required finite-sum input on each independent
transition triangle times plateau rectangle, in both orders. It gives
the original nonzero leading coefficient, uniformly with fixed
parameter derivatives, and keeps both midpoint currents and both
conditional Fourier remainders. Its proof controls the full horizontal
contour by a polynomial positivity test, bounds the vertical pieces,
and extends the normalized holomorphic error from the product boundary.
Thus the isolated phase comparison can now be applied to the complete
finite block. Extra neighboring suppressions and selected-term phase
comparisons remain separate.

The [adjacent-transition source theorem](research_mixed_transition_pair_source.md)
supplies the same complete finite-sum asymptotic when both parameters
lie in transition triangles. Together the four products of transition
triangles and plateau rectangles give a uniform packet on each
independent convex polygon product with real coordinates in
\([.1,.45]\). The root, absolute action, Gaussian coefficient and
normalization agree on the overlaps. Thus the prescribed complex
source domain is now available even for adjacent transitions; the
global comparison of their actions is still required.

The [minimum-level transport argument](research_mixed_minimum_level_transport.md)
now has its complete local input. All 192 unselected half inequalities
passed the canonical 256-bit calculation and separate 320-bit
verification. The latter combines 177 completed domains from the
original implementation with fifteen domains rechecked using an exact
scalar test for the cotangent chamber. The first chamber test had an
unnecessarily wide interval enclosure; the refinement is the identity
that, for \(0<x<1/2\),
\(|\Im\cot(\pi(x+iy))|<1\) is equivalent to
\(\cos(2\pi x)<e^{-2\pi|y|}\). The original and refined
code, full trees, counts and dependencies are retained explicitly.
No failed domain is omitted and no original hypothesis is weakened.

Thus raising all minimum coordinates together is now proved to make
the unselected phase nondecreasing throughout \([.1,.45]^m\),
for every fixed cyclic word. The endpoint lies on the plateau and,
for a point outside it, remains a fixed distance from the geometric
critical point. Strict concavity and the completed source theorem
give a positive exponential loss off the plateau. The original
unselected integral over this whole left region consequently retains
its nonzero central coefficient. This remains a restricted integration
region, not the complete cyclic sum.

The [intermediate selected-height bounds](research_mixed_partial_selected_heights.md)
give the costs for plateau coordinates whose selected heights are
lowered by neighboring transitions. For one selected coordinate at
height \(tH\), with the other at its reference height, the phase
defect is at most \((1-t)q_j(\Im r_j)^2-t/100\), where the
orientation determines \(q_j=11/2\) or \(151/20\).
The proof interpolates the existing reset and selected endpoint
estimates using convexity in the height, separately for each actual
Fourier branch. Two-coordinate versions retain both reset costs.
These formulas can have a positive right side near height zero;
they supply explicit quantities for the remaining assembly, rather
than asserting a selected-term gap by themselves.
