has the complete nonzero boundary asymptotic and common analytic
domains. The \(b_j\)'s have arbitrary signs and magnitudes, and \(B\)
does not depend on them or on the number of stages. A sufficiently
long final scalar closure gives the original Kashaev volume identity
under the original knot and marking conditions.

The proof fixes the order of its choices. First choose the original
bare-edge class and its long-turn threshold \(B_0\). The finitely
many nonzero integers with magnitude below \(B_0\) are treated by
the proved two-boundary kernels, giving a second controlled class.
A long ordinary turn restores the first class even if its input is
known only on the second class's smaller disk: the critical input
angle is \(O(1/n)\), while the output angle belongs to the new bare
edge. Large intervening powers then use the first class's original
theorem; small ones use the finite kernel collection. The final
threshold is chosen only after these two classes are fixed.

This is a general composition result. It leaves out arbitrary
consecutive short nonzero powers and does not remove zero-power
cancellations. Those are still necessary cases for finitely many
exceptions among the original filling assignments.

## A general extension to internal vertices

The [internal-vertex boundary theorem](research_high_degree_short_internal_vertex.md)
now estimates the complete polynomial with all neighboring boundary
angles retained. If the original degree is $d$ and its fixed signed
crossing power is $n$, its sufficient condition is

\[
d^2+n^2\geq\max\{1024,128d\}.
\]

In particular, every fixed power, including zero, is allowed when
$d\geq128$, and every degree is allowed when $|n|\geq64$. The
selected action loses at most $7d/[2(d^2+n^2)]$ from the complete
action. This is smaller than the established loss for an omitted
wire index. The exact trace contour then gives a nonzero leading
term and global decay in every remaining boundary angle.

[The geometric proof](research_isolated_internal_vertex_geometry.md)
keeps the original primitive filling curves and the absolute volume
normalization. Its selected positive branch exists exactly when
$d+|n|>2$. The completed
[isolated-vertex theorem](research_isolated_vertex_coverage_and_assembly.md)
now proves the full quantum estimate on this same domain. The
displayed degree-and-power bound remains the analytic proof of its
unbounded range.

Several additional internal cases now have their own proofs.

- At degree two, crossing powers \(2\) and \(-2\) are covered by
  [an exact formula with two boundary variables](research_degree_two_power_two_formula.md),
  [its full contour estimate](research_degree_two_power_two_boundary_theorem.md),
  and [the geometric phase calculation](research_degree_two_power_two_geometric_phase.md).
  Taking the central trace first moves the stationary point into a
  regular factorial domain. The comparison with the original
  geometric action retains the exact unit phase
  \(e^{\pm i\pi N/2}\).
- At every degree \(d\ge3\), a zero crossing power is covered by
  [the full-circle proof](research_zero_power_internal_boundary_theorem.md).
  The endpoint terms cancel exactly, and positive Laurent
  coefficients control the remaining circle. The proof treats the
  complete sum, including the extreme summation indices. Degree three
  needs a sharper argument: the
  [positive multiplication and Fourier bounds](research_degree_three_zero_wire_tails.md)
  give a strict loss where the previous separate estimates gave none.

Combining these results gives
[long fillings after nonadjacent short fillings](research_nonadjacent_short_fillings_and_long_remainder.md).
One may select any set of original vertices with no edge between
two selected vertices. The complete extension in the
[assembly theorem](research_isolated_vertex_coverage_and_assembly.md#6-a-consequence-that-does-not-require-adjacent-short-fillings)
allows every selected pair satisfying \(d_s+|n_s|>2\).
With at least one vertex
left, independently sufficiently long powers on the remainder give
the original Kashaev volume identity. The proof includes shared
unfilled neighbors, the exact $N^{3/2}$ coefficient power, and the
actual knot-complement volume.

There is also an exact simplification at degree two for powers
zero and $\pm1$. The
[algebraic identities](research_degree_two_short_reductions.md)
now have a corresponding
[proof by marked tangle isotopies](research_marked_degree_two_tangle_moves.md).
Powers $\pm1$ remove the vertex and shift both neighboring powers
by $\mp1$. The isotopy retains the required physical half-turn of a
branch, the order of the tangles, the primitive peripheral curves,
and the framing correction. Thus one such short vertex, with all
other powers independently long, also gives the volume identity by
applying the long-filling theorem to the reduced tree.

The zero-power move merges the neighboring powers by addition.
This is a valid exact reduction, but it is not sufficient for a
finite-exception argument: infinitely many original pairs can have
the same sum. Finitely many unresolved sums could therefore have
infinitely many unresolved preimages.

## Some connected groups of short fillings are covered

The
[joint boundary estimate](research_connected_short_filling_clusters.md)
and [its positive geometric realization](research_connected_short_filling_geometry.md)
also allow adjacent selected vertices. A simple sufficient condition
is the following: if a selected connected component contains \(k\ge2\)
vertices, every vertex of that component has original degree at
least \(256k\). Its fixed crossing powers may then be arbitrary
signed integers, including zero. A more general condition in those
notes uses the degrees and powers together and requires
\(\sqrt{d_v^2+n_v^2}\ge448\) for the geometric chart.

This is a joint estimate for the actual contraction. Its proof bounds
the cumulative loss in the action and all mixed contour faces;
separate estimates at the individual vertices would not suffice.
It retains every boundary variable, a nonzero leading coefficient,
the primitive filling curves, and the absolute volume normalization.

There is now a separate result without a large-degree condition when
all selected powers are zero. Any number of adjacent zero-power
vertices is allowed, provided each has original degree at least
three. The
[full Newton-coordinate theorem](research_all_zero_subtree_newton_packet.md)
retains every original summation index and repeated-root derivative.
It gives a holomorphic boundary asymptotic with a nonzero amplitude,
a strict bound away from the complete boundary, and the negative
boundary Hessian needed for further fillings.

The geometric argument is especially direct. Deleting these zero
boxes as through identities leaves a strict Conway construction,
with each remaining crossing circle and its filling parameter
unchanged. The
[marked deletion proof](research_zero_subtree_conway_geometry.md)
therefore applies the existing strict Conway long-filling theorem.
This is a new application of that theorem. The stronger boundary
result also permits combining these regions with other established
short-filled regions. Its classical Legendre identity identifies the
actual primitive meridian and longitude, including one carrier
correction per remaining original circle.

The proof includes adjacent trivalent zero vertices. In that case an
internal index reaches the endpoint of the former imaginary-angle
description. The primitive Newton state and the strict Conway cells
remain regular, so no extension through a degenerate tetrahedron is
assumed. The
[normalization calculation](../experiments/check_zero_subtree_newton_normalization.py)
checks the exact leading constants for a single trivalent vertex
and for a pair of them. Its finite-level evaluations are supplementary
checks, not the proof of the asymptotic theorem.

Several eligible components may be chosen at once, and they may
share unfilled neighbors. With at least one vertex left, independently
sufficiently long powers at all remaining vertices give the original
Kashaev volume identity. Section 10 of the joint-estimate note now
includes the all-zero components alongside the high-degree and
isolated cases above. Arbitrary connected groups of nonzero short
fillings remain outside this theorem.

## Joining filled pieces without requiring a long central power

The [common-circle composition theorem](research_amplified_finite_block_source.md)
allows already filled pieces to be joined before another crossing circle
is filled. Initially the permitted pieces are terminal vertices with
fixed powers of magnitude at least two and zero-filled subtrees whose
selected original degrees are at least three. Each piece retains its
distinguished boundary angle and its entire finite source. If sufficiently
many of these pieces meet one circle, every fixed signed power at that
circle is allowed. The threshold is independent of the central power.

The proof uses the product of the original boundary polynomials inside
the exact derivative trace. Their negative real curvatures add. This
keeps the selected critical point near the complete boundary even when
the central twist is short. The full contour formula then controls the
other Fourier charges, the vertical boundary integrals and the omitted
real trace nodes. Its leading coefficient is nonzero. The complex
quadratic parts of the block actions are retained; the resulting real
parameter used in the estimates is not substituted for the original
integer crossing power.

[The marked geometric gluing](research_amplified_marked_block_geometry.md)
adds the meridian increments of the pieces around their common circle
while retaining one primitive longitude and one central carrier. The
selected critical point gives the actual cone filling. Integrating
Schläfli's formula from the complete common circle identifies the
absolute action with the knot-complement volume. Previously filled
cores keep angle \(2\pi\) along this deformation.

This gives examples containing adjacent trivalent zero-filled vertices
and a short nonzero central vertex. Such examples are not covered by a
condition requiring every selected vertex to have large degree.

### A uniform theorem for stars

The [uniform terminal-family theorem](research_uniform_terminal_family_and_star_fillings.md)
removes the finite-list restriction on terminal powers. There is a finite
integer \(m_*\) with the following property. In an original star with
\(m\ge m_*\) leaves, give the leaves independently chosen fixed signed
powers \(|p_j|\ge2\), and give the center any fixed signed power.
Whenever the prescribed carrier and strand pattern gives a knot, its
complement is hyperbolic and

\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)|
                       =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K).
\]

There is no later long-filling step in this statement. The proof gives
a nonzero leading term \(\Omega_NN^{3/2}D e^{NS}\), with
\(|\Omega_N|=1\), \(D\ne0\), and
\(2\pi\Re S=\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K)\), through all
large integer levels. The threshold \(m_*\) is independent of the
magnitudes and signs of the chosen powers. The asymptotic error and its
starting level may depend on that fixed assignment.

The additional uniformity is proved using \(s=1/p\) in the original
terminal critical equation. Its phase extends holomorphically to
\(s=0\), and its amplitude becomes nonzero there after removing the
scalar factor \(|p|^{-3/2}\). The contour proof has uniform losses for
the omitted wire indices and outer trace nodes. The loss for higher
Fourier charges can tend to zero as \(|p|\) grows; it only determines
the starting level for a fixed power and is not used as a uniform
eligibility constant. This distinction is necessary for the theorem.

The threshold is specified by inequalities in the established phase
and contour constants. No small numerical value for it is claimed.
The result also permits a bare unfilled edge and any prescribed finite
list of zero-subtree pieces among the branches; remaining circles may
then be filled independently with sufficiently long fixed powers.

This is a theorem about the stated compositions, not a finite-exception
theorem for every template. A general short-filled region need not
decompose in this way. Terminal powers \(0,\pm1\) can reduce a large
star to a smaller core, so those reductions must still be followed
rather than counted as a finite exceptional set.

The [finite composition check](../experiments/check_amplified_zero_block_composition.py)
compares original quotient-algebra contractions with nested physical
derivative traces at both level parities and independent complex
boundary values. Its saved
[120-digit replay](../repro/results/research-amplified-zero-block-composition-root.json)
checks the exact normalization. The all-level asymptotic and the
geometric identification are proved in the notes above, not inferred
from those finite comparisons.

### The composition can be repeated without increasing the degree threshold

The [recursive source theorem](research_recursive_high_valence_source.md)
extends the star result to trees of arbitrary finite size and depth.
There is one finite integer \(M_*\) with the following property.
Root an original circle tree at an internal vertex. The root must have
at least \(M_*\) children, and each other internal vertex must have
at least \(M_*\) children. Assign every terminal a fixed signed power
of magnitude at least two. Every internal power may be any fixed
signed integer, including zero. Whenever the prescribed strand pattern
gives a knot, the knot is hyperbolic and satisfies the original Kashaev
volume identity through all integer levels.

In particular, the hypothesis holds if every internal degree in the
unrooted tree is at least \(M_*+1\). The threshold does not depend on
the number of vertices, tree depth, or filling powers. This improves
on the earlier connected-region criterion whose required degrees
grew with the number of selected vertices. The proof specifies finite
inequalities for a sufficient threshold; it does not provide a small
numerical value.

The reason the estimates survive repeated composition is precise.
Keep one unfilled edge leading from a newly filled vertex to the outside
boundary, whose angle is \(u\). If \(\psi(t,u)\) is that edge's
action and \(t_*(u)\) is the new internal critical angle, then the
boundary action of the entire piece satisfies

\[
 W_{\rm new}'(u)=\psi_u(t_*(u),u).
\]

Thus its normalized boundary response is controlled by the one outgoing
edge, independently of how many vertices lie behind it. The negative
real curvature survives exactly by a Schur-complement inequality.
The same edge supplies the global decay in \(u\), and the output
polynomial still has degree at most \(N-1\). These facts restore the
same complex strip and the same source disk at every stage. The proof
applies the original trace to the full product before estimating it,
retains all boundary currents, and establishes a nonzero amplitude.
Only prefactors, errors and starting levels may depend on the fixed
finite tree.

[The geometric induction](research_recursive_marked_block_geometry.md)
preserves the original face maps, primitive filling curves and positive
core lengths on that same disk. Schläfli's formula fixes the absolute
volume at each step. At the final root no auxiliary circle remains,
and the full source has a nonzero \(N^{3/2}e^{NS}\) leading term with
\(2\pi\Re S\) equal to the knot-complement volume.

The [recursive normalization check](../experiments/check_recursive_original_tree_contraction.py)
compares quotient-algebra recursion with full physical derivative
traces, both for an open complex boundary and for the final closed
root. Its [saved results](../repro/results/research-recursive-original-tree-contraction.json)
test those exact identities; the small test trees are not used as
evidence for the sufficient degree threshold.

This theorem still does not give cofinite assignments on an arbitrary
fixed template. Setting a terminal power to \(0\) or \(\pm1\)
leaves infinitely many possible choices at the other vertices. Their
exact simplifications can expose an untreated small-degree core.
The branching theorem does not remove that obligation.

## A low-degree adjacent nonzero component is now covered

The [boundary theorem for the adjacent pair](research_adjacent_two_crossing_boundary_theorem.md)
proves the complete asymptotic for two consecutive powers equal to
two on a pendant path. The selected vertices have original degrees
one and two, and one boundary angle remains free. The result includes
a nonzero holomorphic leading coefficient, decay throughout the real
boundary period, and the Gaussian complex-strip bound needed for
further fillings. It holds at both parities of the integer level.

The decisive step was to change the contour domain without changing
the finite sum. Its canonical factorial numerator vanishes at every
added lattice point outside the triangular index set. The
[exact rectangular extension](research_adjacent_pair_rectangular_extension.md)
therefore gives a complete first-variable period. Its lower contour
is a full circle, whose normalized integrand is holomorphic inside.
The [complete-circle bound](research_adjacent_pair_full_circle_bound.md)
controls the exponentially small error of restoring the original
normalization. The two vertical sides are combined by the exact
translation law before taking absolute values; its peripheral factor
is retained.

The [remaining contour bounds](research_adjacent_pair_grouped_contour_bounds.md)
control every combined side and endpoint. The proof has written
endpoint estimates and a standalone interval verifier for seven
compact rectangles. All nonprincipal terms have rate below 0.847,
whereas the selected rate is rigorously greater than 0.848851224.
The existing horizontal maximum and Gaussian expansion then give

\[
 Z_N(u)=A(u)e^{NS(u)}(1+O(N^{-1})),\qquad A(0)\ne0,
 \qquad S''(0)=-\frac{\sqrt7+3i}{8\pi}.
\]

The [marked two-edge geometry](research_adjacent_two_crossing_pair.md)
identifies the full germ as \(S(u)=G(u)+i\pi\), with its
absolute volume constant. The factor \((-1)^N\) is retained.
Consequently the three-vertex family \((2,2,n)\) satisfies the
original Kashaev volume identity for every sufficiently long fixed
signed \(n\) of the prescribed knot parity.

More generally, the mixed-component theorem permits any finite number
of these pendant pairs, together with its previously allowed
components, while the remaining original powers are independently
sufficiently long. Pairs may share an unfilled neighboring vertex;
their selected vertices and incident edges are disjoint. This adds
an infinite collection of partial-filling families. It does not cover
arbitrary powers or arbitrary connected groups of short vertices.

The earlier triangular contours and complementary-arc calculation
are preserved in the research notes. Their diagonal corner terms
explain why the first separate absolute estimates did not close.
The completed proof uses the exact full-period identity instead.

Two reusable lemmas have been extracted from this calculation. The
[boundary-order criterion](research_balanced_factorial_boundary_order.md)
determines when a normalized factorial integrand has a removable end
and when it has a pole with a possible residue. It retains signed
factorial slopes and peripheral parameters. Its product formula also
shows why regularity cannot simply be assumed to survive composition.
The [Gaussian strip lemma](research_real_gap_to_gaussian_strip.md)
deduces the required complex-boundary bound from a real angular gap,
a local holomorphic asymptotic, and the degree of the exact polynomial.
Both are proved independently of the particular geometric saddle.

## A general exact representation for arbitrary short powers

The [source compilation theorem](research_arbitrary_power_source_compilation.md)
now treats arbitrary finite Conway expressions and arbitrary signed
crossing powers at the algebraic level. It restores the original
closing functional at each multiplication instead of continuing a
factorial coefficient outside its valid index domain. This matters:
the [divisor calculation](research_factorial_rectangle_divisor_criterion.md)
exhibits a genuine pole in the naive simultaneous continuation of a
Newton multiplication coefficient, even at an added lattice point
where its discrete coefficient is zero.

After restoring the traces, the
[finite Fourier-band theorem](research_newton_interpolation_finite_fourier_band.md)
gives an exact replacement. The continued Newton factor, including
its spectral values and first derivatives, has frequencies

\[
 -(N-1)/2,\;-(N-1)/2+1,\ldots,(N-1)/2.
\]

Each internal index occurs in two factors. Their product has integer
frequencies between \(-(N-1)\) and \(N-1\), so its \(N\)-point
sum is exactly \(N\) times its integral over a full period.
The [network version](research_internal_wire_exact_circle_averaging.md)
applies simultaneously to every internal index, with arbitrary vertex
degrees, turn orientations, and fixed signed powers. All internal-index
side terms and extra Fourier modes cancel exactly after the original
traces. The source and its full boundary polynomial are preserved.

This is a general algebraic result, without a longness assumption.
It does not prove the missing asymptotic. The physical angle integrals
still contain their crossing phases and exact derivative-trace kernels.
Their geometric critical point, contributing cycle, and competing
regions must be controlled. At a genuinely free boundary, the entire
finite Fourier interpolation must also be distinguished from its
factorial representative in the quotient; they are not interchangeable
without a further argument.

The gain for the critical path is precise: internal index corrections
no longer require a separate contour estimate for each short tangle
in this representation. The remaining general problem concerns the
original angle period and its free boundaries.

The [twist-period calculation](research_twist_period_insertion_growth.md)
also determines why finite-level periodicity cannot supply the missing
short-filling theorem. With \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\), the original crossing
satisfies
\[
 R^{n+2Nk}=\eta^kR^n(1+kU_N),\qquad U_N^2=0.
\]
For an isolated vertex of any fixed positive degree and any fixed
signed power, the term containing \(U_N\) has a nonzero boundary
asymptotic at the complete augmented rate. The original source has
a strict loss below that rate. Recovering it from two period-shifted
powers cancels the entire larger term exactly, including every order
of its inverse-level expansion. Thus adding twists proportional to
the level does not extend the theorem for a fixed knot. The proof
keeps the original trace and its first normal derivatives; finite
matrix comparisons check the normalization separately.

There is now also an [exact periodic angle integral](research_polynomial_crossing_fourier_trace.md).
Keeping each crossing as its canonical polynomial in the full pair
algebra makes every angle integrand periodic. The original trace
then has no vertical endpoint currents, and a fixed network has
only finitely many possible Fourier charges, independently of the
level. Its coefficients retain the derivatives at double roots.
This representation preserves the source, but does not remove its
cancellation: in the two-crossing terminal example, charge one is
the only charge, yet one of its crossing-mode summands has twice
the exponential rate of the final answer. The note proves this
using the original kernel and the established terminal theorem.

The [residue formulation](research_actual_source_dualizing_residue.md)
organizes these same finite operations without discarding nilpotents.
The closing functional is a perfect residue pairing, which remains
regular when its repeated spectral roots are separated by independent
parameters. On this generic smoothing, the compiled numerator has a
nonzero residue weight on every spectral branch. Those weights can
still cancel in their sum. They are also not the critical points of
the large-level phase. Passing from this exact spectral residue to
the marked geometric critical period remains necessary before its
algebraic nonvanishing can be used in the volume argument.

The [signed Gaussian shift calculation](research_signed_gaussian_ward_endpoint_packet.md)
now gives the exact endpoint correction for odd as well as even
crossing powers. Even powers give the previously known scalar term
after the original half crossing and quarter-turn. Odd powers also
give the turned spectral idempotent \(T\Pi_0\). Here \(\Pi_0\)
has value one and derivative zero at the first double spectral root,
with all other prescribed values and derivatives zero; \(T\) is the
original geometric quarter-turn. This extra term cannot be discarded.

Its spectral values and first derivatives can nevertheless be computed
exactly. If \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal J}\) is the maximum of the sum of
the absolute value and first derivative at each double root, retaining
only the value at a simple root, the result is

\[
 \|T\Pi_0\|_{\mathcal J}
 \le 2+2H_{\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor}+\frac{N^2-1}{12},
 \qquad H_j=\sum_{r=1}^j\frac1r,\quad H_0=0.
\]

The proof uses a finite partial-fraction identity and a confluent
difference at the paired spectral roots. Thus this particular endpoint
term costs only a polynomial in the full source norm. The result does
not identify an arbitrary contour remainder with that term, and an
estimate for the surrounding contraction is still needed. The
[reproduction script](../experiments/check_signed_gaussian_ward_endpoint_packet.py)
compares the identity against the original crossing matrices and an
independent characteristic-polynomial construction of \(\Pi_0\).
The [120-digit replay](../repro/results/research-signed-gaussian-ward-endpoint-packet-root.json)
checks both level parities and signed powers; the written identities
provide the proof for all levels.

The [logarithmic contour calculation](research_gaussian_logarithmic_contour_transport.md)
now identifies the correction produced by an actual lattice
translation of the Gaussian residue contour. It retains the
derivatives at repeated roots and proves the formula for any number
of lattice steps. It also expresses a one-step correction in a tree
as a finite sum of sources on the components left after deleting the
shifted vertex. The neighboring components retain the required
boundary insertions. These formulas describe the corrections
exactly; a polynomial bound on an insertion does not prove that the
resulting source has a smaller exponential rate.

This distinction is visible in the formulas themselves. Translating
by a full period gives zero correction for an even crossing power
and four times the original normalized source for an odd power.
Thus a long contour translation cannot generally discard the
accumulated endpoint terms.

The [logarithmic-factorial representative](research_odd_ward_logarithmic_factorial.md)
gives a useful analytic expression for the odd correction inside
an original trace. It has exactly the physical values and first
derivatives of \(T\Pi_0\), is \(O(\log N)\) on the physical rectangle,
and has leading term \(2(-1)^N\log N\) near an interior saddle.
Inserting it into an already controlled terminal contour preserves
that contour's exponential rate and gives a nonzero logarithmic
factor. This supplies a concrete reason to retain these corrections,
rather than infer their exponential smallness from their polynomial
norm. The representative is not a periodic free-boundary substitute:
its period defect and poles are specified in the note.

## A general geometric result for connected short fillings

The [positive-edge period theorem](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md)
now treats any connected group of the original circle-tree blocks
with arbitrary fixed signed powers, provided its original eight
tetrahedra per edge remain positive. It proves that the primitive
filling equations have at most one such solution and that its
complex Jacobian is nonsingular. Existence is not assumed to follow
from this uniqueness.

The proof compares any two positive configurations, even when the
straight segment between their original angle coordinates leaves
the positive domain. Each positive edge has two global disk
coordinates. In their associated strip coordinates the period
comparison reduces to the strict monotonicity of
\(f(z)=\arctan(\tanh z)\), whose derivative has positive real part.
The comparisons add over the original graph. Signed filling powers
contribute purely imaginary terms and hence cannot cancel their
positive real pairing.

This comparison survives eliminating an arbitrary positive filled
region. Its interior solution is unique for each realized boundary
assignment, and the resulting holomorphic boundary response is
again strictly monotone. Its derivative is an accretive Schur
complement. The original carrier term is retained once per boundary
circle. Thus the geometric equations have the composition property
needed for iterative partial filling throughout this positive class.

The [convex variational formulation](research_positive_filling_convex_variation.md)
goes further. It expresses angle matching and the imaginary parts of
the primitive filling equations as linear equations on a product of
bounded squares. An explicit strictly convex energy supplies the
remaining real equations and imaginary matching. With strict
feasibility, the closed polytope always has a unique minimizer. An
interior minimum is exactly the positive geometric solution.

Strict feasibility itself has an explicit linear-programming test.
At unit charges and complete outside boundaries it is equivalent to
finding numbers \(0\le\tau_v<1\), with \(|n_v|\tau_v\le2\), such that
\[
 d_v-2+|n_v|\tau_v-
       \sum_{\substack{w\text{ selected}\\w\sim v}}\tau_w>0
 \quad\text{for every selected }v.
\]
Consequently every selected region whose original vertex degrees
are at least three has a unique closed-polytope optimum for arbitrary
signed powers: take \(\tau_v=0\). This removes a large-degree
requirement from the optimization statement. It does not remove
the quantum estimates or guarantee an interior optimum.

The boundary alternative is also classified: each degenerate square
factor of a minimum must be a corner; it cannot lie on an open side.
This distinction is necessary. Two adjacent selected trivalent
vertices with zero powers and complete outside boundaries have
strictly feasible angle data, but their unique minimum has a folded
internal edge. Its positive cone solutions approach that minimum
as the charges tend to one. The previously proved zero-subtree
construction handles this example by a different cell decomposition.
Thus this general optimization formulation does not assume away
the degenerations needed for the finite-exception target.

The [corner optimality conditions](research_positive_filling_corner_kkt.md)
now make this distinction exact. At a square corner, the two signed
components of a supporting covector satisfy
\(U,V>0\) and \(\sinh(2U)\sinh(2V)\ge1\). A finite limit of
the original positive shapes satisfies equality. A strict inequality
can occur at the constrained minimum and does not give geometric
periods. The note proves an example with two adjacent degree-two
vertices and powers \((2,-2)\): the constraints are strictly feasible,
but the unique minimum has a corner with product equal to three.
The [explicit shape calculation](research_square_corner_flat_geometry.md)
shows why interpreting its multipliers as original shapes fails.
This pair also cannot be removed by the integral outside shifts
that suffice for the known zero- and unit-power moves.

There is a general sufficient condition for avoiding this boundary.
At unit charges and complete outside boundaries, an interior
positive solution exists whenever
\[
 d_v^2+n_v^2\ge16|S|d_v\qquad(v\in S),
\]
where \(S\) is the selected region and \(d_v\) is the original
degree. The proof compares an explicit feasible energy with the
fixed energy cost of a corner; it also gives a sharper nonuniform
criterion. This improves the geometric existence test. It does not
replace the stronger conditions in the quantum boundary theorems.

This does not establish the corresponding quantum theorem. Some
hyperbolic partial fillings can require a different or degenerate
cell decomposition. Even when the positive solution exists, its
nonzero coefficient in the original quantum period and the bounds
on competing contributions still need a general proof.

## Exact source coordinates when a geometric edge degenerates

The [Newton boundary transport](research_corner_newton_source_transport.md)
provides an exact expression for two adjacent vertices with any
fixed signed powers. If each endpoint has an external leg, apply
the original turned crossing to one external leg at each end of
the zero-power tensor. This produces the full powered tensor before
any external variables are identified. The transformation is
invertible and retains every repeated-root derivative and carrier
factor. The resulting boundary tensor has rank \(N\) across the
division into left and right legs for every pair of signed powers.

Its factorial expression remains meaningful at the corner of the
old geometric coordinates. Each added crossing has a specified
imaginary quadratic phase. Its real phase \(h\) satisfies
\(2\pi h=\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta_1)+\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta_2)\)
for two explicit positive tetrahedra on the strict real index
triangle. The [two-shape calculation](research_square_corner_flat_geometry.md)
proves this for both crossing signs. The
[marked flag calculation](research_newton_crossing_marked_flags.md)
now identifies the four parabolic meridians and their fixed points
with the original Conway white-transition matrices. It also develops
the two tetrahedra on those actual flags and verifies the cancellation
of their shared face. The
[two-flip attachment](research_newton_crossing_two_flip_attachment.md)
now carries out the attachment at an actual all-white Conway
interface: it specifies all exterior faces, the four output white
transition maps, and the transport of auxiliary primitive curves and
their fixed points. This construction is not asserted at a masked
interface and does not prove that an arbitrary composed source has a
positive geometric saddle. Thus arbitrary powers can be treated in the same
finite source without assigning geometric meaning to an invalid
corner covector. The original canonical crossing graph and its
Casimir torsor were already established in the earlier notes; they
are not new volume results.

The exact transformation does not transfer the existing zero-power
estimate for free. One entry of a single crossing matrix has size
\(N^{-1/2}\exp(NG/\pi)(1+O(N^{-1}))\), where \(G\) is Catalan's
constant. An exponentially small remainder can therefore become
large after transport. The required new estimate must treat the
transformed sum, its stationary point, and its competing terms
together. Neither invertibility nor finite tensor rank proves a
nonzero geometric contribution after the boundary is evaluated.

The same note identifies the term lost by treating an arbitrary free
boundary as a spectral eigenvector. For the Newton value vector
\(v(c)\), the exact difference between the powered crossing and
its scalar spectral value is a polynomial divided difference
multiplied by \(P_N(c)/N^2\). At the complete value \(c=-2\), this
factor is zero at odd levels but equals \(4/N^2\) at even levels.
At odd levels its boundary derivative can still be nonzero. Thus
the spectral torsor alone does not determine the boundary function
needed for another filling. The formula and its derivative have
been checked against the full original matrices at both parities;
no exponential bound is inferred from the factor \(N^{-2}\).

## What is still missing

The complete cyclic three/four trace now has its nonzero geometric
asymptotic at both level parities. The remaining requirements concern
open boundary sources, attachment to other pieces, and arbitrary short
partial fillings; they are not a remaining cyclic cancellation gap.

The [continuation argument](research_dominant_saddle_transport.md)
identifies one possible way to prove a general extension. After
contributions with smaller real action are removed, the original
integration cycle would have to lie in a transported one-dimensional
relative homology group generated by the geometric saddle. If its
coefficient is initially nonzero, the local amplitude stays nonzero,
and the contour ends remain controlled, the leading term persists.
The note proves this implication directly. It does not establish
these hypotheses for arbitrary short fillings.

The [edge Hessian criterion](research_cone_chamber_accretivity.md)
also proves strict horizontal action decay on each convex region
satisfying its explicit inequalities. The stronger global positive
period comparison above no longer needs a convex region for
uniqueness or boundary elimination. Neither statement puts every
competing solution or the original integration cycle in the positive
domain.

In particular, maximal geometric volume only at the beginning and
end of a deformation is insufficient. An explicit cubic integral
in the same note has a selected saddle dominant at both endpoints,
but its contribution disappears along the path. A geometric
comparison along the deformation, and control of poles, ends, and
equal-rate contributions, are still needed for this approach.

The isolated-vertex estimates are complete on \(d+|n|>2\).
Three requirements remain for the full finite-exception goal.

1. **The degenerate local powers and their parameter fibers.**
   Terminal powers \(0,\pm1\) and degree-two power zero have exact
   marked reductions. The resulting short cores still require
   proofs when they give hyperbolic knots. In particular, merging
   two neighboring powers by addition has infinite fibers in the
   original assignment space.
2. **The remaining connected groups of short vertices.** The joint
   theorem covers the explicit degree-and-power range and every
   all-zero component whose original degrees are at least three.
   The recursive theorem above now also covers complete trees of
   arbitrary size when every internal vertex has sufficiently many
   children, with all terminal powers of magnitude at least two.
   Low-degree groups with nonzero powers remain untreated in general.
   Eliminating a terminal changes the function
   at its neighbor; the terminal theorem cannot simply be applied
   again to that new function. We need a theorem stable under these
   changes, or a direct estimate for every required joint contraction.
   The pendant pair \((2,2)\) and, more generally, every same-sign
   pendant chain of powers \(2\) or \(-2\), are now covered. Their
   long-remainder volume conclusion follows from the exact marked
   reduction; their unreduced boundary asymptotic follows from the
   boundary multiplication estimate above. The mixed pendant pair
   \((2,-2)\) now has its complete analytic boundary theorem,
   primitive geometric deformation, and an isotopy identifying
   its original attaching surface with the required geometric
   surface. It and its mirror are valid one-boundary pendant
   pieces. The same-sign pendant pair \((3,3)\) and its mirror
   now have their full boundary asymptotic, a strict whole-period
   bound, and the original marked volume identification. A
   sufficiently long final twist therefore proves the conjecture
   on the original fibers \((2,2,p)\), and their mirrors, apart
   from finitely many values of \(p\) for each fixed outside
   carrier. Arbitrarily many copies may also be used as pendant
   leaves in the enlarged hybrid tree theorem; each attaching
   vertex must still have sufficiently high valence or a
   sufficiently long power. These are the conclusions of
   [the adjacent-three closing theorem](research_three_crossing_long_closing_fiber.md).
   A separate [internal-pair theorem](research_internal_pair_three_full_boundary_packet.md)
   now supplies its two-boundary kernel, nonzero coefficient,
   and full outside-period and complex-strip bounds. This treats
   the fixed \(3,3\) and mirrored blocks. The
   [general positive-pair theorem](research_internal_pair_combined_contour_reduction.md#7-the-full-source-for-every-fixed-pair-of-powers-at-least-seven)
   now gives all these estimates for every fixed \(n,p\ge7\)
   and its mirror. The uniform composition argument now
   allows all these pairs under one common separator threshold;
   a prescribed finite list is no longer required. Zero joins
   with a sufficiently long merged power are also covered.
   It still does not treat every adjacent short pair or
   remove every separating-power condition.
   Independently, the full path source theorem now treats
   consecutive selected powers with \(|n_v|\ge8\), without
   separators and with arbitrary signs; it gives the knot
   limit when every auxiliary vertex is filled and the
   original component tests hold. Positive powers at least
   seven have the corresponding source theorem with a
   stipulated complete outside endpoint. These results leave
   other connected short assignments unresolved.
   The binary negative chains in Theorem 4 of
   [the complementary-word note](research_binary_negative_corridor_positive_reexpression.md)
   are also valid pendant pieces under its explicit run-length
   conditions. This last conclusion uses the existing long-turn
   theorem after an exact marked replacement; it does not cover
   every chain of powers \(-2\) and \(-3\).
   The [marked rational-piece criterion](research_marked_rational_pendant_admissibility.md)
   now also permits a complementary chain ending in \((3,2)\)
   or \((3,3)\), with preceding powers sufficiently long.
   In the original negative presentation this covers arbitrarily
   long binary chains with specified long runs of twos and a
   terminal group \((-3,-3)\) or \((-3,-3,-2)\). Its exact
   cap scalar and outside parameter translation are retained.
   The criterion also allows a first long reset followed by
   the previously proved alternating long and nonzero turns.
   It is a sufficient arithmetic recognition rule for fixed
   rational pieces, not a reduction of every short word to the
   proved library. Other short power
   assignments and general low-degree components still need a proof.
   The [scope calculation](research_finite_exception_scope_audit.md#1-adjacent-short-vertices-and-the-two-crossing-reduction)
   distinguishes these arguments from an unsupported iteration of
   singleton estimates.
3. **The full class of admissible templates.** Circle-tree results
   must be extended to the permitted Conway compositions and their
   degenerations, with the original peripheral data retained.

The finite-exception goal needs these issues resolved for the partial
assignments reached by the finite branching argument. A general
theorem for such partially filled sources would supply all of them
at once. Neither a local geometric critical point nor an upper bound
on the filling operator proves its required nonzero quantum
contribution.

## Assignments and knot types must remain distinct

Section 8 of [the reduction note](research_finite_exceptions_under_partial_fillings.md)
proves an additional constraint. For the enlarged literal strict
Conway grammar, finitely many exceptional **assignments for every
template** would imply the volume identity for every hyperbolic
strict Conway knot. A fixed core can be padded with a zero cap and
a freely varying removable twist, giving infinitely many assignments
of one template that all represent that core.

This uses the enlarged grammar's permission to close an elementary
box against a turned product. The padding argument has not been
asserted for the older subfamily requiring two completed closing
children. The exact type and endpoint checks are included in the
reduction note.

Consequently, an unresolved core cannot be placed on a finite
exception list while infinitely many of its redundant assignments
are left untreated. This does not refute the target; it identifies
its strength. Nor can a nonhyperbolic intermediate exterior simply
be discarded if its remaining fillings still give hyperbolic knots.

Finally, finite exceptions for each fixed template would not by
itself imply finitely many exceptions among all hyperbolic knot
types. That further statement requires control as template
complexity grows.

There is a concrete version of the parameter issue on just four
vertices. If \(K_j\) denotes the knot obtained from a path with
\(j\) vertices in the original turning convention, marked isotopies
give

\[
 K_4(a,0,b,c)\simeq K_2(a+b,c).
\]

For fixed \(s,c\), the assignments \((m,0,s-m,c)\), with one
fixed parity of \(m\), therefore all give \(K_2(s,c)\). There
are infinitely many of them. Consequently a cofinite-assignment
theorem for every four-vertex path would imply the volume identity
for every hyperbolic two-circle knot, including the finitely many
pairs still untreated by the present two-circle theorem. The
[four-path proposition](research_finite_exception_scope_audit.md#2-an-infinite-fiber-on-a-four-vertex-path)
proves this implication without assuming the desired volume theorem.

The [affine-fiber theorem](research_affine_reduction_fibers_and_core_obligation.md)
makes this obstruction decidable on every recorded reduction branch.
Once its affine equations and nonzero subset-sum conditions are fixed,
each nonempty fiber is either a singleton or infinite, according to
the rank of the combined parameter matrix. A finite list of reduced
exceptions therefore cannot be pulled back as a finite list when a
hyperbolic unresolved core has an infinite fiber. In the literal strict
grammar, adding two leaves is enough to give any fixed core such a
fiber. The general per-template target consequently still requires
the volume identity for those cores themselves.
